Distributed Systems from the Ground Up

Cover

Preface

Distributed systems engineering operates under physical and theoretical constraints that single-node abstractions conceal: asynchronous message delivery, unbounded network delay, independent component crashes, clock drift across unsynchronized oscillators, and volatile kernel page caches. Designing reliable infrastructure requires deriving architectures directly from explicit safety and liveness invariants, fault boundaries, and quantitative resource limits rather than informal component sketches.

In this book, I examine the architecture of fault-tolerant distributed systems from first principles. For every system, I establish the actors, verifiable functional contracts, explicit latency and availability Service Level Objectives (SLOs), and storage, compute, and bandwidth envelopes prior to introducing algorithms, wire protocols, or deployment topologies.

Organization of the Text

The twenty-eight chapters are grouped into six thematic parts:

  • Part I (Chapters 1 to 6): Distributed Key-Value Store. In Chapter 1, I specify the system architecture, consistency model, partitioning scheme, and failure-handling contracts of a strongly consistent key-value store. In Chapters 2 to 6, I detail the low-level design and empirical verification of its core mechanisms: durable write-ahead logging, leader-follower quorum replication, Raft leader election with monotonic term fencing, consistent-hash request routing, and group commit.
  • Part II (Chapters 7 to 13): Core Infrastructure Primitives. I analyze foundational platform services that enforce fairness, ordering, caching, coordination, and asynchronous decoupling: distributed rate limiting, unique identifier generation, distributed caching, distributed locking, partitioned message queues, job scheduling, and notification delivery.
  • Part III (Chapters 14 to 18): Content, Media, and Communication Systems. I analyze read-intensive and media-delivery architectures: URL shortening, social news feeds, chunked object storage, adaptive video streaming, and real-time messaging.
  • Part IV (Chapters 19 to 21): Transactional and Marketplace Systems. I analyze domains governed by strict transactional integrity, concurrency control, and real-time spatial state: payment processing with double-entry ledgers, high-contention ticket booking, and geospatial ride-hailing dispatch.
  • Part V (Chapters 22 to 24): Search, Indexing, and Observability. I analyze low-latency prefix indexing, polite distributed web crawling, and high-cardinality metrics ingestion and monitoring.
  • Part VI (Chapters 25 to 28): Synchronization and Low-Latency Streaming. I analyze conflict resolution, operational convergence, deterministic execution, and stream processing: file synchronization, collaborative editing, a single-threaded stock exchange matching engine, and click aggregation.

Architectural Methodology

Across every system design chapter, I adhere to an explicit engineering progression aligned with formal systems documentation standards (ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514):

  1. Requirements and Capacity Bounds: I specify actors, use-case boundaries, numbered functional and non-functional requirements, and order-of-magnitude storage, throughput, and memory calculations upfront.
  2. External and Internal Interface Contracts: I define HTTP/2 or gRPC endpoints, preconditions, idempotency semantics, error payloads, and storage schemas before examining internal optimizations.
  3. Control-Plane and Data-Plane Separation: I isolate low-frequency metadata management, topology coordination, and policy compilation from the latency-critical request path.
  4. Failure Modes, Tail Latency, and Observability: I evaluate network partitions, hot-key skew, lock contention, and gray failures, specifying automated recovery invariants and Service Level Indicators (SLIs) for each failure domain.

Companion Implementations and Prerequisites

The companion code/ directory contains the runnable Part I storage subsystems and the workload simulations cited across Parts II to VI, allowing readers to reproduce the throughput measurements, skew distributions, and crash-recovery experiments reported in the text.

For the system design chapters, I assume foundational knowledge of HTTP semantics, relational databases, data structures, and TCP/IP networking. For the low-level implementation chapters in Part I, I additionally assume reading familiarity with Rust. Every distributed systems primitive is derived when first introduced and consolidated in each chapter’s engineering glossary.

References and Provenance

The protocols and trade-offs presented in this volume draw upon primary distributed systems literature and published production engineering reports, including work on Raft consensus, Dynamo, Spanner, CockroachDB, Stripe’s atomic-phase idempotency and GCRA rate-limiting systems, and classical transaction-processing theory. Full bibliographic citations appear at the close of each chapter.

Arpan Pathak

1. Key-Value Store: System Design

A distributed key-value store provides durable, strongly consistent storage for opaque byte sequences addressed by primary key. Because the store imposes no schema on values, engineers deploy it as the foundational state layer beneath web session stores, cluster membership registries, distributed configuration engines, and object-store metadata indexes. On a single server, we can satisfy this interface in a few hundred lines of code using an in-memory map backed by an append-only file. Distributed systems engineering begins when data volume exceeds a single disk, request throughput exceeds a single processor core, and service continuity must survive power loss, corrupted storage media, and network partitions.

In this chapter, we derive the architecture of a replicated, sharded key-value store directly from its operational requirements and physical constraints. In Chapters 2 through 6, we implement each component in Rust and verify its invariants under controlled crash and partition injection.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, verifiable functional requirements, non-functional SLOs, and storage, disk, and network capacity bounds
  • the client-facing HTTP/2 contract (conditional writes via If-Match, RFC 9457 error objects) and the internal gRPC/Protobuf replication protocol
  • separation of the control plane from the data plane using stateless request routers and partitioned Multi-Raft storage groups
  • formal consistency models (linearizability, tunable quorums, and eventual consistency) and the cost of strong consistency
  • data partitioning via consistent hashing with virtual nodes versus sorted range splits, backed by empirical measurements from ringsim
  • quorum commit, linearizable ReadIndex reads, monotonic term fencing under network partitions, and safe online reconfiguration
  • tail-latency engineering, hot-key mitigation, failure recovery matrices, observability SLIs, and production case studies

1.1 Requirements and Capacity Envelope

Modern application tiers achieve horizontal elasticity by remaining stateless: any web or API server can crash, restart, or scale out without losing client state because we offload all durable data to a shared storage tier. That architectural division concentrates operational complexity inside the storage layer. A load balancer absorbs the failure of a stateless node transparently, whereas any corruption or prolonged outage in the storage tier halts every dependent service simultaneously.

Actors and Use Cases

Three classes of actors interact with the store, each imposing distinct interface and availability contracts (Figure 1-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Application ServicePoint write (PUT), point read (GET), deletion (DELETE)Persist, retrieve, and expire customer session or shopping-cart records across stateless web servers
Application ServiceConditional compare-and-swap (PUT with If-Match)Update a shared counter or cart record without overwriting concurrent mutations from peer servers
Application ServicePaginated prefix listing (GET /v1/keys?prefix=...)Enumerate all active session keys belonging to a specific tenant or account
Cluster OperatorNode addition, graceful drain, host replacement, shard splitExpand storage capacity before peak traffic or replace a host experiencing NVMe hardware faults
Observability PlatformReadiness probes (GET /healthz) and metrics collectionEvict degraded nodes from router pools and alert on latency or error-budget burn rates

Functional Requirements

Each functional requirement defines a deterministic contract verifiable by automated integration tests:

No.Functional Requirement
0A client can store an opaque byte value (0 to 1 MiB) under a key (1 to 256 ASCII characters in [A-Za-z0-9._-]). Every committed mutation assigns a strictly monotonic per-key version (uint64).
1A client can retrieve the latest committed value and its version for a given key, or receive 404 Not Found if the key does not exist or has been deleted.
2A client can delete a key by committing a tombstone record in the shard log, advancing the key version so delayed retries cannot resurrect removed state.
3A client can make any write conditional on an expected version (If-Match: "<version>") or on the absence of the key (If-None-Match: *), guaranteeing atomic compare-and-swap semantics.
4A client can enumerate keys matching a prefix in lexicographic order using bounded, cursor-paginated responses (limit <= 1,000).
5An operator can add, drain, and replace storage nodes across availability zones while the cluster continues serving traffic without downtime.
6Every node exposes machine-readable liveness, readiness, consensus lag, and storage-saturation telemetry.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

A single-host process with one log file satisfies functional requirements 0 through 4 in full yet fails nearly every operational constraint of production infrastructure. The non-functional bounds below dictate the distributed architecture:

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0ConsistencyLinearizable (strong consistency) per keyEvery GET invoked after an acknowledged PUT returns that write or a newer one; enforced via Raft quorum commit and ReadIndex
1DurabilityZero loss of acknowledged writes across any single node, disk, or availability-zone (AZ) failureReplication factor N = 3 across three AZs; synchronous WAL fsync on a majority (2 of 3) before acknowledging the client
2Availability99.95% monthly request availability (<= 21.6 minutes of error budget per 30-day month)Automated leader election (< 1.5 s failover) and active-active multi-AZ stateless routers
3Latency (Intra-Region)Writes: p50 <= 4 ms, p99 <= 20 ms; Reads: p50 <= 1.5 ms, p99 <= 5 msLocal NVMe storage, WAL group-commit batching (Chapter 6), and persistent multiplexed gRPC channels
4Scale10^9 keys (1 KiB mean value), 20,000 writes/s, 100,000 reads/s sustained (3x burst)Multi-terabyte storage footprint and aggregate fsync rate exceeding any single server; mandates Multi-Raft sharding
5ElasticityLinear capacity expansion without service interruptionOnline partition migration using non-voting learners and joint-consensus membership changes

Durability and availability govern orthogonal failure modes, so we analyze them separately. Durability protects data that has already been acknowledged: once a client receives 200 OK or 201 Created, subsequent hardware failures cannot erase that state. Availability governs incoming requests: whether the cluster can accept new traffic at a given instant. Under a network partition that isolates a shard leader from its peers, we deliberately reject requests on the minority side rather than risking divergent writes. In the PACELC classification, we choose a PC/EC design: consistency over availability during partitions, and consistency over minimal latency during normal operation.

Capacity and Resource Envelope

Before selecting internal algorithms, we size storage, disk IOPS, and network bandwidth to establish our minimum hardware footprint:

Resource DimensionDerivationProvisioned Bound
Logical Corpus10^9 keys * (1,024 B value + 64 B key/header)~1.09 TB logical data
Replicated Disk Footprint1.09 TB * 3 replicas * 1.6 (WAL segments, compaction overhead, filesystem reserve)~5.2 TB usable NVMe
Cluster Write Bandwidth20,000 writes/s * 1.1 KiB * 3 (client ingress plus two follower streams)~66 MB/s aggregate
Cluster Read Bandwidth100,000 reads/s * 1.1 KiB~110 MB/s aggregate
Disk fsync CeilingCommodity NVMe sustains 3,000 to 5,000 unbatched fsync/s; 20,000 writes/s * 3 replicas yields 60,000 log appends/sMinimum 24 nodes (8 per AZ) combined with WAL group commit (Chapter 6)
Per-Node Load (24 Nodes)~217 GB disk, ~2,500 replicated appends/s, ~4,167 reads/s (~12,500 reads/s at 3x burst)Commodity hosts (64 GiB RAM, 1 TB NVMe, 10 GbE NIC)

Because 217 GB of per-node storage exceeds 64 GiB of physical RAM, a storage node cannot pin its full value corpus in memory. Instead, RAM holds active working-set entries, Bloom filters, and index blocks, while cold reads resolve against local NVMe in under 150 microseconds and writes achieve durability through sequential WAL appends.

1.2 External API, Wire Protocol, and Data Contracts

We separate the client-facing HTTP/2 interface from the internal cluster replication protocol. External callers benefit from a stable, language-neutral HTTP/2 API with standard caching and precondition headers, whereas node-to-node replication requires compact binary framing, multiplexed streams, and strict schema evolution via gRPC and Protocol Buffers.

Client-Facing HTTP/2 Interface

All external endpoints reside under /v1/, run over mutual TLS (mTLS), communicate object versions through standard HTTP ETag headers, and report failures using RFC 9457 application/problem+json payloads:

OperationMethod and PathPreconditions / HeadersSuccess ResponseError Responses
UpsertPUT /v1/keys/{key}Content-Type: application/octet-stream; optional If-Match: "<ver>" or If-None-Match: *200 OK or 201 Created with ETag400, 412 Precondition Failed, 413 Payload Too Large, 503
ReadGET /v1/keys/{key}Optional If-None-Match: "<ver>"200 OK with ETag, or 304 Not Modified404 Not Found, 503 Service Unavailable
DeleteDELETE /v1/keys/{key}Optional If-Match: "<ver>"204 No Content404, 412 Precondition Failed, 503
Prefix ListGET /v1/keys?prefix={p}&limit={n}&cursor={c}None200 OK (keys[], next_cursor)400 Bad Request, 503
ReadinessGET /healthzNone200 OK503 (draining or partitioned)

Optimistic Concurrency Control and Retry Safety

When two stateless application servers read version 7 of a shopping cart, append different items in memory, and issue unconditional PUT requests, the second write overwrites the first without raising an error. Conditional writes eliminate this lost-update anomaly. By attaching If-Match: "7", the caller instructs the shard leader to evaluate the version predicate atomically before appending to its write-ahead log:

PUT /v1/keys/cart:41 HTTP/2
Host: kv.internal
If-Match: "7"
Content-Type: application/json

{"items": ["tea", "milk", "bread"]}

If the committed version remains 7, the leader commits version 8 to a majority and returns 200 OK with ETag: "8". If a concurrent writer has already advanced the key to 8, the leader rejects the stale write in memory without invoking disk I/O:

HTTP/2 412 Precondition Failed
Content-Type: application/problem+json
ETag: "8"

{
  "type": "/problems/version-mismatch",
  "title": "Precondition Failed",
  "status": 412,
  "detail": "Expected version 7, current committed version is 8."
}

Retry safety follows directly from these semantics. GET and DELETE are naturally idempotent. Conditional PUT with If-Match is safe to retry after a dropped connection: if the initial attempt committed before the reply packet was lost, the retry observes 412 Precondition Failed carrying ETag: "8" rather than applying the mutation twice. Client SDKs should apply truncated exponential backoff with full jitter on 503 Service Unavailable and 429 Too Many Requests, and must never retry deterministic client errors (400, 412, 413).

Internal Replication and Topology Protocol (gRPC / Protobuf)

Storage nodes exchange strictly typed Protobuf messages over persistent HTTP/2 streams (code/proto/store.proto). Before examining Listings 1.1 through 1.3, note the invariants encoded in the message fields:

  • Record.sequence (uint64): The contiguous, strictly monotonic log index assigned by the shard leader. Every replica applies committed records in exact sequence order, guaranteeing identical state-machine convergence.
  • AppendRequest.term (uint64): The sender’s current Raft election epoch. Any follower observing request.term < local_term immediately rejects the RPC and returns its higher term, fencing partitioned former leaders.
  • AppendRequest.previous_sequence and previous_term: The log consistency check. A follower accepts records only if its own log contains an entry at previous_sequence with matching previous_term, guaranteeing by induction that all preceding entries match the leader.
  • Ring.version (uint64): The strictly increasing topology epoch maintained by the metadata control plane. Routers tag forwarded requests with their cached epoch; storage nodes reject stale routing with a typed redirect carrying the current leader address and epoch.

Listing 1.1 Log record persisted in the write-ahead log and replicated across shard peers. proto/store.proto

// A change to one key, as the leader of a shard wrote it to its log.
message Record {
  uint64 sequence = 1;
  oneof change {
    Put put = 2;
    Delete delete = 3;
  }
}

message Put {
  string key = 1;
  bytes value = 2;
}

message Delete {
  string key = 1;
}

Listing 1.2 Leader-to-follower replication and heartbeat RPC contract. proto/store.proto

// Sent by the leader of a shard to each follower.
service Replication {
  // Appends records to the follower's log. A call with no records is a
  // heartbeat: it tells the follower that the leader is alive.
  rpc Append(AppendRequest) returns (AppendResponse);
}

message AppendRequest {
  // The shard, named by the last position it owns.
  fixed64 shard = 1;
  // The term of the sender. A follower rejects a leader of an older term.
  uint64 term = 2;
  // The sequence of the record that precedes `records` in the leader's log.
  uint64 previous_sequence = 3;
  repeated Record records = 4;
  // Every record up to this sequence is on a majority of the replicas.
  uint64 committed_sequence = 5;
  // Added for leader election. The term of the record at previous_sequence,
  // and the id of the sender.
  uint64 previous_term = 6;
  uint32 leader = 7;
}

message AppendResponse {
  uint64 term = 1;
  // False when the follower's log does not end at `previous_sequence`.
  bool appended = 2;
  // The sequence of the last record in the follower's log.
  uint64 last_sequence = 3;
}

Listing 1.3 Versioned cluster topology snapshot stored by the metadata control plane. proto/store.proto

// The ring, as the coordinator stores it. Routers and nodes read it and watch it
// for changes.
message Ring {
  uint64 version = 1;
  repeated Node nodes = 2;
  repeated Shard shards = 3;
}

message Node {
  string id = 1;
  string address = 2;
  // The positions this node owns on the ring.
  repeated fixed64 tokens = 3;
}

// A range of the ring and the nodes that hold its keys.
message Shard {
  // The shard owns the positions from first_token to last_token, both included.
  fixed64 first_token = 1;
  fixed64 last_token = 2;
  uint64 term = 3;
  string leader = 4;
  repeated string followers = 5;
}

1.3 System Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We decouple topology coordination (the control plane) from per-request execution (the data plane). Routing every GET or PUT through a centralized coordinator turns that coordinator into both a latency bottleneck and a single blast-radius dependency. Instead, stateless routers maintain an in-memory copy of the topology snapshot (Ring) synchronized asynchronously via a watch stream, and forward client operations directly to the responsible shard leader (Figure 1-2).

Component Responsibilities and Failure Domains

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
L7 Load BalancerDataActive router pool healthDeployed active-active across three AZs with health-checked failover
Stateless Router Tier (x6)DataCached Ring (epoch v), persistent gRPC channels, per-shard circuit breakersInstant failover to peer routers; continues serving through a full control-plane outage using cached topology and leader redirects
Metadata Raft Cluster (x3)ControlAuthoritative Ring, shard leader directory, node liveness leasesTolerates one host or AZ loss; if metadata quorum is lost, data-plane traffic continues while membership changes pause
Placement ControllerControlDesired vs. observed replica placement, disk and QPS heatmapsStateless leader-elected controller; reconstructs state cleanly from the metadata quorum on restart
Multi-Raft Storage Nodes (x24)DataPer-shard WAL (fsync), LSM/B-Tree engine, Raft log and vote stateEach shard forms an independent 3-replica Raft group spanning AZ-A, AZ-B, and AZ-C; losing any node or entire AZ leaves a 2 of 3 majority intact

End-to-End Request Lifecycle

Tracing a conditional write (PUT /v1/keys/user-1 with If-Match: "7") clarifies how every tier cooperates without touching the control plane on the hot path:

  1. Ingress and Partition Lookup: The L7 load balancer routes the HTTP/2 request to an AZ-local stateless router. The router hashes user-1 and performs an O(log V) binary search over its cached Ring (Epoch v42), resolving Shard 01 and its current leader in AZ-A in under 500 nanoseconds.
  2. Epoch Validation and Local WAL Append: The Shard 01 leader verifies shard ownership at Epoch >= v42, evaluates If-Match: "7" against its in-memory index, allocates log index 42 (key version 8), appends the record to its local WAL, and flushes via group-commit fsync.
  3. Parallel Quorum Replication: In parallel with its local disk flush, the leader streams AppendRequest(term=4, seq=42) to Follower B (AZ-B) and Follower C (AZ-C).
  4. Majority Commit and State-Machine Apply: As soon as one follower acknowledges durable fsync (forming a 2 of 3 majority across two AZs without waiting for the slowest replica), the leader advances committed_sequence = 42, applies the entry to its local storage engine, and replies 200 OK with ETag: "8".
  5. Stale-Epoch Redirect: If a leader election recently moved Shard 01 to AZ-B while the router still held Epoch v42, AZ-A replies immediately with NOT_LEADER(leader_hint=AZ-B, epoch=43). The router updates its local cache and retries against AZ-B transparently within the client deadline.

1.4 Consistency Semantics and Trade-Offs

In distributed storage, engineers use the single word “consistency” for three formally incompatible guarantees. We distinguish them cleanly by considering a read invoked immediately after a write has been acknowledged while one replica still lags behind the leader (Figure 1-3).

Consistency ModelFormal GuaranteePACELC BehaviorTarget Workloads
Linearizability (Strong)Every operation takes effect atomically at a single point between its invocation and completion, preserving global real-time recencyPC/EC: Quorum round trip required; minority partition rejects trafficConfiguration registries, distributed locks, CAS state machines, session auth, ledgers
Tunable Quorum (R + W > N)Leaderless overlap ensures at least one read replica intersects the write set (provided strict non-sloppy quorums and synchronous read-repair hold)PA/EL under sloppy quorums; requires version vectors or conflict resolutionHigh-availability shopping carts, multi-region user profiles
Eventual ConsistencyReplicas converge asynchronously after writes cease; readers may observe arbitrarily stale data during replication lagPA/EL: Local single-node ACK (< 1 ms), remains writable across partitionsDNS caches, view counters, social timelines, CDN metadata

Why Quorum Intersection (R + W > N) Alone Does Not Guarantee Linearizability

In leaderless Dynamo-style stores, engineers frequently assume that configuring N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 achieves linearizability because any two-node read set overlaps any two-node write set. Three edge cases invalidate that assumption in production:

  1. Sloppy Quorums and Hinted Handoff: When a primary replica is unreachable and the coordinator writes to a temporary fallback host to preserve availability, the subsequent R = 2 read against the nominal replica set misses the newly written value entirely.
  2. Non-Monotonic Concurrent Reads: While a write of v2 has reached Replica 1 but not yet Replicas 2 and 3, Reader A querying {R1, R2} observes v2. A later Reader B querying {R2, R3} observes v1, violating real-time linearizability unless Reader A synchronously repairs R2 before returning v2 to its caller.
  3. Physical-Clock Last-Write-Wins (LWW): Ordering concurrent writes with wall-clock timestamps drops valid updates without detection whenever NTP clock drift exceeds the interval between writes.

Because functional requirement 3 mandates atomic compare-and-swap (If-Match), we adopt leader-based Raft linearizability per shard. Serializing every mutation for a key through a single term-fenced leader eliminates concurrent write divergence altogether.

1.5 Partitioning: Consistent Hashing, Virtual Nodes, and Range Splits

A single Raft consensus group hits a hard vertical ceiling at the fsync throughput and network capacity of its leader (5,000 to 15,000 writes/s even with group commit). To sustain 20,000 writes/s and 100,000 reads/s across 5.2 TB of replicated storage, the key space is partitioned into hundreds of independent 3-replica Raft groups (Multi-Raft) distributed across the 24 physical nodes. Each host acts as leader for a balanced fraction of shards and follower for others, utilizing all 24 NVMe drives and network interfaces concurrently.

Consistent Hashing and Empirical Virtual-Node Variance

Modulo partitioning (hash(key) % N) degrades severely during cluster scaling: expanding a 24-node fleet to 25 nodes alters the modulo divisor for nearly every key, forcing 96% of the corpus (~5 TB of data) to migrate simultaneously across the cluster fabric.

Consistent hashing maps keys and physical nodes onto a circular 64-bit hash ring [0, 2^64 - 1]. Walking clockwise from H(key) selects the owning primary token, and continuing clockwise while skipping tokens hosted on already-selected physical machines or availability zones selects the N = 3 fault-isolated replicas (Figure 1-4). Adding one node to a 24-node ring relocates only 1/25 = 4% of keys directly to the new host.

Placing a single token per physical node leaves large random gaps around the circle, producing severe load imbalance. Assigning V virtual nodes (tokens) per host averages out random arc lengths. Executing ringsim across 100,000 keys and 24 nodes measures this convergence directly:

$ cargo run --release -p ringsim
100000 keys on 24 nodes, ideal share 4.17%
     1 tokens per node: smallest share  0.16%, largest share 11.26%
     8 tokens per node: smallest share  1.42%, largest share  7.83%
    64 tokens per node: smallest share  3.35%, largest share  5.07%
   256 tokens per node: smallest share  3.86%, largest share  4.73%
adding node 25 to a ring with 256 tokens per node, ideal movement 4.00%
  on the ring: 4332 keys changed owner (4.33%), 4332 of them to the new node
  hash mod N : 96001 keys changed owner (96.00%)
replicas of user-1: node-10, node-1, node-6
position of user-1: 0x7c7615c11438e5c9

With a single token per node, the fullest machine absorbs 2.7x its ideal share (11.26%), 70x more data than the lightest host (0.16%). Increasing to 256 virtual nodes compresses worst-case load to 4.73% (1.13x ideal), while adding a 25th node moves only 4.33% of keys compared to 96.00% under modulo hashing.

Architectural Trade-Off: Consistent Hashing vs. Range Partitioning

Hash partitioning creates a structural tension with functional requirement 4 (lexicographic prefix listing). Because hashing scatters lexicographically adjacent keys (user:7:sess1 and user:7:sess2) across unrelated shards, answering GET /v1/keys?prefix=user:7: requires a scatter-gather fan-out across every shard followed by a K-way merge at the router. Tail latency then degrades to the slowest shard in the fleet (p99_total ≈ 1 - (1 - p99_shard)^S), making broad scans expensive at large cluster sizes.

Range partitioning (used by CockroachDB, TiKV, and Google Spanner) keeps keys sorted lexicographically across contiguous ranges so prefix scans execute on a single shard in O(log N + K) time. The corresponding liability is write hot-spotting: monotonically increasing keys (timestamps or sequential identifiers) funnel every write onto the rightmost range until the placement controller executes an automated dynamic range split once a shard exceeds 64 MiB or a QPS threshold. Production systems frequently adopt compound keys (Amazon DynamoDB style), hashing the tenant or entity partition key for uniform write spread while sorting sub-keys lexicographically within the shard so tenant-scoped prefix scans remain single-shard operations.

Hot-Key Skew Mitigation

Even with uniform hash distribution, real workloads follow Zipfian popularity curves where a single viral configuration key or celebrity profile attracts 30,000 reads/s on one shard leader. Mitigating hot keys requires explicit workload isolation: read-heavy keys that tolerate milliseconds of staleness can opt into short-TTL router caching or AZ-local follower reads (bounded by a Raft safe-timestamp watermark), while hot write keys are bounded by per-key router admission control so one saturated key cannot starve neighboring keys sharing the same Raft log.

1.6 Replication, Linearizable Reads, and Split-Brain Fencing

Within every shard, we run a 3-node Raft group to guarantee both durability and linearizable state transitions (implemented in detail in Chapters 3 and 4). Every write passes exclusively through the shard leader, which appends to its local WAL and replicates entries via AppendRequest (Figure 1-5).

Quorum Intersection and Term Fencing

For any replication group of size N = 2f + 1 (N = 3, f = 1), any two majorities of size f + 1 = 2 overlap in at least one replica. Raft’s election restriction permits a candidate to win RequestVote only if its log is at least as up-to-date as every voter in its majority. By quorum intersection, any leader elected in Term T + 1 is mathematically guaranteed to possess every record committed in Term <= T. Meanwhile, monotonic term numbers fence stale leaders: if Leader A (Term 4) is isolated in a minority partition while AZ-B and AZ-C elect Leader B (Term 5), Leader A cannot assemble a majority for new writes, and any delayed Term 4 RPC arriving at AZ-B or AZ-C is rejected immediately. When the partition heals, Leader A observes Term 5 and steps down cleanly, discarding any uncommitted minority entries.

Linearizable Reads Without Disk Writes (ReadIndex vs. Leader Leases)

Serving a GET directly from a leader’s local memory without checking quorum status violates linearizability: a partitioned leader unaware that a newer leader has committed writes in Term + 1 would return stale data. Conversely, appending every read to the Raft log preserves linearizability at an unacceptable fsync cost.

Two production mechanisms preserve linearizability on reads without touching disk:

  1. ReadIndex (Clock-Independent Default): Upon receiving GET, the leader snapshots its commit_index as read_index, broadcasts a lightweight empty AppendRequest heartbeat to confirm it still holds majority authority, waits for its local state machine to apply up to read_index, and serves the read from memory. Concurrent reads coalesce into a single heartbeat round trip (< 1 ms intra-AZ/cross-AZ RTT) with zero reliance on physical clock synchronization.
  2. Leader Leases (Clock-Dependent Optimization): The leader avoids the per-read heartbeat RTT by tracking a local time-bounded lease (lease < election_timeout / (1 + max_clock_drift)). Because virtual machine live-migration pauses, garbage-collection stalls, or NTP steps can invalidate local clock bounds and expose stale reads, leader leases are safe only when paired with verified monotonic clock bounds (such as CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW with hardware watchdogs or Spanner’s TrueTime uncertainty intervals).

Storage Engine Internals and Online Membership Changes

Inside each storage node, crash safety rests on an append-only Write-Ahead Log (WAL) protected by per-record CRC32C checksums (Chapter 2) and accelerated by group commit (Chapter 6), which batches concurrent writes into a single fsync call. Once data exceeds RAM, the engine pairs the WAL with either an LSM-Tree (in-memory MemTable flushed to immutable sorted SSTables, merged via leveled compaction, and guarded by per-SSTable Bloom filters to avoid disk reads on absent keys) or a copy-on-write B+Tree (BoltDB/LMDB style).

When replacing a failed disk or rebalancing shards across hosts, transitioning a Raft group directly from configuration C_old to C_new risks allowing two disjoint majorities to form simultaneously. Safe online reconfiguration first catches up the replacement node as a non-voting Learner until its log lag approaches zero, then commits membership changes either one voting server at a time or via Raft joint consensus (C_old,new, requiring majorities in both old and new configurations until committed).

1.7 Failure Modes, Tail Latency, and Observability

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ScenarioBlast RadiusDetection MechanismAutomated Recovery and Client Impact
Single Storage Node CrashShards led by that host (~1/24 of cluster)Missed Raft heartbeats (300 to 500 ms timeout)Surviving majority elects new leader in < 1.5 s; clients retry brief 503 responses with zero data loss
Full Availability Zone OutageOne-third of physical nodes offlineCross-AZ heartbeat timeout and readiness probesEvery shard retains 2 of 3 replicas across the remaining two AZs; affected leaders fail over in < 1.5 s and traffic continues at degraded redundancy
Corrupted NVMe Sector / Bit RotSingle replica WAL or SSTableCRC32C checksum mismatch on replay or readNode halts the corrupted shard immediately (fail-stop); placement controller rebuilds a clean replica from the healthy leader

Metadata Control-Plane OutageCluster membership changes onlyControl-plane quorum alertData plane continues serving uninterrupted via router-cached topology and leader redirects; node joins pause until metadata quorum restores
Slow Disk (Gray Failure)Elevated tail latency on one hostPer-node fsync p99 monitorMajority (2 of 3) masks a slow follower automatically; if a leader’s disk degrades, controller triggers graceful leadership transfer (TimeoutNow)

Tail-Latency Engineering

At 100,000 reads/s, a 0.1% tail anomaly affects 100 operations every second. Sustaining p99 <= 5 ms reads and p99 <= 20 ms writes requires four discipline measures: group-commit batching to amortize NVMe fsync latency across parallel writers (Chapter 6); dedicated gRPC channels separating latency-sensitive Raft heartbeats from bulk gigabyte snapshot transfers so recovery traffic never triggers spurious leader elections; end-to-end deadline propagation (grpc-timeout) so expired requests are discarded before entering disk queues; and bounded proposal queues returning 429 Too Many Requests under overload rather than accumulating unbounded memory until an out-of-memory kill.

Chapter 2: Storage Node and Write-Ahead Logging (LLD)

In Chapter 1, we distributed the key-value store across 24 storage nodes, replicated every shard across three independent failure domains, and derived quorum durability bounds under host crashes and network partitions. That entire distributed architecture depends on a single local-storage invariant: once a storage node acknowledges a write to its caller, that write must remain recoverable after the process crashes or the host loses power. If a single node loses an acknowledged record, then a write counted as stored on two of three replicas may survive on only one, invalidating every replication guarantee layered above it.

In this chapter, I implement the storage node in Rust so that this durability invariant holds unconditionally. A storage node manages the live key-value map and durable log on one host. Its core engineering complexity concentrates in the few milliseconds during which a mutation is in flight and power may fail. We begin by analyzing what a crash can corrupt at each stage of a write, which motivates append-only write-ahead logging (WAL). We then specify the binary record format, implement CRC-32 checksummed encoding and torn-tail recovery, measure the physical latency of write versus fsync, and assemble the in-memory store and HTTP/1.1 interface specified in Chapter 1. Finally, we verify crash durability empirically in three complementary ways: by truncating and bit-flipping every byte of a log in crashsim, by terminating kvd with SIGKILL under active client load on one host, and by repeating the crash test across two separate network hosts.

In this chapter, we cover

  • crash-consistency failure modes at each stage of a mutation and the four invariants of write-ahead logging
  • binary record framing with little-endian length prefixes, monotonic sequence numbers, and CRC-32 checksums
  • deterministic startup recovery, torn-tail truncation via set_len, and parent-directory synchronization
  • kernel page-cache buffering versus physical disk durability (write versus fsync) and empirical NVMe latency via synccost
  • fail-stop error handling when write_all or sync_data returns an I/O fault
  • the BTreeMap-backed Store supporting monotonic versions, conditional If-Match / If-None-Match writes, and cursor-paginated prefix scans
  • the asynchronous axum HTTP server (kvd) offloading blocking disk I/O via spawn_blocking
  • exhaustive byte-truncation and bit-flip verification (crashsim) and live SIGKILL recovery verification (kvctl) on one host and across two hosts

2.1 Durable Storage and Write-Ahead Logging

A storage node holds its active key-value entries in RAM so that point reads (GET) and prefix scans resolve without disk seeks. Because volatile memory disappears when a process terminates or a server loses power, the node must persist every mutation on non-volatile storage in a form from which we can reconstruct the in-memory map deterministically at startup.

Updating a data file in place is unsafe under power loss. Consider replacing a 1 KiB value with a new 1 KiB payload when power fails after half of the new bytes reach disk. On restart, the file contains the first half of the new value concatenated with the second half of the old value. The entry is torn, the prior value is gone, and the raw file carries no structural evidence of corruption.

The defect in an in-place update is that overwriting destroys the old state before the new state becomes complete, creating a vulnerability window in which neither state exists. We eliminate that window by forbidding in-place mutations altogether. Instead, the node appends a self-contained description of each change to the end of an append-only file, called a log, and never modifies previously written bytes. Because we record every change durably in the log before mutating any in-memory index, this design is called write-ahead logging (WAL).

With an append-only log, a crash mid-write can corrupt at most the single record currently being appended at the tail of the file. Every previously acknowledged record resides at an earlier byte offset that the process never touches again.

We enforce four strict invariants on every storage node, regardless of request interleaving or crash timing:

No.Storage Node InvariantOperational Guarantee
0Every mutation is appended to the WAL and confirmed by fsync before the server returns a response to the client.Guarantees durability of acknowledged writes across process termination and power loss.
1Every mutation reaches the durable WAL before the node applies it to the in-memory BTreeMap.Prevents any concurrent reader from observing uncommitted state that could vanish after a crash.
2The in-memory BTreeMap equals the exact result of applying all valid WAL records in sequence order.Ensures that losing RAM loses zero committed state and recovery is deterministic.
3The WAL is modified exclusively by appending; bytes belonging to a confirmed record are never overwritten.Confines crash damage strictly to the tail of the file, where startup recovery detects and truncates incomplete frames.

2.2 Crash Points During a Write

Because invariant 0 and invariant 1 impose a strict total order on the write path (encode frame, append to WAL, call fsync, apply to BTreeMap, send HTTP response), we can enumerate the exact recovery state for a crash at every stage of a mutation (Figure 2-1).

The third case merits explicit analysis. When the node completes fsync and terminates before writing the HTTP response socket, the record survives recovery even though the caller received a connection reset rather than a 201 Created or 204 No Content. This outcome satisfies invariant 0: durability binds acknowledged writes and makes no promise that an unacknowledged write did not commit. From the caller’s perspective, the outcome is indeterminate. As we established in Chapter 1, the caller resolves indeterminate writes safely by retrying with an idempotent PUT or a conditional If-Match version check. We trigger and observe this exact third case experimentally in Section 2.8.

2.3 On-Disk WAL Record Format

When the storage node restarts, the recovery scanner must locate every record boundary across variable-length keys and values, and it must reject any truncated or bit-corrupted record at the end of the file.

We satisfy both requirements by prefixing every serialized payload with an 8-byte frame header: a 4-byte little-endian unsigned payload length (u32) followed by a 4-byte IEEE CRC-32 checksum computed over the payload bytes. Any single-bit flip, torn sector write, or truncated payload changes either the observed length or the recomputed CRC-32 checksum. Figure 2-2 illustrates both the on-disk binary record layout and the synchronous write path from frame encoding through WAL durability to BTreeMap visibility.

Inspecting the raw bytes of data/kv.log after applying two writes to user-1 illustrates the exact wire layout:

$ xxd data/kv.log | head -4
00000000: 1400 0000 8dd3 da1d 0100 0000 0000 0000  ................
00000010: 0106 0075 7365 722d 3161 6461 1d00 0000  ...user-1ada....
00000020: cefd 7d53 0200 0000 0000 0000 0106 0075  ..}S...........u
00000030: 7365 722d 3161 6461 206c 6f76 656c 6163  ser-1ada lovelac

The first four bytes (1400 0000) encode payload length 20 in little-endian byte order, followed by the 4-byte CRC-32 checksum (8dd3 da1d). Inside the 20-byte payload, the 8-byte sequence number 1 precedes the 1-byte operation tag (01 for Put), the 2-byte key length (0600), the 6-byte UTF-8 key (user-1), and the remaining value bytes (ada). At byte offset 28 (0x1c), the second frame opens with length 1d00 0000 (29 bytes).

We implement binary framing in kv/src/record.rs. Listing 2.1 declares the CRC-32 hasher import required for payload integrity verification.

Listing 2.1 Imports of kv/src/record.rs. kv/src/record.rs

use crc32fast::hash;

Before writing the encoder and decoder, we define the core domain types in Listing 2.2. Change represents either a Put with key and value bytes or a Delete tombstone, Record pairs a Change with its strictly monotonic u64 log sequence number, and Decoded partitions every possible decode result into three mutually exclusive outcomes: Ok (a valid record plus byte count consumed), Incomplete (buffer ended before frame or payload completion), or Corrupt (checksum mismatch, unknown tag, or invalid UTF-8 key). Recovery treats Incomplete and Corrupt identically by stopping the scan, whereas post-mortem fault inspection benefits from distinguishing an interrupted tail write from on-disk bit corruption.

Listing 2.2 Core record types and three-way decode outcome in kv/src/record.rs. kv/src/record.rs

/// A change to the store.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Change {
    Put { key: String, value: Vec<u8> },
    Delete { key: String },
}

/// A change with its position in the log. Sequence numbers start at 1 and
/// grow by 1 with each record.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Record {
    pub sequence: u64,
    pub change: Change,
}

/// The result of reading one record from the front of a slice of bytes.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Decoded {
    /// A whole record, and the number of bytes it occupies.
    Record { record: Record, length: usize },
    /// The bytes end before the record does.
    Incomplete,
    /// The checksum does not match the payload, or the payload is malformed.
    Corrupt,
}

/// The bytes of a frame: the length and the checksum.
pub const FRAME: usize = 8;

/// The largest payload a record may have: a key, a value of 1 MiB, and the
/// fixed fields.
pub const MAX_PAYLOAD: usize = (1 << 20) + 1024;

const PUT: u8 = 1;
const DELETE: u8 = 2;

Listing 2.3 defines Record::encode, which serializes the sequence number, operation tag, key length, key bytes, and optional value bytes into a contiguous payload vector, computes its CRC-32 digest, and prepends the 8-byte frame header (len and crc) in little-endian order. The contract guarantees that every encoded frame is self-delimiting and passes Record::decode without allocation ambiguity.

Listing 2.3 Little-endian framing and CRC-32 encoding in kv/src/record.rs. kv/src/record.rs

impl Record {
    /// Returns the record as the bytes that are appended to the log.
    pub fn encode(&self) -> Vec<u8> {
        let (kind, key, value) = match &self.change {
            Change::Put { key, value } => (PUT, key, value.as_slice()),
            Change::Delete { key } => (DELETE, key, &[][..]),
        };

        let mut payload = Vec::with_capacity(11 + key.len() + value.len());
        payload.extend_from_slice(&self.sequence.to_le_bytes());
        payload.push(kind);
        payload.extend_from_slice(&(key.len() as u16).to_le_bytes());
        payload.extend_from_slice(key.as_bytes());
        payload.extend_from_slice(value);

        let mut bytes = Vec::with_capacity(FRAME + payload.len());
        bytes.extend_from_slice(&(payload.len() as u32).to_le_bytes());
        bytes.extend_from_slice(&hash(&payload).to_le_bytes());
        bytes.extend_from_slice(&payload);

        bytes
    }
}

Listing 2.4 implements the inverse contract, Record::decode. It parses a byte slice defensively without trusting any length field read from disk: if fewer than 8 bytes remain or fewer than len payload bytes remain, it returns Decoded::Incomplete; if the recomputed CRC-32 fails, an internal field exceeds payload bounds, the key is invalid UTF-8, or the operation tag is unrecognized, it returns Decoded::Corrupt. Every fixed-width field uses split_first_chunk, ensuring that corrupted length headers never trigger an out-of-bounds panic.

Listing 2.4 Defensive bounds-checked decoding in kv/src/record.rs. kv/src/record.rs

impl Record {
    /// Reads the record at the front of `bytes`.
    pub fn decode(bytes: &[u8]) -> Decoded {
        let Some((length, rest)) = bytes.split_first_chunk::<4>() else {
            return Decoded::Incomplete;
        };
        let Some((checksum, rest)) = rest.split_first_chunk::<4>() else {
            return Decoded::Incomplete;
        };

        let length = u32::from_le_bytes(*length) as usize;

        if length > MAX_PAYLOAD {
            return Decoded::Corrupt;
        }

        let Some(payload) = rest.get(..length) else {
            return Decoded::Incomplete;
        };

        if hash(payload) != u32::from_le_bytes(*checksum) {
            return Decoded::Corrupt;
        }

        match parse(payload) {
            Some(record) => Decoded::Record {
                record,
                length: FRAME + length,
            },
            None => Decoded::Corrupt,
        }
    }
}

/// Splits a payload into its fields. It returns `None` for a payload that is
/// too short for its fields or has an unknown kind.
fn parse(payload: &[u8]) -> Option<Record> {
    let (sequence, rest) = payload.split_first_chunk::<8>()?;
    let (&kind, rest) = rest.split_first()?;
    let (key_length, rest) = rest.split_first_chunk::<2>()?;
    let (key, value) = rest.split_at_checked(u16::from_le_bytes(*key_length) as usize)?;
    let key = String::from_utf8(key.to_vec()).ok()?;

    let change = match (kind, value) {
        (PUT, value) => Change::Put {
            key,
            value: value.to_vec(),
        },
        (DELETE, []) => Change::Delete { key },
        (_unknown, _value) => return None,
    };

    Some(Record {
        sequence: u64::from_le_bytes(*sequence),
        change,
    })
}

2.4 Measuring the Physical Cost of fsync

Invariant 0 requires confirmation from non-volatile storage before replying to a client. Issuing a write system call alone does not satisfy this requirement. write copies bytes from user-space memory into the operating system kernel’s page cache and returns immediately; the kernel flushes dirty pages asynchronously on its own schedule. Calling fsync (or fdatasync, invoked in Rust via File::sync_data) forces the kernel to flush all buffered bytes for that file descriptor to the storage controller and blocks until the device reports completion.

To quantify this durability barrier on real hardware, we build the synccost microbenchmark. Listing 2.5 imports the filesystem, timing, and record types used by synccost.

Listing 2.5 Imports of synccost/src/main.rs. synccost/src/main.rs

use std::env;
use std::error::Error;
use std::fs;
use std::path::Path;
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

use kv::{Change, Log};

Listing 2.6 appends 500 identical records twice to fresh files: once calling write_all alone (sync = false) and once calling write_all followed by sync_data (sync = true), reporting elapsed time, per-record latency, and sustained throughput for each mode.

Listing 2.6 Measuring buffered versus durable WAL append throughput in synccost/src/main.rs. synccost/src/main.rs

const RECORDS: u32 = 500;

/// Appends `RECORDS` records of 100 bytes and returns the time it took.
fn measure(directory: &Path, sync: bool) -> Result<Duration, Box<dyn Error>> {
    let mut log = Log::open(directory, sync)?.0;
    let started = Instant::now();

    for number in 0..RECORDS {
        log.append(Change::Put {
            key: format!("key-{number:06}"),
            value: vec![b'v'; 100],
        })?;
    }

    Ok(started.elapsed())
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let root = env::args()
        .nth(1)
        .ok_or("usage: synccost <directory>")?;

    for (name, sync) in [("without fsync", false), ("with fsync", true)] {
        let directory = Path::new(&root).join(name.replace(' ', "-"));
        let elapsed = measure(&directory, sync)?;
        let each = elapsed.as_secs_f64() * 1000.0 / f64::from(RECORDS);

        println!(
            "{name:13}: {RECORDS} records in {:8.1} ms, {each:.3} ms per record, {:6.0} records per second",
            elapsed.as_secs_f64() * 1000.0,
            1000.0 / each
        );

        fs::remove_dir_all(&directory)?;
    }

    Ok(())
}

Running synccost on an NVMe SSD yields a three-order-of-magnitude latency gap:

$ cargo run --release -p synccost -- /var/tmp/synccost
without fsync: 500 records in      1.4 ms, 0.003 ms per record, 366991 records per second
with fsync   : 500 records in   2697.5 ms, 5.395 ms per record,    185 records per second

Each durable append costs 5.4 ms, roughly 1,900 times longer than copying into the kernel page cache, capping an unbatched single-writer disk at 185 records/s. This measurement anchors the hardware provisioning analysis we established in Chapter 1 and motivates the group-commit batching optimization we implement in Chapter 6. Because durability versus throughput is an explicit operational trade-off, kvd exposes an optional --no-sync flag that skips sync_data. Under --no-sync, acknowledged writes survive a process crash (SIGKILL) via the kernel page cache, yet recent writes can disappear upon host power loss. Defaulting to durable fsync ensures that no operator trades away power-loss safety without an explicit configuration flag.

2.6 The Write-Ahead Log (kv::log)

Log owns the open file descriptor for kv.log and exposes two public operations: open, which recovers the durable prefix and repairs any torn tail, and append, which assigns the next contiguous sequence number and persists the framed record.

Listing 2.8 imports the file I/O traits, path types, and Record codec used by kv/src/log.rs.

Listing 2.8 Imports of kv/src/log.rs. kv/src/log.rs

use std::fs::{self, File, OpenOptions};
use std::io::{self, Read, Write};
use std::path::Path;

use crate::record::{Change, Decoded, Record};

Listing 2.9 defines the Log struct and Recovered return bundle. Log tracks the next sequence number to assign (next), whether sync_data is enabled (sync), and the fail-stop latch (failed). Recovered hands back the open Log, the ordered vector of intact Record entries, and truncated_bytes so operators can observe whether startup repaired a torn tail.

Listing 2.9 Log state and Recovered summary in kv/src/log.rs. kv/src/log.rs

/// The name of the log inside the data directory.
pub const FILE_NAME: &str = "kv.log";

/// An open log, positioned at its end.
pub struct Log {
    file: File,
    /// Whether `append` waits for the disk before it returns.
    sync: bool,
    /// The sequence number of the next record.
    next: u64,
    /// Set by a failed write. A failed log accepts no more records.
    failed: bool,
}

/// What `Log::open` found in the file.
pub struct Recovery {
    /// The complete records, in the order they were written.
    pub records: Vec<Record>,
    /// The bytes after the last complete record, which were removed.
    pub discarded: u64,
}

Startup Scan and Torn-Tail Truncation

At startup, scan reads the raw file buffer from byte offset 0 and invokes Record::decode repeatedly until either all bytes are consumed or the first Incomplete or Corrupt frame is encountered. Listing 2.10 implements this pure decoding loop, returning the valid record vector and the exact byte offset where valid data ends.

Listing 2.10 Sequential record scan in kv/src/log.rs. kv/src/log.rs

/// Reads records from the front of `bytes` until one is incomplete or
/// corrupt. It returns the records and the number of bytes they occupy.
fn scan(bytes: &[u8]) -> (Vec<Record>, usize) {
    let mut records = Vec::new();
    let mut valid = 0;

    while let Decoded::Record { record, length } = Record::decode(&bytes[valid..]) {
        records.push(record);
        valid += length;
    }

    (records, valid)
}

Figure 2-5 traces the complete crash-recovery lifecycle: scanning valid CRC-checked frames from byte 0, truncating the torn tail at the exact valid boundary, replaying the valid prefix into a fresh BTreeMap, and bounding long-term log growth via atomic snapshot compaction.

Listing 2.11 implements Log::open. After opening or creating kv.log, reading its contents, and running scan, it truncates any trailing damaged bytes via file.set_len(valid_end), seeks the write cursor to valid_end, calls file.sync_all(), and synchronizes the parent directory descriptor (sync_dir).

Listing 2.11 Opening the WAL, truncating damaged tails, and syncing the parent directory in kv/src/log.rs. kv/src/log.rs

impl Log {
    /// Opens the log in `directory`, creating both if they do not exist.
    /// Anything after the last complete record is cut off.
    pub fn open(directory: &Path, sync: bool) -> io::Result<(Log, Recovery)> {
        fs::create_dir_all(directory)?;

        let mut file = OpenOptions::new()
            .read(true)
            .append(true)
            .create(true)
            .open(directory.join(FILE_NAME))?;
        let mut bytes = Vec::new();
        file.read_to_end(&mut bytes)?;

        let (records, valid) = scan(&bytes);
        let discarded = (bytes.len() - valid) as u64;

        if discarded > 0 {
            file.set_len(valid as u64)?;
        }

        if sync {
            // The file's length is part of the file. Its name is part of the directory.
            file.sync_all()?;
            File::open(directory)?.sync_all()?;
        }

        let next = records
            .last()
            .map_or(1, |record| record.sequence + 1);

        Ok((
            Log {
                file,
                sync,
                next,
                failed: false,
            },
            Recovery { records, discarded },
        ))
    }
}

Truncating the damaged tail before accepting any new write is mandatory for correctness. If trailing garbage remained in the file, subsequent valid records would be appended past the corrupt offset; on the next restart, scan would halt at the old damage and discard newly acknowledged writes. Both sync_all calls are equally required: synchronizing the file descriptor persists its truncated length and contents, whereas synchronizing the parent directory persists the directory entry linking the filename to its inode. On POSIX filesystems, a newly created log file whose parent directory was never synchronized can vanish entirely after a power loss.

Durable Appends and Fail-Stop Error Handling

Listing 2.12 implements Log::append. Preconditions: self.failed must be false. The method constructs the next Record with sequence number self.next, encodes the frame, writes all bytes to disk, and optionally calls sync_data. Only after disk confirmation succeeds does self.next increment. On any I/O error from write_all or sync_data, the method sets self.failed = true and propagates the error.

Listing 2.12 Durable append with fail-stop latching in kv/src/log.rs. kv/src/log.rs

impl Log {
    /// Appends a change and returns the record that holds it. When the log
    /// was opened with `sync`, the record is on the disk when this returns.
    pub fn append(&mut self, change: Change) -> io::Result<Record> {
        if self.failed {
            return Err(io::Error::other(
                "the log failed on an earlier write and is closed",
            ));
        }

        let record = Record {
            sequence: self.next,
            change,
        };

        if let Err(error) = self.write(&record.encode()) {
            self.failed = true;

            return Err(error);
        }

        self.next += 1;

        Ok(record)
    }

    fn write(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]) -> io::Result<()> {
        self.file.write_all(bytes)?;

        if self.sync {
            self.file.sync_data()?;
        }

        Ok(())
    }

    /// The sequence number of the last record, or 0 for an empty log.
    pub fn last_sequence(&self) -> u64 {
        self.next - 1
    }
}

Latching self.failed = true enforces a fail-stop policy. When write_all or sync_data fails, the on-disk tail state is indeterminate: the bytes may be absent, partially written, or written to a failing sector. Continuing to append risks placing a valid record behind a corrupt frame where recovery will never read it. Retrying fsync is equally unsafe on Linux and similar kernels: after returning an I/O error from fsync, the kernel marks affected page-cache pages clean and discards the error state, so a second fsync call can return Ok(()) even though the data never reached disk. By latching failed = true, the node rejects all further mutations with HTTP 503 Service Unavailable, continues serving in-memory reads, and awaits operator restart or host replacement. In the multi-node cluster of Chapter 1, peer replicas elect a new leader and absorb the failed disk without service outage.

2.7 The In-Memory Store (kv::store)

Store owns both the BTreeMap<String, Entry> index and the underlying Log, funneling every mutation through a single ordered code path. Listing 2.13 declares the map and error imports for kv/src/store.rs.

Listing 2.13 Imports of kv/src/store.rs. kv/src/store.rs

use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use std::io;
use std::ops::Bound;
use std::path::Path;

use thiserror::Error;

use crate::log::Log;
use crate::record::{Change, Record};

Listing 2.14 implements Store::open and the internal apply helper. Store::open delegates WAL recovery to Log::open, allocates an empty BTreeMap, and replays every recovered record through apply. Because startup recovery and live writes invoke the exact same apply function, invariant 2 holds by construction: live state and recovered state cannot diverge.

Listing 2.14 Store startup replay and single-source state application in kv/src/store.rs. kv/src/store.rs

impl Store {
    /// Opens the store in `directory` and applies every record of its log.
    /// It returns the store, the number of records applied, and the number
    /// of bytes that were cut from the end of the log.
    pub fn open(directory: &Path, sync: bool) -> io::Result<(Store, usize, u64)> {
        let (log, recovery) = Log::open(directory, sync)?;
        let applied = recovery.records.len();
        let mut entries = BTreeMap::new();

        for record in recovery.records {
            apply(&mut entries, record);
        }

        Ok((Store { entries, log }, applied, recovery.discarded))
    }
}

/// Makes the change of one record in the map. Recovery and the write path
/// both go through this function, so they cannot disagree.
pub fn apply(entries: &mut BTreeMap<String, Entry>, record: Record) {
    match record.change {
        Change::Put { key, value } => {
            entries.insert(
                key,
                Entry {
                    value,
                    version: record.sequence,
                },
            );
        }
        Change::Delete { key } => {
            entries.remove(&key);
        }
    }
}

Listing 2.15 implements Store::put and Store::delete. Both enforce the exact three-stage contract required by invariants 0 and 1:

  1. Validate the caller’s Condition (Always, Absent, or Version(expected)) against the current BTreeMap entry so rejected writes never touch disk.
  2. Call self.log.append(change)?, returning early on any disk failure before mutating memory.
  3. Apply the durable record to self.entries and return the assigned version.

Notice that an entry’s version equals the exact sequence number of the WAL record that last updated it. Reusing the WAL sequence number eliminates any secondary version counter that could drift out of synchronization across crashes.

Listing 2.15 Check-append-apply write path in kv/src/store.rs. kv/src/store.rs

impl Store {
    /// Sets the value of a key. The change is in the log before it is in
    /// the map.
    pub fn put(
        &mut self,
        key: String,
        value: Vec<u8>,
        condition: Condition,
    ) -> Result<Written, StoreError> {
        let current = self.version(&key);
        check(condition, current)?;

        let record = self
            .log
            .append(Change::Put { key, value })?;
        let version = record.sequence;
        apply(&mut self.entries, record);

        Ok(Written {
            version,
            created: current.is_none(),
        })
    }

    /// Removes a key.
    pub fn delete(&mut self, key: &str, condition: Condition) -> Result<(), StoreError> {
        let current = self.version(key);

        if current.is_none() {
            return Err(StoreError::NotFound);
        }

        check(condition, current)?;

        let record = self.log.append(Change::Delete {
            key: key.to_owned(),
        })?;
        apply(&mut self.entries, record);

        Ok(())
    }

    fn version(&self, key: &str) -> Option<u64> {
        self.entries
            .get(key)
            .map(|entry| entry.version)
    }
}

pub fn check(condition: Condition, current: Option<u64>) -> Result<(), StoreError> {
    let holds = match condition {
        Condition::Always => true,
        Condition::Absent => current.is_none(),
        Condition::Version(version) => current == Some(version),
    };

    holds
        .then_some(())
        .ok_or(StoreError::ConditionFailed { current })
}

Listing 2.16 implements the read path (Store::get, Store::list, and page), which queries self.entries exclusively with zero disk I/O. Because BTreeMap maintains keys in lexicographic order, page executes a bounded range scan starting either at prefix or strictly after cursor, terminating at the first key that no longer starts with prefix. Fetching limit + 1 keys determines whether a subsequent page exists without scanning the remainder of the keyspace.

Listing 2.16 Point lookups and cursor-paginated prefix scans in kv/src/store.rs. kv/src/store.rs

impl Store {
    pub fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<&Entry> {
        self.entries.get(key)
    }

    /// Returns up to `limit` keys that start with `prefix` and sort after
    /// `after`, in order, and whether more keys follow them.
    pub fn list(&self, prefix: &str, after: Option<&str>, limit: usize) -> (Vec<Summary>, bool) {
        page(&self.entries, prefix, after, limit)
    }

    pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
        self.entries.len()
    }

    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        self.entries.is_empty()
    }

    /// The sequence number of the last record in the log.
    pub fn last_sequence(&self) -> u64 {
        self.log.last_sequence()
    }
}

/// One page of a listing over a map of entries.
pub fn page(
    entries: &BTreeMap<String, Entry>,
    prefix: &str,
    after: Option<&str>,
    limit: usize,
) -> (Vec<Summary>, bool) {
    let start = match after {
        Some(key) => Bound::Excluded(key),
        None => Bound::Included(prefix),
    };

    let mut matching = entries
        .range::<str, _>((start, Bound::Unbounded))
        .take_while(|entry| entry.0.starts_with(prefix))
        .map(|(key, entry)| Summary {
            key: key.clone(),
            version: entry.version,
            size: entry.value.len(),
        });

    let page: Vec<Summary> = matching
        .by_ref()
        .take(limit)
        .collect();
    let more = matching.next().is_some();

    (page, more)
}
