Listing 2.44 Complete crashsim/src/main.rs. crashsim/src/main.rs

//! Command crashsim checks what the log recovers after a crash in the middle
//! of a write. It writes a log of 5 records, then damages a copy of it in
//! every way a crash or a bad disk can: it cuts the copy at every length,
//! and it flips 1 bit in every byte. After each, it opens the copy and
//! compares the records that come back with the records that were complete.
//!
//! Run it from code/ with:
//!
//!     cargo run -p crashsim

use std::env;
use std::error::Error;
use std::fs;
use std::path::Path;
use std::process;

use kv::log::FILE_NAME;
use kv::{Change, Log, Record};

/// The changes of the test log.
fn changes() -> Vec<Change> {
    let put = |key: &str, value: &str| Change::Put {
        key: key.into(),
        value: value.into(),
    };

    vec![
        put("user-1", "ada"),
        put("user-2", "grace"),
        put("user-1", "ada lovelace"),
        Change::Delete {
            key: "user-2".into(),
        },
        put("user-3", "barbara"),
    ]
}

/// Writes the changes to a log in `directory`. It returns the bytes of the
/// log and the offset at which each record ends.
fn build(directory: &Path) -> Result<(Vec<u8>, Vec<usize>), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let mut log = Log::open(directory, false)?.0;
    let mut ends = Vec::new();

    for change in changes() {
        let record = log.append(change)?;
        ends.push(ends.last().copied().unwrap_or(0) + record.encode().len());
    }

    Ok((fs::read(directory.join(FILE_NAME))?, ends))
}

/// Replaces the log in `directory` with `bytes` and opens it.
fn recover(directory: &Path, bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<Vec<Record>, Box<dyn Error>> {
    fs::write(directory.join(FILE_NAME), bytes)?;
    let recovery = Log::open(directory, false)?.1;

    Ok(recovery.records)
}

/// Whether `records` are exactly the first `count` changes, in order.
fn is_prefix(records: &[Record], count: usize) -> bool {
    let expected = changes();

    records.len() == count
        && records
            .iter()
            .zip(&expected)
            .enumerate()
            .all(|(index, (record, change))| {
                record.sequence == index as u64 + 1 && &record.change == change
            })
}

/// Cuts the log at every length and checks that recovery returns the records
/// that end at or before the cut.
fn cuts(directory: &Path, log: &[u8], ends: &[usize]) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    for length in 0..=log.len() {
        let complete = ends
            .iter()
            .filter(|&&end| end <= length)
            .count();
        let records = recover(directory, &log[..length])?;

        if !is_prefix(&records, complete) {
            return Err(format!(
                "cut at {length}: expected {complete} records, recovered {}",
                records.len()
            )
            .into());
        }
    }

    println!(
        "cut at every length from 0 to {}: each recovery returned the complete records",
        log.len()
    );

    let mut first = 0;

    for (count, &end) in ends.iter().enumerate() {
        println!("  lengths {first:3} to {:3}: {count} records", end - 1);
        first = end;
    }

    println!("  length  {first:3}       : {} records", ends.len());

    Ok(())
}

/// Flips 1 bit in each byte in turn and checks that recovery returns the
/// records before the damaged one.
fn flips(directory: &Path, log: &[u8], ends: &[usize]) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    for position in 0..log.len() {
        let mut damaged = log.to_vec();
        damaged[position] ^= 0x10;

        let before = ends
            .iter()
            .filter(|&&end| end <= position)
            .count();
        let records = recover(directory, &damaged)?;

        if !is_prefix(&records, before) {
            return Err(format!(
                "flip at {position}: expected {before} records, recovered {}",
                records.len()
            )
            .into());
        }
    }

    println!(
        "1 bit flipped in each of {} bytes: each recovery returned the records before the damage",
        log.len()
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn run(directory: &Path) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let (log, ends) = build(directory)?;
    let boundaries: Vec<String> = ends
        .iter()
        .map(usize::to_string)
        .collect();

    println!(
        "a log of {} records and {} bytes, with records ending at {}",
        ends.len(),
        log.len(),
        boundaries.join(", ")
    );

    cuts(directory, &log, &ends)?;
    flips(directory, &log, &ends)?;

    let records = recover(directory, &log[..ends[1] + 5])?;
    let mut reopened = Log::open(directory, false)?.0;
    let next = reopened.append(Change::Delete {
        key: "user-1".into(),
    })?;

    println!(
        "after a cut at {}: {} records recovered, and the next record has sequence {}",
        ends[1] + 5,
        records.len(),
        next.sequence
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let directory = env::temp_dir().join(format!("crashsim-{}", process::id()));
    let result = run(&directory);

    fs::remove_dir_all(&directory)?;

    result
}

Listing 2.45 presents the complete write versus fsync microbenchmark in synccost/src/main.rs.

Listing 2.45 Complete synccost/src/main.rs. synccost/src/main.rs

//! Command synccost measures what it costs to wait for the disk. It appends
//! the same records to 2 logs, one that calls fsync after each record and
//! one that does not, and prints the time per record.
//!
//! Run it from code/ with:
//!
//!     cargo run --release -p synccost -- /var/tmp/synccost

use std::env;
use std::error::Error;
use std::fs;
use std::path::Path;
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

use kv::{Change, Log};

const RECORDS: u32 = 500;

/// Appends `RECORDS` records of 100 bytes and returns the time it took.
fn measure(directory: &Path, sync: bool) -> Result<Duration, Box<dyn Error>> {
    let mut log = Log::open(directory, sync)?.0;
    let started = Instant::now();

    for number in 0..RECORDS {
        log.append(Change::Put {
            key: format!("key-{number:06}"),
            value: vec![b'v'; 100],
        })?;
    }

    Ok(started.elapsed())
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let root = env::args()
        .nth(1)
        .ok_or("usage: synccost <directory>")?;

    for (name, sync) in [("without fsync", false), ("with fsync", true)] {
        let directory = Path::new(&root).join(name.replace(' ', "-"));
        let elapsed = measure(&directory, sync)?;
        let each = elapsed.as_secs_f64() * 1000.0 / f64::from(RECORDS);

        println!(
            "{name:13}: {RECORDS} records in {:8.1} ms, {each:.3} ms per record, {:6.0} records per second",
            elapsed.as_secs_f64() * 1000.0,
            1000.0 / each
        );

        fs::remove_dir_all(&directory)?;
    }

    Ok(())
}

Further Reading

  • T. Pillai et al., “All File Systems Are Not Created Equal: On the Complexity of Crafting Crash-Consistent Applications”, OSDI 2014.
  • A. Rebello et al., “Can Applications Recover from fsync Failures?”, USENIX ATC 2020.
  • C. Mohan et al., “ARIES: A Transaction Recovery Method Supporting Fine-Granularity Locking and Partial Rollbacks Using Write-Ahead Logging”, ACM Transactions on Database Systems, 1992.
  • A. Petrov, Database Internals, O’Reilly, 2019.

Summary

  • A storage node maintains a BTreeMap in RAM for low-latency reads and an append-only WAL on disk for durability, confirming every write with fsync before modifying memory or acknowledging the client.
  • Append-only logging restricts crash damage exclusively to the trailing record, whereas in-place updates risk tearing previously committed values.
  • Every WAL frame begins with a 4-byte little-endian length and a 4-byte CRC-32 checksum, allowing defensive bounds-checked decoding to reject incomplete or corrupted records without panicking.
  • Startup recovery scans from offset 0, retains the valid prefix, truncates any damaged tail via set_len, and synchronizes both the log file and its parent directory.
  • On NVMe hardware, write copies into the kernel page cache in 0.003 ms, whereas write followed by fsync requires 5.4 ms (185 records/s).
  • Following any write_all or sync_data error, Log latches a fail-stop flag and rejects all further writes, avoiding the hazard of a retried fsync reporting false success after the kernel discards dirty pages.
  • A crash between fsync completion and HTTP response transmission produces a durable yet unacknowledged write, which clients resolve safely via idempotent or conditional retries.
  • Process-kill tests (SIGKILL) leave the kernel page cache intact and therefore cannot distinguish durable fsync writes from buffered --no-sync writes under power loss.

Chapter 3: Leader-Follower Quorum Replication (LLD)

The single storage node we implemented in Chapter 2 preserves every acknowledged write across process crashes and torn WAL tails. Against the permanent loss of the host itself, or of its storage device, a single node provides zero protection: a write-ahead log stored on one disk vanishes when that disk fails. Non-functional requirement 1 of Chapter 1 mandates that every acknowledged write survive the loss of any single host, disk, or availability zone. Meeting that guarantee requires persisting every mutation on at least two independent hosts before acknowledging the caller.

Copying a log file from one host to another in isolation is trivial. Replication becomes a distributed systems engineering problem because messages traverse an asynchronous network that drops, delays, and reorders both requests and replies while hosts halt and restart at arbitrary moments. Across all of those faults, every replica must converge to the exact same sequence of records in the exact same order. A follower that misses record 7 must not append record 8 on top of record 6. A leader whose acknowledgement packet was dropped must neither assume the follower lacks record 7 nor assume the follower holds it. A deposed leader returning from a network partition must be prevented from mutating followers after a successor has taken over.

In this chapter, I implement leader-follower quorum replication for a three-replica shard in Rust. A single local rule on the follower side resolves missed messages, lost acknowledgements, restarts, and empty replicas uniformly without special-case recovery branches. We first specify the Append RPC contract and replica state machine as a pure, network-free library crate (repl) so we can verify every combination of message and reply loss deterministically in replsim (4,096 fault patterns). We then build the networked storage server kvnode over gRPC (tonic) and HTTP (axum), and run live three-node fault experiments: killing a follower under load, severing quorum, destroying the leader’s disk and promoting a survivor, and testing term fencing against a returning former leader.

In this chapter, we cover

  • the Append gRPC/Protobuf contract and its last_sequence self-healing reply invariant
  • replica state separation: durable WAL records, uncommitted suffix, committed watermark, and monotonic term
  • the two-check follower handler (term fencing and exact previous_sequence continuity)
  • leader write serialization (is_settled), per-follower replication streams, and the median majority commit rule
  • exhaustive deterministic fault simulation across 4,096 message-loss and reply-loss patterns (replsim)
  • kvnode: Protobuf compilation, tonic gRPC service, lock-free network I/O, watch-channel commit notifications, and lease-bounded leader reads
  • live three-node fault experiments: follower crash and catch-up, quorum loss (503), permanent leader loss with manual promotion, and stale-term fencing (421)

3.1 Shard Topology and Replication Invariants

Each shard consists of three replicas placed across independent failure domains. One replica serves as the leader and accepts client mutations; the other two act as followers and persist ordered log batches streamed from the leader. Figure 3-1 traces the end-to-end synchronous replication write path from client ingress through local WAL durability, parallel follower replication, majority commit-index advancement, and in-memory state application.

We enforce four invariants across the replicated shard:

No.Replication InvariantArchitectural Guarantee
0Every follower’s log is an exact prefix of its leader’s log (identical records in identical sequence order, possibly shorter).Eliminates gaps, duplicates, and out-of-order entries on followers.
1The leader acknowledges a write to the client only after at least two of the three replicas hold its WAL record durably.Satisfies Chapter 1 durability (non-functional requirement 1) across any single-host or single-disk failure.
2A replica applies a record to its in-memory BTreeMap only after that record is known to reside on a majority of replicas.Prevents reads from returning uncommitted data that could disappear after a failover.
3Every replica rejects any Append RPC carrying a term strictly lower than its own local term.Fences returning former leaders so stale epochs cannot corrupt follower logs.

In this chapter, an operator appoints the initial leader and manually promotes a follower upon leader failure. In Chapter 4, we replace manual promotion with automated Raft leader election built directly onto these log and term mechanisms.

3.2 Replication Protocol Messages

The internal replication protocol requires a single RPC, Append, sent from the leader to each follower for both log shipping and periodic heartbeats. Listing 3.1 specifies the Replication service contract in proto/store.proto.

Listing 3.1 gRPC Replication service definition in proto/store.proto. proto/store.proto

// Sent by the leader of a shard to each follower.
service Replication {
  // Appends records to the follower's log. A call with no records is a
  // heartbeat: it tells the follower that the leader is alive.
  rpc Append(AppendRequest) returns (AppendResponse);
}

message AppendRequest {
  // The shard, named by the last position it owns.
  fixed64 shard = 1;
  // The term of the sender. A follower rejects a leader of an older term.
  uint64 term = 2;
  // The sequence of the record that precedes `records` in the leader's log.
  uint64 previous_sequence = 3;
  repeated Record records = 4;
  // Every record up to this sequence is on a majority of the replicas.
  uint64 committed_sequence = 5;
  // Added for leader election. The term of the record at previous_sequence,
  // and the id of the sender.
  uint64 previous_term = 6;
  uint32 leader = 7;
}

message AppendResponse {
  uint64 term = 1;
  // False when the follower's log does not end at `previous_sequence`.
  bool appended = 2;
  // The sequence of the last record in the follower's log.
  uint64 last_sequence = 3;
}

To keep our core replication logic deterministic and testable without network sockets or Protobuf runtime dependencies, we define pure Rust domain types inside the repl library crate and translate at the gRPC boundary in kvnode. Listing 3.2 declares the kv and standard-library imports of repl/src/lib.rs.

Listing 3.2 Imports of repl/src/lib.rs. repl/src/lib.rs

use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use std::io;
use std::path::Path;

use kv::{Change, Condition, Entry, Log, Record, StoreError, Summary, apply, check, page};

Listing 3.3 defines Append and AppendReply. Every request carries the leader’s term, the previous_sequence immediately preceding the attached records slice, and the leader’s current committed_sequence. Every reply returns term, a boolean appended indicator, and the follower’s exact last_sequence after processing the message.

Listing 3.3 Pure domain message types in repl/src/lib.rs. repl/src/lib.rs

/// The message a leader sends to a follower.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Append {
    /// The term of the sender.
    pub term: u64,
    /// The sequence of the record that precedes `records` in the leader's log.
    pub previous_sequence: u64,
    pub records: Vec<Record>,
    /// Every record up to this sequence is on a majority of the replicas.
    pub committed_sequence: u64,
}

/// The follower's answer.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Appended {
    pub term: u64,
    /// False when the follower's log does not end at `previous_sequence`,
    /// or when the sender's term is older than the follower's.
    pub appended: bool,
    /// The sequence of the last record in the follower's log.
    pub last_sequence: u64,
}
FieldContract and Semantics
termMonotonic leadership epoch; followers reject any request with request.term < local.term.
previous_sequenceLeader log index immediately before records[0]; followers append only when their own log ends at this exact index.
recordsContiguous suffix of records missing from the follower, or an empty slice for a heartbeat.
committed_sequenceHighest sequence number known by the leader to reside on a majority; followers advance their local BTreeMap up to this bound.
appendedtrue if both term and prefix checks passed; false on any refusal.
last_sequenceExact end index of the follower’s WAL after handling the RPC, reported on both acceptance and refusal.

Reporting last_sequence unconditionally on every reply is the linchpin of the protocol. Rather than answering with a bare boolean rejection, the follower tells the leader its exact durable log frontier, allowing the leader to realign its per-follower cursor in one round trip.

3.3 Replica State Machine

A Replica combines its durable WAL (Log), an in-memory vector mirroring all WAL records (records, where sequence n resides at index n - 1), the BTreeMap<String, Entry> reflecting committed state, and two control integers: committed (the highest applied sequence) and term (the highest epoch observed). Figure 3-2 illustrates the separation between the committed prefix (1 to 7) and the uncommitted tail (8 and 9).

A record becomes committed once a majority of replicas (2 of 3) have persisted it to disk. Any two of three replicas share at least one overlapping member, so a committed record survives the failure of any single host. Keeping uncommitted tail records in the WAL without applying them to entries enforces invariant 2: no read can observe a mutation that might vanish after a failover. Figure 3-3 maps each data structure inside Replica to the methods that move data between disk, log buffer, and committed index.

Listing 3.4 implements Replica, Replica::open, commit, and the read methods (get, list). Because commit is the sole caller of kv::store::apply, no uncommitted record can leak into entries. Notice that Replica::open intentionally initializes committed to 0 and leaves entries empty even when kv.log already holds records. Upon restart, a single replica cannot determine from its local disk alone which suffix of its log reached a majority before the crash. A follower learns the committed frontier from its leader’s next Append RPC; a leader re-establishes the committed frontier once followers report their last_sequence values.

Listing 3.4 Replica state machine and committed-only state application in repl/src/lib.rs. repl/src/lib.rs

pub struct Replica {
    log: Log,
    /// Every record of the log, in order. Record `n` is at index `n - 1`.
    records: Vec<Record>,
    /// The result of applying the records up to `committed`.
    entries: BTreeMap<String, Entry>,
    /// The sequence of the last record that is applied to `entries`.
    committed: u64,
    term: u64,
}

impl Replica {
    /// Opens the replica in `directory`. Nothing is applied yet: a replica
    /// that has restarted does not know which of its records are committed.
    pub fn open(directory: &Path, sync: bool, term: u64) -> io::Result<Replica> {
        let (log, recovery) = Log::open(directory, sync)?;

        Ok(Replica {
            log,
            records: recovery.records,
            entries: BTreeMap::new(),
            committed: 0,
            term,
        })
    }

    pub fn term(&self) -> u64 {
        self.term
    }

    pub fn last_sequence(&self) -> u64 {
        self.records.len() as u64
    }

    pub fn committed(&self) -> u64 {
        self.committed
    }

    /// One page of the committed keys.
    pub fn list(&self, prefix: &str, after: Option<&str>, limit: usize) -> (Vec<Summary>, bool) {
        page(&self.entries, prefix, after, limit)
    }

    /// Every record of the log, in order.
    pub fn records(&self) -> &[Record] {
        &self.records
    }

    /// The committed value of a key.
    pub fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<&Entry> {
        self.entries.get(key)
    }

    /// Applies the records up to `sequence` that are not applied yet.
    pub fn commit(&mut self, sequence: u64) {
        let until = sequence.min(self.last_sequence());

        while self.committed < until {
            apply(
                &mut self.entries,
                self.records[self.committed as usize].clone(),
            );
            self.committed += 1;
        }
    }
}

3.4 Follower Rules and Self-Healing Catch-Up

A follower evaluates every incoming Append message against exactly two sequential preconditions (Figure 3-4):

Precondition CheckOutcome on Failure / MatchFollower State ActionReply Returned
msg.term < self.termStale leader detectedNoneappended = false, term = self.term, last_sequence
msg.previous_sequence != self.last_sequence()Log frontier mismatchAdopt msg.termappended = false, term = self.term, last_sequence
Both checks passExact continuationAdopt msg.term, append_records with one fsync, commit(msg.committed_sequence)appended = true, term = self.term, updated last_sequence

Listing 3.5 implements Replica::handle_append. Both refusal paths share the refuse closure, returning the follower’s current term and last_sequence. When both checks pass, Log::append_records writes the entire batch with a single sync_data call, appends the records to self.records, and invokes self.commit(msg.committed_sequence) (which safely clamps to self.last_sequence() if the leader’s commit watermark exceeds this follower’s log length).

Listing 3.5 Follower handle_append validation and batch persistence in repl/src/lib.rs. repl/src/lib.rs

impl Replica {
    /// Processes a message from a leader.
    pub fn handle_append(&mut self, request: Append) -> io::Result<Appended> {
        let refuse = |replica: &Replica| Appended {
            term: replica.term,
            appended: false,
            last_sequence: replica.last_sequence(),
        };

        if request.term < self.term {
            return Ok(refuse(self));
        }

        self.term = request.term;

        if request.previous_sequence != self.last_sequence() {
            return Ok(refuse(self));
        }

        if !request.records.is_empty() {
            self.log
                .append_records(&request.records)?;
            self.records.extend(request.records);
        }

        self.commit(request.committed_sequence);

        Ok(Appended {
            term: self.term,
            appended: true,
            last_sequence: self.last_sequence(),
        })
    }
}

This single exact-continuation check preserves invariant 0 across every network and crash anomaly: restarted followers, dropped requests, dropped replies, and brand-new empty replicas. None requires bespoke recovery logic; all reduce to a single mismatch where the follower reports its actual last_sequence and the leader resends the missing suffix from that exact index. Figure 3-5 contrasts this clean stale-follower catch-up (Mode A) against the split-brain hazard that arises if an operator or uncoordinated failover promotes a second leader without consensus term fencing (Mode B).

Follower batch persistence builds directly on kv::log from Chapter 2. Listing 3.6 recalls the imports of kv/src/log.rs, and Listing 3.7 defines Log::append_records, which verifies contiguous incoming sequence numbering, encodes every record in the batch into the file, calls sync_data once for the entire batch, and enforces the same fail-stop latch (self.failed = true) on any I/O error.

Listing 3.6 Imports of kv/src/log.rs. kv/src/log.rs

use std::fs::{self, File, OpenOptions};
use std::io::{self, Read, Write};
use std::path::Path;

use crate::record::{Change, Decoded, Record};

Listing 3.7 Batched follower record persistence in kv/src/log.rs. kv/src/log.rs

impl Log {
    /// Appends records that another node numbered, in one write and with one
    /// wait for the disk. The first record must follow the last record of
    /// this log.
    pub fn append_records(&mut self, records: &[Record]) -> io::Result<()> {
        if self.failed {
            return Err(io::Error::other(
                "the log failed on an earlier write and is closed",
            ));
        }

        let misplaced = (self.next..)
            .zip(records)
            .find(|(expected, record)| record.sequence != *expected);

        if let Some((expected, record)) = misplaced {
            return Err(io::Error::other(format!(
                "record {} cannot follow record {}",
                record.sequence,
                expected - 1
            )));
        }

        let bytes: Vec<u8> = records
            .iter()
            .flat_map(Record::encode)
            .collect();

        if let Err(error) = self.write(&bytes) {
            self.failed = true;

            return Err(error);
        }

        self.next += records.len() as u64;

        Ok(())
    }
}

3.5 Leader Proposal, Dispatch, and Majority Commit Rule

The leader orchestrates three responsibilities: validating and appending local proposals, constructing per-follower catch-up or heartbeat messages, and advancing the global commit watermark whenever a majority confirms a sequence number.

Proposing a Record (propose)

Because conditional writes (If-Match and If-None-Match) evaluate their version preconditions against self.entries, and self.entries contains only committed records, the leader accepts a new write only when self.is_settled() holds (every record in the leader’s local WAL is already committed). Accepting a second write while an earlier record remained uncommitted would evaluate the second precondition against stale state, violating linearizability for conditional updates. Listing 3.8 enforces this contract: propose verifies is_settled, rejects Delete on absent keys, validates Condition via kv::store::check, appends the record to the leader’s local WAL, and pushes it onto self.records without mutating self.entries.

Listing 3.8 Leader proposal validation and local WAL append in repl/src/lib.rs. repl/src/lib.rs

impl Replica {
    /// Whether every record of the log is committed. A leader accepts a new
    /// write only in this state, so that the condition of the write is
    /// checked against the result of all earlier writes.
    pub fn is_settled(&self) -> bool {
        self.committed == self.last_sequence()
    }

    /// Checks the condition of a write and appends its record to the
    /// leader's log. The record is not applied: it is not committed yet.
    pub fn propose(&mut self, change: Change, condition: Condition) -> Result<u64, StoreError> {
        let key = match &change {
            Change::Put { key, .. } | Change::Delete { key } => key,
        };
        let current = self
            .entries
            .get(key)
            .map(|entry| entry.version);

        if matches!(change, Change::Delete { .. }) && current.is_none() {
            return Err(StoreError::NotFound);
        }

        check(condition, current)?;

        let record = self.log.append(change)?;
        let sequence = record.sequence;
        self.records.push(record);

        Ok(sequence)
    }
}

Serializing writes until settled restricts a single shard to one unbatched commit per replication round trip. Production systems can evaluate preconditions against speculative uncommitted tails; in Chapter 6, we recover high write throughput cleanly via WAL group commit.

Constructing Follower Messages (append_for)

For each follower, the leader maintains its last reported sequence number (after). Listing 3.9 implements append_for, slicing every record after after into an Append request (yielding an empty records vector for heartbeats when the follower is caught up) and clamping after to self.last_sequence() in case a newly started leader holds a shorter log than a stale hint.

Listing 3.9 Constructing incremental replication and heartbeat messages in repl/src/lib.rs. repl/src/lib.rs

impl Replica {
    /// The message that brings a follower whose log ends at `follower_last`
    /// up to the end of this log. With nothing to send it is a heartbeat.
    pub fn append_for(&self, follower_last: u64) -> Append {
        let from = follower_last.min(self.last_sequence()) as usize;

        Append {
            term: self.term,
            previous_sequence: from as u64,
            records: self.records[from..].to_vec(),
            committed_sequence: self.committed,
        }
    }
}

The Majority Commit Rule (majority_sequence)

Given the leader’s own last_sequence and each follower’s reported last_sequence, sorting all replica frontier indices in descending order places the highest majority-replicated sequence at index n / 2 (Figure 3-6). For a three-replica shard with frontiers [10, 7, 9], descending sort yields [10, 9, 7], and index 3 / 2 = 1 selects 9: at least two replicas hold records 1 through 9, whereas record 10 resides on only one replica and stays uncommitted.

Listing 3.10 implements majority_sequence generically for any odd or even cluster size n.

Listing 3.10 Generalized majority commit calculation in repl/src/lib.rs. repl/src/lib.rs

/// The highest sequence that is stored on a majority, given the last
/// sequence of every replica, the leader included.
pub fn majority_sequence(mut last_sequences: Vec<u64>) -> u64 {
    last_sequences.sort_unstable_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a));

    last_sequences
        .get(last_sequences.len() / 2)
        .copied()
        .unwrap_or(0)
}

3.6 Exhaustive Deterministic Fault Simulation (replsim)

Real network faults occur unpredictably and rarely reproduce on demand. Because repl performs zero network I/O, we can embed a three-node cluster inside a single deterministic simulator (replsim) that controls the fate of every RPC exchange: delivered cleanly, request dropped, or request persisted on the follower while its reply is dropped.

Listing 3.11 declares the imports for replsim/src/main.rs.

Listing 3.11 Imports of replsim/src/main.rs. replsim/src/main.rs

use std::env;
use std::error::Error;
use std::fs;
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
use std::process;

Listing 3.12 defines the in-process Cluster harness with one leader, two followers, per-follower cursor tracking, and a three-way fault injector (Delivery::Ok, DropRequest, DropReply).

Listing 3.12 Single-process deterministic cluster harness in replsim/src/main.rs. replsim/src/main.rs

/// What happens to one exchange between the leader and a follower.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum Fate {
    Delivered,
    /// The follower does not receive the message.
    RequestLost,
    /// The follower processes the message, and its answer does not arrive.
    AnswerLost,
}

/// A leader, 2 followers, and what the leader knows about each follower.
struct Cluster {
    leader: Replica,
    followers: Vec<Replica>,
    /// The last sequence each follower has reported.
    reported: Vec<u64>,
}

impl Cluster {
    fn open(root: &Path) -> Result<Cluster, Box<dyn Error>> {
        let open = |name: &str| Replica::open(&root.join(name), false, 1);

        Ok(Cluster {
            leader: open("leader")?,
            followers: vec![open("follower-1")?, open("follower-2")?],
            reported: vec![0, 0],
        })
    }

    /// One exchange with a follower: the leader sends what the follower
    /// lacks, as far as it knows, and commits what a majority now holds.
    fn exchange(&mut self, follower: usize, fate: Fate) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
        let message = self
            .leader
            .append_for(self.reported[follower]);

        if fate == Fate::RequestLost {
            return Ok(());
        }

        let answer = self.followers[follower].handle_append(message)?;

        if fate == Fate::AnswerLost {
            return Ok(());
        }

        self.reported[follower] = answer.last_sequence;

        let stored = vec![
            self.leader.last_sequence(),
            self.reported[0],
            self.reported[1],
        ];
        self.leader
            .commit(majority_sequence(stored));

        Ok(())
    }

    /// A write: the leader appends the record and makes one exchange with
    /// each follower. It returns whether the write was acknowledged, or
    /// `None` when the leader could not accept it.
    fn write(
        &mut self,
        key: &str,
        value: &str,
        fates: [Fate; 2],
    ) -> Result<Option<bool>, Box<dyn Error>> {
        if !self.leader.is_settled() {
            return Ok(None);
        }

        let change = Change::Put {
            key: key.into(),
            value: value.into(),
        };
        let sequence = self
            .leader
            .propose(change, Condition::Always)?;

        self.exchange(0, fates[0])?;
        self.exchange(1, fates[1])?;

        Ok(Some(self.leader.committed() >= sequence))
    }

    /// The last sequence of the leader and of each follower.
    fn lasts(&self) -> [u64; 3] {
        [
            self.leader.last_sequence(),
            self.followers[0].last_sequence(),
            self.followers[1].last_sequence(),
        ]
    }
}

Listing 3.13 executes targeted scenarios exercising steady-state replication, single-follower outage and one-round-trip catch-up, dropped replies followed by exact-continuation realignment, total quorum loss with deferred commit upon recovery, and stale-term rejection.

Listing 3.13 Scenario verification suite in replsim/src/main.rs. replsim/src/main.rs

const BOTH: [Fate; 2] = [Fate::Delivered, Fate::Delivered];

fn cases(root: &Path) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let mut cluster = Cluster::open(root)?;
    let show = |cluster: &Cluster| {
        format!(
            "logs end at {:?}, committed {}",
            cluster.lasts(),
            cluster.leader.committed()
        )
    };

    for key in ["a", "b", "c"] {
        cluster.write(key, "1", BOTH)?;
    }

    println!("3 writes, every message delivered: {}", show(&cluster));

    for key in ["d", "e", "f"] {
        cluster.write(key, "1", [Fate::RequestLost, Fate::Delivered])?;
    }

    println!(
        "3 writes while follower 1 is unreachable: {}",
        show(&cluster)
    );

    cluster.exchange(0, Fate::Delivered)?;
    println!("follower 1 returns, 1 exchange: {}", show(&cluster));

    for key in ["g", "h", "i"] {
        cluster.write(key, "1", [Fate::AnswerLost, Fate::Delivered])?;
    }

    println!(
        "3 writes while the answers of follower 1 are lost: {}",
        show(&cluster)
    );
    println!(
        "  the leader believes that the log of follower 1 ends at {}",
        cluster.reported[0]
    );

    cluster.exchange(0, Fate::Delivered)?;
    println!(
        "  next exchange: the leader sends records 7 to 9, follower 1 refuses and reports {}",
        cluster.reported[0]
    );

    cluster.exchange(0, Fate::Delivered)?;
    println!("  the exchange after it: {}", show(&cluster));

    let acknowledged =
        cluster.write("j", "1", [Fate::RequestLost, Fate::RequestLost])? == Some(true);
    println!(
        "1 write while both followers are unreachable: acknowledged {acknowledged}, {}",
        show(&cluster)
    );
    println!(
        "  the leader reads j as {:?}",
        cluster
            .leader
            .get("j")
            .map(|entry| entry.version)
    );

    let accepted = cluster
        .write("k", "1", [Fate::RequestLost, Fate::RequestLost])?
        .is_some();
    println!("  the leader accepts another write: {accepted}");

    cluster.exchange(1, Fate::Delivered)?;
    println!("follower 2 returns: {}", show(&cluster));
    println!(
        "  the leader reads j as {:?}",
        cluster
            .leader
            .get("j")
            .map(|entry| entry.version)
    );

    let mut newer = Replica::open(&root.join("newer"), false, 2)?;
    let answer = newer.handle_append(cluster.leader.append_for(0))?;
    println!(
        "a replica at term 2 receives a message of term 1: appended {}, its term {}",
        answer.appended, answer.term
    );

    Ok(())
}

Listing 3.14 runs an exhaustive sweep over three sequential writes: each write triggers two follower exchanges, and each of the six exchanges chooses from four 2-bit fault encodings, covering all 4^6 = 4,096 patterns. After every single pattern, the harness asserts invariant 0 (every follower log is a prefix of the leader log) and invariant 1 (every acknowledged record exists on at least two replicas), then heals the network and asserts full three-way log equality.

Listing 3.14 Exhaustive 4,096-pattern fault sweep in replsim/src/main.rs. replsim/src/main.rs

const WRITES: usize = 3;

/// The fate of exchange number `index` under a pattern: 2 bits for each.
fn fate(pattern: u32, index: usize) -> Fate {
    match (pattern >> (2 * index)) & 3 {
        0 | 1 => Fate::Delivered,
        2 => Fate::RequestLost,
        3.. => Fate::AnswerLost,
    }
}

/// Runs 3 writes under one pattern of losses and checks the replicas. It
/// returns the number of writes that were acknowledged.
fn run(root: &Path, pattern: u32) -> Result<usize, Box<dyn Error>> {
    let mut cluster = Cluster::open(root)?;
    let mut acknowledged = Vec::new();

    for number in 0..WRITES {
        let fates = [fate(pattern, 2 * number), fate(pattern, 2 * number + 1)];

        if cluster.write(&format!("key-{number}"), "1", fates)? == Some(true) {
            acknowledged.push(cluster.leader.last_sequence());
        }
    }

    for &sequence in &acknowledged {
        let holders = cluster
            .lasts()
            .iter()
            .filter(|&&last| last >= sequence)
            .count();

        if holders < 2 {
            return Err(format!(
                "pattern {pattern}: record {sequence} was acknowledged and is in {holders} log"
            )
            .into());
        }
    }

    for follower in &cluster.followers {
        if !cluster
            .leader
            .records()
            .starts_with(follower.records())
        {
            return Err(format!(
                "pattern {pattern}: a follower's log is not the beginning of the leader's"
            )
            .into());
        }
    }

    for _ in 0..2 {
        cluster.exchange(0, Fate::Delivered)?;
        cluster.exchange(1, Fate::Delivered)?;
    }

    let [leader, first, second] = cluster.lasts();

    if first != leader || second != leader || !cluster.leader.is_settled() {
        return Err(format!(
            "pattern {pattern}: the logs differ after every message was delivered"
        )
        .into());
    }

    Ok(acknowledged.len())
}

fn exhaustive(root: &Path) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let patterns = 1u32 << (4 * WRITES);
    let mut by_acknowledged = [0; WRITES + 1];

    for pattern in 0..patterns {
        let directory = root.join(format!("pattern-{pattern}"));
        by_acknowledged[run(&directory, pattern)?] += 1;
        fs::remove_dir_all(&directory)?;
    }

    println!("{patterns} patterns of lost messages over {WRITES} writes:");
    println!("  every acknowledged record was in at least 2 of the 3 logs");
    println!("  every follower's log was the beginning of the leader's log");
    println!("  after the losses stopped, the 3 logs were equal and every record was committed");

    for (count, patterns) in by_acknowledged.iter().enumerate() {
        println!("  {count} of {WRITES} writes acknowledged: {patterns} patterns");
    }

    Ok(())
}

Listing 3.15 invokes both the targeted scenarios and the exhaustive 4,096-pattern verification from main.

Listing 3.15 Entry point of replsim/src/main.rs. replsim/src/main.rs

fn directory() -> PathBuf {
    env::temp_dir().join(format!("replsim-{}", process::id()))
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let root = directory();
    let result = cases(&root.join("cases")).and_then(|()| exhaustive(&root));

    fs::remove_dir_all(&root)?;

    result
}

Observed OutputVerified Protocol Behavior
3 writes while follower 1 is unreachable: logs end at [6, 3, 6], committed 6Leader plus one surviving follower maintain write availability under invariant 1.
follower 1 returns, 1 exchange: logs end at [6, 6, 6]Leader ships records 4 to 6 in a single batch based on its stored follower frontier.
next exchange: the leader sends records 7 to 9, follower 1 refuses and reports 7Exact-continuation check rejects duplicate record 7 and realigns the leader cursor in one round trip.
1 write while both followers are unreachable: acknowledged false, committed 9Single-replica record 10 stays uncommitted and invisible to reads (j reads as None).
follower 2 returns: logs end at [10, 9, 10], committed 10Uncommitted record 10 commits automatically upon quorum restoration even though the original caller received an error.

4096 patterns of lost messages over 3 writesInvariants 0 and 1 hold across every possible loss permutation, and all three replicas converge once delivery resumes.

Notice the operational consequence of record 10: a write that returned an error during quorum loss remained in the leader’s WAL and committed later when a follower reconnected. Consequently, clients of a replicated store must treat a 503 timeout as an indeterminate outcome, identical to a dropped TCP connection, and resolve it via read-after-error or idempotent conditional retry.

3.7 Low-Level Architecture of kvnode

Having verified the pure state machine in repl, we wrap it in a networked server binary kvnode that pairs an external HTTP API (axum) with an internal gRPC replication service (tonic).

Low-level design: replication

Crates

CrateKindResponsibilities
repllibraryPure domain messages, Replica, follower handler, leader propose/append_for, and majority_sequence
replsimbinaryDeterministic fault simulator covering targeted anomalies and 4,096 exhaustive loss patterns
kvnodebinaryNetworked replica combining rpc (gRPC service), node (leader replication tasks, write/read coordination), and main (HTTP API)

Shared Node State (kvnode::node::Node)

FieldTypeResponsibility
replicaMutex<Replica>Synchronizes access to the WAL, in-memory log vector, committed BTreeMap, and term
peersVec<Peer>Tracks each follower’s gRPC endpoint, last reported sequence, and last contact timestamp
turntokio::sync::Mutex<()>Serializes concurrent client writes so each evaluates preconditions against a settled log
committedwatch::Sender<u64>Broadcasts commit-index advances to wake awaiting HTTP write handlers
appendedNotifySignals per-follower replication tasks immediately after a local WAL append
deposedAtomicBoolLatched when any follower replies with a strictly higher term, halting stale leader writes

Timing Constants

ConstantValueRole
HEARTBEAT100 msIdle interval between empty heartbeat RPCs to each follower
ANSWER500 msPer-RPC deadline waiting for a single follower’s Append reply
COMMIT1 sClient write quorum timeout and maximum lease window for serving leader reads

HTTP Error Semantics

Runtime ConditionHTTP Status
Client sends PUT, DELETE, or GET to a follower421 Misdirected Request
Client writes to a leader deposed by a higher-term reply421 Misdirected Request
Proposed record fails to reach a majority within 1 s503 Service Unavailable
Client reads from a leader without majority contact in the past 1 s503 Service Unavailable

Listing 3.21 implements bidirectional conversion between generated Protobuf structs and kv/repl domain types. Any wire Record missing its oneof change payload is rejected immediately with Status::invalid_argument.

Listing 3.21 Wire-to-domain conversions in kvnode/src/rpc.rs. kvnode/src/rpc.rs

impl From<&Record> for proto::Record {
    fn from(record: &Record) -> Self {
        let change = match record.change.clone() {
            Change::Put { key, value } => proto::record::Change::Put(proto::Put { key, value }),
            Change::Delete { key } => proto::record::Change::Delete(proto::Delete { key }),
        };

        proto::Record {
            sequence: record.sequence,
            change: Some(change),
        }
    }
}

impl TryFrom<proto::Record> for Record {
    type Error = Status;

    fn try_from(record: proto::Record) -> Result<Self, Status> {
        let change = match record.change {
            Some(proto::record::Change::Put(put)) => Change::Put {
                key: put.key,
                value: put.value,
            },
            Some(proto::record::Change::Delete(delete)) => Change::Delete { key: delete.key },
            None => return Err(Status::invalid_argument("a record without a change")),
        };

        Ok(Record {
            sequence: record.sequence,
            change,
        })
    }
}

impl From<Append> for proto::AppendRequest {
    fn from(message: Append) -> Self {
        proto::AppendRequest {
            shard: 0,
            term: message.term,
            previous_sequence: message.previous_sequence,
            records: message
                .records
                .iter()
                .map(proto::Record::from)
                .collect(),
            committed_sequence: message.committed_sequence,
            // The fields that leader election added are not used by this program.
            previous_term: 0,
            leader: 0,
        }
    }
}

impl From<proto::AppendResponse> for Appended {
    fn from(answer: proto::AppendResponse) -> Self {
        Appended {
            term: answer.term,
            appended: answer.appended,
            last_sequence: answer.last_sequence,
        }
    }
}

Listing 3.22 implements the follower-side Replication gRPC server. Because Replica::handle_append executes synchronous WAL fsync, the handler wraps the critical section inside tokio::task::block_in_place so Tokio can migrate sibling async tasks off the blocking worker thread.

Listing 3.22 Follower-side Append gRPC handler in kvnode/src/rpc.rs. kvnode/src/rpc.rs

/// The server side of `Append`, which a follower runs.
pub struct Follower {
    pub node: Arc<Node>,
}

#[tonic::async_trait]
impl Replication for Follower {
    async fn append(
        &self,
        request: Request<proto::AppendRequest>,
    ) -> Result<Response<proto::AppendResponse>, Status> {
        let request = request.into_inner();
        let records = request
            .records
            .into_iter()
            .map(Record::try_from)
            .collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>()?;

        let message = Append {
            term: request.term,
            previous_sequence: request.previous_sequence,
            records,
            committed_sequence: request.committed_sequence,
        };

        // Appending waits for the disk, so it runs where blocking is allowed.
        let answer = task::block_in_place(|| {
            self.node
                .replica
                .lock()
                .handle_append(message)
        })
        .map_err(|error| Status::unavailable(error.to_string()))?;

        Ok(Response::new(proto::AppendResponse {
            term: answer.term,
            appended: answer.appended,
            last_sequence: answer.last_sequence,
        }))
    }
}

Leader Replication Tasks and Lock-Free Network I/O (kvnode/src/node.rs)

Figure 3-7 traces the internal concurrency structure of a leader node: HTTP write handlers serialize on turn, append locally via propose, wake per-follower background tasks via appended, and await commit advancement on the committed watch channel.

Listing 3.23 imports the async primitives and RPC helpers in kvnode/src/node.rs, and Listing 3.24 defines Role, Peer, Node, and NodeError.

use std::sync::Arc;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, AtomicU64, Ordering};
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

use kv::{Change, Condition, Entry, Summary, Written};
use kvd::api::ApiError;
use parking_lot::Mutex;
use repl::{Appended, Replica, majority_sequence};
use tokio::sync::{Notify, watch};
use tokio::task;
use tokio::time::{sleep, timeout};
use tonic::transport::{Channel, Endpoint};

use crate::rpc::{ReplicationClient, proto};

Listing 3.24 Node role, peer tracking, and shared concurrency state in kvnode/src/node.rs. kvnode/src/node.rs

/// How often a leader sends a message to a follower that has nothing new to receive.
const HEARTBEAT: Duration = Duration::from_millis(100);

/// How long a leader waits for the answer to one message.
const ANSWER: Duration = Duration::from_millis(500);

/// How long a write waits for its record to reach a majority.
const COMMIT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(1);

/// What the leader knows about one follower.
pub struct Peer {
    pub address: String,
    /// The last sequence the follower has reported.
    reported: AtomicU64,
    /// When the follower last answered.
    heard: Mutex<Option<Instant>>,
}

pub struct Node {
    pub replica: Mutex<Replica>,
    pub leader: bool,
    pub peers: Vec<Peer>,
    /// The sequence the log ended at when the node started. A leader serves
    /// reads once this much is committed.
    ready: u64,
    /// Held by the write that is in progress, so that writes take turns.
    turn: tokio::sync::Mutex<()>,
    /// The committed sequence, for writes that wait for it to advance.
    committed: watch::Sender<u64>,
    /// Signalled when the leader has appended a record.
    appended: Notify,
    /// Set when a follower answers with a newer term: another leader exists.
    deposed: AtomicBool,
}

impl Node {
    pub fn new(replica: Replica, leader: bool, followers: Vec<String>) -> Arc<Node> {
        let peer = |address| Peer {
            address,
            reported: AtomicU64::new(0),
            heard: Mutex::new(None),
        };

        Arc::new(Node {
            ready: replica.last_sequence(),
            replica: Mutex::new(replica),
            leader,
            peers: followers
                .into_iter()
                .map(peer)
                .collect(),
            turn: tokio::sync::Mutex::new(()),
            committed: watch::Sender::new(0),
            appended: Notify::new(),
            deposed: AtomicBool::new(false),
        })
    }
}

The leader spawns one dedicated follow task per follower (Listing 3.25). Each loop iteration follows a strict three-phase lock discipline:

  1. Acquire replica briefly to build the next Append request via append_for and immediately release the mutex.
  2. Issue the gRPC Append call over the network with a 500 ms timeout while holding zero locks.
  3. Pass the reply to record; if the follower still lags behind the leader’s WAL, loop immediately without sleeping, otherwise await either an appended wakeup or the 100 ms HEARTBEAT timer.

Releasing the mutex prior to network I/O is critical for fault isolation: a partitioned or hung follower stalls only its own task while the surviving follower continues committing writes at full speed.

Listing 3.25 Per-follower background replication loop in kvnode/src/node.rs. kvnode/src/node.rs

impl Node {
    /// Starts one task for each follower. A task sends the follower what it
    /// lacks, again and again, for as long as the node runs.
    pub fn lead(self: &Arc<Node>) -> Result<(), tonic::transport::Error> {
        for index in 0..self.peers.len() {
            let channel = Endpoint::from_shared(self.peers[index].address.clone())?
                .connect_timeout(ANSWER)
                .connect_lazy();

            tokio::spawn(Arc::clone(self).follow(index, ReplicationClient::new(channel)));
        }

        Ok(())
    }

    async fn follow(self: Arc<Node>, index: usize, mut client: ReplicationClient<Channel>) {
        let peer = &self.peers[index];

        loop {
            let message = self.replica.lock().append_for(
                peer.reported
                    .load(Ordering::Relaxed),
            );
            let request = proto::AppendRequest::from(message);

            let answer = timeout(ANSWER, client.append(request)).await;

            // An answer that did not come counts as a peer that is up to date:
            // the next round is a heartbeat, which finds out more.
            let behind = answer
                .ok()
                .and_then(Result::ok)
                .is_some_and(|answer| self.record(peer, answer.into_inner().into()));

            if !behind {
                // Wait for a new record, or send a heartbeat when none comes.
                tokio::select! {
                    () = self.appended.notified() => {}
                    () = sleep(HEARTBEAT) => {}
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

Listing 3.26 implements record. If a follower replies with reply.term > local.term, the leader immediately latches deposed = true so subsequent client writes receive 421 Misdirected Request. Otherwise, record updates the peer’s last_sequence and contact timestamp, recomputes majority_sequence, calls replica.commit, and publishes the new watermark on the committed watch channel.

Listing 3.26 Recording follower replies, term fencing, and advancing the commit watermark in kvnode/src/node.rs. kvnode/src/node.rs

impl Node {
    /// Takes note of a follower's answer and commits what a majority now
    /// holds. It returns whether the follower still lacks records.
    fn record(&self, peer: &Peer, answer: Appended) -> bool {
        let mut replica = self.replica.lock();

        if answer.term > replica.term() {
            self.deposed
                .store(true, Ordering::Relaxed);

            return false;
        }

        peer.reported
            .store(answer.last_sequence, Ordering::Relaxed);
        *peer.heard.lock() = Some(Instant::now());

        let mut stored: Vec<u64> = self
            .peers
            .iter()
            .map(|peer| {
                peer.reported
                    .load(Ordering::Relaxed)
            })
            .collect();
        stored.push(replica.last_sequence());

        replica.commit(majority_sequence(stored));
        self.committed
            .send_replace(replica.committed());

        answer.last_sequence < replica.last_sequence()
    }
}

Leader Write and Lease-Bounded Read Paths

Listing 3.27 implements Node::write. An HTTP handler acquires the async turn mutex, verifies leadership (!deposed), waits if necessary for any prior uncommitted record to settle, invokes Replica::propose via block_in_place, notifies all follower tasks (appended.notify_waiters()), and waits up to COMMIT (1 s) on committed.wait_for(|&c| c >= seq). If quorum does not confirm within 1 s, the handler returns 503 Service Unavailable; the record remains in the leader’s WAL and commits automatically once a follower reconnects.

Listing 3.27 Leader write coordination in kvnode/src/node.rs. kvnode/src/node.rs

impl Node {
    /// A write on the leader: wait for a turn, append the record, and wait
    /// until a majority of the replicas hold it.
    pub async fn write(&self, change: Change, condition: Condition) -> Result<Written, ApiError> {
        self.must_lead()?;

        let turn = self.turn.lock().await;
        let last = self.replica.lock().last_sequence();
        self.wait_for(last).await?;

        let proposed = task::block_in_place(|| {
            let mut replica = self.replica.lock();
            let created = match &change {
                Change::Put { key, .. } | Change::Delete { key } => replica.get(key).is_none(),
            };

            replica
                .propose(change, condition)
                .map(|version| Written { version, created })
        })?;

        self.appended.notify_waiters();
        self.wait_for(proposed.version)
            .await?;
        drop(turn);

        Ok(proposed)
    }

    /// Waits until the record with this sequence is committed.
    async fn wait_for(&self, sequence: u64) -> Result<(), ApiError> {
        let mut committed = self.committed.subscribe();

        let reached = committed.wait_for(|&committed| committed >= sequence);
        let in_time = timeout(COMMIT, reached)
            .await
            .is_ok_and(|reached| reached.is_ok());

        if in_time {
            Ok(())
        } else {
            Err(ApiError::Unavailable(format!(
                "record {sequence} is not on a majority of the replicas"
            )))
        }
    }

    fn must_lead(&self) -> Result<(), ApiError> {
        if !self.leader {
            return Err(ApiError::Misdirected("this node is a follower".into()));
        }

        if self.deposed.load(Ordering::Relaxed) {
            return Err(ApiError::Misdirected(
                "a leader of a newer term exists".into(),
            ));
        }

        Ok(())
    }
}

Listing 3.28 implements Node::get, Node::list, and the must_serve_reads guard. An isolated leader partitioned from both followers cannot detect whether an operator or election has appointed a newer leader. must_serve_reads therefore requires two conditions before serving reads from RAM: (1) a majority of replicas (the leader plus at least one follower) responded within the last COMMIT (1 s) window, and (2) the leader’s startup log has fully settled (committed >= initial_last_sequence) so a restarted leader never returns stale empty responses before re-establishing its commit watermark. Bounding stale-read exposure to 1 s assumes no successor leader is promoted sooner than 1 s after the old leader loses contact; stricter linearizable reads (ReadIndex) confirm quorum on every read at the cost of one network round trip.

Listing 3.28 Leader read path and quorum-contact guard in kvnode/src/node.rs. kvnode/src/node.rs

impl Node {
    /// A leader serves reads while a majority of the replicas, itself
    /// included, has answered within the last second, and once everything
    /// its log held at start is committed.
    fn must_serve_reads(&self) -> Result<(), ApiError> {
        self.must_lead()?;

        let recently = |peer: &&Peer| {
            peer.heard
                .lock()
                .is_some_and(|at| at.elapsed() < COMMIT)
        };
        let reachable = 1 + self
            .peers
            .iter()
            .filter(recently)
            .count();

        if 2 * reachable <= self.peers.len() + 1 {
            return Err(ApiError::Unavailable(
                "this leader cannot reach a majority of the replicas".into(),
            ));
        }

        if self.replica.lock().committed() < self.ready {
            return Err(ApiError::Unavailable(
                "the records from before the restart are not committed yet".into(),
            ));
        }

        Ok(())
    }

    pub fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Result<Entry, ApiError> {
        self.must_serve_reads()?;

        self.replica
            .lock()
            .get(key)
            .cloned()
            .ok_or(ApiError::NotFound)
    }

    pub fn list(
        &self,
        prefix: &str,
        after: Option<&str>,
        limit: usize,
    ) -> Result<(Vec<Summary>, bool), ApiError> {
        self.must_serve_reads()?;

        Ok(self
            .replica
            .lock()
            .list(prefix, after, limit))
    }

    /// The last sequence each follower has reported.
    pub fn reported(&self) -> Vec<u64> {
        self.peers
            .iter()
            .map(|peer| {
                peer.reported
                    .load(Ordering::Relaxed)
            })
            .collect()
    }
}

Wiring the HTTP Surface (kvnode/src/main.rs)

The HTTP handlers reuse kvd::api from Chapter 2 for RFC 9457 error formatting and If-Match / If-None-Match parsing, forwarding requests directly to Node. Listing 3.29 implements the PUT, DELETE, and GET handlers.

Listing 3.29 HTTP mutation and point-read handlers in kvnode/src/main.rs. kvnode/src/main.rs

async fn put_key(
    State(node): State<Arc<Node>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    body: Bytes,
) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;
    let condition = write_condition(&headers)?;

    let written = node
        .write(
            Change::Put {
                key,
                value: body.to_vec(),
            },
            condition,
        )
        .await?;
    let status = if written.created {
        StatusCode::CREATED
    } else {
        StatusCode::NO_CONTENT
    };

    Ok((status, [(ETAG, etag(written.version))]).into_response())
}

async fn delete_key(
    State(node): State<Arc<Node>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
) -> Result<StatusCode, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;
    let condition = write_condition(&headers)?;

    node.write(Change::Delete { key }, condition)
        .await?;

    Ok(StatusCode::NO_CONTENT)
}

async fn get_key(
    State(node): State<Arc<Node>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;
    let cached = version_header(&headers, IF_NONE_MATCH)?;
    let entry = node.get(&key)?;
    let tag = [(ETAG, etag(entry.version))];

    if cached == Some(Condition::Version(entry.version)) {
        return Ok((StatusCode::NOT_MODIFIED, tag).into_response());
    }

    Ok((
        tag,
        [(CONTENT_TYPE, "application/octet-stream")],
        entry.value,
    )
        .into_response())
}

Listing 3.30 implements prefix listing (GET /v1/keys) and the /healthz endpoint exposing role, term, last_sequence, committed, and per-follower match indices.

Listing 3.30 Prefix-listing and health endpoints in kvnode/src/main.rs. kvnode/src/main.rs

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct ListQuery {
    #[serde(default)]
    prefix: String,
    after: Option<String>,
    limit: Option<usize>,
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Item {
    key: String,
    version: u64,
    size: usize,
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Page {
    keys: Vec<Item>,
    next_after: Option<String>,
}

async fn list_keys(
    State(node): State<Arc<Node>>,
    Query(query): Query<ListQuery>,
) -> Result<Json<Page>, ApiError> {
    let limit = query
        .limit
        .unwrap_or(100)
        .clamp(1, 1000);
    let (page, more) = node.list(&query.prefix, query.after.as_deref(), limit)?;
    let next_after = if more {
        page.last()
            .map(|last| last.key.clone())
    } else {
        None
    };
    let keys = page
        .into_iter()
        .map(|item| Item {
            key: item.key,
            version: item.version,
            size: item.size,
        })
        .collect();

    Ok(Json(Page { keys, next_after }))
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Health {
    role: &'static str,
    term: u64,
    last_sequence: u64,
    committed: u64,
    /// The last sequence each follower has reported to this leader.
    followers: Vec<u64>,
}

async fn health(State(node): State<Arc<Node>>) -> Json<Health> {
    let replica = node.replica.lock();

    Json(Health {
        role: if node.leader { "leader" } else { "follower" },
        term: replica.term(),
        last_sequence: replica.last_sequence(),
        committed: replica.committed(),
        followers: node.reported(),
    })
}

Listing 3.31 bootstraps either a follower (starting the tonic gRPC listener alongside HTTP) or a leader (spawning one follow task per peer alongside HTTP).

Listing 3.31 Server bootstrap for leader and follower roles in kvnode/src/main.rs. kvnode/src/main.rs

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let options = Options::parse();
    let replica = Replica::open(&options.data, !options.no_sync, options.term)?;

    println!(
        "term {}, log ends at {}",
        replica.term(),
        replica.last_sequence()
    );

    let node = Node::new(replica, options.role == Role::Leader, options.followers);

    match options.role {
        Role::Leader => node.lead()?,
        Role::Follower => {
            let service = ReplicationServer::new(Follower {
                node: Arc::clone(&node),
            });

            tokio::spawn(
                Server::builder()
                    .add_service(service)
                    .serve(options.replication),
            );
            println!("accepting records on {}", options.replication);
        }
    }

    let routes = Router::new()
        .route("/v1/keys", get(list_keys))
        .route(
            "/v1/keys/{key}",
            get(get_key)
                .put(put_key)
                .delete(delete_key),
        )
        .route("/healthz", get(health))
        .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(MAX_VALUE))
        .with_state(node);

    let listener = TcpListener::bind(options.listen).await?;
    println!("listening on {}", listener.local_addr()?);

    axum::serve(listener, routes).await?;

    Ok(())
}

All three WAL files match byte for byte. In the following four experiments, all three processes share one local NVMe disk; deploying across three separate hosts requires only replacing 127.0.0.1 with each host’s network address.

Experiment 1: Throughput Cost of Synchronous Quorum Replication

$ time ./target/release/kvctl load --server http://127.0.0.1:7001 --count 300 --acked acked.txt
300 writes acknowledged
3.89 s, 77 writes per second

Throughput drops from 185 writes/s (single node, Chapter 2) to 77 writes/s on the same physical disk because every write now blocks on two sequential fsync barriers (first on the leader, then on a follower) plus a gRPC round trip.

Experiment 2: Single Follower Crash and Automatic Catch-Up

Terminating follower 7002 with SIGKILL mid-load causes zero write errors because the leader and follower 7003 maintain a 2 of 3 majority. Restarting 7002 automatically ships the 283 missed records in one exchange:

Experiment 3: Total Quorum Loss (PC/EC Refusal)

Killing both followers strips the leader of its majority. Writes time out after 1 s with 503, subsequent writes reject immediately while record 701 stays unsettled, and reads reject with 503 once the quorum contact window expires. Restarting a single follower commits record 701 automatically:

Promoting the follower with the longest log is mandatory: by invariant 1, every acknowledged write resides on at least one survivor, so the longer log holds all acknowledged records whereas a shorter survivor could miss the most recent writes.

Finally, we start a stale term 1 leader against the term 2 followers to verify term fencing:

$ ./target/release/kvnode --role leader --term 1 --listen 127.0.0.1:7009 --data /var/tmp/n9 \

Both followers reject the term 1 messages and echo term 2, causing the stale leader to latch deposed = true and reject writes with 421 while the legitimate term 2 leader continues serving traffic uninterrupted.

3.10 Residual Limitations

Five structural limitations remain in kvnode, each addressed directly in upcoming chapters:

No.Current LimitationEngineering ConsequenceResolution
0Leader promotion is manual.Shard writes halt after leader failure until an operator intervenes, violating our 99.95% availability SLO.Automated Raft leader election (Chapter 4).
1A returning former leader cannot rejoin with uncommitted conflicting tail records.Because Append checks only previous_sequence (not previous_term), a former leader with a divergent tail must wipe its disk before rejoining.Per-record term tagging and Raft log-matching conflict truncation (Chapter 4).
2Writes execute strictly one at a time (is_settled).Single-shard write throughput caps at one write per replication round trip (77 writes/s).WAL group commit (Chapter 6).
3Every replica retains its entire WAL in RAM (records: Vec<Record>).Memory footprint grows linearly with total historical mutations.Periodic snapshotting and log compaction (Chapter 1).
4Leader reads rely on a 1 s quorum-contact window.Linearizability requires that no new leader take over within 1 s of partition onset.Raft ReadIndex quorum heartbeat validation (Chapters 1 and 4).

3.11 Complete Source Listings

Listings 3.32 through 3.37 present the complete source files for the replication library, deterministic fault simulator, and kvnode server (kv::log and kv::store appear in Chapter 2).

Listing 3.32 presents the complete pure replication state machine (Append, AppendReply, Replica, handle_append, propose, append_for, and majority_sequence) in repl/src/lib.rs.

Listing 3.32 Complete repl/src/lib.rs. repl/src/lib.rs

//! Replication of a log from a leader to its followers.
//!
//! A `Replica` is one copy of a shard: a log, and the entries that result
//! from the records that are known to be on a majority of the copies. The
//! same type serves as leader and as follower. This module does no I/O on
//! the network. It builds the messages and processes them, and the caller
//! carries them between replicas.

use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use std::io;
use std::path::Path;

use kv::{Change, Condition, Entry, Log, Record, StoreError, Summary, apply, check, page};

/// The message a leader sends to a follower.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Append {
    /// The term of the sender.
    pub term: u64,
    /// The sequence of the record that precedes `records` in the leader's log.
    pub previous_sequence: u64,
    pub records: Vec<Record>,
    /// Every record up to this sequence is on a majority of the replicas.
    pub committed_sequence: u64,
}

/// The follower's answer.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Appended {
    pub term: u64,
    /// False when the follower's log does not end at `previous_sequence`,
    /// or when the sender's term is older than the follower's.
    pub appended: bool,
    /// The sequence of the last record in the follower's log.
    pub last_sequence: u64,
}

pub struct Replica {
    log: Log,
    /// Every record of the log, in order. Record `n` is at index `n - 1`.
    records: Vec<Record>,
    /// The result of applying the records up to `committed`.
    entries: BTreeMap<String, Entry>,
    /// The sequence of the last record that is applied to `entries`.
    committed: u64,
    term: u64,
}

impl Replica {
    /// Opens the replica in `directory`. Nothing is applied yet: a replica
    /// that has restarted does not know which of its records are committed.
    pub fn open(directory: &Path, sync: bool, term: u64) -> io::Result<Replica> {
        let (log, recovery) = Log::open(directory, sync)?;

        Ok(Replica {
            log,
            records: recovery.records,
            entries: BTreeMap::new(),
            committed: 0,
            term,
        })
    }

    pub fn term(&self) -> u64 {
        self.term
    }

    pub fn last_sequence(&self) -> u64 {
        self.records.len() as u64
    }

    pub fn committed(&self) -> u64 {
        self.committed
    }

    /// One page of the committed keys.
    pub fn list(&self, prefix: &str, after: Option<&str>, limit: usize) -> (Vec<Summary>, bool) {
        page(&self.entries, prefix, after, limit)
    }

    /// Every record of the log, in order.
    pub fn records(&self) -> &[Record] {
        &self.records
    }

    /// The committed value of a key.
    pub fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<&Entry> {
        self.entries.get(key)
    }

    /// Applies the records up to `sequence` that are not applied yet.
    pub fn commit(&mut self, sequence: u64) {
        let until = sequence.min(self.last_sequence());

        while self.committed < until {
            apply(
                &mut self.entries,
                self.records[self.committed as usize].clone(),
            );
            self.committed += 1;
        }
    }
}

impl Replica {
    /// Whether every record of the log is committed. A leader accepts a new
    /// write only in this state, so that the condition of the write is
    /// checked against the result of all earlier writes.
    pub fn is_settled(&self) -> bool {
        self.committed == self.last_sequence()
    }

    /// Checks the condition of a write and appends its record to the
    /// leader's log. The record is not applied: it is not committed yet.
    pub fn propose(&mut self, change: Change, condition: Condition) -> Result<u64, StoreError> {
        let key = match &change {
            Change::Put { key, .. } | Change::Delete { key } => key,
        };
        let current = self
            .entries
            .get(key)
            .map(|entry| entry.version);

        if matches!(change, Change::Delete { .. }) && current.is_none() {
            return Err(StoreError::NotFound);
        }

        check(condition, current)?;

        let record = self.log.append(change)?;
        let sequence = record.sequence;
        self.records.push(record);

        Ok(sequence)
    }
}

impl Replica {
    /// The message that brings a follower whose log ends at `follower_last`
    /// up to the end of this log. With nothing to send it is a heartbeat.
    pub fn append_for(&self, follower_last: u64) -> Append {
        let from = follower_last.min(self.last_sequence()) as usize;

        Append {
            term: self.term,
            previous_sequence: from as u64,
            records: self.records[from..].to_vec(),
            committed_sequence: self.committed,
        }
    }
}


/// The highest sequence that is stored on a majority, given the last
/// sequence of every replica, the leader included.
pub fn majority_sequence(mut last_sequences: Vec<u64>) -> u64 {
    last_sequences.sort_unstable_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a));

    last_sequences
        .get(last_sequences.len() / 2)
        .copied()
        .unwrap_or(0)
}

impl Replica {
    /// Processes a message from a leader.
    pub fn handle_append(&mut self, request: Append) -> io::Result<Appended> {
        let refuse = |replica: &Replica| Appended {
            term: replica.term,
            appended: false,
            last_sequence: replica.last_sequence(),
        };

        if request.term < self.term {
            return Ok(refuse(self));
        }

        self.term = request.term;

        if request.previous_sequence != self.last_sequence() {
            return Ok(refuse(self));
        }

        if !request.records.is_empty() {
            self.log
                .append_records(&request.records)?;
            self.records.extend(request.records);
        }

        self.commit(request.committed_sequence);

        Ok(Appended {
            term: self.term,
            appended: true,
            last_sequence: self.last_sequence(),
        })
    }
}
