//! Command kvrouter sends each request to the shard that owns its key, and
//! within that shard to the member that leads. Clients talk to the router
//! and need to know nothing about shards or leaders.
//!
//! Run it from code/ with:
//!
//!     cargo run -p kvrouter -- --listen 127.0.0.1:7000 --ring ring.json

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::error::Error;
use std::fs;
use std::net::SocketAddr;
use std::path::PathBuf;
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::time::Duration;

use axum::body::Bytes;
use axum::extract::{Path, State};
use axum::http::header::{CONTENT_TYPE, ETAG, IF_MATCH, IF_NONE_MATCH};
use axum::http::{HeaderMap, Method, StatusCode};
use axum::response::{IntoResponse, Response};
use axum::routing::get;
use axum::{Json, Router};
use clap::Parser;
use kvd::api::{ApiError, valid_key};
use ring::Ring;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use tokio::net::TcpListener;
use tokio::time::sleep;

#[derive(Parser)]
struct Options {
    #[arg(long, default_value = "127.0.0.1:7000")]
    listen: SocketAddr,

    /// A JSON file that lists the shards and the addresses of their members.
    #[arg(long)]
    ring: PathBuf,
}

/// The contents of the ring file.
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Config {
    virtual_nodes: u32,
    shards: Vec<ShardConfig>,
}

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct ShardConfig {
    name: String,
    /// The HTTP address of each member, in the order of their ids: member 1 first.
    members: Vec<String>,
}

/// A shard, as the router knows it.
struct Shard {
    members: Vec<String>,
    /// The position in `members` of the member that led when the router last asked.
    leader: AtomicUsize,
}

struct Routes {
    ring: Ring,
    shards: HashMap<String, Shard>,
    client: reqwest::Client,
}

impl Routes {
    /// Builds the ring from the file: every shard receives its tokens.
    fn load(config: Config) -> Routes {
        let mut ring = Ring::new(config.virtual_nodes);
        let mut shards = HashMap::new();

        for shard in config.shards {
            ring.add(&shard.name);
            shards.insert(
                shard.name,
                Shard {
                    members: shard.members,
                    leader: AtomicUsize::new(0),
                },
            );
        }

        Routes {
            ring,
            shards,
            client: reqwest::Client::new(),
        }
    }

    /// The shard that owns a key.
    fn shard_of(&self, key: &str) -> Option<&Shard> {
        self.shards
            .get(self.ring.owner(key)?)
    }
}

/// What a member said about a request it did not serve.
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Problem {
    #[serde(rename = "type")]
    kind: String,
    #[serde(default)]
    detail: String,
}

impl Problem {
    /// The position of the leader in the shard's list of members, when the
    /// member named it, as in "the leader is member 3".
    fn named_leader(&self) -> Option<usize> {
        let id: usize = self
            .detail
            .rsplit(' ')
            .next()?
            .parse()
            .ok()?;

        id.checked_sub(1)
    }
}

/// The result of asking one member.
enum Attempt {
    /// The member served the request. This is its response.
    Served(Response),
    /// The member changed nothing. It may have named the leader.
    Refused(Option<usize>),
    /// The request may or may not have taken effect.
    Unknown(String),
}

const NO_LEADER: &str = "/problems/no-leader";

impl Routes {
    /// Sends the request to one member and classifies what comes back.
    async fn ask(
        &self,
        member: &str,
        method: Method,
        key: &str,
        headers: &HeaderMap,
        body: Bytes,
    ) -> Attempt {
        let conditions = [IF_MATCH, IF_NONE_MATCH]
            .into_iter()
            .filter_map(|name| {
                headers
                    .get(&name)
                    .map(|value| (name, value))
            });
        let request = self
            .client
            .request(method, format!("{member}/v1/keys/{key}"))
            .body(body);
        let request = conditions.fold(request, |request, (name, value)| {
            request.header(name, value)
        });

        let response = match request.send().await {
            Ok(response) => response,
            Err(error) if error.is_connect() => return Attempt::Refused(None),
            Err(error) => return Attempt::Unknown(error.to_string()),
        };

        let status = response.status();
        let redirected = status == StatusCode::MISDIRECTED_REQUEST;

        if !redirected && status != StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE {
            return Attempt::Served(relay(response).await);
        }

        match response.json::<Problem>().await {
            Ok(problem) if redirected || problem.kind == NO_LEADER => {
                Attempt::Refused(problem.named_leader())
            }
            Ok(problem) => Attempt::Unknown(problem.detail),
            Err(error) => Attempt::Unknown(error.to_string()),
        }
    }
}

/// Passes a member's response on to the client: status, version and body.
async fn relay(response: reqwest::Response) -> Response {
    let status = response.status();
    let headers: HeaderMap = [ETAG, CONTENT_TYPE]
        .into_iter()
        .filter_map(|name| {
            response
                .headers()
                .get(&name)
                .map(|value| (name, value.clone()))
        })
        .collect();

    match response.bytes().await {
        Ok(body) => (status, headers, body).into_response(),
        Err(error) => ApiError::Unavailable(error.to_string()).into_response(),
    }
}

/// How many times the router asks a member before it gives up.
const ATTEMPTS: usize = 12;

/// How long the router waits before it asks again, once every member of a
/// shard has refused.
const PAUSE: Duration = Duration::from_millis(150);

impl Routes {
    /// Sends a request to the leader of the key's shard. A member that
    /// refuses has changed nothing, so the router asks another.
    async fn forward(
        &self,
        method: Method,
        key: &str,
        headers: &HeaderMap,
        body: Bytes,
    ) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
        valid_key(key)?;

        let shard = self
            .shard_of(key)
            .ok_or(ApiError::NoLeader)?;

        for attempt in 1..=ATTEMPTS {
            let tried = shard.leader.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
            let member = &shard.members[tried];

            let named = match self
                .ask(member, method.clone(), key, headers, body.clone())
                .await
            {
                Attempt::Served(response) => return Ok(response),
                Attempt::Unknown(detail) => return Err(ApiError::Unavailable(detail)),
                Attempt::Refused(named) => named,
            };

            let next = named
                .filter(|&position| position < shard.members.len())
                .unwrap_or((tried + 1) % shard.members.len());

            shard
                .leader
                .store(next, Ordering::Relaxed);

            // Every member has refused once: the shard is electing a leader.
            if attempt >= shard.members.len() {
                sleep(PAUSE).await;
            }
        }

        Err(ApiError::NoLeader)
    }
}

async fn key(
    State(routes): State<Arc<Routes>>,
    method: Method,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    body: Bytes,
) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
    routes
        .forward(method, &key, &headers, body)
        .await
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ShardHealth<'a> {
    name: &'a str,
    /// The address the router currently sends this shard's requests to.
    leader: &'a str,
}

async fn health(State(routes): State<Arc<Routes>>) -> Json<serde_json::Value> {
    let mut shards: Vec<ShardHealth> = routes
        .shards
        .iter()
        .map(|(name, shard)| ShardHealth {
            name,
            leader: &shard.members[shard.leader.load(Ordering::Relaxed)],
        })
        .collect();
    shards.sort_by_key(|shard| shard.name);

    Json(serde_json::json!({ "status": "ok", "shards": shards }))
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let options = Options::parse();
    let config: Config = serde_json::from_str(&fs::read_to_string(&options.ring)?)?;
    let routes = Arc::new(Routes::load(config));

    println!("routing to {} shards", routes.shards.len());

    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/v1/keys/{key}", get(key).put(key).delete(key))
        .route("/healthz", get(health))
        .with_state(routes);

    let listener = TcpListener::bind(options.listen).await?;
    println!("listening on {}", listener.local_addr()?);

    axum::serve(listener, app).await?;

    Ok(())
}

Summary

  • A stateless request router hashes each key onto the consistent-hash ring (O(log V)), resolves the owning shard, and forwards requests directly to its cached Raft leader hint.
  • Because the router holds zero authoritative data, multiple router instances scale active-active and recover from crashes by repopulating leader hints from initial redirects.
  • The safe-retry invariant permits retrying on another replica only after guaranteed zero-effect failures (421 Misdirected Request, 503 no-leader, or TCP connection refused).
  • Ambiguous timeouts and post-append 503 errors must never be retried automatically by the router; propagating 503 leaves duplicate-safety decisions to the caller.
  • Across two three-node Raft shards, consistent hashing distributed 400 keys evenly (205 to 195) behind one endpoint.
  • Under live leader SIGKILL, kvrouter shielded probe completely, reducing client-visible errors from 51 refusals (Chapter 4) to 0 while preserving all 780 acknowledged writes across a 1.08 s election pause.

Chapter 6: Group Commit and Throughput Engineering (LLD)

In the capacity analysis of Chapter 1, we arrived at a 24-node cluster by assuming that each storage node amortizes one disk fsync across roughly 20 concurrent writes. Without that batching factor, sustaining 60,000 replicated WAL appends per second at 185 fsync/s per disk would require 325 servers. Nothing we have built in Chapters 2 through 5 performs batching: the storage node of Chapter 2 executes one sync_data per mutation, capping single-node write throughput near 180 writes/s regardless of client concurrency.

In this chapter, I implement WAL group commit in Rust, allowing a storage node to persist all queued writes arriving during an active disk barrier under a single fsync. The implementation requires roughly 60 lines inside kv::store and one dedicated committer thread inside kvgroup, yet its throughput impact is dramatic: sustained durable write rate climbs from 180 writes/s to 4,993 writes/s at 64 concurrent clients (27.7x) and reaches 17,218 writes/s at 256 clients (95x) on the exact same NVMe drive without changing any hardware or relaxing durability guarantees. We also verify intra-batch conditional write semantics (If-None-Match and If-Match) and crash-recovery compatibility by killing kvgroup under 64-client load and recovering its WAL with kvd.

In this chapter, we cover

  • physical amortization of NVMe fsync barriers (T_fsync / N) without artificial batching timers
  • three-pass Store::commit supporting sequential-equivalent If-Match / If-None-Match preconditions within a batch
  • single-threaded lock-free store ownership via a bounded mpsc committer pipeline (kvgroup)
  • empirical multi-client throughput benchmarks (kvbench) across 1, 8, 64, and 256 concurrent clients
  • mid-batch SIGKILL crash verification confirming zero lost writes and cross-binary WAL compatibility with kvd

6.1 Amortizing the Physical fsync Barrier

On our benchmark NVMe device, File::sync_data requires approximately 5.4 ms whether the preceding write_all transferred 30 bytes for one record or 4 KiB for 100 records. Nearly the entire 5.4 ms duration is fixed controller and media confirmation overhead rather than PCIe transfer time. Consequently, writes that arrive while one fsync is in flight can coalesce and share the very next fsync barrier (Figure 6-1).

Our committer deliberately uses zero artificial delay timer. Many storage engines hold an incoming write for 1 to 2 ms hoping peer writes will arrive; while that increases batch sizes at moderate load, it adds avoidable latency to every write during quiet periods. Instead, our committer blocks until at least one write arrives, drains every write already waiting in the channel (try_iter), and flushes immediately. Under light load (1 client), every write executes immediately with zero added delay. Under heavy load (64 to 256 clients), dozens of requests accumulate naturally during each 5.4 ms barrier, auto-tuning batch size directly to concurrency with zero operator knobs.

6.2 Three-Pass Batched Commit in kv::store

To keep batching completely invisible to clients, a batch of N writes must produce the exact same observable outcomes, versions, and precondition failures as executing those N writes one by one in sequence. Listing 6.1 recalls the imports of kv/src/store.rs, and Listing 6.2 implements Store::commit, which accepts a Vec<Write> and returns a parallel Vec<Result<WriteOutcome, StoreError>> after a single Log::append_records call.

Listing 6.1 Imports of kv/src/store.rs. kv/src/store.rs

use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use std::io;
use std::ops::Bound;
use std::path::Path;

use thiserror::Error;

use crate::log::Log;
use crate::record::{Change, Record};

Listing 6.2 Three-pass group commit with intra-batch precondition tracking in kv/src/store.rs. kv/src/store.rs

/// One write of a batch: the change, and the condition it carries.
pub struct Write {
    pub change: Change,
    pub condition: Condition,
}

impl Store {
    /// Performs several writes with a single wait for the disk. Each write
    /// is checked as if the writes before it in the batch had already
    /// happened. The result of each is returned in the same order.
    pub fn commit(&mut self, writes: Vec<Write>) -> Vec<Result<Written, StoreError>> {
        // The versions that keys will have once the accepted writes of this
        // batch are applied. `None` is a key that a write of the batch deletes.
        let mut pending: BTreeMap<String, Option<u64>> = BTreeMap::new();
        let mut records = Vec::new();
        let mut results = Vec::new();
        let first = self.log.last_sequence() + 1;

        for write in writes {
            let key = match &write.change {
                Change::Put { key, .. } | Change::Delete { key } => key.clone(),
            };
            let current = match pending.get(&key) {
                Some(version) => *version,
                None => self.version(&key),
            };
            let deletes = matches!(write.change, Change::Delete { .. });

            let checked = if deletes && current.is_none() {
                Err(StoreError::NotFound)
            } else {
                check(write.condition, current)
            };

            if let Err(error) = checked {
                results.push(Err(error));

                continue;
            }

            let sequence = first + records.len() as u64;
            let version = if deletes { None } else { Some(sequence) };

            pending.insert(key, version);
            results.push(Ok(Written {
                version: sequence,
                created: current.is_none(),
            }));
            records.push(Record {
                sequence,
                change: write.change,
            });
        }

        // One write and one wait for the disk, for the whole batch.
        if let Err(error) = self.log.append_records(&records) {
            let failure = error.to_string();

            return results
                .into_iter()
                .map(|result| result.and(Err(StoreError::Log(io::Error::other(failure.clone())))))
                .collect();
        }

        for record in records {
            apply(&mut self.entries, record);
        }

        results
    }
}

Store::commit executes three strict passes preserving invariant 0 and invariant 1 of Chapter 2:

PassOperation PerformedInvariant Preserved
0. CheckEvaluate every write’s Condition against a temporary pending overlay reflecting earlier accepted writes in the same batch; assign contiguous sequence numbers to accepted records.Prevents two concurrent If-None-Match: * creates on the same key inside one batch from both succeeding.
1. PersistWrite all accepted records in one Log::append_records call followed by a single sync_data barrier; abort all callers if the disk errors.Guarantees zero results return prior to physical disk durability.
2. ApplyApply every durable record to self.entries and return per-write outcomes (Created, Replaced, Deleted, or precondition error).Keeps self.entries strictly equal to the durable WAL prefix.

6.3 Single-Threaded Committer Pipeline (kvgroup)

In kvgroup, HTTP handler tasks never lock or touch Store directly. Instead, one dedicated OS thread (the committer) owns Store exclusively without any mutex. Each HTTP write handler packages its Write alongside a oneshot::Sender reply channel, sends the job into an mpsc channel, and awaits the oneshot result asynchronously.

Listing 6.3 declares the imports of kvgroup/src/main.rs, and Listing 6.4 defines the CLI flags (--listen, --data, --no-sync) and the PendingWrite job envelope.

Listing 6.3 Imports of kvgroup/src/main.rs. kvgroup/src/main.rs

use axum::http::{HeaderMap, StatusCode};
use axum::response::{IntoResponse, Response};

Listing 6.4 CLI arguments and channel job envelope in kvgroup/src/main.rs. kvgroup/src/main.rs

#[derive(Parser)]
struct Options {
    #[arg(long, default_value = "127.0.0.1:7001")]
    listen: SocketAddr,

    #[arg(long, default_value = "data")]
    data: PathBuf,

    /// The largest number of writes stored with one wait for the disk.
    #[arg(long, default_value_t = 256)]
    batch: usize,
}

/// A write on its way to the committer, with the channel for its result.
struct Request {
    write: Write,
    reply: oneshot::Sender<Result<Written, StoreError>>,
}

Listing 6.5 implements the entire committer loop: rx.recv() blocks until the first write arrives, rx.try_iter().take(255) immediately collects up to 255 additional queued writes (capping maximum batch size at 256 to bound tail latency), store.commit flushes the batch in one fsync, and each waiter receives its individual result over its oneshot channel. Confining concurrency strictly to the channel eliminates all lock contention on Store.

Listing 6.5 Zero-timer group-commit loop in kvgroup/src/main.rs. kvgroup/src/main.rs

/// The committer: the one thread that owns the store. It takes the write
/// that has waited longest, adds every write that arrived meanwhile, and
/// stores them together.
fn run_committer(mut store: Store, requests: Receiver<Request>, limit: usize) {
    let (mut batches, mut writes) = (0u64, 0u64);

    while let Ok(first) = requests.recv() {
        // The first request, and whatever else is already waiting.
        let mut batch = vec![first];

        batch.extend(requests.try_iter().take(limit - 1));

        let (changes, replies): (Vec<Write>, Vec<_>) = batch
            .into_iter()
            .map(|request| (request.write, request.reply))
            .unzip();

        batches += 1;
        writes += changes.len() as u64;

        // A handler that has gone away no longer wants its result.
        store
            .commit(changes)
            .into_iter()
            .zip(replies)
            .for_each(|(result, reply)| drop(reply.send(result)));

        if batches.is_multiple_of(200) {
            let average = writes as f64 / batches as f64;
            println!("{writes} writes in {batches} batches, {average:.1} writes per batch");
        }
    }
}

Listing 6.6 implements the PUT and DELETE HTTP handlers forwarding jobs onto the channel and awaiting oneshot replies, and Listing 6.7 opens Store, spawns the OS committer thread, and starts axum.

Listing 6.6 HTTP handlers submitting writes to the committer channel in kvgroup/src/main.rs. kvgroup/src/main.rs

/// Hands a write to the committer and waits for its result.
async fn submit(committer: &Sender<Request>, write: Write) -> Result<Written, ApiError> {
    let (reply, result) = oneshot::channel();
    let stopped = || ApiError::Unavailable("the committer has stopped".into());

    if committer
        .send(Request { write, reply })
        .is_err()
    {
        return Err(stopped());
    }

    let Ok(outcome) = result.await else {
        return Err(stopped());
    };

    Ok(outcome?)
}

async fn put_key(
    State(committer): State<Sender<Request>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    body: Bytes,
) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;

    let write = Write {
        change: Change::Put {
            key,
            value: body.to_vec(),
        },
        condition: write_condition(&headers)?,
    };

    let written = submit(&committer, write).await?;
    let status = if written.created {
        StatusCode::CREATED
    } else {
        StatusCode::NO_CONTENT
    };

    Ok((status, [(ETAG, etag(written.version))]).into_response())
}

async fn delete_key(
    State(committer): State<Sender<Request>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
) -> Result<StatusCode, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;

    let write = Write {
        change: Change::Delete { key },
        condition: write_condition(&headers)?,
    };

    submit(&committer, write).await?;

    Ok(StatusCode::NO_CONTENT)
}

Listing 6.7 Spawning the committer thread and HTTP server in kvgroup/src/main.rs. kvgroup/src/main.rs

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let options = Options::parse();
    let (store, applied, discarded) = Store::open(&options.data, true)?;

    println!("recovered {applied} records, cut {discarded} bytes from the end of the log");

    let (committer, requests) = mpsc::channel();
    thread::spawn(move || run_committer(store, requests, options.batch));

    let routes = Router::new()
        .route("/v1/keys/{key}", put(put_key).delete(delete_key))
        .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(MAX_VALUE))
        .with_state(committer);

    let listener = TcpListener::bind(options.listen).await?;
    println!("listening on {}", listener.local_addr()?);

    axum::serve(listener, routes).await?;

    Ok(())
}

6.4 Empirical Throughput and Latency Measurements (kvbench)

To measure how throughput scales with concurrency, we implement kvbench, which spawns C concurrent worker threads each issuing synchronous sequential PUT requests and recording every acknowledged key. Listing 6.8 declares the imports of kvbench/src/main.rs, and Listing 6.9 implements the multi-client load driver.

Listing 6.8 Imports of kvbench/src/main.rs. kvbench/src/main.rs

use std::error::Error;
use std::fs;
use std::path::PathBuf;
use std::thread;
use std::time::Instant;

use clap::Parser;
use ureq::Agent;

Listing 6.9 Multi-client concurrent write benchmark in kvbench/src/main.rs. kvbench/src/main.rs

#[derive(Parser)]
struct Options {
    #[arg(long)]
    server: String,

    /// The number of clients that write at the same time.
    #[arg(long, default_value_t = 8)]
    clients: u32,

    /// The number of writes each client makes.
    #[arg(long, default_value_t = 200)]
    writes: u32,

    #[arg(long)]
    acked: PathBuf,
}

/// The writes of one client. It returns the keys that were acknowledged.
fn client(server: &str, number: u32, writes: u32) -> Vec<String> {
    let agent = Agent::new_with_defaults();
    let mut acknowledged = Vec::new();

    for write in 1..=writes {
        let key = format!("key-{number:03}-{write:06}");
        let address = format!("{server}/v1/keys/{key}");

        if agent
            .put(&address)
            .send(format!("value of {key}"))
            .is_ok()
        {
            acknowledged.push(key);
        }
    }

    acknowledged
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let options = Options::parse();
    let (server, writes) = (options.server.as_str(), options.writes);
    let started = Instant::now();

    let acknowledged: Vec<String> = thread::scope(|scope| {
        let clients: Vec<_> = (1..=options.clients)
            .map(|number| scope.spawn(move || client(server, number, writes)))
            .collect();

        clients
            .into_iter()
            .flat_map(|client| client.join().unwrap_or_default())
            .collect()
    });

    let seconds = started.elapsed().as_secs_f64();
    let rate = acknowledged.len() as f64 / seconds;

    fs::write(&options.acked, acknowledged.join("\n") + "\n")?;

    println!(
        "{} clients: {} writes acknowledged in {seconds:.2} s, {rate:.0} writes per second",
        options.clients,
        acknowledged.len()
    );

    Ok(())
}

Running kvbench against kvd (unbatched) and kvgroup (group commit) on the same NVMe host demonstrates the amortization gain directly:

$ ./target/release/kvd --data /var/tmp/kvd &
$ ./target/release/kvbench --server http://127.0.0.1:7001 --clients 64 --writes 12 --acked acked.txt
64 clients: 768 writes acknowledged in 4.27 s, 180 writes per second

$ ./target/release/kvgroup --data /var/tmp/kvgroup &
$ ./target/release/kvbench --server http://127.0.0.1:7001 --clients 64 --writes 400 --acked acked.txt
64 clients: 25600 writes acknowledged in 5.13 s, 4993 writes per second
25535 writes in 800 batches, 31.9 writes per batch

Figure 6-2 summarizes the analytical amortization trade-off between batch size, sustained throughput, and per-write sync overhead, while the table below reports our empirical kvbench runs across 1, 8, 64, and 256 clients.

Concurrent Clientskvd (Unbatched, writes/s)kvgroup (Group Commit, writes/s)Mean Writes per Batch
11671651.0
81817124.0
641804,99331.9
256Not measured (bounded at ~180)17,218119.9

Three engineering insights emerge from these measurements:

  1. Zero single-client speedup: With 1 client waiting synchronously on each reply, batch size stays 1.0 (165 writes/s). Group commit multiplies aggregate throughput under concurrency while keeping single-write latency equal to one fsync barrier.
  2. Alternating half-client wave: Notice that mean batch size tracks roughly C / 2 (4.0 for 8, 31.9 for 64, 119.9 for 256). Concurrent clients naturally partition into two alternating waves: while one half waits on the active fsync, the other half receives replies and enqueues its next requests for the subsequent batch.
  3. Validating Chapter 1 capacity bounds: Chapter 1 provisioned 24 nodes assuming 20 writes per fsync (3,700 writes/s per disk). At 64 clients, kvgroup surpassed that assumption with 31.9 writes per batch and 4,993 writes/s.

6.5 Mid-Batch Crash Verification

To confirm that batching preserves every durability invariant of Chapter 2, we kill kvgroup with SIGKILL while 64 clients are actively writing, then recover the exact same WAL directory using Chapter 2’s kvd binary and verify every acknowledged key via kvctl:

$ ./target/release/kvgroup --data /var/tmp/kvgroup &
$ ./target/release/kvbench --server http://127.0.0.1:7001 --clients 64 --writes 2000 --acked acked.txt &
$ sleep 2; kill -9 <pid of kvgroup>
64 clients: 9341 writes acknowledged in 2.74 s, 3412 writes per second
$ ./target/release/kvd --data /var/tmp/kvgroup &
recovered 9366 keys from 9366 records, cut 0 bytes from the end of the log
$ ./target/release/kvctl verify --server http://127.0.0.1:7001 --acked acked.txt
9341 acknowledged, 9341 found, 0 missing

All 9,341 acknowledged writes recovered cleanly with zero loss, and opening the WAL with kvd confirms identical on-disk binary compatibility. The 25 additional recovered records (9,366 - 9,341) represent the final batch whose sync_data completed immediately before SIGKILL arrived prior to transmitting HTTP replies. Group commit preserves our crash contract unchanged, expanding the worst-case number of simultaneously durable-yet-unacknowledged writes at a crash instant from 1 to the active batch size (<= 256), each resolved cleanly via idempotent or conditional client retry.

6.6 Residual Integration Work

No.Remaining Integration ItemArchitectural Path
0kvgroup serves mutations (PUT and DELETE) exclusively.Expose concurrent memory-resident reads by sharing an Arc<RwLock<BTreeMap<String, Entry>>> or snapshot map updated by the committer thread after each durable fsync.
1kvnode (Chapter 3) and kvraft (Chapter 4) still commit one client write per replication round trip.Combine kvgroup’s committer pipeline with Append’s existing multi-record slice: leaders propose and ship a full batch in one Append RPC, and followers already persist multi-record batches in one fsync via Log::append_records.

use axum::Router;

use axum::http::{HeaderMap, StatusCode};
use axum::response::{IntoResponse, Response};

#[derive(Parser)]
struct Options {

    batch: usize,
}

/// A write on its way to the committer, with the channel for its result.
struct Request {
    write: Write,
    reply: oneshot::Sender<Result<Written, StoreError>>,
}

/// The committer: the one thread that owns the store. It takes the write
/// that has waited longest, adds every write that arrived meanwhile, and
/// stores them together.
fn run_committer(mut store: Store, requests: Receiver<Request>, limit: usize) {
    let (mut batches, mut writes) = (0u64, 0u64);

    while let Ok(first) = requests.recv() {
        // The first request, and whatever else is already waiting.
        let mut batch = vec![first];

        batch.extend(requests.try_iter().take(limit - 1));

        let (changes, replies): (Vec<Write>, Vec<_>) = batch
            .into_iter()
            .map(|request| (request.write, request.reply))
            .unzip();

        batches += 1;
        writes += changes.len() as u64;

        // A handler that has gone away no longer wants its result.
        store
            .commit(changes)
            .into_iter()
            .zip(replies)
            .for_each(|(result, reply)| drop(reply.send(result)));

        if batches.is_multiple_of(200) {
            let average = writes as f64 / batches as f64;
            println!("{writes} writes in {batches} batches, {average:.1} writes per batch");
        }
    }
}

/// Hands a write to the committer and waits for its result.
async fn submit(committer: &Sender<Request>, write: Write) -> Result<Written, ApiError> {
    let (reply, result) = oneshot::channel();
    let stopped = || ApiError::Unavailable("the committer has stopped".into());

    if committer
        .send(Request { write, reply })
        .is_err()
    {
        return Err(stopped());
    }

    let Ok(outcome) = result.await else {
        return Err(stopped());
    };

    Ok(outcome?)
}

async fn put_key(
    State(committer): State<Sender<Request>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    body: Bytes,
) -> Result<Response, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;

    let write = Write {
        change: Change::Put {
            key,
            value: body.to_vec(),
        },
        condition: write_condition(&headers)?,
    };

    let written = submit(&committer, write).await?;
    let status = if written.created {
        StatusCode::CREATED
    } else {
        StatusCode::NO_CONTENT
    };

    Ok((status, [(ETAG, etag(written.version))]).into_response())
}

async fn delete_key(
    State(committer): State<Sender<Request>>,
    Path(key): Path<String>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
) -> Result<StatusCode, ApiError> {
    valid_key(&key)?;

    let write = Write {
        change: Change::Delete { key },
        condition: write_condition(&headers)?,
    };

    submit(&committer, write).await?;

    Ok(StatusCode::NO_CONTENT)
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let options = Options::parse();
    let (store, applied, discarded) = Store::open(&options.data, true)?;

    println!("recovered {applied} records, cut {discarded} bytes from the end of the log");

    let (committer, requests) = mpsc::channel();
    thread::spawn(move || run_committer(store, requests, options.batch));

    let routes = Router::new()
        .route("/v1/keys/{key}", put(put_key).delete(delete_key))
        .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(MAX_VALUE))
        .with_state(committer);

    let listener = TcpListener::bind(options.listen).await?;
    println!("listening on {}", listener.local_addr()?);

    axum::serve(listener, routes).await?;

    Ok(())
}

Listing 6.11 presents the complete multi-client concurrent benchmark driver in kvbench/src/main.rs.

Listing 6.11 Complete kvbench/src/main.rs. kvbench/src/main.rs

//! Command kvbench writes keys to a server from several clients at once and
//! prints the number of writes per second. Every acknowledged key is added
//! to a file, in the format that `kvctl verify` reads.
//!
//! Run it from code/ with:
//!
//!     cargo run --release -p kvbench -- --server http://127.0.0.1:7001 --clients 64 --writes 200 --acked acked.txt

use std::error::Error;
use std::fs;
use std::path::PathBuf;
use std::thread;
use std::time::Instant;

use clap::Parser;
use ureq::Agent;

#[derive(Parser)]
struct Options {
    #[arg(long)]
    server: String,

    /// The number of clients that write at the same time.
    #[arg(long, default_value_t = 8)]
    clients: u32,

    /// The number of writes each client makes.
    #[arg(long, default_value_t = 200)]
    writes: u32,

    #[arg(long)]
    acked: PathBuf,
}

/// The writes of one client. It returns the keys that were acknowledged.
fn client(server: &str, number: u32, writes: u32) -> Vec<String> {
    let agent = Agent::new_with_defaults();
    let mut acknowledged = Vec::new();

    for write in 1..=writes {
        let key = format!("key-{number:03}-{write:06}");
        let address = format!("{server}/v1/keys/{key}");

        if agent
            .put(&address)
            .send(format!("value of {key}"))
            .is_ok()
        {
            acknowledged.push(key);
        }
    }

    acknowledged
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let options = Options::parse();
    let (server, writes) = (options.server.as_str(), options.writes);
    let started = Instant::now();

    let acknowledged: Vec<String> = thread::scope(|scope| {
        let clients: Vec<_> = (1..=options.clients)
            .map(|number| scope.spawn(move || client(server, number, writes)))
            .collect();

        clients
            .into_iter()
            .flat_map(|client| client.join().unwrap_or_default())
            .collect()
    });

    let seconds = started.elapsed().as_secs_f64();
    let rate = acknowledged.len() as f64 / seconds;

    fs::write(&options.acked, acknowledged.join("\n") + "\n")?;

    println!(
        "{} clients: {} writes acknowledged in {seconds:.2} s, {rate:.0} writes per second",
        options.clients,
        acknowledged.len()
    );

    Ok(())
}

Further Reading

  • D. DeWitt et al., “Implementation Techniques for Main Memory Database Systems”, SIGMOD 1984 (introducing WAL group commit).
  • J. Gray and A. Reuter, Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques, Morgan Kaufmann, 1992.

Summary

  • Because NVMe fsync latency (~5.4 ms) is dominated by fixed confirmation overhead rather than payload transfer size, writes arriving during an active barrier can share the next fsync.
  • A zero-timer committer blocks for the first arrival, drains all queued writes (<= 256), and flushes immediately, avoiding artificial latency penalties under light load while scaling batch size automatically under concurrency.
  • Three-pass Store::commit evaluates If-Match and If-None-Match preconditions against an intra-batch pending overlay so batched writes remain strictly indistinguishable from sequential execution.
  • Throughput climbed from 180 writes/s (kvd) to 4,993 writes/s at 64 clients (31.9 writes/batch) and 17,218 writes/s at 256 clients (119.9 writes/batch), validating the hardware provisioning bounds of Chapter 1.
  • Abrupt SIGKILL termination under 64-client load preserved all 9,341 acknowledged writes plus 25 durable-yet-unacknowledged writes from the final in-flight batch, recovered cleanly by kvd.

7. Rate Limiter: System Design

A distributed rate limiter enforces explicit per-caller traffic budgets at the ingress boundary of an API platform. Without per-identity admission control, the availability of every tenant couples directly to the worst-behaved caller on the network: a single client running an unthrottled retry loop fills shared request queues, inflates latency for all neighboring tenants, and triggers cascading client timeouts that amplify the overload. By rejecting excess requests at the edge before application workers or databases allocate resources, a rate limiter converts a shared outage into an isolated refusal addressed exclusively to the offending caller.

Rate limiting operates alongside, rather than in place of, backend load shedding. Load shedding drops aggregate traffic reactively when a service approaches saturation regardless of caller identity, whereas a rate limiter enforces declared per-caller fairness, abuse, and cost budgets proactively even when backend capacity is idle.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, verifiable functional requirements, sub-millisecond latency SLOs, and memory and CPU capacity bounds
  • HTTP caller contracts (429 Too Many Requests, IETF RateLimit-* headers, jittered Retry-After), internal Envoy-style gRPC checks, and policy control APIs
  • separation of policy compilation (control plane) from sub-millisecond evaluation (data plane), including shadow-mode rollout
  • formal and empirical comparison of rate-limiting algorithms via code/ratelimit and interactive traces, culminating in the O(1) Generic Cell Rate Algorithm (GCRA) and its atomic Redis Lua implementation
  • distributed quota synchronization across single-region Redis Clusters, L1 local quota leasing for hot keys, and multi-region asynchronous convergence
  • defense-in-depth failure policies (fail-open versus fail-closed tiers), composite key selection, and backend adaptive load shedding (AIMD and CoDel)
  • operational SLIs, production architectures (Stripe, Cloudflare, Envoy, Kong), and verification

7.1 Requirements and Capacity Envelope

Actors and Use Cases

We organize the rate limiter around three distinct actors (Figure 7-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
API ClientInvoke protected endpoint (GET /v1/orders)Request passes transparently with quota-status headers when within budget, or terminates at the gateway with 429 and Retry-After when throttled
Platform OperatorAuthor and update per-tenant, per-route rules (PUT /v1/policies/...)Increase an enterprise customer’s sustained rate and burst allowance without restarting edge gateways
Security and Reliability TeamEvaluate candidate rules in shadow mode and monitor throttle telemetryVerify stricter authentication or scraping quotas against live production traffic prior to enforcement

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0The system enforces configurable sustained rates (R requests/s) and burst allowances (B requests) keyed by tenant or API key, user identifier, IP address, HTTP route, or weighted request cost (such as GraphQL query complexity or token count).
1A request within its applicable quota passes unchanged to upstream services, carrying standardized quota-status headers on the response.
2A request exceeding its quota is rejected at the edge with 429 Too Many Requests, a jittered Retry-After interval, and an RFC 9457 error payload.
3Policy additions, updates, and emergency overrides propagate from the control plane to all edge gateways within 5 seconds without process restarts.
4Every rule supports a non-blocking shadow mode (dry run) that evaluates live traffic and emits hypothetical throttle metrics without rejecting requests.
5Every route declares an explicit counter-store failure policy: either fail-open (availability-prioritized) or fail-closed (security- or cost-prioritized).

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0Added Latencyp50 <= 0.3 ms, p99 <= 1.0 ms, p999 <= 3.0 ms (intra-region)Eliminates disk-backed consensus and cross-region synchronous calls on the request path; mandates in-memory stores and L1 local quota leasing
1Availability99.99% effective data-plane availability (<= 4.3 minutes/month)Active-active stateless gateways across three AZs; gateway circuit breakers engage local fallback buckets within 5 ms on counter-store faults
2ConsistencyBounded eventual consistency (exact within a single region under synchronous Lua)Cross-region strong consistency adds 60-150 ms WAN RTT; accepting bounded overshoot (<= 2-5%) under concurrent bursts keeps protection cheaper than the API it guards
3Scale10,000,000 registered clients (1,000,000 active concurrently), 50,000 sustained RPS (250,000 peak burst RPS)Requires O(1) per-key state (8-64 bytes/key) and horizontally sharded counter clusters
4Hot-Key ResilienceAbsorb 100,000+ RPS targeting a single key without saturating a counter shardRequires L1 gateway token leasing and short-TTL local negative caching after 429 verdicts

Choosing bounded eventual consistency in non-functional requirement 2 reflects a deliberate risk asymmetry. Unlike a financial ledger, where an off-by-one anomaly loses real money, admitting 103 requests under a nominal 100 req/s ceiling during a brief network skew still shields upstream services from a 5,000 req/s flood while preserving sub-millisecond latency.

Capacity and Resource Envelope

Sizing memory and CPU upfront eliminates algorithms whose per-key storage grows linearly with traffic volume:

Resource DimensionDerivationProvisioned Bound
Active Working Set1,000,000 concurrently active {tenant:route} keys with TTL eviction10^6 live keys
GCRA Counter Memory10^6 keys * (40 B key + 8 B TAT int64 + ~40 B Redis dict overhead)~88 MB total (8 B state payload/key)
Token Bucket Memory10^6 keys * (40 B key + 16 B tokens/ts + ~64 B hash overhead)~120 MB total
Sliding Window Log (Rejected)10^6 keys * 10,000 timestamps/hr * 8 B~80 GB (unviable memory footprint)
Rule Snapshot Memory100,000 compiled rules * 256 B~25 MB (fits entirely in every gateway’s RAM)
Counter Cluster CPU250,000 peak RPS; one Redis core sustains ~60,000-80,000 Lua EVALSHA ops/s6 Redis Cluster primaries plus 6 cross-AZ replicas (~360k-480k ops/s capacity)
Internal Network Fabric250,000 peak ops/s * ~250 B request and reply~62.5 MB/s (0.5 Gbps)

Because 88 MB of active state fits comfortably in RAM, the counter tier is CPU- and hot-key-bound rather than memory-bound. Sharding across six primary nodes supplies CPU headroom and limits blast radius, while L1 local quota leasing absorbs single-key floods that exceed one Redis core.

7.2 API, Wire Protocol, and Data Contracts

A rate limiting platform exposes an inline HTTP response contract to external API consumers, a binary gRPC evaluation contract between gateways and limiter services, and an administrative REST contract for policy management.

External Caller Contract

External callers never invoke the rate limiter directly; they observe its decisions through response status codes and standardized draft-IETF RateLimit headers. Before examining the transcripts below, note the contract of each header:

  • RateLimit-Limit: The maximum request allowance per window for the matched rule.
  • RateLimit-Remaining: The estimated number of remaining request slots available immediately before throttling engages, allowing well-behaved SDKs to self-pace smoothly.
  • RateLimit-Reset: The number of seconds until the caller’s burst budget fully replenishes.
  • Retry-After (on 429): The minimum wait duration in seconds before retrying. When thousands of callers exhaust a shared quota simultaneously, returning identical integer wait durations triggers a synchronized retry storm at the next second boundary. Gateways therefore inject small random jitter (+0 to 250 ms on sub-second resets or randomized backoff spreads) and client SDKs apply full-jitter exponential backoff.

Allowed response:

HTTP/2 200 OK
RateLimit-Limit: 100
RateLimit-Remaining: 42
RateLimit-Reset: 1

Throttled response (terminated at the gateway before reaching backend servers):

HTTP/2 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 2
RateLimit-Limit: 100
RateLimit-Remaining: 0
RateLimit-Reset: 2
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "/problems/rate-limit-exceeded",
  "title": "Too Many Requests",
  "status": 429,
  "detail": "Quota of 100 requests/s (burst 200) exceeded for route GET /v1/orders."
}

Internal Evaluation RPC and Policy Management API

Gateways query the stateless Rate Limiter Service over persistent HTTP/2 gRPC channels (ShouldRateLimitRequest carrying typed descriptors such as tenant=acct_42, route=GET:/v1/orders, and cost=1, returning {decision, remaining, reset_ms, leased_tokens}).

Operators manage policies through an idempotent control-plane API backed by durable relational or etcd storage:

PUT /v1/policies/acct_42/routes/orders HTTP/2
Host: ratelimit-control.internal
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "rate_per_second": 100,
  "burst_capacity": 200,
  "cost_unit": "requests",
  "failure_mode": "fail_open",
  "enforcement_mode": "enforce"
}

Separating durable Policy configuration from ephemeral QuotaState counters is foundational. Policy records change rarely, must survive restarts, and are read millions of times per second from gateway RAM. QuotaState mutates on every request and carries an automatic expiration TTL (ceil(burst / rate) + margin): losing a counter shard resets active callers to a fresh burst without corrupting any persistent business state.

7.3 System Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We decouple rule authoring and compilation (control plane) from per-request quota enforcement (data plane) so that a control-plane database upgrade or outage never degrades hot-path latency or availability (Figure 7-2).

Component Responsibilities and Failure Domains

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Policy API and Config DBControlAuthoritative versioned tenant and route rulesData plane continues enforcing its last compiled snapshot indefinitely; only policy edits pause
Rule Compiler and xDS PushControlImmutable compiled rule trie/hash bundlesStreams rule revisions to gateways over persistent gRPC/xDS connections with polling fallback
Shadow and Telemetry PipelineControlSampled allow/deny counters and Count-Min Sketch heavy-hitter mapsDecoupled via non-blocking ring buffers; never delays request handling
API Gateway (Envoy)DataAuthN verifier, compiled rules, L1 local quota leases, circuit breakerStateless multi-AZ fleet; rejects 429 traffic at ingress before upstream connection allocation
Rate Limiter Service (gRPC)DataStateless evaluator, Redis Cluster slot map, request coalescing buffersHorizontally auto-scaled across three AZs; may also run embedded inside the gateway process
Sharded Redis Cluster (3 AZs)DataPer-key GCRA TAT timestamps with TTL (8 B payload/key)Six primaries plus six cross-AZ replicas; gateway circuit breaker triggers route fallback within 5 ms on shard fault

Request Path Walkthrough

  1. Pre-Authentication Coarse Filter: Edge L4/L7 filters enforce generous per-IP/CIDR ceilings (via eBPF/XDP or gateway-local memory) to discard volumetric floods before JWT parsing or TLS handshake amplification consumes CPU.
  2. Identity and Key Derivation: The API Gateway authenticates the caller and constructs the canonical composite key (for example, {acct_42}:GET:/v1/orders).
  3. L1 Local Quota Lease Check: If the route permits local leasing and the gateway holds unexpired prefetched tokens in L1 RAM, it decrements atomically in ~10 microseconds and forwards immediately, refilling asynchronously in the background.
  4. Centralized Atomic Evaluation: For strict single-region routes or on an L1 lease miss, the gateway issues ShouldRateLimit (gRPC) to the Rate Limiter Service, which executes a pre-loaded Redis Lua script (EVALSHA) against the owning Redis Cluster shard.
  5. Enforcement and Response Headers: On ALLOW, the gateway forwards the request upstream and injects RateLimit-* headers into the reply. On DENY, the gateway returns 429 Too Many Requests immediately and optionally sets a short-TTL local negative cache entry if the caller is actively flooding.

7.4 Rate-Limiting Algorithms and GCRA Formulation

The natural-language specification “5 requests per second” admits multiple incompatible implementations until two degrees of freedom are fixed: burst tolerance (whether all 5 requests may arrive in the same millisecond or must be spaced evenly every 200 ms) and window alignment (calendar-aligned clock seconds versus every rolling 1,000 ms span).

Empirical Comparison of Classical Algorithms

The repository’s code/ratelimit simulation subjects five classical algorithms to identical traffic at 5 requests/s (20 simultaneous requests, 10 requests straddling the 1,000 ms clock boundary, and 30 requests arriving at 10 req/s over 3 seconds):

Interactive Step-by-Step Algorithm Walkthroughs

Advancing through the interactive traces below illustrates how four algorithms respond to the same 11 requests arriving between 600 ms and 1,250 ms across the 1,000 ms clock boundary under a 5 req/s quota:

Formal Derivation: Generic Cell Rate Algorithm (GCRA)

Standardized originally for Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) networks, the Generic Cell Rate Algorithm (GCRA) is mathematically isomorphic to a continuous-refill token bucket while collapsing its two mutable variables (tokens and last_refill_timestamp) into a single 64-bit integer timestamp termed the Theoretical Arrival Time (TAT) (Figure 7-3).

Given sustained rate R (requests/s) and burst capacity B (requests), we define the emission interval tau = 1 / R (the time required to earn one request slot) and the burst tolerance T = B * tau (when deducting cost prior to admission, or (B - 1) * tau when checking prior to incrementing). Intuitively, TAT records the instant at which the caller’s bucket will next be completely full. When a request of weight cost arrives at time t_now:

  1. Initialization: If no TAT exists (the caller has been idle longer than T), we initialize TAT = t_now.
  2. Candidate Advance: We compute new_tat = max(t_now, TAT) + cost * tau and the earliest admissible arrival time allow_at = new_tat - T.
  3. Admission Decision: We permit the request if and only if t_now >= allow_at. Upon admission, we persist new_tat with expiration TTL new_tat - t_now. Upon refusal, we leave TAT unchanged and return exact wait time retry_after = allow_at - t_now.

Atomic Redis Lua Contract and Implementation

Executing GET, computing new_tat inside a stateless gateway, and writing back via SET introduces a distributed Read-Modify-Write (RMW) race: two concurrent gateways reading an identical TAT both admit requests and overwrite one another’s updates, doubling effective burst allowance under concurrency.

Embedding GCRA inside a pre-cached Redis Lua script (EVALSHA) eliminates the RMW race because Redis executes Lua scripts atomically on its single-threaded event loop in one network round trip. Before examining the script below, note its input and output contract:

  • KEYS[1]: Composite key wrapped in a Redis Cluster hash tag ({tenant_id:route_id}) so multi-key policies hash to the exact same slot (CRC16(tag) mod 16384).
  • ARGV[1..3]: emission_interval_us (tau in microseconds), burst_tolerance_us (T in microseconds), and integer request cost (default 1).
  • Time Source: Calling redis.call("TIME") reads the Redis server’s clock directly, preventing NTP skew across gateway hosts from corrupting quotas.
  • Return Tuple: {allowed (0|1), remaining_tokens, retry_after_us}.
local now_parts = redis.call("TIME")
local now_us = tonumber(now_parts[1]) * 1000000 + tonumber(now_parts[2])

local tau   = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local tol   = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local cost  = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local incr  = cost * tau

local tat = tonumber(redis.call("GET", KEYS[1])) or now_us
local new_tat = math.max(tat, now_us) + incr
local allow_at = new_tat - tol

if now_us < allow_at then
    local retry_after_us = allow_at - now_us
    return { 0, 0, retry_after_us }
end

local ttl_ms = math.max(1000, math.ceil((new_tat - now_us) / 1000))
redis.call("PSETEX", KEYS[1], ttl_ms, new_tat)

local remaining = math.floor((now_us - (new_tat - tol)) / tau)
return { 1, remaining, 0 }

Self-cleaning TTLs via PSETEX ensure that idle keys disappear automatically once their burst capacity has replenished (new_tat - now_us), bounding Redis memory strictly to currently active callers.

7.5 Distributed Synchronization, Hot Keys, and Multi-Region Scaling

Synchronous Redis Lua evaluation satisfies 50,000-250,000 RPS within a single geographic region, but two operational regimes exceed its bounds: extreme hot keys (a single tenant driving 100,000+ RPS onto one Redis primary core) and multi-region active-active deployments (where synchronous cross-WAN RTT of 60-150 ms breaks the 1 ms latency SLO by two orders of magnitude). We select among three synchronization topologies by route tier (Figure 7-4).

Local Quota Leasing (Batch Token Prefetching)

Under local quota leasing, each gateway amortizes network round trips by reserving a small batch of k tokens (for example, k = 50 or 1% of the tenant’s per-second quota, capped at a 100 ms lease TTL) in one Redis Lua invocation (cost = k). Subsequent requests decrement a lock-free atomic counter (AtomicI64) in gateway RAM in ~10 microseconds, triggering an asynchronous background refill when remaining local tokens fall below 20%.

This pattern reduces Redis QPS by 10x-50x and lifts single-key ceilings into millions of RPS. Its cost is an explicit, mathematically bounded overshoot: if N gateways simultaneously hold unexpired leases of size k, instantaneous overshoot cannot exceed N * k. Gateways therefore adapt k dynamically from observed per-key QPS (k = 1 for low-rate security endpoints, scaling upward only for hot public-API keys).

Multi-Region Global Quotas

Active-active deployments across US-East, EU-West, and AP-Southeast execute all hot-path checks against regional Redis Clusters (< 1 ms RTT) and reconcile global usage off the request path through two mechanisms:

  1. Asynchronous Delta-CRDT / Gossip Sync: Each region broadcasts compact per-key usage deltas (PN-Counter or window increments) to peer regions every 100-500 ms. Worst-case global overshoot during a simultaneous multi-region spike is bounded linearly by R_burst * sync_interval.
  2. Dynamic Regional Quota Allocation: A control-plane loop monitors each region’s traffic proportion every few seconds and assigns proportional local sub-budgets (for example, US: 60%, EU: 30%, AP: 10%), rapidly shifting unused quota when traffic moves across continents.

7.6 Defense-in-Depth: Failure Policies, Keying, and Load Shedding

Rate limiting is one layer in a broader traffic-control hierarchy (Figure 7-5). Applying one blanket fallback rule to every endpoint, or expecting per-caller quotas to prevent aggregate overload, leads directly to avoidable outages.

Tiered Failure Policies (Fail-Open vs. Fail-Closed)

When a Redis shard becomes unreachable, the gateway circuit breaker opens within 5 ms and executes the route’s declared failure contract:

  • Fail-Open with Local Fallback (General and Revenue APIs): Catalog, search, and read endpoints continue serving traffic guarded by an in-process per-gateway local token bucket configured to max(1, global_limit / active_gateway_count). A counter-store fault never disrupts normal business traffic.
  • Fail-Closed (Security and High-Cost Endpoints): Login, OTP verification, password reset, and high-cost compute or payment creation routes reject calls with 503 Service Unavailable and Retry-After if global enforcement is blind, preventing credential-stuffing attacks or unbounded third-party billing.

Composite Key Selection

Key design governs both fairness and abuse resistance. Keying exclusively by IP address fails in both directions: corporate proxies, universities, and carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT) aggregate thousands of legitimate users behind one IP address (causing widespread collateral refusals), whereas distributed botnets rotate across tens of thousands of residential IPs. Production gateways reserve IP-keyed limits strictly for coarse pre-authentication DDoS defense, authenticate callers first, and key primary quotas on (tenant_id, route_group) weighted by explicit request cost (cost = 1 for a point lookup, cost = 25 for a bulk export).

Rate Limiting vs. Adaptive Load Shedding

Even if every tenant respects its individual quota, 10,000 legitimate tenants arriving concurrently during a global traffic spike can saturate a downstream database. Backend services therefore complement ingress rate limiting with adaptive concurrency limiting grounded in Little’s Law (L = lambda * W, relating concurrency L, arrival rate lambda, and service time W):

  • AIMD Concurrency Control: Services continuously track baseline minimum latency (RTT_noload) against current queueing latency, increasing their in-flight concurrency ceiling additively while latency stays flat and reducing it multiplicatively as soon as queue depth builds.
  • CoDel and Priority Shedding: Controlled Delay (CoDel) monitors request sojourn time inside work queues and sheds queued work exceeding a latency threshold, prioritizing P0 interactive checkout calls over P3 batch exports and scrapers to bound p999 tail latency.

7.7 Failure Modes, Observability, Production Systems, and Verification

Single Hot-Key Flood (100k+ RPS)One Redis shard core saturates at 100% CPU, elevating p99 for co-located tenantsGateway activates L1 local quota leasing (k = 50) plus 500 ms local negative caching on rejected keys, shielding the shard

Observability: SLIs and Alerts

Four operational signals govern day-two reliability: hot-path latency SLI (p99 check duration alerted above 1.0 ms for 5 minutes), circuit-breaker activation alerts (ratelimit_circuit_breaker_open_total > 0, ensuring fail-open fallback never masks a prolonged counter outage), per-route throttle ratios paired with a Count-Min Sketch of top-throttled keys (distinguishing one runaway client from a misconfigured global rule), and shadow-mode delta dashboards verifying hypothetical 429 volume before promoting any policy from shadow to enforce.

Chapter 8: Unique ID Generator

Nearly every record in a distributed storage system requires an unambiguous primary key so that orders, invoices, ledger entries, and foreign-key indexes reference exactly one entity across the lifetime of the platform. On a single relational database, a monotonic BIGSERIAL or AUTO_INCREMENT sequence satisfies uniqueness, compactness, and chronological sort order in one atomic page increment. Once we shard writes across dozens of database nodes and multiple availability zones, routing every record creation through one central sequence reintroduces both a throughput bottleneck and a single point of failure.

In this chapter, I design a distributed 64-bit unique identifier generator that produces roughly time-ordered keys without cross-node coordination on the request path. We begin by establishing requirements, actors, and capacity bounds, then specify wire contracts and separate Raft-backed worker-ID leasing (control plane) from lock-free local generation (data plane). In the deep dives, we derive the 64-bit Snowflake bit budget, compare it against ticket servers, range-block allocators, and UUIDv7, and harden the generator against NTP backward clock steps, leap seconds, and crash-restart reuse using monotonic guards, disk epoch checkpoints, and Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, functional contracts, sub-millisecond latency SLOs, non-goals, and arithmetic capacity bounds
  • HTTP/gRPC single and batched allocation contracts, 64-bit integer string encoding for JSON safety, and lease schemas
  • separation of consensus-backed worker-ID leasing (control plane) from shared-nothing local generation (data plane)
  • comparative analysis of database counters, multi-master ticket servers, range-block allocators, UUIDv4, UUIDv7, and 64-bit Snowflake layouts
  • bit-level Snowflake allocation, per-millisecond sequence exhaustion, B-tree append locality, and range-sharded hotspot trade-offs
  • defenses against NTP clock regressions, leap seconds, VM restarts, and worker-ID collisions via epoch checkpoints and Hybrid Logical Clocks
  • operational failure modes, SLIs, production deployments (Twitter Snowflake, Instagram, Discord, Sonyflake), and simulation verification

8.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Actors and Use Cases

We organize the unique ID generator around three operational actors: application services requesting identifiers on the hot write path, generator nodes leasing exclusive worker slots during startup, and platform operators auditing clock skew and sequence saturation (Figure 8-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Application ServiceRequest single ID (GET /v1/ids/next) or batch (POST /v1/ids/batch)Mint primary keys for newly created orders, chat messages, or telemetry events across sharded databases
Application ServiceDecode embedded metadataExtract creation timestamp and originating node bits during incident triage or time-range log correlation
Generator NodeLease and renew a 10-bit worker_id (0 to 1023)Acquire an exclusive worker slot from the etcd control plane at process startup and checkpoint its high-water timestamp
Platform OperatorMonitor clock drift, sequence exhaustion, and lease churnDetect NTP stepping faults or approaching sequence saturation before client requests experience wait delays

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0We guarantee global uniqueness across all active, retired, and restarted generator nodes for the entire operational lifetime of the system.
1Every generated identifier fits inside a signed 64-bit integer (int64, non-negative 0 to 2^63 - 1) so it maps natively to relational BIGINT primary keys and compact B-tree indexes.
2Identifiers are roughly time-ordered (k-sortable): an ID minted later sorts numerically greater than an ID minted earlier whenever their creation times differ by more than the maximum inter-node clock skew.
3The service supports both single-ID allocation and batched block allocation (count up to 4,096 per call) over HTTP/2 and gRPC, as well as an embeddable in-process library mode.
4Any node can decode the creation timestamp (millisecond precision), datacenter/worker identifier, and per-millisecond sequence number directly from an ID without external lookups.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0Latencyp50 <= 0.2 ms, p99 <= 1.0 ms over local-AZ RPC; < 1 microsecond embedded in-processProhibits cross-node consensus or database round trips on the generation path; generation uses strictly local memory and atomic instructions
1Availability99.999% data-plane availability (<= 5.26 minutes/year downtime)Shared-nothing fleet across three availability zones; an active generator continues minting IDs even if the control plane and all peer generators fail
2Throughput and ScaleSustained 1,000,000 IDs/s cluster-wide; peak 4,096,000 IDs/s per generator node across up to 1,024 nodesRequires a 12-bit per-millisecond sequence counter (2^12 = 4,096 IDs/ms/node) and a 10-bit worker address space
3Uniqueness ConsistencyAbsolute (zero duplicates under crashes, restarts, and NTP regressions)Requires linearizable Raft-backed worker_id leasing at startup, monotonic clock guards in RAM, and durable high-water timestamp checkpoints
4Ordering ConsistencyApproximate across hosts (bounded by inter-node NTP skew, typically 2 to 20 ms); strict within one nodeCallers requiring causal or total order across nodes must obtain sequence numbers from a consensus log rather than inferring causality from IDs

Non-Goals and Scope Boundaries

To keep the generation path fast and verifiable, we exclude the following properties from this system:

  • Strict gap-free sequentiality: Sequence numbers reset to 0 on every millisecond tick, and idle milliseconds produce numeric gaps. Callers must never subtract two IDs to count records.
  • Cryptographic unpredictability: Time-prefixed IDs are enumerable and expose millisecond creation timestamps. Authentication tokens, password-reset links, and public unguessable slugs require a separate CSPRNG token generator (at least 128 random bits).
  • Cross-node causal ordering: Physical clocks drift across hosts. We do not attempt to use ID comparisons as a substitute for vector clocks, Lamport timestamps, or database transaction commit order.
  • Dynamic bit-field resizing after launch: Reassigning bit widths between timestamp, worker, and sequence fields after issuing production IDs risks overlapping numeric ranges.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

We size the bit budget, throughput ceiling, network bandwidth, and control-plane state from first principles before writing a schema:

Resource DimensionArithmetic DerivationProvisioned Bound
Timestamp Horizon (41 bits)2^41 ms / (1,000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 365.25)69.73 years from custom epoch (for example, 2025-01-01T00:00:00Z lasts until 2094)
Per-Node Peak Rate (12 bits)2^12 = 4,096 IDs/ms * 1,000 ms/s4,096,000 IDs/s per generator node
Cluster Maximum Rate (10 bits)2^10 = 1,024 nodes * 4,096,000 IDs/s4.19 billion IDs/s theoretical ceiling
Baseline Fleet Sizing1,000,000 IDs/s target at <= 25% per-node capacity load across 3 AZs12 generator nodes (4 per AZ, ~83,333 IDs/s/node; ~2% of 4.09M ceiling, leaving huge burst headroom)
RPC Network Bandwidth1,000,000 single calls/s * 128 B gRPC frame (or 10,000 batches of 100 IDs * 1 KB)128 MB/s (1.02 Gbps) single-call; 10 MB/s (80 Mbps) batched
