Even 12 lightweight generator instances sustain an order of magnitude above our 1,000,000 IDs/s baseline while leaving over 1,000 worker slots spare for rolling deployments, canary instances, and cooldown quarantine windows.

8.2 External API and Data Contracts

We expose a binary gRPC interface for internal microservices, an HTTP/2 REST API for language-agnostic clients, and an embeddable library interface for ultra-low-latency callers that register directly as leased workers.

External HTTP/2 and gRPC Contracts

Whenever an ID travels over JSON, we serialize the 64-bit integer as a decimal string. IEEE 754 double-precision floating-point numbers used by JavaScript engines and many JSON parsers represent integers exactly only up to 2^53 - 1 (9,007,199,254,740,991). Returning a raw 64-bit JSON number causes browsers to round distinct IDs to the same value, corrupting client-side state.

Single ID allocation (GET /v1/ids/next):

GET /v1/ids/next HTTP/2
Host: idgen.internal
Accept: application/json

HTTP/2 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
X-Worker-Id: 7

{
  "id": "8388636672",
  "timestamp_ms": 2000,
  "worker_id": 7,
  "sequence": 0
}

Batched ID allocation (POST /v1/ids/batch):

Batching amortizes network round trips and allows callers to keep a small local buffer without maintaining their own etcd lease. An Idempotency-Key header prevents retries from double-charging accounting quotas, though minting a fresh unused ID is harmless for uniqueness.

POST /v1/ids/batch HTTP/2
Host: idgen.internal
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: checkout-pod-19-batch-402

{
  "count": 100
}

HTTP/2 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "ids": ["8388636672", "8388636673"],
  "count": 100,
  "worker_id": 7
}

When a generator node detects a severe backward clock jump exceeding its safe wait threshold (for example, > 15 ms), it rejects requests immediately with 503 Service Unavailable and Retry-After: 1 while removing itself from load-balancer health checks so local-AZ routers fail over to healthy peers.

Internal gRPC contract (Protocol Buffers):

syntax = "proto3";
package idgen.v1;

service IdGeneratorService {
  rpc NextId(NextIdRequest) returns (NextIdResponse);
  rpc NextBatch(NextBatchRequest) returns (NextBatchResponse);
}

message NextIdRequest {}
message NextIdResponse {
  int64 id = 1; // Wire-encoded as varint/fixed64; zero precision loss in gRPC
}

message NextBatchRequest {
  uint32 count = 1; // Bounded to [1, 4096]
}
message NextBatchResponse {
  repeated int64 ids = 1;
}

Control-Plane Lease and Checkpoint Schema

In the etcd control plane, we maintain two key namespaces per worker slot w in [0, 1023]:

/idgen/workers/{worker_id}/lease      -> { "host": "az-a-node-04", "lease_id": 918273, "started_at_ms": 1763612000000 }  [TTL = 30s]
/idgen/workers/{worker_id}/checkpoint -> { "max_ts_ms": 1763612045000, "retired_at_ms": 0 }                                [Persistent]

The /lease key is attached to an etcd ephemeral lease (TTL = 30 s, renewed every 10 s). The /checkpoint key persists indefinitely so that no future host acquiring worker_id can ever mint an ID at a millisecond earlier than max_ts_ms.

8.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We decouple worker-ID assignment and high-water epoch persistence (control plane) from per-request identifier generation (data plane). Once a generator node holds a valid 10-bit worker ID, it performs zero network I/O to produce identifiers (Figure 8-2).

Component Responsibilities and Failure Domains

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Worker-ID Lease Coordinator (3-node etcd)ControlAuthoritative map of leased worker_id slots (0 to 1023) and durable max_ts_ms checkpointsTolerates 1 node failure transparently. If quorum is lost, running generators continue minting IDs uninterrupted; only new node startups pause until quorum returns
Epoch Checkpoint StoreControlHighest timestamp horizon promised by each worker slot, updated asynchronously every 2 to 5 sPrevents a restarted or reassigned worker from reusing timestamps after a backward NTP correction
Zone-Aware Edge Router (L7 Proxy)DataStateless routing table with local-AZ affinity and active health probesKeeps caller RTT below 0.5 ms by preferring same-AZ generators; automatically drains any node reporting clock regression (503)
Snowflake Generator Fleet (Multi-AZ)DataLeased 10-bit worker_id, atomic (last_ms, sequence) 64-bit state word, local disk checkpoint fileShared-nothing across nodes. Losing one node reduces fleet capacity by 1/N with zero coordination overhead and zero lost uniqueness

Hot Data Path Walkthrough

  1. Startup Lease Acquisition (Off Hot Path): When a generator starts, it runs a compare-and-swap transaction in etcd to claim an unleased worker_id whose quarantine cooldown (retired_at_ms + 60,000 ms) has elapsed. It reads checkpoint.max_ts_ms and refuses to mark itself healthy until its local wall clock strictly exceeds max_ts_ms.
  2. Zone-Local Request Routing: An application service sends NextId or NextBatch over a persistent HTTP/2 gRPC channel to a same-AZ generator (or calls the in-process library directly).
  3. Lock-Free Bit Packing: The generator reads its wall clock and monotonic clock delta, verifies the timestamp has not regressed below last_ms, increments sequence (wrapping and awaiting the next millisecond if sequence == 4096), and packs the 64-bit integer in nanoseconds.
  4. Periodic Horizon Checkpointing (Background): A background thread writes now_ms + 5,000 ms to local disk and etcd every 2 seconds. If the process crashes and restarts within 5 seconds on a drifted clock, startup recovery waits until the clock clears the persisted horizon.

8.4 Comparative Design Space and 64-Bit Snowflake Layout

Before committing to a composite time-worker-sequence layout, we evaluate the four classical families of distributed ID generation against our requirements.

Comparing the Four Classical Approaches

  1. Single Database Sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT): Produces compact, gap-free 64-bit integers with exact global ordering. However, every write across the entire platform must serialize on one primary database instance, turning ID generation into a global availability bottleneck.
  2. Multi-Master Ticket Servers (Flickr Pattern): Deploying N databases where server i starts at i and steps by N (1, 3, 5... and 2, 4, 6...) removes the single point of failure. Its operational weakness is rigidity: changing N online requires coordinated step reconfiguration without range overlap, and cross-node time order disappears as traffic skews between masters.
  3. Coordinator Range-Block Allocator (Segment Mode): A durable coordinator hands out blocks of 1,000 to 10,000 contiguous integers to each worker, reducing coordinator RPCs by three to four orders of magnitude. Double-buffering (prefetching the next block at 20% remaining) hides network stalls. However, worker crashes discard unused block tails, and IDs from slow workers lag far behind busy workers, destroying chronological ordering.
  4. Random and Time-Prefixed 128-Bit UUIDs (UUIDv4 and UUIDv7):
    • UUIDv4 uses 122 random bits and requires zero coordination. By the birthday paradox, generating 10^15 IDs (1,000,000 IDs/s for 31.7 years) yields a collision probability of roughly n^2 / 2^123, or ~1 in 10,000,000. Its practical costs are double storage overhead (16 bytes in every primary key, foreign key, and secondary index) and uniform random distribution across B-tree leaf pages. Once an index outgrows RAM, random primary-key inserts trigger a disk read and dirty-page eviction on nearly every write.
    • UUIDv7 (RFC 9562, 2024) places a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp in the most significant bits followed by 4 version bits, 12 sub-millisecond/counter bits, 2 variant bits, and 62 random bits. UUIDv7 restores B-tree append locality while keeping zero startup coordination. Its sole drawback for our contract is size: 128 bits cannot fit in a 64-bit BIGINT column.
DimensionSingle DB SequenceTicket Servers (step = N)Range Blocks (Segment)UUIDv4 (128-bit)UUIDv7 (128-bit)64-Bit Snowflake (Chosen)
Width64 bits64 bits64 bits128 bits128 bits64 bits
Hot-Path Network I/O1 RTT per ID1 RTT per ID1 RTT per blockNoneNoneNone
Time OrderingExactNoneNoneNoneK-sorted (ms)K-sorted (ms)
B-Tree Index LocalitySequential appendSequential per shardFragmented by workerRandom page thrashingSequential appendSequential append
Control-Plane OutageTotal outageSurvives N - 1 lossContinues until block emptiesUnaffectedUnaffectedRunning nodes unaffected
Primary Failure HazardSPOF bottleneckRigid cluster resizingGaps and cross-node skewCloned PRNG seed; index bloat16 B key footprintDuplicate worker_id or clock rollback

We choose the 64-bit Snowflake layout because requirement 1 mandates a 64-bit integer key, requirement 2 demands k-sortable B-tree locality, and non-functional requirement 1 demands zero hot-path network coordination.

64-Bit Field Layout and Uniqueness Proof

Figure 8-3 details the bit allocation across the 64-bit signed big-endian integer:

  • Bit 63 (1 bit, sign): Permanently 0 so the value stays non-negative across signed 64-bit integer types in Java, PostgreSQL (BIGINT), and Go (int64).
  • Bits 62..22 (41 bits, timestamp): Milliseconds elapsed since a custom system epoch (epoch_ms). Placing the timestamp in the most significant bits ensures that ordinary integer comparison orders IDs chronologically.
  • Bits 21..12 (10 bits, datacenter and worker ID): Uniquely identifies up to 1,024 concurrent generator instances (commonly split into 3 to 5 bits for datacenter/AZ and 5 to 7 bits for host slot so operators can identify the originating zone by bitmasking).
  • Bits 11..0 (12 bits, per-millisecond sequence): Monotonically increments from 0 to 4,095 within each millisecond on a given node and resets to 0 on the next millisecond tick.
id = ((timestamp_ms - epoch_ms) << 22) | (worker_id << 12) | sequence

Uniqueness follows by case analysis on any two identifiers A and B:

  1. If A and B are generated by different nodes, they differ in bits 21..12, provided Invariant 1 holds: no two active generators share the same worker_id within the same clock window.
  2. If A and B are generated by the same node in different milliseconds, they differ in bits 62..22, provided Invariant 2 holds: the node’s emitted timestamp never returns to a millisecond it has already used.
  3. If A and B are generated by the same node in the same millisecond, they differ in bits 11..0, provided Invariant 3 holds: the node never lets the 12-bit sequence overflow into the adjacent worker_id bits.

Advancing through Interactive Trace 8.A demonstrates two independent nodes minting six globally unique, roughly time-ordered IDs with zero inter-node communication:

When a busy node exhausts all 4,096 sequence values in a single millisecond, letting the 12-bit counter wrap or carry into bit 12 would corrupt the worker_id field without warning and impersonate a neighboring node. Instead, the generator spins or yields until the clock advances to last_ms + 1 and resets sequence = 0, bounding caller delay to under 1 ms.

Storage Engine Trade-Off: B-Tree Locality vs. Range-Partitioned Hotspots

On single-primary or hash-sharded databases backed by B-trees (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, RocksDB memtables), time-prefixed Snowflake keys append exclusively to the rightmost leaf page. The working set of dirty index pages stays compact in RAM, avoiding random disk I/O.

In range-partitioned distributed databases such as Google Cloud Spanner, CockroachDB, and Bigtable, monotonically increasing primary keys create the opposite pathology: every write across the entire cluster targets the single rightmost tablet range, saturating one storage server while all other tablets sit idle. For range-partitioned stores, engineers either prepend a shard hash prefix (hash(tenant_id) mod S), composite-key on (tenant_id, snowflake_id), or bit-reverse the timestamp prefix to scatter inserts evenly across tablets.

8.5 Clock Regression, Crash Recovery, and Worker-ID Safety

Because Snowflake trades network coordination for local invariants, violating Invariant 1 or Invariant 2 causes duplicate IDs without triggering any runtime exception inside the generator. Production systems harden all three failure surfaces systematically.

Handling NTP Backward Steps and Leap Seconds

Hardware quartz oscillators drift by 10 to 100 parts per million (~1 to 8 seconds per day). Time synchronization daemons (chronyd, ntpd) correct drift either by slewing (adjusting clock frequency smoothly without jumping backward) or by stepping (jumping CLOCK_REALTIME backward abruptly when offset exceeds a threshold, or during an unsmeared POSIX leap second).

Interactive Trace 8.B walks through a 3 ms backward wall-clock jump and the generator’s refusal to reuse millisecond 2000:

We implement a tiered clock-regression policy using both CLOCK_REALTIME (for epoch alignment) and CLOCK_MONOTONIC (which the OS kernel guarantees never moves backward):

  1. Zero-Regression Normal Operation via Monotonic Anchoring: At startup, the generator anchors (anchor_wall_ms, anchor_mono) once. During operation, it advances timestamps via anchor_wall_ms + elapsed(anchor_mono), slewing gently toward CLOCK_REALTIME only when wall time moves ahead. Small backward NTP steps on CLOCK_REALTIME never cause the emitted timestamp to step backward.
  2. Tier 1 Small Drift (delta <= 15 ms): If a raw wall-clock check detects a small regression (now_ms < last_ms by <= 15 ms), the generator waits 2 * delta milliseconds for physical time to catch up before issuing the next ID.
  3. Tier 2 Medium Drift (15 ms < delta <= 500 ms) via Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC) Borrowing: Rather than stalling callers, an HLC-enhanced generator keeps its logical timestamp pinned at last_ms and continues incrementing the 12-bit sequence (or borrows 1 ms forward) up to a strict drift ceiling (500 ms), emitting an urgent metric so operators inspect NTP health.
  4. Tier 3 Severe Drift (delta > 500 ms): The node fails its readiness probe, rejects requests with 503 Service Unavailable, and alerts SRE immediately. Accepting multi-second future drift risks breaking k-ordering guarantees and exhausting timestamp headroom.
  5. Leap-Second Smearing: Fleet NTP servers must run uniform leap-second smearing (spreading the extra second over 24 hours, as practiced by Google and AWS Time Sync Service) so CLOCK_REALTIME never repeats a full second.

Surviving Restarts and Preventing Worker-ID Collisions

In-memory last_ms state vanishes on a crash or container restart. Consider a generator that mints an ID at t = 5000 ms, crashes, suffers a 50 ms backward NTP step during host reboot, and restarts at t = 4970 ms. Without durable state, it would reissue IDs for milliseconds 4970 through 5000.

We close this window with three coordinated mechanisms:

  1. Future-Horizon Checkpointing: Every 2 seconds, each generator asynchronously persists horizon_ms = now_ms + 5,000 ms to local NVMe and to its etcd /checkpoint record. On startup, the node reads max(local_horizon, etcd_horizon) and sleeps until its clock exceeds that horizon (or fails startup if the delta exceeds 10 seconds).
  2. Lease-Backed Exclusive worker_id Ownership: We never derive worker_id from ephemeral IP octets or static VM templates that can be cloned. Instead, each generator acquires an ephemeral etcd lease (TTL = 30 s, renewed every 10 s). If the node loses lease connectivity and cannot renew within 20 s (before the 30 s server expiry), it self-fences immediately and stops issuing IDs, eliminating split-brain dual ownership.
  3. Quarantine Cooldown on Slot Reuse: When a worker lease expires or releases cleanly, the control plane marks retired_at_ms = now_ms and forbids reassigning that worker_id to any other host for 60 seconds (far exceeding maximum inter-node NTP skew). With 1,024 slots and 12 to 100 active nodes, plenty of fresh slots remain available for immediate replacement startups.

Security, Privacy, and Information Leakage

Because Snowflake IDs encode creation time and worker origin in plaintext, external clients can inspect traffic volume and record creation times. Where business confidentiality forbids exposing timestamps or insertion volume (for example, external invoice URLs or tenant counts), we keep Snowflake as the internal BIGINT clustered primary key for database speed and map it at the API boundary through either a format-preserving cipher (such as Feistel permutation over 64 bits) or a separate random public UUID column. Regardless of ID format, endpoints must always enforce explicit authorization checks and never treat an identifier as a capability secret.

8.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ModeOperational SymptomAutomated Mitigation
Small NTP Backward Step (<= 15 ms)Brief 1 to 15 ms tail latency bump on affected nodeMonotonic clock anchoring prevents timestamp rollback; fallback wait loop pauses until now_ms > last_ms
Severe Clock Jump (> 500 ms)Node returns 503 Service Unavailable and logs clock-fault alertReadiness probe fails within 2 s; local-AZ proxy shifts traffic to healthy peers; operator repairs chronyd
Control-Plane (etcd) Quorum LossNew generator pods block in startup; existing fleet latency unaffectedActive generators keep serving from local memory while leases remain valid; alerts page on-call to restore etcd before lease expiry
Per-Millisecond Sequence Exhaustion (> 4,096/ms)Micro-burst callers experience < 1 ms wait on one nodeSequence overflow check blocks until next millisecond tick; autoscaler adds generator pods if sequence_high_water > 3,000
Generator Crash and Rapid RestartBrief pod restart; risk of clock overlap with prior processStartup checks persisted horizon_ms checkpoint and sleeps until clock clears the high-water mark before accepting traffic
Split-Brain Worker Lease ExpiryNetwork partition isolates a generator from etcdGenerator self-fences after 20 s without renewal (10 s safety margin before 30 s lease expiry); control plane quarantines slot for 60 s

Key SLIs and Operational Alerts

We monitor four production signals continuously:

  • Generation Latency SLI: p99 <= 1.0 ms over local-AZ gRPC (alert if p99 > 2.0 ms for 5 minutes).
  • Clock Skew and Regression Counter: idgen_clock_backward_ms_total and host NTP offset (alert if NTP offset exceeds 10 ms or any backward step > 5 ms occurs).
  • Sequence Saturation Ratio: max(sequence_per_ms) / 4096 per node (page at > 75% sustained so we scale out before microsecond throttling begins).
  • Lease Renewal Headroom: lease_ttl_remaining_seconds (alert if any active generator drops below 15 s, well ahead of its 10 s self-fencing cutoff).

Real-World Production Systems

Instagram Sharded IDs (2012)41 ms + 13 logical shard + 10 seq (64-bit)Embedded PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL function per logical shardZero external ID service; database shards mint IDs directly inside INSERT triggers
Discord Snowflake42 ms (epoch 2015-01-01) + 5 worker + 5 process + 12 seqCluster configuration and process managerEmbeds worker and process identity for tracing across Elixir/Rust message pipelines
Sonyflake (Sony)39 bits (10 ms units, 174 yr) + 8 seq + 16 machine (64-bit)Lower 16 bits of private IPv4 (or custom callback)Trades per-ms burst capacity (256 / 10 ms) for 65,536 machines and a 174-year lifetime
Meituan Leaf (Segment + Snowflake)Dual mode: DB range blocks and ZooKeeper SnowflakeZooKeeper persistent sequential nodes + local disk cacheCombines future-timestamp checkpointing with dual-buffer segment caching for heterogeneous workloads

8.7 Simulation Verification

To validate per-millisecond sequence exhaustion, global uniqueness across independent nodes, chronological ordering, and backward clock-step refusal, we execute the repository’s idgen simulation (code/idgen/src/main.rs). The test drives 3 independent generator nodes, requesting 5,000 IDs per node across 100 milliseconds (1,500,000 total requests), and then injects a 2 ms backward clock jump on node 7:

$ cargo run --release -p idgen
ids made: 1228800, different ids: 1228800
requests refused because a millisecond was full: 271200
node 7 at time 2000: Some(8388636672), then Some(8388636673)
node 7 at time 2001: Some(8392830976)
node 7 at time 1999, after its clock went back: None
ids sort by time: true

Three exact invariants emerge from the observed output:

  1. Zero Collisions Under Exhaustion: 3 nodes * 100 ms * 4,096 IDs/ms = 1,228,800 minted IDs, with 1,228,800 distinct values (0 duplicates). The excess 3 * 100 * (5,000 - 4,096) = 271,200 calls are cleanly refused rather than overflowing into the worker-ID bits.
  2. Bit-Exact Encoding: At t = 2000 ms, worker_id = 7, seq = 0, (2000 << 22) | (7 << 12) | 0 = 8,388,608,000 + 28,672 = 8,388,636,672, followed by 8,388,636,673 for seq = 1, and 8,392,830,976 at t = 2001 ms.
  3. Strict Monotonic Guard: When node 7 observes t = 1999 ms after already emitting at t = 2001 ms, it returns None instead of reissuing IDs from a past millisecond.

Run the unique ID generator simulation. Execute cargo run --release -p idgen in code/ (code/idgen/src/main.rs) to reproduce the 1,228,800-ID uniqueness, sequence-exhaustion, and clock-regression checks above.

8.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Snowflake IDA 64-bit composite integer concatenating a sign bit (0), a millisecond timestamp, a unique node/worker identifier, and a per-millisecond sequence counter.
K-Sortable (Roughly Time-Ordered)An ordering property where any two identifiers separated by more than the maximum inter-node clock skew sort in true chronological order.
Monotonic Clock (CLOCK_MONOTONIC)An OS-provided elapsed-time counter guaranteed never to step backward, used to measure elapsed duration safely across NTP adjustments.
Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC)A timestamp mechanism combining physical wall time with a logical counter so timestamps remain monotonic and close to physical time even across small clock regressions.
Self-FencingA generator node voluntarily halting ID allocation before its control-plane lease expires when heartbeat renewal fails, preventing dual worker-ID ownership.
Epoch CheckpointA durably persisted high-water timestamp horizon that prevents a crashed and restarted node from emitting IDs earlier than timestamps used before the crash.
UUIDv7 (RFC 9562)A 128-bit universally unique identifier embedding a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp in its leading bits to preserve B-tree index locality.
Leap-Second SmearingGradually slewing NTP clock frequency over hours to absorb an inserted leap second without repeating a second on CLOCK_REALTIME.

Chapter 9: Distributed Cache

Every read against a durable database pays for disk I/O, index traversal, lock acquisition, or multi-table joins. When thousands of callers request the same product catalog item or user profile within a few seconds, repeating identical database work wastes backend CPU and bounds overall platform throughput to storage IOPS. A distributed cache keeps hot copies in RAM across a fleet of memory-optimized nodes, answering repeat reads in under a millisecond and insulating backing databases from 90% to 99% of aggregate read volume.

That speedup creates a subtle architectural dependency. Every cached value is a mutable copy that can diverge from its source of truth, memory is finite so the cache must continuously evict entries, and a database sized for 1% of read traffic collapses immediately if a cold restart or synchronized expiry drops the hit ratio to 0%. In this chapter, I design a horizontally sharded distributed cache from first principles. We establish capacity bounds and wire contracts, separate ring-membership management (control plane) from sub-millisecond data lookup (data plane), analyze eviction policies from LRU to W-TinyLFU, and engineer defenses against stale-value races, thundering-herd stampedes, hot-key skew, penetration, and cascading avalanches.

In this chapter, we cover

  • hit-ratio amplification arithmetic, actors, functional contracts, sub-millisecond latency SLOs, non-goals, and fleet memory sizing
  • binary/HTTP cache-aside wire contracts, conditional lease tokens (CAS), and CDC-driven invalidation interfaces
  • separation of consistent hash ring membership and hot-key detection (control plane) from direct-routed in-memory serving (data plane)
  • cache topologies (cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind) and eviction mechanics (LRU, LFU, Sampled-LRU, and W-TinyLFU)
  • consistent hashing with virtual nodes and bounded loads, hot-key L1 near-caching, and key replication
  • stampede defense via singleflight request coalescing and probabilistic early expiration (XFetch), plus cache-aside race prevention, Bloom filters, and TTL jitter
  • failure recovery (gutter pools, cold-cluster warmup), SLIs, production architectures (Facebook Memcache/Mcrouter, Redis, Caffeine), and simulation verification

9.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Actors and Use Cases

We organize the distributed cache around three actors: application services reading and invalidating cached entries, an asynchronous Change Data Capture (CDC) invalidation pipeline draining database commit logs, and platform operators managing cluster ring membership and eviction health (Figure 9-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Application ServiceLookup (GET), populate (SET with TTL), and delete (DEL)Serve user profiles and product pages in < 1 ms while collapsing concurrent cold misses through singleflight
CDC Invalidation WorkerStream committed database writes to cache DEL commandsRemove stale cache entries reliably even when an application process crashes immediately after committing a database transaction
Platform OperatorScale ring membership, warm replacement nodes, and tune evictionAdd cache shards with minimal key migration using virtual nodes and track hit ratios, eviction rates, and hot-key skew

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0Callers can store an opaque byte value under a string key with a mandatory positive Time-To-Live (TTL) expiration bound.
1Callers can fetch a single key or a pipelined batch of keys (MGET), receiving either the cached payload or an explicit miss response.
2Callers and CDC pipelines can explicitly delete keys (DEL) and execute conditional lease-guarded fills (CAS / lease token) to prevent stale writes from overwriting newer invalidations.
3When a cache node reaches its memory ceiling, it evicts entries automatically according to an admission and eviction policy (LRU or W-TinyLFU) without blocking concurrent reads.
4The client routing layer coalesces concurrent cache misses for the same key (singleflight) and supports probabilistic early refresh to protect backing databases from stampedes.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0Latencyp50 <= 0.3 ms, p99 <= 1.0 ms, p999 <= 3.0 ms (intra-AZ)Pure in-memory storage, persistent connection pools, direct single-hop client-to-shard routing via smart client or local proxy (zero central load balancer hop)
1Throughput and Capacity100 GB active working set; 200,000 sustained reads/s (600,000 peak burst reads/s)Sharded across 8 memory-optimized cache nodes (16 GB RAM each) using consistent hashing with 256 virtual nodes per shard
2ConsistencyBounded eventual consistency; staleness upper-bounded strictly by entry TTLExplicit invalidation via write path plus CDC handles the common case; TTL acts as an unconditional safety net
3Availability and Blast RadiusSingle-node loss affects <= 1/N (12.5%) of keyspace with zero durable data lossCache holds volatile copies only; gutter fallback nodes and origin concurrency limits shield the database during node failure
4Hit-Ratio SensitivitySustain >= 98% hit ratio on Zipfian read traffic (10x to 50x DB load reduction)Requires scan-resistant eviction (W-TinyLFU) and consistent hashing so topology changes do not flush the entire fleet

Non-Goals and Scope Boundaries

  • Durable source-of-truth persistence: We do not write synchronous WAL files to disk or run Raft consensus per write. Every entry is a reconstructible copy of data stored durably in a primary database.
  • Strong linearizable reads after write: Financial ledger balances, inventory reservation counts, and permission revocation checks must read the authoritative database (or bypass the cache) rather than tolerating a staleness window.
  • Complex secondary queries or range joins: The cache serves point lookups (GET key) and batched key fetches (MGET) only.

Hit-Ratio Arithmetic and Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

Understanding hit-ratio nonlinearity governs every sizing decision in a caching tier. If a cache hit takes 1 ms and a database read takes 20 ms, lifting the hit ratio from 90% to 99% lowers mean latency from 2.9 ms to 1.19 ms, but more importantly cuts database read volume by 10x (from 10% of requests down to 1%). Conversely, if a cache cluster empties completely, database traffic jumps by 100x.

Resource DimensionArithmetic DerivationProvisioned Bound
Target Working Set100,000,000 cached items * 1 KB average value (+ ~100 B key and allocator metadata)~110 GB gross memory footprint
Usable RAM per Node16 GB physical cache RAM * 0.85 (reserving 15% for slab fragmentation, metadata, and OS buffers)13.6 GB usable per node
Minimum Shard Count110 GB / 13.6 GB = 8.09 -> provision 9 nodes (3 per AZ)9 shards (122.4 GB usable capacity)
Per-Node Read Throughput200,000 sustained RPS / 9 nodes (600,000 peak / 9)22,222 sustained RPS/node (66,667 peak RPS/node; well below 150k+ single-node Memcached/Redis ceiling)
Network Egress per Node66,667 peak RPS * 1 KB payload66.7 MB/s (~0.53 Gbps per node; fits comfortably inside 10 Gbps NICs)
Backing DB Miss Load200,000 RPS * (1 - 0.99) at 99% hit ratio2,000 DB reads/s steady state; surges to 22,222 DB reads/s on 1-node loss unless guttered

9.2 External API and Data Contracts

Production caches serve hot-path reads over lightweight binary protocols (Memcached binary protocol or Redis RESP3) to avoid HTTP header and JSON parsing overhead. For clarity across service boundaries, we document the equivalent RESTful contract alongside the conditional lease primitive used to close stale-value races.

Lookup, Lease-Guarded Fill, and Invalidation Contracts

Read key (GET /v1/entries/{key}):

On a cache miss, the cache server issues a unique 64-bit X-Cache-Lease token alongside 404 Not Found. Any subsequent DELETE on that key invalidates all outstanding lease tokens for that key.

GET /v1/entries/product:8821 HTTP/2
Host: cache-shard-03.internal

HTTP/2 404 Not Found
X-Cache-Lease: 90481122
X-Cache-Status: MISS

Conditional populate (PUT /v1/entries/{key}):

The caller fetches the fresh row from the backing database and supplies If-Match-Lease together with a jittered Cache-Control: max-age TTL. If a writer invalidated product:8821 while the reader was querying the database, the shard rejects the stale write with 412 Precondition Failed, preserving cache correctness.

PUT /v1/entries/product:8821 HTTP/2
Host: cache-shard-03.internal
Cache-Control: max-age=317
If-Match-Lease: 90481122
Content-Type: application/octet-stream

<serialized product payload>

HTTP/2 204 No Content

Explicit invalidation (DELETE /v1/entries/{key}):

Writers issue DELETE only after the primary database transaction commits.

DELETE /v1/entries/product:8821 HTTP/2
Host: cache-shard-03.internal

HTTP/2 204 No Content

In-Memory Entry Metadata Layout

Each shard stores compact metadata per entry in slab-allocated memory to avoid heap fragmentation:

EntryHeader {
    key_hash:      u64,   // 64-bit xxHash / SipHash for O(1) bucket probe
    expires_at_ms: u64,   // Absolute monotonic expiry timestamp (enforces TTL)
    lease_epoch:   u64,   // Monotonic per-key invalidation version (for CAS/lease checks)
    flags:         u16,   // Compression flag (LZ4/Zstd) + negative-cache tombstone bit
    val_len:       u32,   // Opaque payload length in bytes
}

9.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We separate cluster topology management, health probing, and hot-key detection (control plane) from direct client-to-shard reads and writes (data plane) so that a configuration-store hiccup never interrupts sub-millisecond reads (Figure 9-2).

Component Responsibilities and Failure Domains

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Ring and Health CoordinatorControlAuthoritative shard membership map, consistent hash ring epoch (v18), and active health checksSmart clients and proxies cache the latest ring snapshot in RAM; control-plane outage pauses scaling edits without affecting reads or writes
Hot-Key Detector and Auto-ScalerControlSampled heavy-hitter sketches (Top-K keys per shard) and memory-pressure telemetryPushes hot-key identifiers to L1 near-cache allowlists and triggers key replication before one shard NIC saturates
Smart Client / Proxy Tier (Mcrouter)DataLocal ring map, L1 tiny hot-key cache (1 to 5 s TTL), singleflight wait table, circuit breakersRuns co-located as a sidecar or library inside application hosts; eliminates extra network hops and isolates dead shards within 5 ms
Sharded Cache Fleet (Multi-AZ)DataSlab-allocated key-value entries, W-TinyLFU frequency sketch, TTL expiration heapsLosing one shard causes misses for 1/N of keys; proxy routes misses for the failed shard to standby gutter nodes rather than overloading peer shards
CDC Invalidation RelayDataDatabase WAL / binlog offset and idempotent delete queueReplays committed mutations as cache DEL calls asynchronously, repairing any dropped application-level invalidation

Read and Write Path Walkthrough

  1. L1 Hot-Key Near-Cache Check: The application’s smart client checks a tiny process-local L1 cache (holding only top 1,000 hot keys with a 1 to 2 s TTL) in ~10 microseconds.
  2. Consistent Hash Lookup: On an L1 miss, the client hashes the key (xxHash64) onto the consistent hash ring (with 256 virtual nodes per shard) and sends a direct GET over a persistent TCP pool to the owning cache node.
  3. Singleflight Coalescing on Miss: On a 404 miss with X-Cache-Lease, the client acquires an in-process singleflight gate for that key. Concurrent threads requesting the same key await the leader’s result instead of issuing redundant database queries.
  4. Origin Fetch and Conditional Fill: The winning caller reads the backing database, populates the cache shard with PUT carrying If-Match-Lease and a jittered TTL, and broadcasts the value to all waiting local callers.
  5. Write-Path Invalidation: On a mutation, the application commits to the primary database first and then issues DELETE to the cache shard (backed up asynchronously by the CDC invalidation relay).

9.4 Cache Topologies, Eviction Policies, and Sharding Mechanics

Choosing Cache-Aside Over Write-Through and Write-Behind

We evaluate four canonical arrangements between cache and database:

PatternCache PopulationWrite OrderStaleness ProfileCache-Outage Behavior
Cache-Aside (Chosen)Application populates lazily on missUpdate DB first, then DELETE cache keyBounded by TTL (and race-protected via leases)Degrades cleanly to DB reads (protected by DB concurrency caps)
Read-ThroughCache proxy fetches DB on missApplication updates DB and invalidates cacheIdentical to cache-asideReads fail unless application maintains a fallback path
Write-ThroughCache populates synchronously on every writeWrite cache + DB synchronouslyNear-zero for writes routed through cacheWrites fail or stall on cache outage; pollutes RAM with cold keys never read
Write-Behind (Write-Back)Cache accepts write immediately; async DB flushWrite cache now, batch-flush DB laterCache is newest; DB lags asynchronouslyData loss if cache node crashes before flush completes

Cache-aside keeps the cache strictly optional, loads only keys that callers actually read, and avoids write-behind durability loss.

Eviction Policies: From LRU and LFU to W-TinyLFU

A steady-state cache is perpetually full; every insertion evicts an existing entry. Choosing the victim governs hit ratio across shifting and scan-heavy workloads.

Least Recently Used (LRU) orders entries in a doubly linked list, promoting an entry to the head on every access and evicting from the tail. Advancing through Interactive Trace 9.A reveals LRU’s structural weakness: a single sequential scan of cold keys (B, C, D) flushes a genuinely hot key (A) that was accessed three times in a row.

Least Frequently Used (LFU) tracks per-entry access counts and evicts the lowest-count item. As Interactive Trace 9.B illustrates on the exact same sequence, LFU preserves hot key A across the scan. However, plain LFU suffers from cache pollution by historical popularity: an item accessed 10,000 times yesterday occupies RAM indefinitely even when no longer requested, starving newly trending keys whose count begins at 1.

Two production algorithms resolve these trade-offs:

  1. Approximated Sampled-LRU (Redis): Updating a global doubly linked list on every read creates lock contention across CPU cores and consumes 16 bytes of pointers per key. Redis instead samples k = 5 to 10 random keys and evicts the one with the oldest 24-bit idle timestamp, approaching true LRU hit ratios at a fraction of the memory and locking overhead.
  2. Window TinyLFU (W-TinyLFU, used in Caffeine): Combines recency and frequency with tiny memory overhead:
    • New entries enter a small Window LRU (1% of cache capacity) to capture sudden bursty locality.
    • Evictions from the Window compete against the eviction victim of the Main Segmented LRU (SLRU) (99% of capacity, split 20% probation / 80% protected) using an admission filter backed by a 4-bit Count-Min Sketch plus a Bloom doorkeeper.
    • The newcomer displaces the main victim only if its estimated frequency exceeds the victim’s frequency. Periodically halving all sketch counters ages out historical popularity, preventing stale heavy hitters from lingering permanently.
Eviction PolicyPer-Key MetadataScan ResistanceAdaptation to Popularity ShiftProduction Use
Strict LRU16 B list pointersPoor (flushed by sequential scans)FastMemcached slab LRU (segmented Hot/Warm/Cold)
Decaying LFU8 to 16 B counterHighSlow without aggressive decayRedis allkeys-lfu (Morris logarithmic counter)
Sampled-LRU (k = 5)3 B idle clockPoorFastRedis default allkeys-lru
W-TinyLFU~1 to 2 B amortized sketchExcellent (rejects one-hit wonders at admission)Fast (Window LRU + periodic halving)Caffeine (JVM), Otter (Go), modern L1/L2 caches

Consistent Hashing with Virtual Nodes and Bounded Loads

Assigning keys via hash(key) mod N remaps (N - 1) / N of all keys whenever one shard joins or leaves, causing an instant fleet-wide cache flush. We instead place every physical shard at 256 deterministic positions (virtual nodes) around a 2^64 consistent hash ring. Adding a 10th node to 9 shards moves roughly 1/10 (10%) of the keyspace while keeping key-count variance across nodes below 5%.

Standard consistent hashing still breaks under hot-key skew: if one celebrity profile or flash-sale SKU draws 120,000 RPS, the single shard owning that ring token saturates its NIC and CPU while peer shards remain idle. Two production techniques mitigate skew:

  1. Consistent Hashing with Bounded Loads (Mirrokni et al., Google): Each shard enforces an explicit load cap ceil((1 + epsilon) * average_load) (for example, 1.25x average load). When a target shard hits its cap, the proxy walks clockwise along the ring to the next shard with available headroom, bounding maximum skew mathematically while preserving cache locality.
  2. Hot-Key Replication and L1 Near-Caching: For extreme single-key floods (> 50,000 RPS on one key), the control-plane heavy-hitter detector flags the key. Clients either cache the value locally in L1 RAM for 1 to 2 seconds or scatter reads across K replicated key suffixes (product:8821#0 through product:8821#7), trading K invalidations on write for K-fold read scalability.

9.5 Consistency Races, Stampedes, Penetration, and Avalanches

Closing the Cache-Aside Stale-Value Race

Under cache-aside, writers update the database first and then DELETE the cache key (rather than overwriting the cache directly, which lets two out-of-order concurrent writers leave the older value cached). Even with UPDATE DB -> DELETE cache, an interleaving between a slow reader and a fast writer can leave a stale value cached permanently until TTL expiry, as demonstrated in Interactive Trace 9.C:

We layer three defenses against this race:

  1. Mandatory TTL Bound: Every entry carries an explicit expiration, guaranteeing that even a dropped invalidation or undetected race heals automatically within bounded time.
  2. Lease-Guarded Conditional Fill (Facebook Memcache Leases): On a miss, the cache returns a 64-bit lease_epoch token. Any DELETE invalidates all outstanding tokens for that key. When the delayed reader in Interactive Trace 9.C attempts to store stale price 10 using its invalidated lease token, the shard rejects the write with 412 Precondition Failed.
  3. CDC Log-Tailing Invalidation (Delayed Double-Delete Alternative): Streaming committed changes from the database write-ahead log (via Debezium or Maxwell) guarantees that cache deletes happen in exact commit order even if the originating application server crashes between COMMIT and DELETE.

Defending Against Cache Stampedes (Thundering Herd)

When a hot entry receiving 1,000 reads/s expires and takes 12 ms to recompute from the database, 12 to 1,000 concurrent callers miss simultaneously and launch duplicate origin queries, creating a positive-feedback latency spiral. We deploy two complementary defenses (Figure 9-3):

  1. Singleflight Request Coalescing (Cold-Miss Collapse): Inside each application host or cache proxy, an in-memory map of in-flight miss keys ensures that at most one caller per proxy queries the origin database for a given key. All concurrent local callers subscribe to that singleflight future and receive the populated value together. Across a fleet of 100 hosts, pairing local singleflight with Memcache per-key miss leases (1 token issued per 10 s per shard; other missers receive a short retry hint) collapses global origin load to a single query.
  2. Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch, Vattani et al.): For hot keys with measurable recomputation time delta, we avoid the expiry cliff altogether. Whenever a reader hits a cached entry storing (value, delta, expiry), it triggers an early background recomputation if:
current_time - delta * beta * ln(rand(0, 1)) >= expiry

Because ln(rand(0, 1)) is negative, -delta * beta * ln(rand(0, 1)) adds a random positive lookahead proportional to recomputation cost delta (with tuning factor beta >= 1.0). As current_time approaches expiry, the probability that one reader refreshes the key early rises smoothly while all other callers keep receiving fast hits, eliminating cold expiry spikes with zero distributed locks.

Defending Against Penetration and Avalanches

  • Cache Penetration (Nonexistent Keys): Malicious scanners or broken clients querying nonexistent IDs bypass positive caches completely and hammer the database. We combine short-TTL negative caching (30 to 60 s tombstones for absent keys) with a front-door Bloom filter (for 10^9 valid keys at 1% false-positive rate, ~1.2 GB of bitset memory rejects 99% of invalid keys before they touch cache or database).
  • Cache Avalanche (Mass Simultaneous Expiry or Node Loss): Loading a catalog batch with an identical 3,600 s TTL causes all entries to expire together. Adding uniform TTL jitter (base_ttl + rand(0, 0.15 * base_ttl)) spreads expiration evenly. Against single-shard crashes, Facebook’s Gutter Pool routes failed-shard misses to a small 1% fleet of standby cache nodes with short TTLs instead of reshuffling keys onto healthy primary shards (which could trigger cascading OOMs). Finally, an independent origin database concurrency bulkhead guarantees that even a 0% hit ratio degrades gracefully via shedding rather than taking down storage.

9.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ModeOperational SymptomAutomated Mitigation
Single Cache Shard Crash1/N (11%) of requests miss; origin DB read QPS jumps ~11xSmart client trips circuit breaker in 5 ms and routes failed shard’s keys to standby gutter pool with short TTL; origin bulkhead caps DB concurrency
Cold Cluster Restart (Avalanche)Hit ratio plunges to 0%; DB CPU spikes toward 100%Progressive traffic ramp (5% -> 25% -> 100%) or peer-cluster cold warmup (reading from an adjacent warm region before hitting DB)
Hot-Key Flood (100k+ RPS)Single shard saturates CPU/NIC while peer shards sit idleControl-plane heavy-hitter detector enables 1 to 2 s L1 near-caching and bounded-load overflow or K-way key replication
Batch Scan PollutionHit ratio collapses after analytics job reads millions of cold keysW-TinyLFU admission sketch rejects one-hit keys; batch pipelines explicitly bypass cache via direct read replicas
Dropped Application DELETEReaders observe stale entry after DB writeCDC WAL invalidation pipeline deletes key asynchronously within < 500 ms; mandatory TTL bounds worst-case staleness
Penetration Attack (Random IDs)Cache miss rate rises sharply; DB spends CPU on empty lookupsFront-door Bloom filter rejects 99% of nonexistent keys; 30 s negative tombstones absorb repeated misses

Key SLIs and Operational Alerts

  • Cache Hit Ratio by Keyspace: Tracked separately per namespace (alert if hit ratio drops > 3% below rolling 7-day baseline, because a drop from 99% to 96% quadruples DB read traffic).
  • Shard Tail Latency (p99 and p999): Alert when intra-AZ p99 > 1.5 ms for 3 minutes (early warning of hot-key CPU contention or memory swapping).
  • Eviction Rate and Item Lifetime: Alert if mean time-to-eviction falls below 50% of configured TTL (indicating an undersized working set causing thrashing).
  • Singleflight Coalesce Ratio and Origin Miss QPS: Tracks how many concurrent misses collapsed per DB query and alerts if origin miss QPS approaches database read capacity.

Real-World Production Systems

Production SystemCore Eviction / RoutingStampede & Consistency MechanismArchitectural Distinction

Redis Cluster / Valkey16,384 hash slots + Sampled-LRU (k = 5) or Morris decaying LFUSingle-threaded atomic Lua scripts + optional client-side tracking invalidationsRich in-memory data structures (hashes, sorted sets, Bloom modules) alongside raw key-value caching
Caffeine (JVM) / Otter (Go)W-TinyLFU (Window LRU + Count-Min Sketch + Segmented LRU)Lock-free ring buffers for read/write metadata batchingNear-optimal hit ratios across both recency-heavy and scan-heavy workloads

9.7 Simulation Verification

To measure empirically how cache capacity translates into hit ratio under skewed Zipfian popularity, we run the repository’s cachesim benchmark (code/cachesim/src/main.rs), which replays 1,000,000 read requests across 100,000 distinct keys against an LRU cache sized at 1%, 5%, 10%, and 25% of the keyspace:

$ cargo run --release -p cachesim
1000000 requests for 100000 keys, a few of them popular
  cache holds  1% of the keys:  5.7% of requests answered from the cache
  cache holds  5% of the keys: 24.7% of requests answered from the cache
  cache holds 10% of the keys: 42.2% of requests answered from the cache
  cache holds 25% of the keys: 72.7% of requests answered from the cache

Holding 25% of the keyspace (25,000 keys) absorbs 72.7% of all requests, cutting backing-store traffic by 3.66x. Under steeper real-world Zipfian exponents (alpha >= 1.0), 5% to 10% of the keyspace routinely exceeds 95% to 99% hit ratios. In practice, operators must always benchmark miss-ratio curves against real production access traces before finalizing fleet RAM budgets.

Run the distributed cache hit-ratio simulation. Execute cargo run --release -p cachesim in code/ (code/cachesim/src/main.rs) to reproduce the 1,000,000-request Zipfian hit-ratio curve across 1%, 5%, 10%, and 25% cache capacities.

9.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Cache-AsideA topology in which the application checks the cache on reads, queries the database on misses to populate the cache, and deletes the cache key after committing database writes.
W-TinyLFUA scan-resistant admission and eviction policy combining a small Window LRU, a Count-Min Sketch frequency filter, and a Segmented Main LRU.
Consistent Hashing with Bounded LoadsA hash-ring routing algorithm that caps per-shard traffic at (1 + epsilon) times average load and overflows hot traffic clockwise to neighboring shards.
Singleflight CoalescingDeduplicating concurrent in-flight cache misses for the same key within a host or proxy so only one request queries the backing database.
Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch)Refreshing a cached entry asynchronously before its TTL expires with probability rising exponentially as remaining lifetime shrinks relative to recomputation time.
Memcache LeaseA 64-bit token issued by a cache shard on a miss that both throttles concurrent origin queries and rejects stale SET operations invalidated by an intervening DELETE.
Cache PenetrationSustained queries for nonexistent keys that miss the cache on every attempt and hit the backing database directly; mitigated by Bloom filters and negative caching.
Cache AvalancheA sudden fleet-wide collapse in hit ratio caused by synchronized TTL expiry or shard failure; mitigated by TTL jitter, gutter pools, and origin load shedding.
Gutter PoolA small standby cluster that absorbs misses for a failed cache shard with short TTLs, protecting the database without overloading healthy cache primaries.

References

Chapter 10: Distributed Lock Service

Inside a single operating-system process, a mutex guarantees mutual exclusion because the kernel mediates both thread scheduling and shared memory access. Across a distributed network, no global kernel exists. A worker holding a lock may crash without releasing it, stall for tens of seconds during a stop-the-world garbage collection pause or VM live migration, or lose network connectivity while continuing to send buffered packets toward shared storage. Observers on the network cannot distinguish a dead holder from a slow or paused holder.

In this chapter, I design a linearizable distributed lock service modeled on Google Chubby, Apache ZooKeeper, and etcd. We first separate locks taken for efficiency from locks required for correctness, then establish requirements, capacity bounds, and lease APIs. After detailing a five-node Raft consensus architecture across three availability zones, we examine why time-bounded leases alone cannot guarantee mutual exclusion, evaluate Martin Kleppmann’s critique of Redlock, and complete the safety proof by enforcing monotonic fencing tokens directly at the protected storage layer.

In this chapter, we cover

  • efficiency locks versus correctness locks, actors, functional contracts, linearizability SLOs, non-goals, and state sizing
  • HTTP/gRPC lease acquisition, heartbeat keepalive, conditional release, and storage-layer fencing DDL contracts
  • five-node Raft consensus control plane, monotonic Raft-index token generation, and watch-stream session management
  • why process pauses, VM migrations, and clock skew break lease-only mutual exclusion and why Redlock cannot guarantee correctness
  • end-to-end fencing token enforcement at the storage layer, conditional release/renewal races, and progress-coupled keepalives
  • fair waiter queues (ephemeral sequential watch chains) that eliminate release thundering herds, and when optimistic concurrency replaces locking
  • failure modes, SLIs, production coordination services (Chubby, ZooKeeper, etcd, DynamoDB Lock Client), and simulation verification

10.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Efficiency Locks vs. Correctness Locks

Before provisioning consensus hardware, we distinguish two fundamentally different uses of mutual exclusion:

  • Locks for Efficiency: Prevent redundant work (for example, avoiding duplicate cache recomputations or running an idempotent analytics summary twice). If a lock occasionally fails under a network partition, the cost is extra compute rather than corrupted state.
  • Locks for Correctness: Prevent concurrent mutations that corrupt persistent data (for example, two database primaries accepting conflicting writes, or two billing workers double-charging a ledger). An occasional mutual-exclusion failure causes permanent data loss or financial inconsistency.

In this chapter, we design for correctness, which requires both strongly consistent consensus inside the lock service and monotonic fencing enforcement inside the protected resource.

Actors and Use Cases

We organize the lock service around three actors: distributed workers contending for exclusive leases, downstream storage systems validating monotonic fencing tokens on every write, and platform operators auditing Raft quorum health and active lease holders (Figure 10-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Worker / ApplicationAcquire lease (POST /v1/locks/{k}), renew (PUT /v1/leases/{id}/keepalive), release (DELETE)Elect a single active leader for a sharded database partition or serialize a nightly settlement batch
Protected Storage ResourceValidate monotonic fencing token (token >= max_seen_token)Reject delayed writes arriving from a paused worker whose lease already expired
Platform OperatorAudit Raft leader, term, quorum latency, and lock wait queuesDetect network partitions, stalled holders renewing indefinitely, or excessive fine-grained lock contention

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0A worker can attempt to acquire an exclusive lease on a named lock key; at most one worker holds an active lease for that key at any point in linearizable history.
1Every granted lease carries a bounded server-enforced Time-To-Live (TTL) and a globally strictly increasing 64-bit fencing token (token_new > token_prev).
2A lease holder can extend its active lease via conditional heartbeat keepalive (PUT /v1/leases/{id}/keepalive) and release it voluntarily only if it still owns the matching lease token.
3Waiting workers can subscribe to ordered watch notifications so lock handoff wakes exactly the next waiter in FIFO order without polling or thundering-herd contention.
4Once a lease expires or is released, another worker can acquire the lock with a strictly higher fencing token.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0ConsistencyStrictly linearizable (CP under CAP) for lock acquisition, lease expiration, and monotonic token assignmentMandates quorum consensus (5-node Raft group committing every grant and token increment to 3 of 5 nodes before returning)
1Availability99.99% across three availability zones; tolerates 2 simultaneous node failures (or 1 full AZ loss + 1 rolling restart)Five-node Raft cluster placed 2 + 2 + 1 across three AZs; minority partition refuses grants rather than risking split-brain
2Latencyp50 <= 4 ms, p99 <= 15 ms for acquire/release (1 cross-AZ Raft quorum round trip plus WAL fsync)Coarse-grained locks held for seconds to hours; unsuitable for microsecond per-row hot-path locking
3ScaleUp to 1,000,000 active locks (~100 MB RAM) and 10,000 lock ops/sEntire active lock table fits inside Raft state-machine RAM backed by NVMe WAL and periodic snapshots

Non-Goals and Scope Boundaries

  • Fine-grained, high-frequency per-row locking: Calling a Raft consensus group 500,000 times per second on every HTTP request saturates leader WAL fsync bandwidth. Per-record concurrency belongs in database row locks or optimistic compare-and-set.
  • Correctness without storage-layer cooperation: No lock service can prevent an already-transmitted TCP packet from a paused client from reaching an unfenced third-party API. If the downstream resource cannot check fencing tokens, callers must redesign mutations to be idempotent.
  • Unbounded eternal locks: Every lock must attach to a bounded lease so a permanently crashed worker never deadlocks the cluster.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

Resource DimensionArithmetic DerivationProvisioned Bound
Per-Lock Memory50 B key + 30 B holder ID + 8 B fencing token + 8 B expiry + 32 B index/watch overhead~128 B per active lock
Active State Footprint1,000,000 concurrent locks * 128 B~128 MB RAM (fits entirely in Raft state-machine memory)
Quorum Write Throughput10,000 acquires/renewals/s; batched Raft WAL commits sustain 20,000 to 40,000 ops/s on NVMe5 Raft nodes (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, dedicated NVMe WAL volume)
Heartbeat Bandwidth100,000 active sessions renewing every 10 s = 10,000 keepalives/s * 128 B1.28 MB/s (~10 Mbps total; negligible network cost)
Raft Snapshot Size128 MB compressed with LZ4~40 MB snapshot written asynchronously every 100,000 log entries

10.2 External API and Data Contracts

Every mutation carries explicit identity and fencing metadata so retries and late requests remain safe.

Lock Service HTTP/gRPC Contracts

Acquire exclusive lease (POST /v1/locks/{key}):

Supplying Idempotency-Key guarantees that if the response to a granted lock is dropped on the network, the same worker retrying receives its existing lease and fencing token rather than failing with 409 Conflict.

POST /v1/locks/nightly-billing HTTP/2
Host: locks.internal
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: worker-a-session-9102

{
  "holder": "worker-a",
  "ttl_seconds": 30
}

HTTP/2 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "lock_key": "nightly-billing",
  "lease_id": 42,
  "fencing_token": 34,
  "expires_in_seconds": 30
}

If another worker already holds an active lease, the service responds with 409 Conflict and an RFC 9457 error payload (or blocks via a streaming gRPC watch queue if wait=true is specified):

HTTP/2 409 Conflict
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "/problems/lock-held",
  "title": "Lock Currently Held",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "Lock nightly-billing is held under fencing_token 34; retry or attach a watch."
}

Renew lease heartbeat (PUT /v1/leases/{lease_id}/keepalive):

PUT /v1/leases/42/keepalive HTTP/2
Host: locks.internal
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "holder": "worker-a",
  "fencing_token": 34,
  "extend_seconds": 30
}

HTTP/2 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "lease_id": 42,
  "fencing_token": 34,
  "expires_in_seconds": 30
}

Conditional release (DELETE /v1/locks/{key}?token={fencing_token}):

The Raft state machine deletes the lock key if and only if the currently stored fencing_token equals the query parameter (34). A stale holder presenting token 33 receives 412 Precondition Failed instead of deleting its successor’s lock.

Protected Storage Fencing Contract (SQL / KV DDL)

To complete end-to-end correctness, every table or object protected by a distributed lock stores the highest accepted fence_token and validates it atomically on every mutation:

CREATE TABLE billing_ledger_state (
    partition_id   BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    last_fence_tok BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    payload        BYTEA  NOT NULL,
    updated_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);

-- Atomic fenced update executed by the lock holder:
UPDATE billing_ledger_state
   SET payload        = $1,
       last_fence_tok = $2,
       updated_at     = NOW()
 WHERE partition_id   = $3
   AND last_fence_tok <= $2;

If the UPDATE affects 0 rows because another worker already committed with a higher token (last_fence_tok > $2), the storage layer has safely fenced off the stale holder, and the worker aborts its batch immediately.

10.3 High-Level Architecture: Consensus Plane and Fenced Data Path

Unlike a stateless cache or rate limiter, the lock service cannot run with asynchronous replication. If a primary confirms a lock grant and crashes before replicating that entry to a follower, the newly promoted leader sees the lock as free and grants it to a second worker simultaneously. We therefore build the lock service on a five-node Raft consensus group spread across three availability zones, while keeping the protected storage tier completely off the consensus data path except for token validation (Figure 10-2).

Component Responsibilities and Failure Domains

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Raft Leader (1 of 5 nodes)Consensus / ControlAuthoritative lock table, active lease expiry wheel, monotonic Raft log index counterCommits every acquire, renew, expire, and release to a quorum (3 of 5) before replying. On crash, surviving majority elects a new leader within 1 to 3 s with zero lost locks
Raft Followers (4 nodes across 3 AZs)Consensus / ControlReplicated WAL + lock state machine + read-only watch proxiesTolerate up to 2 node crashes simultaneously while maintaining quorum; minority nodes reject all lock writes
Lease Expiry Wheel & Watch StreamConsensus / ControlHierarchical timer wheel tracking lease deadlines and FIFO watch queues per lock keyWhen a lease deadline passes, the leader commits an explicit EXPIRE log entry through Raft and notifies exactly the head waiter
Protected Storage LayerDataBusiness records plus last_fence_tok column per protected resourceEnforces incoming_token >= last_fence_tok atomically on every write; completely eliminates split-brain corruption

Request Path Walkthrough

  1. Quorum Lock Acquisition: Worker A sends POST /v1/locks/nightly-billing to the Raft leader. The leader checks that the lock is unheld, appends (ACQUIRE, key="nightly-billing", holder="worker-a", ttl=30s) to the Raft log at log index 34, replicates to at least two followers, and commits.
  2. Monotonic Token Assignment: Because every committed Raft log entry has a globally unique, strictly increasing 64-bit log index (or key create_revision in etcd), the leader returns fencing_token = 34 directly from the replicated log without any external sequence generator.
  3. Periodic Lease Keepalive: Every 10 s (one-third of the 30 s lease TTL), Worker A sends a keepalive tied to active work progress so two dropped network packets do not trigger premature expiration.
  4. Fenced Storage Writes: Worker A attaches fencing_token = 34 to every write sent directly to the protected database or object store. The storage layer persists last_fence_tok = 34 and refuses any write carrying a token < 34.
  5. Conditional Release and Ordered Handoff: When finished, Worker A sends DELETE /v1/locks/nightly-billing?token=34. The leader commits the release through Raft and pushes a single watch event to the next queued waiter.

10.4 Process Pauses, Fencing Tokens, and the Redlock Critique

Why Time-Bounded Leases Cannot Guarantee Mutual Exclusion

A common design mistake assumes that a worker can guarantee safety by checking its local clock right before writing: “My lease expires at t = 30 s, my clock currently reads t = 12 s, therefore I still hold the lock.” That check is structurally unsound in any asynchronous system.

Between the line of code that checks the lease expiration and the moment the resulting network packet arrives at the storage engine, an unbounded pause can occur without the worker’s knowledge:

  • Stop-the-World Garbage Collection: A JVM or Go GC pause can freeze all application threads for 10 to 45 seconds right after the check passes.
  • Hypervisor / VM Live Migration or CPU Starvation: A cloud host migrating a virtual machine or swapping memory pages stalls execution invisibly.
  • Network Buffer Delay: A TCP packet already emitted by the kernel can sit queued inside a congested switch or retransmitted over a flapping link for longer than the remaining lease TTL.

During that pause, the lock service’s lease timer expires and legitimately grants the lock to Worker B. When Worker A resumes, both workers believe they hold exclusive access. As Figure 10-3 and Interactive Trace 10.A demonstrate, only a monotonic fencing token checked at the storage boundary closes this failure mode completely.

Note what fencing tokens change structurally: we no longer require the lock service to solve the impossible problem of preventing two clients from running concurrently across asynchronous pauses. We require the lock service only to issue strictly increasing numbers through Raft consensus, and we enforce mutual exclusion at the single point where mutations become durable: the storage engine itself.

Evaluating Redlock and Martin Kleppmann’s Critique

Because running a dedicated Raft cluster adds operational footprint, Salvatore Sanfilippo proposed Redlock, an algorithm attempting distributed locking over N = 5 completely independent, non-replicated Redis nodes:

  1. A client records its local start time T1 and attempts SET resource_key random_value NX PX ttl sequentially on all 5 independent Redis instances with short per-node timeouts.
  2. The client computes elapsed time elapsed = T2 - T1 and considers the lock acquired if it succeeded on a majority (>= 3 nodes) and elapsed < ttl, setting effective validity time to ttl - elapsed - clock_drift.

In his 2016 formal analysis, Martin Kleppmann demonstrated two fundamental defects that make Redlock unsafe for correctness locks:

  1. Dependence on Bounded Timing and Synchronized Clocks: Redlock assumes bounded network delays, bounded process pauses, and bounded clock drift rates across all five independent nodes. If Node C experiences a forward NTP clock jump that expires its key early, a second client can acquire the lock on Nodes {C, D, E} while the first client still believes its lock is valid on {A, B, C}. Even without clock jumps, a GC pause on Client 1 right after acquiring the majority leaves both clients active simultaneously.
  2. Absence of a Monotonic Fencing Token Generator: Because the five Redis instances are independent and run no consensus protocol, no single node knows the highest token issued by other majorities. Redlock therefore cannot generate globally monotonic fencing tokens, leaving storage engines unable to distinguish stale holders from current holders.

Sanfilippo countered that monotonic clocks (CLOCK_MONOTONIC) avoid NTP step jumps on Redis TTLs and that delayed restarts can prevent crash-recovery loss of lock state. Nevertheless, the core systems conclusion stands: Redlock is acceptable for efficiency locks (deduplicating best-effort work), whereas correctness locks require a consensus-backed lock service (Chubby, ZooKeeper, etcd) paired with storage-layer fencing tokens.

10.5 Safe Release, Progress-Coupled Renewal, and Fair Waiter Queues

Conditional Release and Progress-Coupled Keepalives

Releasing a lock by issuing an unconditional DELETE key introduces a classic concurrency bug illustrated in Interactive Trace 10.B: Worker A stalls past its lease deadline, Worker B acquires the lock, and Worker A wakes up and deletes Worker B’s active lock, allowing Worker C to enter immediately while Worker B is still running.

We prevent this by requiring every DELETE and every keepalive renewal to execute an atomic compare-and-delete (DELETE IF current_token == T) inside the Raft state machine (or inside a Redis Lua script for efficiency locks).

A subtle liveness hazard also arises with background lease-renewal threads. If an SDK spawns an independent daemon thread that renews a lease every 10 s unconditionally while the main worker thread deadlocks on a mutex or stalls on an infinite loop, the deadlocked worker holds the lock forever, reintroducing the original infinite-lock defect. Production lock clients tie renewal strictly to explicit work-progress heartbeats (the renewal loop extends the lease only if the worker updated a monotonic progress counter within the last lease window) and cap maximum total lease hold duration.

Eliminating the Release Herd with Ephemeral Sequential Queues

If 200 workers watch a single lock key directly, releasing that key broadcasts 200 watch notifications simultaneously. All 200 workers stampede the Raft leader with POST /v1/locks/{k} requests, 1 succeeds, and 199 fail and re-register watches (O(N^2) network messages to drain N waiters).

ZooKeeper and etcd solve this with ephemeral sequential waiter chains (O(N) total messages, strict FIFO fairness):

  1. Every contending worker creates an ephemeral key tied to its active session lease under a prefix with a monotonically assigned Raft sequence suffix: /locks/nightly-billing/0000000101, /0000000102, /0000000103.
  2. The worker lists children under /locks/nightly-billing/. If its sequence number is the smallest, it holds the lock (using its sequence number as the fencing token).
  3. Otherwise, the worker places a watch strictly on the single immediate predecessor (0000000102 watches only 0000000101).
  4. When 0000000101 finishes (or its session expires after a crash), the lock service notifies exactly 0000000102, waking one worker per transition with zero contention spikes.

When to Avoid Distributed Locks Entirely

Because correctness locking requires Raft quorum latency, fencing-token plumbing, and lease lifecycle management, we evaluate three lighter primitives before introducing a distributed lock:

  • Idempotent Mutations: If processing a payment or webhook twice produces the exact same durable state via an idempotency key (Chapter 13 and Chapter 19), mutual exclusion is unnecessary.
  • Optimistic Concurrency Control (CAS): For single-row or single-document updates, UPDATE items SET qty = qty - 1, version = version + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND version = $v achieves linearizable safety in one database round trip with zero lock service dependency.
  • Deterministic Ownership Partitioning: Assigning each key partition to one active consumer or shard leader (Chapter 11) provides exclusive ownership structurally without per-item lock negotiation.

10.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ModeOperational SymptomAutomated Mitigation
Worker Crashes While Holding LockWork stalls until lease TTL elapses (<= 30 s)Raft leader expiry wheel commits EXPIRE at deadline and notifies next queued waiter with token + 1
Worker Suffers 45 s GC PauseLease expires and transfers to Worker B; Worker A resumes lateWorker A’s stale writes carry token 33 < 34 and are rejected by storage fencing; Worker A detects 412 / 0 rows updated and halts
Single Raft Node or Entire AZ FailsBrief 1 to 3 s leader election if leader was in failed AZRemaining 3 or 4 nodes preserve quorum (3 of 5) across surviving AZs with zero lost locks or token regressions
Minority Network Partition Isolates LeaderIsolated leader cannot commit keepalives or new acquiresRaft ReadIndex / leader lease check fails; partitioned leader steps down and refuses lock grants, preventing split-brain
Deadlocked Worker with Background RenewerLock held indefinitely with zero output progressProgress-coupled keepalive stops renewing when work heartbeat stalls; maximum lease duration cap forces eventual reclamation
Lock Key Contention Spike (1,000 waiters)Elevated CPU on lock service if polling or broadcast watchingEphemeral sequential watch chain ensures 1 notification per release (O(1) wakeups)

Key SLIs and Operational Alerts

  • Quorum Commit Latency (p99): Alert if Raft fsync + quorum append p99 > 25 ms for 2 minutes (disk latency spikes cause false session expirations across the fleet).
  • Raft Leader Elections per Hour: Alert immediately on > 1 unexpected leader election per hour (signals network instability or disk I/O stalls).
  • Fencing Rejection Rate (storage_fence_rejections_total): Every rejected stale token proves the safety net worked, but a sudden spike indicates fleet-wide GC pauses, undersized lease TTLs, or network jitter.
  • Lease Hold Duration (p99): Alert when active leases approach their maximum hold threshold, surfacing stuck workers early.

Real-World Production Systems

Production SystemConsensus ProtocolFencing Token PrimitiveArchitectural Distinction
Google Chubby (2006)Multi-Paxos (5 replicas)Sequencer ({lock_name, mode, generation_number})Pioneered coarse-grained advisory locks, keepalive leases, and client-side read caching with invalidations
Apache ZooKeeperZab (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast)Ephemeral sequential zxid / node sequence numberWait-free FIFO lock recipes using predecessor-only watches to prevent herd wakeups

10.7 Simulation Verification

To verify end-to-end fencing safety under a long process pause, we execute the repository’s locksim simulation (code/locksim/src/main.rs). In this trace, client-a acquires the lock at t = 0 with a 10 s lease and fencing token 1, then freezes for 15 seconds at t = 2. At t = 12, after the lease expires, client-b acquires the lock with token 2 and writes to storage at t = 13. When client-a wakes at t = 17 and attempts to write with token 1, the storage engine rejects the stale write:

$ cargo run --release -p locksim
t=0   client-a acquires the lock: token Some(1), lease until t=10
t=1   client-b asks for the lock: None
t=2   client-a stops for 15 seconds (a long pause of its process)
t=12  the lease has ended. client-b acquires the lock: token Some(2)
t=13  client-b writes with token 2: accepted true
t=17  client-a wakes up, still believes it holds the lock, writes with token 1: accepted false
the storage holds: written by client-b

Without storage-layer token verification, client-a’s write at t = 17 would overwrite client-b’s committed data without detection. With monotonic fencing enforced at storage, 1 < 2 triggers an unconditional refusal (accepted false), preserving written by client-b regardless of pause duration or clock skew.

Run the distributed lock and fencing simulation. Execute cargo run --release -p locksim in code/ (code/locksim/src/main.rs) to reproduce the 15-second pause, lease transfer, and storage-layer token rejection trace above.

10.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
LeaseA time-bounded lock that expires automatically if its holder fails to renew it before the deadline, preventing deadlocks after worker crashes.
Fencing TokenA strictly monotonic integer issued by a consensus-backed lock service on every grant and validated by the protected storage layer to reject delayed writes from expired holders.
Process PauseAny involuntary suspension of worker execution (GC stop-the-world, VM migration, OS page fault, or network buffering) during which a lease can expire without the worker’s knowledge.
LinearizabilityThe strongest single-object consistency guarantee, ensuring every lock acquisition, expiration, and release appears to take effect atomically at a single point in real time.
RedlockAn algorithm acquiring locks across a majority of independent Redis nodes without consensus; relies on timing assumptions and cannot generate monotonic fencing tokens.
Ephemeral Sequential Watch ChainA FIFO queue of session-bound numbered keys where each waiter watches only its immediate predecessor, eliminating release thundering herds.
Optimistic Concurrency Control (CAS)Conditional state updates (WHERE version = expected) that detect concurrent writes at commit time without acquiring an external distributed lock.

References

  • M. Burrows, “The Chubby Lock Service for Loosely-Coupled Distributed Systems”, USENIX OSDI, 2006.
  • P. Hunt, M. Konar, F. P. Junqueira, and B. Reed, “ZooKeeper: Wait-free Coordination for Internet-scale Systems”, USENIX ATC, 2010.
  • D. Ongaro and J. Ousterhout, “In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft)”, USENIX ATC, 2014.
  • M. Kleppmann, “How to Do Distributed Locking”, martin.kleppmann.com, 2016.
  • S. Sanfilippo, “Is Redlock Safe?”, antirez.com, 2016.
  • C. Gray and D. Cheriton, “Leases: An Efficient Fault-Tolerant Mechanism for Distributed File Cache Consistency”, ACM SOSP, 1989.
