Chapter 11: Distributed Message Queue

When an order service calls billing, inventory, fraud scoring, and email delivery synchronously over RPC, its availability becomes the product of every downstream dependency and its tail latency becomes the sum of the slowest responders. A spike in checkout traffic overflows downstream worker pools, while a maintenance restart of a non-critical analytics service blocks customer purchases. Placing a durable, partitioned message queue between producers and consumers breaks temporal coupling, absorbs burst traffic into disk-backed backlogs, and enables independent downstream teams to consume the same event stream at their own pace.

In this chapter, I design a high-throughput, Kafka-style distributed commit-log message queue. We establish functional contracts, durability SLOs, and multi-terabyte storage bounds, specify producer and consumer wire protocols, and separate KRaft metadata coordination (control plane) from zero-copy partitioned log brokers (data plane). In the deep dives, we dissect sequential disk I/O and sendfile() page-cache mechanics, In-Sync Replica (ISR) replication with acks=all, cooperative sticky consumer group rebalancing, delivery semantics (at-most-once, at-least-once, and idempotent effectively-once), idempotent producers, and the transactional outbox pattern.

In this chapter, we cover

  • temporal decoupling, task queues versus durable commit logs, actors, durability SLOs, non-goals, and storage/broker capacity bounds
  • partitioned produce, long-poll fetch, idempotent offset commit, and consumer group coordination wire contracts
  • separation of KRaft metadata controller and group coordinator (control plane) from partitioned append-only brokers (data plane)
  • sequential log segments, OS page-cache zero-copy sendfile() transfers, key-based partition ordering, and log compaction
  • In-Sync Replica (ISR) replication, acks=all, min.insync.replicas, High Watermark (HW) visibility, and broker failover
  • cooperative sticky consumer group rebalancing (zero stop-the-world pauses), offset commit ordering, idempotent producers, transactional outbox, and dead-letter queues
  • operational failure modes, lag SLIs, production brokers (Apache Kafka, Apache Pulsar, Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ), and simulation verification

11.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Task Queues vs. Partitioned Commit Logs

Two architectures share the label “message queue” while serving distinct workloads:

  • Task Queue (Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ): Hands each message to one worker, hides it during a visibility timeout, and deletes it permanently upon acknowledgment. Independent consumers cannot replay historical events, and parallel workers scramble strict per-entity ordering.
  • Partitioned Append-Only Log (Apache Kafka, Redpanda, Apache Pulsar): Appends immutable records sequentially to partitioned disk segments identified by monotonic 64-bit offsets. Reading does not delete records; each consumer group tracks its own offset cursor independently, enabling multi-subscriber fan-out, deterministic replay after bug fixes, and strict per-key ordering within each partition.

In this chapter, I design a partitioned append-only commit log because modern microservice platforms require durable multi-consumer fan-out, replayability, and ordered per-key event streams.

Actors and Use Cases

We organize the message queue around three actors: producer services appending keyed batches, consumer groups polling ordered partitions and committing offsets, and platform operators managing topic partitions, replication factors, and retention policies (Figure 11-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Producer ServiceAppend keyed batch (PRODUCE with acks=all)Publish order-7:created, order-7:paid, and order-7:shipped into the same partition with durable replication
Consumer GroupPoll ordered segments (FETCH), commit offsets (COMMIT), join rebalanceBilling, warehouse, and analytics services each read the full orders topic independently at their own throughput
Platform OperatorProvision topics, configure retention/compaction, monitor consumer lagSet RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, 7-day retention, and expand partitions before consumer lag breaches retention

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0Producers append messages to a named topic with an optional partition key; all records sharing a key land in the same partition and remain strictly ordered by monotonically increasing 64-bit offsets.
1Consumers pull batches sequentially from any offset within their assigned partitions and commit durable group offsets so restarted consumers resume without losing position.
2Multiple independent consumer groups read the same topic concurrently at independent offsets; within a single group, each partition is owned by at most one consumer at a time.
3Brokers retain committed messages durably for a configurable retention window (7 days default) or compact topics by key to preserve the latest value per key indefinitely.
4Producers support idempotent retries via sequence numbers so network timeouts never append duplicate records to a partition log.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0Throughput and Scale100,000 messages/s sustained (1 KB average = 100 MB/s ingress); 300,000 peak burst messages/sPartitioned append-only logs using sequential disk I/O, producer batch compression (LZ4/Zstd), and zero-copy sendfile() reads
1DurabilityZero committed data loss across 1 broker or 1 full AZ failure (RF = 3, min.insync.replicas = 2)Synchronous replication across 3 AZs with acks=all; consumers read only up to the committed High Watermark (HW)
2Latencyp50 <= 5 ms, p99 <= 20 ms end-to-end produce-to-consume under normal lagDirect producer/consumer connections to partition leaders (zero central proxy hop) and long-polling fetches
3Consistency and OrderingStrong total order within each partition; no global order across partitionsEvery consumer observes identical records at identical offsets inside a partition; cross-partition ordering is explicitly omitted
4Delivery SemanticsAt-least-once broker delivery; effectively-once end-to-end with idempotent producers and idempotent consumersBrokers prioritize zero data loss over duplicate avoidance when consumers crash between work and offset commit

Non-Goals and Scope Boundaries

  • Global total ordering across partitions: Enforcing total order across an entire topic collapses throughput to a single partition leader. Callers requiring strict ordering among related events must assign them the same partition key.
  • Per-message arbitrary deletion or SQL querying: Offsets advance monotonically; consumers cannot delete an individual message in the middle of a log segment.
  • Broker-side push delivery: Brokers never push messages to consumers; pull-based fetching lets each consumer apply natural backpressure matched to its own CPU and downstream database capacity.

Resource DimensionArithmetic DerivationProvisioned Bound

7-Day Retention (RF = 3)8.64 TB/day * 7 days * 3 replicas181.44 TB total raw replicated disk
Broker Fleet Sizing (Disk)181.44 TB / (4 TB usable NVMe * 0.75 headroom) = 60.5 -> provision 63 brokers (21 per AZ) or 24 brokers with 12 TB NVMe24 brokers (8 per AZ, 12 TB NVMe each = 288 TB raw, 63% steady disk occupancy)

11.2 External API and Data Contracts

Production brokers speak a compact binary TCP protocol supporting pipelined batched frames, CRC32C checksums, and zero-copy disk slicing. Below we specify the semantic equivalents for produce, long-poll fetch, and idempotent offset commit.

Produce, Fetch, and Commit Contracts

Produce a keyed batch (POST /v1/topics/{topic}/messages):

Producers attach (producer_id, producer_epoch, base_sequence) so the partition leader detects and drops retried batches idempotently.

POST /v1/topics/orders/messages HTTP/2
Host: broker-04.internal
Content-Type: application/json
X-Producer-Id: 40912
X-Producer-Epoch: 3
X-Base-Sequence: 1088
X-Acks: all

{
  "key": "order-7",
  "records": [
    { "event_type": "order_paid", "amount_cents": 4900 }
  ]
}

HTTP/2 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "topic": "orders",
  "partition": 1,
  "base_offset": 2,
  "high_watermark": 2
}

Long-poll fetch from partition leader (GET /v1/topics/{topic}/partitions/{p}/messages):

To avoid busy-wait polling when a partition is quiet, the broker holds the fetch open up to max_wait_ms until at least min_bytes of committed data (offset <= high_watermark) become available.

GET /v1/topics/orders/partitions/1/messages?offset=0&max_bytes=1048576&max_wait_ms=500 HTTP/2
Host: broker-04.internal

HTTP/2 200 OK
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
X-High-Watermark: 6
X-Next-Offset: 6

Idempotent offset commit (PUT /v1/topics/{topic}/partitions/{p}/offsets/{group}):

PUT /v1/topics/orders/partitions/1/offsets/billing-service HTTP/2
Host: group-coordinator.internal
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "generation_id": 14,
  "member_id": "billing-pod-02",
  "committed_offset": 6
}

HTTP/2 204 No Content

Validating generation_id acts as a fencing token against zombie consumers: if billing-pod-02 stalled past its session timeout and lost partition 1 in generation 15, the coordinator rejects its late offset commit with 409 Conflict, preventing it from rewinding or overwriting the new owner’s progress.

On-Disk Log Segment Schema

Each partition directory on a broker consists of fixed-size rolling segments (for example, 1 GB each) paired with sparse offset and timestamp indexes:

/var/lib/queue/orders-1/
  00000000000000000000.log       # Sequential append-only record batches (CRC32C, offset, ts, key, value)
  00000000000000000000.index     # Sparse 8-byte (relative_offset: u32, file_position: u32) every 4 KB
  00000000000000000000.timeindex # Sparse (timestamp_ms: u64, relative_offset: u32) for time-based seek

Retention cleanup deletes entire closed .log segments in O(1) unlink() calls rather than compacting individual records inside active files.

11.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We decouple cluster metadata consensus and consumer group coordination (control plane) from high-volume sequential log appends and zero-copy reads (data plane) so metadata churn never stalls broker disk I/O (Figure 11-2).

Component Responsibilities and Failure Domains

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
KRaft Metadata Controller (3-node Raft)ControlAuthoritative topic configs, partition leader epochs, and In-Sync Replica (ISR) listsReplaces external ZooKeeper; tolerates 1 node loss with sub-second controller failover; running data plane caches partition leader map
Group Coordinator & __offsets TopicControlConsumer group membership, generation IDs, partition assignments, and compacted committed offsetsHosted on replicated internal partitions (RF = 3); failover triggers brief rebalance without losing committed offsets
Partitioned Broker Fleet (Multi-AZ)DataAppend-only .log segments, sparse indexes, OS page-cache hot tail, per-producer sequence tableEach partition has 1 leader and 2 followers across 3 AZs; losing one broker shifts leadership to an in-sync follower in < 2 s
Producers & Consumer GroupsDataCached cluster metadata map, producer sequence numbers, local batch compression buffersConnect directly to partition leaders; refresh metadata automatically upon NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION responses

Hot Data Path Walkthrough

  1. Keyed Partition Routing: A producer computes partition = murmur2(key) mod P, compresses a batch of records (for example, 16 KB or 5 ms linger), and transmits directly to the leader broker for that partition.
  2. Leader Sequential Append: The leader verifies (producer_id, epoch, seq) for duplicates, assigns consecutive offsets, and appends the batch sequentially to the active .log segment (landing directly in Linux page cache).
  3. ISR Replication & High Watermark Advance: Follower brokers continuously pull new batches from the leader. Once every replica in the current ISR (at least min.insync.replicas = 2 across distinct AZs) has appended the offset, the leader advances the High Watermark (HW) and sends 201 Created (acks=all).
  4. Zero-Copy Consumer Fetch: A consumer polls the leader from its committed offset. The broker locates the byte range via binary search on the .index file and invokes sendfile() so the kernel transfers bytes directly from the OS page cache to the NIC socket buffer via DMA, bypassing user-space copies entirely.
  5. Offset Commit: After processing the batch, the consumer commits next_offset with its fenced generation_id to the Group Coordinator.

11.4 Storage Mechanics, Replication (ISR), and Cooperative Rebalancing

Why Sequential Logs and Zero-Copy sendfile() Deliver High Throughput

Random disk writes require seek overhead and fragmented flash translation updates, whereas modern NVMe drives and even spinning disks sustain sequential appends at hundreds of megabytes to gigabytes per second. By writing strictly to the end of active .log segments and relying on the OS page cache rather than duplicating buffers inside application heap memory, brokers avoid GC overhead and cache cold starts across process restarts.

On the read path, a conventional read-then-write loop copies each byte four times (disk -> kernel page cache -> user-space buffer -> kernel socket buffer -> NIC). Invoking Linux sendfile() collapses this into a zero-copy DMA path: the kernel streams pages directly from the page cache to the network interface card with zero user-space context copies, saturating 25 Gbps links with minimal CPU usage.

In-Sync Replicas (ISR), acks=all, and High Watermark Visibility

A pure Raft quorum requires 2f + 1 replicas to tolerate f failures (3 replicas for 1 failure, 5 replicas for 2 failures). For multi-hundred-terabyte event logs, storing 5 copies is expensive. Kafka-style brokers use an In-Sync Replica (ISR) protocol coordinated by the KRaft controller:

  • A partition configures RF = 3 (one replica in each AZ) and min.insync.replicas = 2.
  • Every follower that stays caught up within replica.lag.time.max.ms (for example, 10 s) remains in the ISR. A stalled follower is removed from ISR by the leader via the KRaft controller so one slow disk does not halt the entire partition.
  • With acks=all, the leader confirms a write only after all replicas currently in the ISR replicate it, and refuses writes (NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS) if |ISR| < min.insync.replicas. This guarantees every acknowledged message exists on at least 2 failure domains before the producer sees success.
  • High Watermark (HW) Isolation: Consumers may fetch records strictly up to offset <= HW. Never exposing uncommitted leader-only entries prevents consumers from acting on phantom messages that disappear if the leader crashes before replication completes.

Consumer Groups and Cooperative Sticky Rebalancing

Within a consumer group, each partition belongs to exactly one consumer instance, preserving strict per-key processing order and capping effective parallelism at the partition count P. Interactive Trace 11.A walks through partition ownership across joins and departures:

Historically, eager rebalancing stopped the entire consumer group whenever any single pod restarted or scaled out: every member revoked all its partitions simultaneously, waited for everyone to rejoin, and then received a fresh assignment (stop-the-world rebalance pause). On large groups with 500 partitions, rolling deployments caused cascading minutes of lag.

Modern brokers eliminate this pause using Incremental Cooperative Sticky Rebalancing (Figure 11-3):

  1. Stage 1 (Join Without Global Revoke): When Consumer C3 joins, existing consumers C1 ({P0, P1}) and C2 ({P2, P3}) keep processing their current partitions uninterrupted.
  2. Stage 2 (Selective Revocation): The coordinator computes the minimal delta needed to balance the group (C2 should transfer only P3 to C3). C2 finishes its current batch on P3, commits its offset, and revokes P3 while P0, P1, and P2 experience zero pause.
  3. Stage 3 (Incremental Handoff): On the second micro-rebalance round, the coordinator assigns freed P3 to C3. Combined with a dedicated background heartbeat thread (separated from the processing thread so a slow batch does not expire the session) and static group membership (group.instance.id), rolling restarts avoid rebalance storms altogether.

11.5 Delivery Semantics, Idempotent Producers, and Transactional Outbox

At-Least-Once vs. At-Most-Once Offset Ordering

A consumer performs two non-atomic side effects across two independent systems: executing business work (writing to a database or calling an API) and committing its new offset to the queue. Because the consumer can crash between those two steps, only two execution orders exist:

  1. Work First, Commit Second (At-Least-Once): Demonstrated in Interactive Trace 11.B. If the consumer crashes after billing an order and before committing offset 0, its replacement re-reads from offset 0 and processes the message again. Zero messages are lost; duplicates must be handled idempotently.
  1. Commit First, Work Second (At-Most-Once): Demonstrated in Interactive Trace 11.C. If the consumer crashes after committing offset 1 and before processing it, the replacement begins at offset 2 and the message is lost permanently. Appropriate only for ephemeral telemetry or sensor metrics where dropping an occasional reading is harmless.

Achieving Effectively-Once Side Effects: No broker can make an external email or payment API transactional with its offset store. Production systems obtain effectively-once processing by pairing at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers: the consumer records (topic, partition, offset) or a business event_id inside the exact same ACID database transaction as its business update (INSERT INTO processed_events(event_id) ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING). A redelivered message hits the uniqueness constraint and becomes a no-op.

Idempotent Producers and the Transactional Outbox

Two additional seams require care on the producer side:

  • Idempotent Producer Retries: If a producer times out waiting for acks=all, the broker may have committed the batch and lost only the network ACK. With idempotence enabled (enable.idempotence=true), the broker assigns each producer a unique producer_id (PID) and tracks the last 5 committed sequence numbers per (PID, partition). A retried batch with an already-seen sequence number returns 201 immediately without appending a duplicate record.
  • Dual-Write Atomicity via Transactional Outbox: An order service that writes to PostgreSQL and then calls PRODUCE can crash between the two calls, leaving an orphan database row with no event (or an orphan event if published first and the DB rolls back). With the transactional outbox, the service writes both the domain row (orders) and the serialized event row (outbox_events) inside a single local ACID database transaction. A Change Data Capture (CDC) relay (such as Debezium tailing PostgreSQL WAL) streams committed outbox rows to the message queue at-least-once, where idempotent consumers complete the end-to-end guarantee.
  • Poison Pills, DLQ, and Log Compaction: A permanently malformed message causes infinite retry loops that stall its entire partition. After N bounded attempts (for example, 5), the consumer routes the payload plus error metadata to a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) topic and advances the offset (accepting a localized ordering break for that single key unless the topic halts deliberately). For state-snapshot topics (such as latest user addresses), log compaction retains the newest record per key indefinitely while garbage-collecting superseded older values.

11.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ModeOperational SymptomAutomated Mitigation
Partition Leader Broker Crash1 to 2 s write pause on partitions led by dead brokerKRaft controller promotes an in-sync follower (ISR) to leader; producers/consumers refresh metadata and resume cleanly with zero data loss
Slow Follower Falls Out of ISRUnder-replicated partition (URP > 0) metric risesLeader shrinks ISR after replica.lag.time.max.ms so writes continue uninterrupted on remaining 2 AZs; alert triggers operator disk check
Consumer Crash Before Offset CommitBrief lag bump on owned partitions during cooperative rebalanceGroup coordinator reassigns partitions; successor replays from last committed offset and idempotent consumer skips already-applied event_ids
Poison Pill MessagePartition lag climbs continuously while consumer throws repeated exceptionsConsumer retries 5 times with backoff, then emits payload + stack trace to <topic>.dlq and commits past the poison offset
Hot Partition Key SkewOne partition lags heavily while sibling partitions remain idleIdentify skew via per-partition lag metrics; split hot keys with explicit sub-key salting (tenant#0..7) if cross-subkey ordering is unneeded
Retention Overflow on Sustained LagConsumer lag approaches 7-day retention boundary; imminent data lossPage on-call at 50% retention age; scale consumer instances up to partition count P or temporarily extend topic retention TTL

Key SLIs and Operational Alerts

  • Consumer Group Lag (Messages and Time-Lag Seconds): Alert when time-lag exceeds SLO (for example, > 60 s for real-time billing) or approaches 25% of topic retention age.
  • Under-Replicated Partitions (URP): Alert if URP > 0 for more than 5 minutes (signals loss of redundancy ahead of a second failure).
  • Offline Partitions (offline_partitions_count): Immediate P0 page whenever > 0 (indicates a partition has zero available ISR replicas).
  • Produce p99 Latency and acks=all Error Rate: Alert if p99 > 50 ms or NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS errors occur.

11.7 Simulation Verification

To verify partition-key ordering, at-least-once crash recovery, and idempotent consumer deduplication, we execute the repository’s queuesim simulation (code/queuesim/src/main.rs). Six order lifecycle events append sequentially into partition 1 (offsets 0 through 5). The consumer processes all 6 events and crashes right before committing its offset; upon restarting from committed offset 0, it replays all 6 records, recognizes each previously processed event ID, and skips duplicate side effects before committing offset 6:

$ cargo run --release -p queuesim
produced order-7 created: partition 1, offset 0
produced order-8 created: partition 1, offset 1
produced order-7 paid: partition 1, offset 2
produced order-9 created: partition 1, offset 3
produced order-7 shipped: partition 1, offset 4
the consumer reads partition 1 and crashes before it commits
  offset 0: order-7 created -> acted on
  offset 1: order-8 created -> acted on
  offset 2: order-7 paid -> acted on
  offset 3: order-9 created -> acted on
  offset 4: order-7 shipped -> acted on
  offset 5: order-7 delivered -> acted on
it restarts and reads from the committed offset, which is still 0
  offset 0: order-7 created -> seen before, skipped
  offset 1: order-8 created -> seen before, skipped
  offset 2: order-7 paid -> seen before, skipped
  offset 3: order-9 created -> seen before, skipped
  offset 4: order-7 shipped -> seen before, skipped
  offset 5: order-7 delivered -> seen before, skipped
messages in the partition: 6, actions taken: 6, committed offset: 6

The final summary confirms end-to-end effectively-once semantics under a crash right before offset commit: messages in the partition: 6, actions taken: 6, and committed offset: 6.

Run the partitioned message queue simulation. Execute cargo run --release -p queuesim in code/ (code/queuesim/src/main.rs) to reproduce ordered partition appends, consumer crash redelivery, and idempotent deduplication.

11.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Partitioned Commit LogA topic split into multiple independent append-only ordered log files distributed across brokers for horizontal write and read parallelism.
OffsetA monotonically increasing 64-bit integer uniquely identifying a record’s sequential position inside its partition.
In-Sync Replicas (ISR)The dynamic set of partition replicas caught up with the leader within the configured lag threshold; acks=all waits for every replica in the ISR.
High Watermark (HW)The highest offset replicated across all in-sync replicas; consumers are permitted to read strictly up to HW.
Zero-Copy (sendfile())An OS kernel system call transferring log segment bytes directly from page cache to the network card via DMA without copying through user space.
Cooperative Sticky RebalanceAn incremental consumer-group rebalance protocol that revokes and transfers only the minimal subset of partitions needed, avoiding stop-the-world pauses.
Transactional OutboxWriting domain state changes and outbound event rows in one local ACID database transaction, followed by asynchronous CDC relay publishing to the queue.
Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ)A quarantine topic receiving poison messages that repeatedly fail processing so they do not stall healthy partition traffic.
Log CompactionBackground retention mode rewriting closed log segments to retain at least the latest record per unique key indefinitely.

References

  • Apache Kafka Improvement Proposals: KIP-98 (“Exactly Once Delivery and Transactional Messaging”), KIP-429 (“Kafka Consumer Incremental Rebalance Protocol”), and KIP-500 (“Replace ZooKeeper with a Self-Managed Metadata Quorum”).

Chapter 12: Distributed Job Scheduler

Large backend systems execute millions of tasks asynchronously outside the lifecycle of any user-facing HTTP request: transcoding uploaded videos, erasing closed accounts after a 30-day compliance window, reconciling nightly financial ledgers at 02:00 UTC, or orchestrating multi-stage data pipelines. A distributed job scheduler accepts one-shot, delayed, recurring (cron), and DAG-chained jobs, persists them durably, dispatches each due execution to a worker fleet, and recovers automatically when workers crash or stall mid-flight.

The core systems challenge is partial observability. Once the scheduler hands a job to a worker, it cannot observe the worker’s CPU or memory directly; it observes only network heartbeats and completion reports. A silent worker may have crashed, suffered a long pause, or completed the job while losing its completion response on the wire. In this chapter, I design a durable, horizontally scalable distributed job scheduler. We define actors, requirements, and capacity bounds, specify job/lease APIs and PostgreSQL FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED schemas, separate the DAG/cron registry (control plane) from sharded timing-wheel dispatchers (data plane), and engineer lease fencing, cron DST/idempotency guarantees, priority fairness, and dead-letter recovery.

In this chapter, we cover

  • job lifecycle state machine, actors, functional contracts, dispatch latency SLOs, non-goals, and throughput/storage bounds
  • REST/gRPC job submission, worker lease claiming, heartbeat extension, result fencing, and relational job-store DDL
  • separation of DAG and cron registry (control plane) from sharded DB pollers, hashed timing wheels, and worker pools (data plane)
  • hierarchical timing wheels versus sharded database polling with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  • lease-based claiming, monotonic attempt_id fencing against zombie workers, and at-least-once idempotent execution
  • recurring cron idempotency, UTC scheduling against Daylight Saving Time discontinuities, missed-run policies, priority aging, and per-tenant fair queuing
  • operational failure modes, lag SLIs, production schedulers (Google Distributed Cron, Temporal, Apache Airflow, Quartz), and simulation verification

12.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Actors and Use Cases

We organize the distributed job scheduler around three actors: job authors and upstream services submitting one-shot, cron, or DAG workflows; stateless execution workers claiming bounded leases and reporting outcomes; and platform operators auditing dispatch lag and replaying dead-letter jobs (Figure 12-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Job Author / ServiceSubmit one-shot, delayed, cron, or DAG jobs (POST /v1/jobs); pause/cancel (PATCH)Schedule a 30-day account purge, a nightly 02:00 UTC ledger close, or a 3-step ETL pipeline
Execution WorkerClaim lease (POST /v1/leases), extend TTL heartbeat, report ACK/NACK (PUT)Pull due jobs matched to its queue pool, renew leases during long runs, and return fenced outcomes
Platform OperatorInspect and replay dead-letter jobs; audit dispatch lag and retry spikesDiagnose a defective worker release causing mass DLQ growth and replay failed runs after rollback

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0Callers can submit immediate jobs, delayed future jobs (run_at), recurring cron schedules, and parent-child DAG workflows with explicit retry budgets and priority tiers.
1The scheduler dispatches each due job under a time-bounded lease with a monotonic attempt_id so at most one worker is actively assigned a given run at claim time.
2Workers renew active leases via periodic heartbeats for long-running tasks and submit completion or failure results fenced by attempt_id.
3Transient worker crashes, lease timeouts, or retryable errors requeue the job with jittered exponential backoff; exhausting max_attempts (5 default) transitions the job to a durable Dead-Letter Queue (DEAD) state for inspection and manual replay.
4Callers and operators can query live job state, attempt history, and last failure diagnostics, and can pause, cancel, or trigger ad-hoc runs.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0DurabilityZero lost submitted jobs across scheduler node or storage primary crashesAll job definitions and state transitions persist to a synchronously replicated multi-AZ job store before returning 201 Created
1Dispatch Latency (Precision)p50 <= 200 ms, p99 <= 1.0 s lag from scheduled run_at to worker lease claimPure cold DB polling at 5-second intervals misses sub-second precision; requires sharded 60-second lookahead buffers feeding in-memory hashed timing wheels
2State ConsistencyStrongly consistent job-state transitions (`PENDING -> LEASED -> RUNNING -> SUCCEEDEDDEAD`)
3Execution SemanticsAt-least-once execution (never dropped without notice; jobs must be idempotent)Because lease expiration cannot distinguish a crashed worker from a stalled worker, safe jobs enforce idempotency keys
4Scale10,000,000 jobs/day (116 avg jobs/s, 1,160 peak jobs/s); 500,000 active recurring cron definitionsHorizontally sharded job-run tables (16 to 64 partitions by hash(job_id) and run_at) and stateless auto-scaled dispatchers/workers

Non-Goals and Scope Boundaries

  • Exactly-once side effects without job cooperation: No scheduler can guarantee an uncooperative external side effect runs once across worker network partitions. Jobs performing financial or external mutations must carry deterministic idempotency keys (Chapter 10 and Chapter 11).
  • Sub-millisecond real-time control loops: Networked distributed schedulers operate at 100 ms to 1 s dispatch precision, rather than hard real-time microsecond kernel interrupts.
  • Arbitrary unbounded worker execution without heartbeats: Workers running multi-hour jobs must checkpoint progress and renew short leases rather than requesting 24-hour fixed leases that block crash recovery for a full day.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

Resource DimensionArithmetic DerivationProvisioned Bound
Average / Peak Job Rate10,000,000 jobs / 86,400 s = 115.7 avg/s; 10x burst factor116 avg jobs/s; 1,160 peak jobs/s (top-of-the-hour cron spikes can hit 5,000 jobs/s for 10 s)
State-Transition Write IOPSEach job averages 4 state updates (INSERT, CLAIM, HEARTBEAT, COMPLETE) * 1,160 peak~4,640 transactional DB writes/s peak (1 high-IOPS primary or 4 sharded primaries easily sustain 20,000+ TPS)
30-Day Hot Run Storage10,000,000 jobs/day * 30 days * 1.5 KB (payload + audit + indexes)450 GB hot NVMe storage (1.35 TB across 3 replicas); older completed runs archive to object storage
60-Second Lookahead Wheel RAM5,000 peak jobs/s * 60 s * 256 B timer entry~76.8 MB across dispatch fleet (fits comfortably inside RAM)
Worker Fleet SizingAssuming 2 s mean job duration at 1,160 peak jobs/s -> 2,320 concurrent in-flight jobs; 10 concurrent slots/worker~232 stateless workers (auto-scaled horizontally by queue depth and dispatch lag)

12.2 External API and Data Contracts

We design the scheduler around pull-based worker claiming (POST /v1/leases) so overloaded or draining workers stop requesting work automatically without requiring the scheduler to maintain a live capacity registry for every worker container.

Submission, Lease Claim, Heartbeat, and Fenced Result APIs

Submit a job (POST /v1/jobs):

Callers supply Idempotency-Key so retrying after a network timeout returns the original job ID rather than scheduling duplicate work.

POST /v1/jobs HTTP/2
Host: scheduler.internal
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: video-transcode-88412

{
  "queue": "media-transcode",
  "priority": 1,
  "run_at": "2026-10-14T09:00:00Z",
  "max_attempts": 5,
  "lease_ttl_seconds": 30,
  "payload": { "asset_id": "vid_992", "profiles": ["720p", "1080p"] }
}

HTTP/2 201 Created
Location: /v1/jobs/8231
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "job_id": "8231",
  "state": "PENDING",
  "attempt_id": 0,
  "run_at": "2026-10-14T09:00:00Z"
}

Claim a due job lease (POST /v1/leases):

Returns 201 Created with the job payload and monotonic attempt_id, or 204 No Content when no jobs are due.

POST /v1/leases HTTP/2
Host: scheduler.internal
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "worker_id": "worker-az-a-04",
  "queues": ["media-transcode"],
  "lease_ttl_seconds": 30
}

HTTP/2 201 Created
Location: /v1/leases/771
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "lease_id": "771",
  "job_id": "8231",
  "attempt_id": 1,
  "expires_in_seconds": 30,
  "payload": { "asset_id": "vid_992", "profiles": ["720p", "1080p"] }
}

Extend lease heartbeat (PUT /v1/leases/{lease_id}/heartbeat) and Report fenced outcome (PUT /v1/jobs/{job_id}/results/{attempt_id}):

PUT /v1/jobs/8231/results/1 HTTP/2
Host: scheduler.internal
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "worker_id": "worker-az-a-04",
  "outcome": "SUCCEEDED",
  "retryable": false
}

HTTP/2 204 No Content

If attempt_id = 1 has already been superseded by a reclaimer reissuing attempt_id = 2, the scheduler rejects the stale completion with 409 Conflict, preventing the zombie worker from corrupting the active attempt’s state.

Relational Job-Run Schema and Atomic Claim Query

CREATE TABLE job_runs (
    job_id          BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    idempotency_key TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    queue_name      TEXT NOT NULL,
    tenant_id       TEXT NOT NULL,
    priority        SMALLINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 5,
    state           TEXT NOT NULL,          -- PENDING, LEASED, RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, DEAD
    attempt_id      INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    max_attempts    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 5,
    run_at          TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    lease_owner     TEXT,
    lease_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    payload         JSONB NOT NULL,
    last_error      TEXT
);

-- Covering partial index so due-job queries touch only PENDING rows:
CREATE INDEX idx_job_runs_due
    ON job_runs (queue_name, priority ASC, run_at ASC)
    WHERE state = 'PENDING';

-- Covering partial index for fast lease-expiry reclamation:
CREATE INDEX idx_job_runs_expired_leases
    ON job_runs (lease_expires_at ASC)
    WHERE state IN ('LEASED', 'RUNNING');

12.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We separate durable schedule validation, cron rule parsing, and DAG dependency storage (control plane) from high-frequency timer dispatch, lease claiming, and worker execution (data plane) (Figure 12-2).

Component Responsibilities and Failure Domains

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Scheduler API TierControlStateless validators, cron parser, DAG acyclicity checkerHorizontally scaled behind L7 load balancers across 3 AZs; node loss has zero state impact
Metadata and Run DB (Sharded SQL)Control / DurableAuthoritative cron_specs, dag_edges, and job_runs tables replicated synchronously across 3 AZsPrimary crash triggers automatic synchronous replica failover in < 10 s with zero lost jobs
Sharded Time-Wheel DispatchersDataIn-memory 60-second lookahead hashed timing wheel partitioned by shard_idCompletely reconstructible state; if a dispatcher crashes, its shard lease transfers to a standby dispatcher that reloads the next 60 s window from the DB
Lease Reclaimer DaemonDataStateless sweep loop querying idx_job_runs_expired_leases every 2 sActive-standby via distributed lock (Chapter 10); because reclaiming uses conditional WHERE attempt_id = $a, momentary dual execution is completely harmless
Worker Pools (Per Queue / Priority)DataEphemeral task execution context and active lease heartbeat loopWorker crash leaves job leased until lease_expires_at, when the reclaimer returns it to PENDING with incremented backoff

Hot Data Path Walkthrough

  1. Durable Submission: A client sends POST /v1/jobs. The Scheduler API verifies Idempotency-Key, checks DAG acyclicity if parent dependencies exist, and inserts a PENDING row into the synchronously replicated Run DB.
  2. 60-Second Lookahead Prefetch: Sharded DB Pollers query their assigned partition every 10 seconds for PENDING jobs whose run_at <= NOW() + 60 seconds, buffering lightweight (job_id, run_at, priority) handles into an in-memory Hashed Timing Wheel.
  3. Sub-Second Wheel Release & Atomic Claim: When the timing wheel tick reaches run_at, the dispatcher makes the job claimable. A worker calls POST /v1/leases, executing an atomic FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED claim that transitions state = 'LEASED', increments attempt_id, and sets lease_expires_at = NOW() + 30 s.
  4. Execution, Heartbeat, and DAG Fan-Out: The worker executes the task, renewing lease_expires_at every 10 s while progress advances. On PUT /v1/jobs/{id}/results/{attempt_id}, the Run DB validates attempt_id, marks SUCCEEDED, and atomically decrements remaining-parent counters for any downstream DAG child jobs, promoting ready children to PENDING.

12.4 Scheduling Engines: Hierarchical Timing Wheels vs. SKIP LOCKED Polling

Scaling Delayed Execution with Hierarchical Timing Wheels

Querying a central SQL table every 100 ms across 50 dispatchers to fire delayed jobs creates severe B-tree read contention, whereas polling every 10 seconds violates our <= 1 s dispatch precision SLO.

We solve both problems with a two-tier architecture pairing durable relational storage with in-memory Hashed and Hierarchical Timing Wheels (Varghese and Lauck, SOSP 1987):

  • Long-Horizon Storage (Database): Millions of jobs scheduled hours, days, or months ahead stay cheaply on disk in job_runs indexed by (shard_id, run_at) without consuming RAM.
  • Short-Horizon Precision (Hierarchical Timing Wheel in RAM): Each shard dispatcher maintains an in-memory circular array of buckets (for example, 600 buckets at 100 ms resolution covering 60 seconds, plus a coarse upper wheel if wider horizons are needed). Inserting a job into bucket (current_tick + delta_ticks) mod 600 takes O(1) time, and advancing the tick pointer every 100 ms harvests all due timers in O(1) amortized work per timer rather than O(log N) heap sift operations.

Because the database remains the durable source of truth, a dispatcher crash loses zero jobs: the replacement dispatcher reads the next 60 seconds of PENDING rows from idx_job_runs_due and rebuilds its wheel in milliseconds.

Lock-Free Worker Claiming with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED

Transitioning a job from PENDING to LEASED must guarantee that at most one worker claims each due run. Reading a PENDING row and issuing a separate UPDATE introduces a classic check-then-act race illustrated in Interactive Trace 12.A, where two idle workers both read Job 1 as waiting and both start executing it simultaneously.

A single compare-and-set update (UPDATE job_runs SET state = 'LEASED' WHERE job_id = $1 AND state = 'PENDING') prevents double claiming, but under 200 concurrent workers polling the same queue, 199 workers collide on the oldest job, fail their CAS, and retry in a lockstorm.

PostgreSQL and MySQL 8 eliminate worker contention natively with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED:

WITH claimed AS (
    SELECT job_id
      FROM job_runs
     WHERE queue_name = $1
       AND state = 'PENDING'
       AND run_at <= NOW()
     ORDER BY priority ASC, run_at ASC
     LIMIT 1
       FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE job_runs j
   SET state            = 'LEASED',
       attempt_id       = j.attempt_id + 1,
       lease_owner      = $2,
       lease_expires_at = NOW() + make_interval(secs => $3)
  FROM claimed
 WHERE j.job_id = claimed.job_id
RETURNING j.job_id, j.attempt_id, j.payload;

When Worker 1 locks row 8231, Worker 2 skips locked row 8231 immediately without blocking and locks row 8232 on its first round trip. Throughput scales linearly with worker concurrency with zero lock-wait stalls.

12.5 Leases, Attempt Fencing, Cron Hazards, and Multi-Tenant Fairness

Lease Reclamation and Monotonic attempt_id Fencing

Figure 12-3 and Interactive Trace 12.B trace the full lifecycle of a worker crash and lease recovery. When Worker 1 crashes mid-execution, its lease expires at lease_expires_at. The reclaimer executes an atomic conditional update transitioning the job back to PENDING (with jittered exponential backoff run_at = NOW() + backoff) so Worker 2 claims it with attempt_id = 2.

Because lease expiry cannot prove that Worker 1 is dead (it may have stalled on a slow RPC or GC pause), every state update from a worker carries its attempt_id as a fencing token:

UPDATE job_runs
   SET state = 'SUCCEEDED', lease_owner = NULL
 WHERE job_id = $1
   AND attempt_id = $2
   AND state IN ('LEASED', 'RUNNING');

If zombie Worker 1 wakes up after Worker 2 has already claimed attempt_id = 2, Worker 1’s report with attempt_id = 1 matches 0 rows and receives 409 Conflict. Workers also distinguish permanent non-retryable failures (malformed JSON, deleted user account, HTTP 400) from transient failures (503, timeouts), moving permanent errors directly to DEAD without wasting four retries.

Recurring Cron Jobs: Idempotency, UTC vs. DST, and Missed-Run Policies

Evaluating recurring cron schedules across multiple scheduler nodes introduces three classic production bugs:

  1. Duplicate Firing Across Scheduler Replicas: Relying solely on leader election risks double-firing during leadership handoffs. Instead, every cron trigger constructs a deterministic idempotency key from (schedule_id, scheduled_epoch_utc) (for example, cron:nightly-billing:2026-10-14T02:00:00Z) and inserts into job_runs with ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING. Any number of scheduler nodes can evaluate the same minute tick concurrently, and the database guarantees exactly one run row is created.
  2. Daylight Saving Time (DST) Discontinuities: A job scheduled at 02:30 local time does not exist on the spring-forward night and occurs twice on the fall-back night. We store and evaluate all schedules internally in UTC (or require explicit timezone-aware policies defining skip vs. shift semantics for DST transitions).
  3. Explicit Missed-Run Policy (misfire_policy): If the cluster is unavailable from 01:55 to 02:10, every recurring job must declare one of three explicit policies:
    • RUN_ONCE (default for nightly reports): fire a single catch-up run on recovery.
    • SKIP (for ephemeral notifications or minute-level health pings): discard missed ticks and wait for the next future tick.
    • CATCH_UP (for hourly billing partitions): materialize every missed slot sequentially (capped by a concurrency limit so 180 missed ticks do not launch simultaneously).

Priority Aging and Per-Tenant Fair Queuing

Strict priority ordering (ORDER BY priority ASC) causes starvation when continuous P0 traffic prevents P3 maintenance jobs from ever executing. Similarly, a shared FIFO queue lets one noisy tenant submitting 500,000 export jobs delay every other tenant’s interactive jobs for hours. We counter both pathologies with:

  • Dedicated Priority Pools + Priority Aging: Reserve explicit minimum worker capacity for each tier (for example, 60% P0, 30% P1, 10% P2/P3) and compute an effective score effective_priority = base_priority - floor(wait_seconds / aging_interval) so neglected jobs climb steadily in urgency.
  • Per-Tenant Concurrency Caps and Weighted Fair Queuing: Track active_running_jobs[tenant_id] and enforce a per-tenant in-flight ceiling (max_concurrent_per_tenant) while selecting across active tenant queues via Deficit Round Robin (DRR).

12.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ModeOperational SymptomAutomated Mitigation
Worker Crash Mid-JobJob remains RUNNING until lease_expires_at (30 s)Reclaimer detects expired lease via partial index, transitions job to PENDING with jittered backoff, and dispatches attempt N + 1
Zombie Worker Stalls Past LeaseTwo workers execute concurrently; late worker reports stale resultattempt_id fencing rejects late completion with 409 Conflict; idempotent job handlers prevent duplicate external side effects
Dispatcher Crash (Lost Timing Wheel)< 2 s dispatch pause for 1/S of shardsStandby dispatcher claims shard lease and reloads the next 60 s window from job_runs in < 200 ms with zero job loss
Top-of-Hour Cron Thundering Herd (00:00)50x burst of recurring jobs firing at the exact same secondSupport hash-jittered cron windows (H * * * *) spreading non-time-critical jobs across the minute, plus worker pool autoscaling
Defective Worker Deploy (Mass Failures)Dead-Letter Queue (DEAD) spike across a specific queueDLQ rate alert pages on-call within 2 minutes; operators pause queue consumption, roll back worker image, and batch-replay DEAD runs
Noisy Tenant Submits 500k JobsSingle tenant queue depth spikes; other tenants remain unaffectedPer-tenant concurrency cap and DRR fair queuing isolate latency strictly to the flooding tenant

Key SLIs and Operational Alerts

  • Dispatch Lag (actual_claim_time - scheduled_run_at): p99 <= 1.0 s for P0 queues (alert if p99 > 5.0 s for 3 minutes).
  • Lease Expiration / Reclamation Rate: Tracks crashed or overloaded workers (alert if > 1% of jobs expire leases, indicating under-provisioned lease TTLs or failing heartbeat loops).
  • Dead-Letter Queue Growth Rate (jobs_dead_total): Immediate alert on any sustained increase above baseline.
  • Queue Depth Age (Oldest PENDING Job): Alerts immediately on worker starvation or pool exhaustion before backlogs breach SLAs.

Real-World Production Systems

12.7 Simulation Verification

To verify lease claiming, worker crash recovery via deadline expiration, and bounded attempt accounting, we run the repository’s jobsim simulation (code/jobsim/src/main.rs). Six jobs enter the queue with three workers (worker 0, worker 1, worker 2). At t = 0, all three workers claim jobs 0, 1, and 2. Worker 1 crashes while holding job 1; at t = 3, its lease expires and the reclaimer returns job 1 to the queue. At t = 4, worker 0 claims job 1 on its second attempt and completes it at t = 6:

$ cargo run --release -p jobsim
t= 0  worker 0 takes job 0
t= 0  worker 1 takes job 1
t= 0  worker 2 takes job 2
t= 2  worker 0 finishes job 0: accepted true
t= 2  worker 0 takes job 3
t= 2  worker 2 finishes job 2: accepted true
t= 2  worker 2 takes job 4
t= 3  job 1 was held by worker 1 past its deadline: back in the queue
t= 4  worker 0 finishes job 3: accepted true
t= 4  worker 0 takes job 1
t= 4  worker 2 finishes job 4: accepted true
t= 4  worker 2 takes job 5
t= 6  worker 0 finishes job 1: accepted true
t= 6  worker 2 finishes job 5: accepted true
jobs done: 6 of 6, attempts per job: 1 2 1 1 1 1

All 6 of 6 jobs finish cleanly despite the mid-flight worker failure, with attempts per job: 1 2 1 1 1 1 confirming exact attempt tracking on job 1.

Run the distributed job scheduler simulation. Execute cargo run --release -p jobsim in code/ (code/jobsim/src/main.rs) to reproduce worker crash detection, lease reclamation, and fenced completion above.

12.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Job LeaseA time-bounded assignment lending a job run to one worker until a deadline; if unrenewed, the reclaimer returns the job to PENDING.
Attempt Fencing (attempt_id)A monotonically increasing per-job execution counter checked on every worker heartbeat and result report to reject late updates from zombie workers.
Hashed / Hierarchical Timing WheelAn O(1) in-memory circular bucket structure firing large numbers of short-horizon timers without O(log N) priority-queue overhead.
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKEDA SQL row-locking clause letting concurrent worker transactions skip already-claimed rows instead of blocking, enabling lock-free queue claiming.
Misfire PolicyExplicit behavior (RUN_ONCE, SKIP, or CATCH_UP) governing how a recurring cron schedule handles ticks missed during an outage.
Priority AgingGradually increasing a waiting job’s effective priority over time to prevent low-priority starvation under sustained high-priority load.
Dead-Letter Queue (DEAD State)Terminal quarantine state holding jobs that exhausted retry limits or encountered permanent errors, preserving error traces for manual replay.

References

  • S. Davidovic and K. Guliani, “Reliable Cron Across the Planet”, ACM Queue, 2015.
  • G. Varghese and A. Lauck, “Hashed and Hierarchical Timing Wheels: Data Structures for the Efficient Implementation of a Timer Facility”, ACM SOSP, 1987.
  • PostgreSQL Documentation, “SELECT: The Locking Clause (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)”.
  • Temporal Technologies Documentation, “Workflow Execution, Deterministic Replay, and Event History”.
  • Apache Airflow Documentation, “Scheduler High Availability and DAG Serialization”.

Chapter 13: Multi-Channel Notification Service

Nearly every product service needs to notify users across push notifications (APNs, FCM), SMS carriers (Twilio, Vonage), email relays (Amazon SES, SendGrid), and customer webhooks. If checkout, authentication, billing, and marketing services each integrate directly with external providers, every team duplicates credential management, localization templates, legal opt-out checks, quiet-hour scheduling, and retry logic. Worse, when an external SMS gateway slows to 15 seconds per call, synchronous callers inherit that latency directly.

The defining engineering challenge of a notification platform is that its final delivery step leaves our trust boundary and runs on unreliable third-party infrastructure with strict rate ceilings, partial timeouts, and asynchronous delivery receipts. In this chapter, I design a high-throughput, multi-channel notification platform. We specify requirements, actors, and capacity bounds, design an idempotent 202 Accepted ingestion contract, separate preference/template policy management (control plane) from priority-isolated fan-out and provider dispatch (data plane), and engineer full-jitter exponential backoff, per-provider token buckets and circuit breakers, bounce suppression, and batched campaign fan-out.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, priority tiers (P0 OTP versus P3 marketing), functional contracts, latency SLOs, non-goals, and daily volume capacity bounds
  • idempotent 202 Accepted ingestion API, user preference and quiet-hour schemas, and asynchronous provider webhook contracts
  • separation of template, preference, and provider routing policy (control plane) from deduplication, priority queues, and sender bulkheads (data plane)
  • priority lane isolation eliminating head-of-line blocking, per-provider leaky-bucket pacing, and active-passive multi-provider failover
  • transient versus permanent provider error taxonomy, exponential backoff with full jitter, retry budgets, and three-state circuit breakers
  • user preferences, legal opt-out and bounce suppression lists, frequency capping, quiet-hour deferral, and two-stage batched fan-out for 10M+ campaigns
  • operational failure modes, SLIs, production architectures (Amazon SNS/Pinpoint, Courier, Knock), and simulation verification

13.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Actors and Use Cases

We organize the notification service around four actors: upstream product services emitting notification events, end users managing channel opt-outs and Do-Not-Disturb (DND) quiet hours, external delivery providers (APNs, FCM, SES, Twilio) accepting outbound sends and returning asynchronous delivery webhooks, and platform operators configuring templates and provider failover weights (Figure 13-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Product ServiceSubmit notification (POST /v1/notify with dedup_id and priority)Trigger a P0 login OTP SMS within 2 s, a P1 order-shipped email, or a P3 promotional push campaign
End UserConfigure channel opt-outs, locale, and quiet hours (PUT /v1/users/{id}/preferences)Mute promotional pushes between 22:00 and 08:00 local time while keeping security alerts enabled
External ProviderAccept outbound API sends; emit asynchronous delivery/bounce webhooksApple APNs, Google FCM, Amazon SES, and Twilio report delivered, bounced, or unregistered device tokens
Platform OperatorAuthor versioned i18n templates; tune provider weights and circuit thresholdsShift SMS traffic from degraded primary carrier to backup carrier without redeploying application services

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0Product services submit notifications targeting a user_id (or bulk audience segment) with a template ID, template parameters, priority class (P0 critical, P1 transactional, P2 lifecycle, P3 promotional), and mandatory Idempotency-Key (dedup_id).
1The ingestion tier deduplicates repeated requests carrying the same dedup_id within a 24-hour window, returning the original tracking ID without queueing a duplicate send.
2Before dispatch, the service centrally enforces user opt-out preferences, legal unsubscribe/bounce suppression lists, local quiet hours (deferring non-P0 messages until morning), and daily promotional frequency caps (<= 3 promos/user/day).
3The dispatch tier routes notifications to isolated per-priority, per-channel queues, paces outbound calls within each provider’s rate limit, retries transient failures with jittered exponential backoff up to 5 attempts, and quarantines exhausted sends to a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ).
4The service exposes an idempotent webhook endpoint ingesting provider delivery receipts, hard bounces, and invalid push tokens to update delivery state and maintain suppression lists automatically.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0Ingestion Availability & Latency99.99% availability; p99 <= 25 ms to return 202 AcceptedStrict asynchronous decoupling: ingestion validates, deduplicates, and writes to durable queues via transactional outbox; never calls external providers inline
1End-to-End Dispatch LatencyP0 (OTP/security): p99 <= 3 s; P1 (transactional): p99 <= 15 s; P3 (marketing): minutes to hoursPhysically separate priority topics and dedicated sender worker pools (bulkheads) prevent a 10M-user campaign from delaying login codes
2ConsistencyStrongly consistent deduplication store (SETNX / unique index) and opt-out enforcement; eventually consistent delivery statusTwo API nodes must agree strictly on whether dedup_id was seen; provider delivery receipts arrive asynchronously out of order via webhooks
3Delivery GuaranteeAt-least-once to external providers; at-most-once acceptance per dedup_id from caller perspectivePropagate dedup_id to providers supporting idempotency keys; accept rare duplicates after provider timeouts rather than dropping OTPs unnoticed
4Scale50,000,000 notifications/day (579 avg/s; 5,790 sustained peak/s; 50,000 burst campaign fan-out/s)Sharded Redis/SQL dedup store, partitioned Kafka priority queues, and auto-scaled stateless channel sender pools

Non-Goals and Scope Boundaries

  • Guaranteed human readership: A provider returning 200 OK confirms only handoff to the carrier, never that a user saw or read the message. Critical incident escalation (such as on-call paging) requires explicit human acknowledgment loops with automated escalation timers outside this service.
  • Synchronous delivery confirmation in POST /v1/notify: Callers receive 202 Accepted and poll GET /v1/notifications/{id} or subscribe to status events rather than holding open HTTP connections while SMTP or SMS networks negotiate.
  • Unthrottled instant campaign blasts: Dispatching 10,000,000 push notifications in 10 seconds violates provider quotas and triggers a self-inflicted traffic storm when millions of users open the app simultaneously. Bulk campaigns are always paced over minutes or hours.

Asynchronous Ingestion and Preference Contracts

Submit notification (POST /v1/notify):

Preference, Suppression, and Delivery State Schema

CREATE TABLE user_notification_prefs (
    user_id            TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    locale             TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'en-US',
    timezone           TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'UTC',
    promo_opt_in       BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
    quiet_start_minute SMALLINT,     -- Minutes past midnight local time (e.g., 1320 = 22:00)
    quiet_end_minute   SMALLINT,     -- e.g., 480 = 08:00
    updated_at         TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE address_suppression_list (
    channel            TEXT NOT NULL, -- email | sms | apns | fcm
    destination_hash   TEXT NOT NULL, -- SHA-256 of normalized email/phone/device token
    reason             TEXT NOT NULL, -- HARD_BOUNCE | SPAM_COMPLAINT | UNREGISTERED_TOKEN | STOP_SMS
    suppressed_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (channel, destination_hash)
);

13.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We decouple template authoring, user preference configuration, and provider SLA routing policy (control plane) from high-volume ingestion, deduplication, priority queuing, and provider dispatch (data plane) (Figure 13-2).

Component Responsibilities and Failure Domains

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Preference & Suppression StoreControlAuthoritative user opt-outs, quiet hours, frequency caps, and bounce suppression lists (SQL + Redis cache)Cache miss falls back to SQL; fail-closed on promotional opt-out uncertainty (never violate legal unsubscribe rules), fail-open for P0 security OTPs
Template & Routing Policy DBControlVersioned i18n message templates and per-channel provider health/weight tablesCompiled templates cached in API/sender RAM; control-plane outage pauses edits while live sending continues uninterrupted
Notification Ingestion APIDataStateless validators + strongly consistent dedup_id outbox store (24 h TTL)Multi-AZ stateless fleet; writes dedup_id and outbox event atomically so crashes never drop accepted requests
Priority-Isolated Queues (Kafka)DataDedicated topics per (priority, channel) pair (notify.p0.sms, notify.p3.email, etc.)Buffers hours of backlog during third-party outages; prevents bulk traffic from blocking urgent OTPs
Channel Sender BulkheadsDataPer-provider leaky-bucket rate limiters, three-state circuit breakers, HTTP/2 connection poolsIsolated per channel and priority so a dead SMS carrier cannot exhaust threads needed by APNs or SES
Webhook Receipt IngestorDataIdempotent callback verifier (HMAC signature validation) updating audit logs and suppression listRetried by providers for hours; updates `HANDED_TO_PROVIDER -> DELIVERED

Request Path Walkthrough

  1. Atomic Deduplication & Outbox Intake: The Ingestion API checks dedup:{id} atomically (persisting key + outbox row in one transaction so a crash never records a key without enqueuing the send) and returns 202 Accepted in < 25 ms.
  2. Policy, Preference, and Cap Gate: The enrichment stage checks the user’s opt-outs, hard-bounce suppression list, daily promotional frequency cap (INCR freq:{user}:{yyyy-mm-dd}), and local quiet hours. P0 security/OTP alerts bypass quiet hours and frequency caps; P2/P3 messages arriving during quiet hours are deferred via the delayed job scheduler (Chapter 12) until 08:00 local time.
  3. Localized Template Rendering & Priority Routing: The worker renders the versioned template in the user’s locale and publishes the concrete channel payload onto the matching priority topic (P0, P1, P2, or P3).
  4. Paced Provider Dispatch: A dedicated sender from that lane’s bulkhead consumes the message, acquires a token from the provider’s leaky-bucket pacer, verifies the provider’s circuit breaker is Closed, and transmits over HTTP/2.
  5. Asynchronous Delivery Verification: Provider webhooks later update the notification record from SENT_TO_PROVIDER to DELIVERED or HARD_BOUNCED (automatically adding invalid emails or unregistered APNs/FCM tokens to address_suppression_list).

13.4 Priority Lane Isolation, Provider Pacing, and Circuit Breakers

Eliminating Head-of-Line Blocking with Priority Lanes and Bulkheads

A single shared queue fails catastrophically as soon as marketing triggers a 10,000,000-user announcement: every P0 two-factor login SMS lands behind millions of promotional jobs and arrives 40 minutes late, locking users out of their accounts. Figure 13-3 illustrates our three-stage isolation pipeline:

  • Dedicated Topics and Worker Bulkheads: P0 (OTP, fraud, password reset), P1 (order confirmations, receipts), and P2/P3 (digests, promotions) run on physically separate queue topics, separate thread pools, and separate provider sub-accounts (so marketing email reputation never contaminates transactional IP reputation).
  • Per-Provider Leaky-Bucket Pacing: External providers enforce strict rate limits (for example, 500 SMS/s on Twilio or 1,000 emails/s on SES) and return 429 Too Many Requests when exceeded. Rather than colliding with provider 429 walls, senders pace outbound calls slightly below contracted limits (90% ceiling) using a distributed leaky bucket (Chapter 7), letting excess volume sit safely inside Kafka partitions.
  • Two-Stage Batched Campaign Fan-Out: A 10,000,000-user broadcast never executes as one giant loop. Stage 1 chunks the audience query into 10,000 batch jobs of 1,000 users each (each checkpointed independently). Stage 2 workers expand each batch into individual P3 notifications carrying deterministic idempotency keys (campaign:{camp_id}:user:{uid}) paced over a configured rollout window (30 to 120 minutes), protecting both provider limits and our own app servers from a click-through stampede.

Three-State Circuit Breakers and Multi-Provider Failover

When an external provider hangs instead of returning fast errors, every sender thread blocks for the full 10-second socket timeout, starving healthy traffic and cascading timeouts upstream. Placing a three-state circuit breaker in front of each provider isolates outages in microseconds, as traced in Interactive Trace 13.A:

  • Closed: All calls flow through while tracking rolling error rate and consecutive timeouts. Crossing the threshold (for example, 5 consecutive timeouts or > 50% 5xx over 20 requests) trips the breaker to Open.
  • Open: All calls fail fast in microseconds without opening sockets to the dead provider, protecting sender threads and giving the provider room to recover. For P0 SMS OTPs, an open primary-carrier breaker automatically routes traffic to a pre-warmed secondary SMS carrier (active-passive failover).
  • Half-Open: After a 30-second cooldown, the breaker admits a small probe (1 to 3 trial sends). Success resets the breaker to Closed; failure re-opens it for another cooldown window.

13.5 Error Taxonomy, Full-Jitter Exponential Backoff, and Delivery Truth

Permanent vs. Transient Provider Failures

Retrying every error damages both sender throughput and external deliverability reputation. Senders classify every provider response strictly into four actions:

Provider ResponseClassificationSender Action
200 / 202 AcceptedAccepted for relayMark HANDED_TO_PROVIDER, store provider_message_id, await webhook receipt
Invalid Email, Hard Bounce, APNs 410 Unregistered, FCM UNREGISTERED, SMS STOPPermanent FailureZero retries; mark FAILED_PERMANENT; write destination to address_suppression_list immediately to protect sender IP reputation
429 Too Many Requests, 500/502/503/504, Connection ResetTransient FailureSchedule retry via exponential backoff with full jitter (respecting Retry-After if larger) up to max_attempts = 5
Client Read Timeout (Ambiguous Outcome)Ambiguous TransientRetry with backoff, passing provider-side idempotency header where supported; accept rare duplicate over silent OTP loss

Exponential Backoff with Full Jitter and Retry Budgets

Immediate retries keep an overloaded provider pinned at 100% saturation. Doubling the wait after each failure (1 s -> 2 s -> 4 s -> 8 s -> 16 s, capped at 60 s) lets brief blips recover on attempt 2 while shedding load rapidly during long outages, as demonstrated in Interactive Trace 13.B:

Deterministic doubling alone still synchronizes retries across thousands of senders that failed during the same second, striking a recovering provider with periodic thundering-herd waves. Following Marc Brooker’s AWS simulation analysis, we apply Full Jitter:

sleep_seconds = random_uniform(0, min(cap_seconds, base_seconds * 2^(attempt - 1)))

Full jitter flattens synchronized spikes into a smooth trickle while halving mean retry wait time. To protect against prolonged brownouts where retries still multiply steady-state traffic, we pair full jitter with a per-provider retry budget (Google SRE practice): total retry requests across a sender pool may never exceed 10% of normal first-attempt traffic. Exhausted notifications enter the Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) (or expire automatically when their business validity TTL elapses, as with a 5-minute OTP code that would confuse a user if delivered two hours late).

Separating “Sent” from “Delivered”

Accepting a 200 OK from SES, APNs, or Twilio means only that the provider accepted responsibility to attempt delivery. Actual inbox placement, carrier handset delivery, or soft/hard bounces arrive seconds to hours later via asynchronous webhooks (POST /v1/webhooks/{provider}). Because providers retry webhooks at-least-once and out of order, our webhook handler verifies cryptographic signatures (HMAC-SHA256), enforces monotonic state transitions (QUEUED -> SENT_TO_PROVIDER -> DELIVERED | BOUNCED), and updates suppression lists idempotently.

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ModeOperational SymptomAutomated Mitigation
Primary SMS Carrier OutageConsecutive timeouts / 503 on SMS sender poolCircuit breaker opens after 5 consecutive failures; P0 SMS pool fails over immediately to pre-warmed secondary SMS carrier
10M-User Marketing Campaign LaunchP3 queue depth surges to millionsDedicated P0/P1 topics and sender bulkheads keep OTP latency < 3 s; P3 campaign paces smoothly over 60 minutes

Stale P0 OTP Delayed by Prolonged OutageOTP arrives 15 minutes late, confusing userEvery message carries a business valid_until deadline; senders drop expired OTPs cleanly instead of delivering stale codes

Key SLIs and Operational Alerts

  • End-to-End Dispatch Latency by Priority (p99): P0 <= 3 s (page immediately at > 5 s), P1 <= 15 s, P3 <= 30 minutes.
  • Provider Circuit-Breaker State (provider_breaker_open): Immediate alert whenever any primary provider circuit opens or failover engages.
  • Email Bounce and Spam-Complaint Rates: Page if hard bounce rate exceeds 2.0% or complaint rate exceeds 0.08% (well below ISP/SES suspension limits of 5% and 0.1%).
  • DLQ Volume and Dedup Conflict Rate: Alert on rising DLQ entries (broken template variables or invalid provider credentials) and monitor dedup hit rate for upstream retry loops.

13.7 Simulation Verification

To verify caller idempotency deduplication, exponential retry pacing, and bounded DLQ quarantine, we execute the repository’s notifysim simulation (code/notifysim/src/main.rs). Five requests enter the notification service against a simulated provider configured with distinct transient failure counts per key:

$ cargo run --release -p notifysim
order-7-shipped   sent on try 1, 0 seconds after the first try
order-8-shipped   sent on try 3, 3 seconds after the first try
order-7-shipped   submitted before: not sent again
order-9-shipped   sent on try 5, 15 seconds after the first try
order-10-shipped  failed 5 times: set aside for a person to look at

Every core delivery invariant appears in the five-line trace:

  1. Immediate Healthy Path: order-7-shipped succeeds on try 1 at t = 0 s.
  2. Idempotent Deduplication: Submitting order-7-shipped a second time is recognized by its idempotency key and suppressed (not sent again).
  3. Exponential Backoff Timing: order-8-shipped fails twice and succeeds on try 3 after 1 + 2 = 3 s; order-9-shipped fails four times and succeeds on try 5 after 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 s.
  4. Bounded Retry Quarantine (DLQ): order-10-shipped fails all 5 permitted attempts and moves to the dead-letter set for human inspection rather than looping indefinitely.

Run the notification delivery simulation. Execute cargo run --release -p notifysim in code/ (code/notifysim/src/main.rs) to reproduce idempotency suppression, exponential backoff schedules, and five-try dead-letter isolation above.

Engineering Glossary

Priority Lane Isolation (Bulkhead)Physically separating queues, worker pools, and provider quotas across priority tiers (P0 OTP vs P3 marketing) to eliminate head-of-line blocking.
Full-Jitter Exponential BackoffChoosing each retry delay uniformly at random in [0, min(cap, base * 2^(attempt - 1))], eliminating synchronized retry waves.
Circuit BreakerA three-state (Closed, Open, Half-Open) guard that stops sending traffic to a failing external provider, failing fast or triggering failover until trial probes succeed.
Retry BudgetA global cap limiting retry volume to a small percentage (for example, 10%) of healthy first-attempt traffic to prevent cascading overload.
Suppression ListA durable opt-out and hard-bounce registry preventing further sends to unsubscribed users, invalid addresses, or uninstalled device tokens.
