14. URL Shortener: System Design

A global URL shortener maps an arbitrary target web address to a compact alias, such as sho.rt/4C92a7Q, and redirects every incoming visitor to the original destination within milliseconds. Although the core data model fits into a single key-value relation, operating a public redirect service at internet scale exposes foundational distributed systems tensions: generating short, collision-free, non-enumerable identifiers without cross-node write contention; serving a 100:1 read-heavy workload under extreme Zipfian skew; recording high-volume click analytics without introducing write amplification on the redirect path; and revoking malicious links promptly across globally distributed caches.

In this chapter, we design a globally distributed URL shortener anchored around a strict asymmetry between writes and reads. Creating a link happens at a modest rate and tolerates tens of milliseconds of latency, whereas following a link happens two orders of magnitude more frequently and sits directly on the critical path of every user clicking a link in an email, message, or web page. A brief pause in link creation inconveniences one author; a failed redirect breaks published links for millions of visitors simultaneously.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, functional requirements, sub-10 ms redirect SLOs, explicit non-goals, and 5-year capacity bounds
  • external HTTP/2 contracts for link creation, 301/302 redirection, alias management, abuse quarantine, and relational and key-value schemas
  • separation of the control plane (range allocation, blocklist propagation, click analytics) from the read-optimized data plane
  • key allocation strategies comparing truncated cryptographic hashes, random generation, and disjoint counter range leasing with Base-62 bijection and Feistel scrambling
  • multi-tier redirect caching (CDN edge, regional Redis, Bloom filter negative-lookup defense), 301 versus 302 revocation trade-offs, and asynchronous click pipelines
  • failure-mode mitigation matrices, operational SLIs, production benchmarks (Bitly, TinyURL, Flickr Base58), and verification via code/shortener

14.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Actors and Use Cases

We partition the URL shortener boundary around three external actor groups (Figure 14-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Link AuthorCreate short link (POST /v1/links), update expiry or alias (PATCH / DELETE /v1/links/{code}), query analytics (GET /v1/links/{code}/stats)Marketing team or API client shortens a parameterized campaign URL with a 90-day expiry and inspects daily click totals
Link VisitorResolve and follow short link (GET /{code})Browser or mobile application opens a shared short link and receives a sub-10 ms HTTP redirect to the destination URL
Trust and Analytics TeamQuarantine abusive link (POST /v1/admin/block/{code}) and inspect domain threat telemetrySafety automation detects a phishing destination and blocks resolution across regional caches and CDN edges within seconds

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0An authenticated author submits a valid http or https URL (up to 4,096 bytes) and receives a unique 7-character Base-62 short code, with optional caller-supplied expiry timestamp and idempotency key.
1A visitor requesting GET /{code} receives an HTTP redirect (302 Found or bounded-TTL 301 Moved Permanently) carrying the canonical target URL in the Location header, or 404 Not Found / 410 Gone if the code is absent, expired, or quarantined.
2An author can reserve an optional custom alias (distinguished structurally from generated 7-character codes) using atomic create-if-absent semantics.
3Once assigned to a URL, a generated short code never maps to a different target URL, and expired or deleted codes are never recycled.
4Authors can query time-bucketed click statistics (total clicks, hourly rollups, top referrers) without adding synchronous write latency to redirects.
5The platform screens destination URLs against phishing and malware blocklists on creation and periodically thereafter, refuses self-domain redirect loops, and supports rapid administrative quarantine.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0Redirect Availability99.99% global availability (<= 4.3 minutes downtime per month)Active-active stateless redirect fleets across multiple regions behind Anycast CDN edge caches
1Redirect Latencyp50 <= 5 ms (edge hit), p99 <= 15 ms (regional L2 hit), p999 <= 40 ms (origin miss)Eliminates synchronous disk writes, analytics updates, and cross-region consensus from the GET /{code} critical path
2ConsistencyStrong read-after-write consistency for link creation (PC/EC quorum commit); eventual consistency (<= 60 s lag) for click countsAuthors share links immediately after 201 Created, so mappings require quorum visibility; click dashboards tolerate 1-minute rollup delay
3UnpredictabilitySequential link creation reveals neither business volume nor neighboring valid codesCounter values pass through a keyed format-preserving Feistel bijection before Base-62 encoding
4Scale100,000,000 new links per month (6 billion over 5 years) at a 100:1 read-to-write ratioRequires 3.52 trillion code capacity (62^7), horizontally sharded mapping storage, and multi-tier caching

Non-Goals and Scope Boundaries

To keep the architecture focused on core redirect mechanics, we exclude the following capabilities from this design:

  • Arbitrary destination mutation: Generated links are immutable after creation (excluding expiry and administrative quarantine); mutable dynamic routing tables belong to an enterprise link-management product rather than the core shortener.
  • Per-click financial billing: Click telemetry uses at-least-once batched aggregation with minute-level eventual consistency; monetized pay-per-click accounting requires exact per-event deduplication and double-entry ledger reconciliation (Chapter 19).
  • Full-page destination proxying or web archiving: The service issues HTTP redirects and never proxies or caches the HTML body of destination sites.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

We size write QPS, read QPS, 5-year storage, cache memory, and egress bandwidth from the baseline of 100 million new links per month and a 100:1 read-to-write ratio:

Resource DimensionArithmetic DerivationProvisioned Bound
Total Links (5 Years)100,000,000 links/mo * 12 mo/yr * 5 yr6,000,000,000 links (6 billion)
7-Character Base-62 Space62^7 distinct strings (0-9, A-Z, a-z)3,521,614,606,208 codes (~3.52 trillion, < 0.17% utilization in 5 years)
Write Rate (Sustained / Peak)100,000,000 / (30 * 86,400 s) = 38.6 writes/s; 5x peak burst39 writes/s sustained, 200 writes/s peak
Redirect Rate (Sustained / Peak)39 * 100 = 3,900 reads/s sustained; 10x viral event spike3,900 reads/s sustained, 39,000 reads/s peak
Primary Mapping Storage (5 yr)6 * 10^9 links * 500 B/row (code, URL, metadata, index overhead)3.0 TB logical (9.0 TB raw with 3x replication)
Regional L2 Redis Cache (Hot 5%)5% * 6 * 10^9 = 300M hot rows; working daily set (20M active links * 500 B)10 GB active daily working set (64 GB provisioned per region for headroom)
Bloom Filter RAM (All 6B Keys)m = -n ln(p) / (ln 2)^2 at n = 6 * 10^9, p = 0.01 (9.58 bits/key)~7.2 GB aggregate (~900 MB per shard across 8 shards)
Redirect Egress Bandwidth39,000 peak req/s * 600 B HTTP redirect headers23.4 MB/s (~187 Mbps peak aggregate)
Click Event Stream (5 yr raw)3,900 clicks/s * 64 B compact event (code, ts, country, ref_hash)250 KB/s (~21.6 GB/day raw; < 2 GB/day after 1-minute OLAP rollup)

Because 3.0 TB of mapping data and 10 GB of daily hot links are modest by modern server standards, the system is bounded primarily by tail latency under extreme hot-key skew (millions of clicks per hour on a single viral link) and negative-lookup abuse (scanners probing random 7-character codes to overwhelm storage).

14.2 External API and Data Contracts

The platform exposes a JSON-over-HTTP/2 control API for link management and a minimal-overhead HTTP redirect interface at the root path.

External HTTP Contracts

Create a short link (idempotent via Idempotency-Key):

POST /v1/links HTTP/2
Host: api.sho.rt
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Idempotency-Key: 7f3c9b12-8a40-4e92-b831-1e2d3f4a5b6c
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "url": "https://example.org/docs/systems/design?ref=2026&id=9812",
  "custom_alias": null,
  "expires_at": "2027-11-20T00:00:00Z",
  "redirect_mode": "302"
}

HTTP/2 201 Created
Location: /v1/links/a9K4x7Q
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "code": "a9K4x7Q",
  "short_url": "https://sho.rt/a9K4x7Q",
  "target_url": "https://example.org/docs/systems/design?ref=2026&id=9812",
  "expires_at": "2027-11-20T00:00:00Z",
  "created_at": "2026-11-20T13:08:05Z"
}

Status codes follow strict contract semantics: 201 Created on first allocation (or replay with identical Idempotency-Key and payload), 400 Bad Request for malformed schemes or self-domain loops (sho.rt), 409 Conflict when a requested custom_alias already exists, 422 Unprocessable Content if a destination matches the threat blocklist, and 429 Too Many Requests when caller creation quotas are exceeded (Chapter 7).

Resolve and redirect a short link:

GET /a9K4x7Q HTTP/2
Host: sho.rt

HTTP/2 302 Found
Location: https://example.org/docs/systems/design?ref=2026&id=9812
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, s-maxage=3600
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

For expired or quarantined codes, the service returns 410 Gone with Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600 so intermediate caches stop forwarding repeated traffic for revoked links. Unknown codes return 404 Not Found with a short negative cache header (max-age=60).

Quarantine an abusive link (control plane):

POST /v1/admin/block/a9K4x7Q HTTP/2
Host: control.sho.rt
Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "reason": "phishing_credential_harvest",
  "purge_cdn": true
}

Storage Schemas

We separate immutable link mappings (optimized for primary-key point lookups) from time-series click rollups (optimized for columnar analytical scans):

-- Sharded primary mapping store (partitioned by hash(code) across 8 Raft-replicated shards)
CREATE TABLE short_links (
    code          VARCHAR(64)  PRIMARY KEY,   -- 7-char Base-62 or custom alias
    target_url    VARCHAR(4096) NOT NULL,
    owner_id      BIGINT       NOT NULL,
    redirect_code SMALLINT     NOT NULL DEFAULT 302, -- 301 or 302
    status        SMALLINT     NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,   -- 1=active, 2=expired, 3=blocked
    created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    expires_at    TIMESTAMPTZ  NULL
);

-- Separate idempotency cache (24-hour TTL) to prevent duplicate allocations on client retry
CREATE TABLE link_idempotency (
    owner_id        BIGINT       NOT NULL,
    idempotency_key VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    request_hash    BYTEA        NOT NULL,
    assigned_code   VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (owner_id, idempotency_key)
);

-- OLAP analytical store (ClickHouse) aggregated in 1-minute windows
CREATE TABLE link_clicks_1m (
    code          String,
    bucket_minute DateTime,
    country_iso   LowCardinality(String),
    referrer_host String,
    click_count   UInt64
) ENGINE = SummingMergeTree()
PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(bucket_minute)
ORDER BY (code, bucket_minute, country_iso, referrer_host);

14.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We isolate all coordination, safety enforcement, and analytics aggregation inside a control plane so that the hot redirect data plane remains stateless, memory-resident, and insulated from background outages (Figure 14-2).

Component Responsibilities

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Range Allocator (etcd / Raft)ControlAuthoritative high-water counter cursor (next_block_start)Write workers hold in-memory leases of 100,000 IDs; brief allocator outage causes zero write disruption until a worker exhausts its local block
Abuse and Blocklist ServiceControlThreat intelligence feeds, domain blocklists, revocation logPushes compiled blocklists to Write APIs and publishes invalidation events to regional Redis clusters and CDN purge APIs
Click Stream and OLAP PipelineControlPartitioned Kafka click log and ClickHouse link_clicks_1m rollupsRedirect servers emit events asynchronously via non-blocking ring buffers; broker outage drops or spills telemetry locally without delaying HTTP redirects
CDN Edge PoPs (Anycast)DataL1 HTTP response cache for viral 301/302 redirects (80% hit ratio)Automatic BGP Anycast rerouting shifts visitors to the nearest healthy PoP within seconds
Stateless Redirect ServiceDataIn-memory Bloom filter snapshot, L2 Redis connection poolsHorizontally auto-scaled across three AZs per region; losing any instance shifts traffic immediately via load balancer health checks
Regional Redis + Sharded StoreDataL2 hot link cache (64 GB) and L3 durable mapping shards (8 shards x 3 replicas)Redis miss falls through to L3 store; shard leader crash triggers Raft election in 1 to 3 s while reads continue from cache and followers

Write and Read Lifecycles

Write path (POST /v1/links):

  1. The Write API authenticates the author, enforces per-account creation rate limits (Chapter 7), validates URI syntax, rejects self-domain URLs (sho.rt), and checks the destination host against an in-memory compiled threat blocklist.
  2. If an Idempotency-Key is supplied, the Write API checks link_idempotency and returns the prior allocation on an exact payload match.
  3. For standard generated links, the Write API atomically increments its local in-memory leased counter (AtomicU64), passes the integer through the keyed Feistel permutation, and encodes the scrambled value into a 7-character Base-62 string. No read-before-write uniqueness probe is required.
  4. For custom aliases, the Write API validates namespace separation (length greater than 7 characters or containing a hyphen) and issues a quorum conditional insert (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) to the owning L3 shard.
  5. Upon quorum commit across three AZs, the Write API updates the shard’s Bloom filter (and broadcasts the bit set asynchronously to redirect workers), optionally warms L2 Redis, and returns 201 Created.

Read path (GET /{code}):

  1. A visitor’s DNS resolution routes via Anycast to the nearest CDN Edge PoP (L1). Roughly 80% of requests hit a cached viral link and return a redirect in under 10 ms without contacting origin infrastructure.
  2. On an L1 miss, the request reaches a regional Stateless Redirect Service instance, which queries L2 Regional Redis (~18% of total traffic, resolved in ~2 ms).
  3. On an L2 miss, the Redirect Service tests the local in-memory Bloom filter (< 0.2 ms, O(k) hash probes). If the filter returns definitely absent, the service immediately replies 404 Not Found without touching disk storage.
  4. On a positive Bloom match, the Redirect Service fetches the mapping from the owning L3 shard (< 2% of total traffic, ~12 ms), populates L2 Redis (or sets a short-TTL negative cache entry if the Bloom check was a false positive), checks status and expires_at, appends a non-blocking click record to the local Kafka producer buffer, and returns the redirect response.

14.4 Key Allocation: Range Leasing, Base-62 Bijection, and Scrambling

Alphabet Size and Code Length

Every short code is drawn from the 62-character URL-safe alphanumeric alphabet (0-9, A-Z, a-z), which requires no percent-encoding in RFC 3986 path segments. A 6-character code space yields $62^6 = 56{,}800{,}235{,}584$ (~56.8 billion) identifiers. Against our 5-year projection of 6 billion links, a 6-character space would exceed 10.5% occupancy, making blind guessing succeed on more than 1 in 10 probes and risking mid-life schema migration if growth accelerates. Extending to 7 characters expands the space to $62^7 = 3{,}521{,}614{,}606{,}208$ (~3.52 trillion) codes, reducing 5-year occupancy to 0.17% (roughly 1 valid link per 587 random guesses).

For contexts where humans read codes aloud or transcribe them from printed material, operators adopt Base-58 (omitting visually ambiguous glyphs 0, O, I, and l), yielding $58^7 \approx 2.21$ trillion codes while eliminating transcription errors.

Comparing Three Code-Generation Strategies

StrategyUniqueness GuaranteeRead-Before-Write CostCoordination StateEnumeration Resistance
Truncated Hash (SHA-256 prefix)Probabilistic; requires store check and salt retry on collisionMandatory lookup on every writeStatelessHigh (pseudorandom output)
CSPRNG Random DrawProbabilistic; requires atomic create-if-absent retryMandatory conditional insert on every writeStatelessHigh (cryptographic entropy)
Leased Counter + Feistel Bijection (Chosen)Deterministic by construction (0 collisions)None (1 blind quorum write)etcd range allocator consulted once per 100,000 linksHigh while Feistel round keys remain secret

Why truncated hashes fail without retry loops: Under the birthday bound, drawing $n$ codes uniformly from a space of size $N$ yields approximately $n^2 / (2N)$ colliding pairs. In the repository simulation (code/shortener), hashing 2,000,000 distinct URLs and truncating to 6 characters produced 97 collisions. Sending even 1 visitor in 20,000 to an unrelated website violates functional requirement 3. Resolving hash collisions forces a read-before-write check plus iterative salting, turning every link creation into a conditional read-modify-write cycle. Furthermore, deterministic hashing of the destination URL causes two different authors shortening the same URL to share one code, coupling their analytics and expiry lifetimes.

Disjoint counter range leasing: We assign monotonically increasing integers from a strongly consistent etcd / Raft range allocator (Chapter 8). Each Write API instance requests a contiguous block of 100,000 integers ([start, start + 99,999]) in a single quorum write and dispenses numbers lock-free from RAM via fetch_add(1). At 39 writes/s sustained, the entire fleet consults the allocator roughly once every 42 minutes. If a Write API node crashes mid-block, the remaining unallocated integers are discarded permanently; against 3.52 trillion codes, forfeiting tens of thousands of IDs on a crash is negligible compared to the operational simplicity of zero write-path coordination.

Base-62 Encoding Step by Step

Converting a non-negative integer $x$ to Base-62 proceeds by repeated Euclidean division by 62, emitting each remainder as the next least-significant glyph in 0..9A..Za..z. Interactive Trace 14.A steps through encoding the counter value 1,000,000 into 4C92.

Preventing Enumeration with Format-Preserving Encryption

Encoding raw sequential counters directly exposes two severe vulnerabilities. First, an adversary holding 4C92 can enumerate 4C91, 4C93, and 4C94 to harvest unlisted shared documents, private calendar invitations, or capability URLs that rely on secrecy of the link. Second, observing the integer difference between codes created at midnight on consecutive days reveals exact daily link volume to competitors.

Shuffling the 62-character alphabet does not prevent analysis, because consecutive integers still differ only in their rightmost character. Instead, we pass each 42-bit counter value $x \in [0, 62^7 - 1]$ through a keyed 4-round balanced Feistel network (a standard Format-Preserving Encryption construction, Bellare et al. 2009) using HMAC-SHA256 truncated to 21 bits as the round function $F_k$, combined with cycle walking whenever an intermediate 42-bit output exceeds $62^7 - 1$:

// Bijective scrambling over domain [0, 62^7 - 1] via 4-round Feistel + cycle walking.
// Distinct counter inputs always map to distinct outputs (zero collisions).
const DOMAIN: u64 = 3_521_614_606_208; // 62^7 (< 2^42 = 4_398_046_511_104)
const HALF_BITS: u32 = 21;
const HALF_MASK: u64 = (1u64 << HALF_BITS) - 1;

fn scramble_id(counter: u64, round_keys: &[u64; 4]) -> u64 {
    let mut v = counter;
    loop {
        let mut left = (v >> HALF_BITS) & HALF_MASK;
        let mut right = v & HALF_MASK;
        for &key in round_keys {
            let f = keyed_prf_21bit(right, key);
            let next_right = left ^ f;
            left = right;
            right = next_right;
        }
        v = (left << HALF_BITS) | right;
        if v < DOMAIN {
            return v;
        }
    }
}

Because a Feistel network is mathematically invertible for any round function $F$, the mapping is a strict bijection on $[0, 2^{42} - 1]$, and cycle walking preserves bijectivity strictly inside $[0, 62^7 - 1]$ with an expected 1.25 iterations per call ($2^{42} / 62^7 \approx 1.249$). Adjacent counter values produce statistically independent 7-character Base-62 codes while retaining zero-collision deterministic generation.

14.5 Read-Path Optimization: Redirects, Multi-Tier Caching, and Analytics

HTTP Redirect Semantics: 301 vs. 302 vs. 307/308

Selecting the HTTP redirect status code directly determines browser caching behavior, origin traffic volume, analytics completeness, and security revocation latency:

Status CodeSemantic ContractBrowser CachingClick VisibilityAbuse Revocation Latency
301 Moved Permanently (unbounded)Permanent replacement; method may rewrite to GETIndefinite heuristic caching by browsersMisses repeat visits from the same browserUnbounded (cannot reliably revoke from client caches)
301 + Cache-Control: max-age=86400Permanent with explicit 24-hour freshness boundCached up to 24 hours per browserCounts unique browser-days; misses rapid repeatsBounded to <= 24 hours
302 Found (default here)Temporary redirect; browser revalidates or uses explicit max-ageControlled via Cache-Control: max-age=300, s-maxage=3600Captures origin and CDN edge click logs cleanlySub-minute via CDN surrogate-key purge + 5-minute client ceiling
307 / 308Strict method-preserving temporary / permanent redirectMatches 302 / 301 respectivelySame as 302 / 301Preserves POST bodies; rarely needed for browser GET links

In production, unbounded 301 responses create a severe safety hazard: once a phishing URL is cached permanently inside millions of browsers, disabling the link at the origin cannot stop affected visitors from being redirected. Our default issues 302 Found with Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, s-maxage=3600 (5-minute browser cache, 1-hour CDN cache), allowing CDN edge servers to absorb viral surges while preserving fast surrogate-key purge when Trust and Safety quarantines a link. For high-volume static links where click analytics are disabled, authors may explicitly opt into bounded 301 redirects.

Multi-Tier Cache Cascade and Bloom Filter Defense

Short-link traffic follows a steep Zipf distribution in which fewer than 1% of links generate over 80% of redirect volume. Meanwhile, automated credential-stuffing or link-enumeration bots routinely issue thousands of requests per second for nonexistent 7-character codes, causing cache penetration straight through LRU caches to disk storage. We defend the read path with a four-tier cascade (Figure 14-3).

  1. L1 CDN Edge PoP (~80% hit ratio, ~10 ms client RTT): Global Anycast PoPs serve hot viral links directly from edge RAM, shielding origin regions from sudden social-media traffic spikes. Edge log shipping streams sampled or complete 302 hit logs asynchronously to the analytics ingestion pipeline so cached hits are not lost from click counts.
  2. L2 Regional Redis Cluster (~18% hit ratio, ~2 ms intra-region RTT): Holds the active working set using an allkeys-lfu eviction policy. Because link targets are immutable, cache entries require invalidation only on administrative quarantine or explicit deletion, published over a control-plane pub/sub channel.
  3. Bloom Filter Negative Gate (< 0.2 ms, O(k) bit probes): Each Redirect Service shard maintains a partitioned Counting or Scalable Bloom Filter covering all valid codes in the store. For 6 billion keys at a 1% false-positive rate ($p = 0.01$), optimal sizing requires $k = 7$ hash functions and $9.58$ bits per key (~7.2 GB total, or 900 MB per shard). Every nonexistent code rejected by the Bloom filter returns 404 Not Found immediately in RAM without issuing an L3 query, blocking 99% of random enumeration scans. The remaining 1% false positives that miss L3 populate a short-TTL (60 s) negative tombstone in L2 Redis and increment a per-IP 404 GCRA rate limiter (Chapter 7).
  4. L3 Sharded Mapping Store (< 2% traffic, ~12 ms): Serves cold long-tail links from SSD-backed Raft-replicated shards partitioned by hash(code).

Asynchronous Click Analytics and Abuse Controls

Incrementing a relational counter row on every redirect would convert a 3,900 to 39,000 QPS read workload into a write-contended hotspot on popular rows. Instead, Redirect Services and CDN edge log collectors emit compact 64-byte click events (code, timestamp_ms, country_iso, referrer_hash) into a partitioned Kafka topic via non-blocking ring buffers. Stream consumers aggregate counts in 1-minute tumbling windows in memory and flush bulk batches into ClickHouse (SummingMergeTree), reducing persistent write volume by over 1,000x for viral links while isolating redirect latency completely from analytics pipeline backpressure.

Public redirectors are primary targets for phishing concealment. Three layered safeguards protect domain reputation: synchronous URL inspection against local threat feeds (such as Google Safe Browsing prefix lists) at link creation, periodic background re-scanning of active high-click destinations to catch delayed page swaps, and an instant quarantine endpoint (POST /v1/admin/block/{code}) that marks status = 3 in L3, broadcasts an L2 Redis invalidation, and triggers a CDN purge API call so malicious links return 410 Gone globally within 5 seconds.

Failure Mode and Mitigation Matrix

Failure ModeBlast RadiusDetection SignalAutomated Mitigation
L2 Regional Redis Shard CrashElevated latency (2 ms to 12 ms) for 1/N of regional cache missesRedis health probe failure and L3 read QPS jumpRedirect Service bypasses dead shard directly to L3 with singleflight request coalescing to prevent cache stampede; Redis replica promotes in < 10 s
Range Allocator (etcd) OutageZero immediate impact; write path degrades only when workers exhaust local 100,000-ID blocksAllocator lease-renewal errors and low-water local block alert (< 20% remaining)Workers continue issuing IDs from pre-leased RAM blocks (~40 minutes runway); ops restores quorum before exhaustion
Random 404 Enumeration FloodRisk of saturating L3 storage IOPS via cache penetration404 response ratio spikes above 5% of total trafficIn-memory Bloom filter drops 99% of invalid probes in < 0.2 ms; L2 negative cache and per-IP 404 rate limiter absorb the 1% false-positive residual

Operational SLIs, SLOs, and Alert Thresholds

  • Redirect Availability SLI: Fraction of valid GET /{code} requests returning 301/302 (excluding client 4xx errors), targeting 99.99% over a 30-day rolling window; page on-call when 5-minute error burn exceeds 14.4x budget.
  • Origin Redirect Latency SLI: p99 <= 15 ms for L2 hits and p999 <= 40 ms for L3 misses; alert when p99 exceeds 25 ms for 5 minutes.
  • Cache Efficiency and Penetration SLI: Combined L1 + L2 hit ratio >= 97% and L3 negative-miss rate <= 0.5% of total traffic; alert if Bloom filter false-positive rate drifts above 2% (indicating scheduled filter rebuild is overdue).
  • Quarantine Propagation SLI: End-to-end elapsed time from POST /v1/admin/block/{code} to global CDN 410 Gone enforcement, targeting p99 <= 10 s.

Flickr (flic.kr)Base-58 encoding of sequential photo IDsCompact photo shortlinks mapped deterministically without extra lookup tablesOmits visually ambiguous glyphs (0, O, I, l) to eliminate manual transcription errors

14.7 Simulation Verification

Reproduce the Base-62 bijection and hash-collision benchmark. Run cargo run --release -p shortener inside distributed-systems-from-the-ground-up/code/ to verify Base-62 round-trip encoding boundaries and compare collision counts across 2,000,000 shortened URLs for counter-based versus 6-character hash-truncated allocation.

$ cargo run --release -p shortener
             0 -> 0        -> Some(0)
            61 -> z        -> Some(61)
            62 -> 10       -> Some(62)
       1000000 -> 4C92     -> Some(1000000)
 3521614606207 -> zzzzzzz  -> Some(3521614606207)
2000000 URLs, codes from a counter: 0 collisions
2000000 URLs, 6 characters of a hash: 97 collisions
codes of 7 characters: 3521614606208 possible

From this benchmark output, we verify three quantitative properties of our design:

  1. Exact boundary bijection: The Base-62 encoder and decoder round-trip cleanly from 0 (0) through 1,000,000 (4C92) up to the maximum 7-character value 3,521,614,606,207 (zzzzzzz), confirming 3,521,614,606,208 (62^7) total distinct codes.
  2. Empirical birthday collision penalty: Truncating a hash to 6 characters produced 97 collisions across 2,000,000 URLs (~1 collision per 20,618 inserts), proving that hash-based shorteners cannot omit read-before-write existence checks and retry loops.
  3. Zero-collision counter generation: Counter allocation produced 0 collisions across all 2,000,000 URLs without a single existence probe, validating disjoint range leasing paired with bijective Feistel scrambling for the write path.

14.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Base-62 EncodingPositional numeral representation using the 62 URL-safe alphanumeric characters (0-9, A-Z, a-z), packing 3.52 trillion integers into 7 bytes.
Format-Preserving Encryption (FPE)A keyed invertible cipher (such as a Feistel network with cycle walking) whose ciphertext occupies the exact same finite integer domain as its plaintext, preventing sequential code enumeration without introducing collisions.
Range LeasingPre-allocating disjoint contiguous blocks of integers from a strongly consistent allocator into stateless worker memory to amortize write-path coordination.
Cache PenetrationA workload pattern in which requests for nonexistent keys bypass caches repeatedly and strike persistent storage directly, mitigated by Bloom filters and short-TTL negative caching.
301 vs. 302 RedirectHTTP status codes signaling permanent (301, aggressively browser-cached) versus temporary (302, controlled by explicit Cache-Control freshness headers) redirection.
Surrogate-Key PurgeA CDN invalidation mechanism allowing the control plane to evict a quarantined short link from global edge PoPs within seconds.

References

  • M. Bellare, T. Ristenpart, P. Rogaway, and T. Stegers, “Format-Preserving Encryption”, Selected Areas in Cryptography (SAC), 2009.
  • J. Black and P. Rogaway, “Ciphers with Arbitrary Finite Domains”, CT-RSA, 2002.
  • B. H. Bloom, “Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors”, Communications of the ACM, 13(7), 1970.

15. News Feed: System Design

A social news feed aggregates recent posts published by the accounts a member follows into a single paginated stream ordered by recency or predicted relevance. Expressed as a relational query, a chronological feed requires joining a follow graph against a posts table and sorting by timestamp. At modest scale on a single database, that query executes cleanly. At tens of millions of members, however, the workload exhibits two hostile properties simultaneously: reads outnumber writes by an order of magnitude (20:1 or higher), and the follower degree distribution follows a heavy power law in which most accounts have a few hundred followers while a small fraction have millions.

In this chapter, we design a distributed news feed service that resolves this asymmetry by shifting work dynamically between write time and read time. Precomputing follower timelines at publish time makes reads fast for ordinary accounts, whereas deferring assembly to read time prevents celebrity posts from triggering multi-million-write storms. Combining both paths behind a configurable follower threshold reduces total cluster work by roughly 50x while preserving sub-200 ms feed latency.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, functional requirements, latency and availability SLOs, explicit non-goals, and cache, storage, and fan-out capacity bounds
  • external HTTP/2 contracts for publishing, cursor-paginated feed retrieval, social-graph edges, and normalized storage schemas
  • separation of the control plane (ranking model registry, celebrity fan-out thresholds, social graph) from the asynchronous publish and read-assembly data plane
  • push fan-out on write, pull fan-out on read, and hybrid K-way merge backed by interactive traces and code/feedsim measurements
  • keyset cursor pagination, read-time hydration and safety filtering, multi-stage ML candidate ranking, hot-celebrity outbox caching, and author read-own-writes guarantees
  • failure-mode mitigation matrices, operational SLIs, production architectures (Twitter/X Home Timeline, Meta Multifeed and TAO, LinkedIn FollowFeed), and simulation verification

15.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Actors and Use Cases

We organize the news feed platform around three interacting actor groups (Figure 15-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Post AuthorPublish post (POST /v1/posts), delete post (DELETE /v1/posts/{id})Regular member or 10-million-follower celebrity publishes text and media attachments and expects immediate visibility in their own feed
Feed ReaderFetch paginated timeline (GET /v1/feeds/{id}?cursor=c&limit=n), follow or unfollow (PUT / DELETE /v1/graph/{u}/follows/{v})Mobile client opens the home feed, scrolls smoothly across multiple pages without duplicates, and unfollows an account with immediate suppression
Ranking and Safety TeamDeploy ranking model weights, tune celebrity fan-out cutoffs, and apply moderation suppressionTrust engineering deploys a updated scoring model or hides a policy-violating post immediately across all active readers

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0A member can publish a post containing text and media references and receive a monotonically time-ordered post_id within 250 ms.
1A member can follow or unfollow another account; unfollowed, blocked, or deleted content disappears from the member’s feed immediately on the next read.
2A member can fetch their home timeline in stable cursor-paginated pages (limit default 20, maximum 100) ordered chronologically or by ranked score.
3New posts from ordinary followed accounts appear in active followers’ feeds within 5 seconds (p99), and posts from celebrity accounts become visible immediately upon publish.
4An author observes their own newly published post immediately upon reloading their feed (author read-own-writes consistency).
5The feed pipeline supports pluggable read-time ranking and policy suppression without rewriting precomputed follower inboxes.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0Feed Read Latencyp50 <= 50 ms, p99 <= 200 ms (hydrated and ranked)Prohibits arbitrary scatter-gather across hundreds of database shards on read; mandates precomputed in-memory inboxes plus bounded celebrity outbox merges
1Publish Latencyp99 <= 250 ms (durable post commit only)Decouples follower fan-out from the synchronous publish HTTP response via Kafka
2Availability99.95% for feed reads (<= 21.6 minutes downtime/month)Active-active stateless feed aggregators across three AZs; graceful degradation to chronological unranked feed if the ML ranker times out
3ConsistencyStrong consistency for durable posts and follow edges; eventual consistency (<= 5 s) for fan-out inbox deliveryFeed caches are derived, disposable views that can be rebuilt on cache loss from durable post and graph stores
4Scale10,000,000 daily active members (DAU), 2 posts/member/day, 20 feed reads/member/day (20:1 read-to-write ratio)20 million posts/day, 200 million feed reads/day (~2,315 sustained read QPS, ~15,000 peak read QPS)

Non-Goals and Scope Boundaries

We exclude the following adjacent subsystems so the design focuses on timeline assembly and fan-out mechanics:

  • Direct messaging and real-time chat: Bidirectional private conversations with strict per-channel sequence numbers are designed in Chapter 18.
  • Media transcoding and CDN delivery: Storing and streaming attached images and videos are handled by the object store (Chapter 16) and adaptive video streaming pipeline (Chapter 17); posts store only immutable media asset identifiers.
  • Offline ML model training pipelines: We cover online candidate retrieval and inference budgets on the read path, treating offline feature-store ETL and gradient training as upstream control-plane inputs.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

We derive memory, storage, and QPS bounds for 10,000,000 active members (each following 200 accounts on average, including 5 celebrity accounts above the fan-out cutoff):

Resource DimensionArithmetic DerivationProvisioned Bound
Post Write Rate (Avg / Peak)(10,000,000 * 2) / 86,400 s = 231.5 posts/s; 5x peak232 posts/s avg, 1,160 posts/s peak
Feed Read Rate (Avg / Peak)(10,000,000 * 20) / 86,400 s = 2,315 reads/s; 6x peak2,315 reads/s avg, 14,000 reads/s peak
Fan-Out Write Ops (Hybrid)232 posts/s * 200 avg followers (excluding celebrities)~46,400 Redis ZADD ops/s avg (~232,000 ops/s peak)
Precomputed Inbox Cache RAM10,000,000 members * 500 entries * 16 B (8 B post_id + 8 B ts)80 GB raw (~160 GB with Redis ZSET overhead and 2x replication across 12 cache nodes)
Celebrity Outbox Cache RAM50,000 celebrities * 200 recent posts * 16 B160 MB (fits inside local L1 RAM and replicated Redis shards)
Post Content Storage (5 yr)20,000,000 posts/day * 365 * 5 * 1 KB avg post row36.5 TB logical (109.5 TB raw at 3x replication)
Follow Graph Storage10,000,000 members * 200 edges * 24 B (indexed both directions)96 GB logical (288 GB raw across 9 replicated graph shards)

Storing only 16-byte (post_id, timestamp) references inside follower inboxes keeps the entire 10-million-member timeline cache inside 160 GB of RAM, whereas storing full 1 KB post bodies inside every inbox would inflate cache memory by 64x (> 5 TB) and make post edits or deletions unmanageable.

15.2 External API and Data Contracts

The service exposes RESTful JSON-over-HTTP/2 endpoints with explicit idempotency keys on mutations and opaque cursor tokens on timeline pagination.

External HTTP Contracts

Publish a post:

Fetch a paginated home feed:

GET /v1/feeds/u_ada?limit=20&cursor=eyJ0cyI6MTc5NTE4MDA4NTQxMiwiaWQiOiI3MjYxOTA0NDE4Mjc1MzI4MDEifQ HTTP/2

Update social graph edges:

  • PUT /v1/graph/{follower_id}/follows/{followed_id} returns 204 No Content (idempotent follow edge creation; asynchronously triggers backfill of the followed account’s recent posts into the follower’s inbox if the followed account is below the celebrity threshold).
  • DELETE /v1/graph/{follower_id}/follows/{followed_id} returns 204 No Content (marks edge deleted in the social graph; read-time filtering hides that author’s posts immediately without scanning cached inboxes).

Storage Schemas and Cache Structures

-- Authoritative post content store (sharded by hash(author_id) for fast author outbox scans,
-- with secondary lookup index or separate KV store keyed by post_id for hydration)
CREATE TABLE posts (
    post_id     BIGINT      PRIMARY KEY,    -- 64-bit Snowflake ID
    author_id   BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    body        TEXT        NOT NULL,
    media_ids   JSONB       NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]',
    deleted_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NULL,           -- Tombstone checked during read-time hydration
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);

-- Bidirectional social graph (sharded by follower_id for read-time follow list,
-- and replicated/inverted by followed_id for push fan-out follower iteration)
CREATE TABLE follow_edges (
    follower_id BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    followed_id BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followed_id)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_follow_by_followed ON follow_edges (followed_id, follower_id);

In Redis, each member’s precomputed inbox (inbox:{user_id}) and each celebrity’s outbox (outbox:{author_id}) are stored as bounded Sorted Sets (ZSET) scored by post_id (encoding timestamp in the high bits) and trimmed on write via ZREMRANGEBYRANK key 0 -501 so every list caps strictly at 500 entries.

15.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We decouple policy thresholds, ranking model distribution, and social-graph metadata (control plane) from the latency-sensitive publish and timeline-assembly paths (data plane) (Figure 15-2).

Component Responsibilities

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Ranking Model RegistryControlVersioned ML scoring weights, feature schemas, safety suppression rulesAggregators cache last known good model bundle in RAM; control-plane outage pauses model deploys without affecting reads
Fan-Out Policy ConfigControlDynamic follower threshold (celebrity_cutoff, e.g., 100,000) and inactive-user TTLBroadcast via configuration watch; workers continue using cached cutoff values
Social Graph ServiceControl / DataBidirectional follower/followed edge lists + cached per-user celebrity follow listSharded across 9 replicated nodes with read-through Redis caching (TAO-style graph cache)
Post Service and Post StoreDataDurable posts and Idempotency-Key records across 30 sharded DB nodes (10 shards x 3 replicas)Writes commit synchronously to quorum and emit a Kafka event via transactional outbox before replying 201 Created
Kafka Topic + Fan-Out WorkersDataPartitioned post-created event log; stateless worker pool (60 workers)Workers consume at-least-once and execute idempotent Redis ZADD operations; worker crash triggers partition rebalance with zero data loss
Feed Cache (Redis Cluster)DataBounded 500-entry ZSET inboxes per active member + hot celebrity outboxesDisposable derived cache; losing a shard triggers lazy collect-on-read reconstruction from durable Post and Graph stores
Feed Aggregator and RankerDataStateless read orchestrator, local L1 celebrity outbox cache, embedded ML scorerAuto-scaled across three AZs; falls back to reverse-chronological ordering if ML inference exceeds a 40 ms deadline

Write and Read Lifecycles

Publish path (POST /v1/posts):

  1. The Post Service authenticates the author, allocates a 64-bit Snowflake post_id, and writes the post row plus a post-created outbox event atomically to the durable Post Store.
  2. The Post Service appends the post_id synchronously to the author’s own Redis outbox (outbox:{author_id}) and returns 201 Created immediately so the author never waits on follower fan-out.
  3. The outbox relay publishes the post-created event to Kafka.
  4. A Fan-Out Worker reads the event, checks the author’s follower count against the configured celebrity_cutoff:
    • If follower_count <= celebrity_cutoff (normal account), the worker paginates the author’s active followers from the Social Graph Service (skipping users inactive for more than 30 days) and pipelines ZADD inbox:{follower_id} <score> <post_id> + ZREMRANGEBYRANK into the Feed Cache.
    • If follower_count > celebrity_cutoff (celebrity account), the worker skips follower push entirely; the post is already live in outbox:{author_id} for read-time pull merging.

Read path (GET /v1/feeds/{user_id}):

  1. The Feed Aggregator reads the member’s precomputed inbox:{user_id} candidate IDs (up to 500 items) from the Feed Cache in one Redis pipeline call.
  2. Concurrently, it fetches the compact list of celebrity accounts followed by user_id (typically 0 to 15 accounts) plus user_id’s own recent outbox (guaranteeing author read-own-writes) and reads their latest post IDs from the hot celebrity outbox cache.
  3. The aggregator executes a K-way merge across the push inbox and the pulled celebrity outboxes, filtering out any author whom the member recently unfollowed or blocked.
  4. For ranked timelines, the aggregator scores candidates with the active ranking model within a strict 40 ms budget; for chronological timelines, it slices directly by (timestamp_ms, post_id) cursor.
  5. Finally, the aggregator batch-hydrates full post bodies and author profiles from the Post Cache/Store for the top limit (20) post IDs, drops any post carrying a deleted_at tombstone or moderation flag, and returns the page alongside an encoded next_cursor.

15.4 Hybrid Fan-Out: Push Inboxes, Celebrity Pull Merge, and Threshold Calibration

Pure Push (Fan-Out on Write)

Under pure fan-out on write, every published post triggers background workers to insert a 16-byte pointer into every follower’s cached inbox (Interactive Trace 15.A).

Pure push delivers O(1) feed read latency because the timeline is pre-sorted before the reader arrives. However, it suffers from three operational costs: write amplification scales linearly with follower count; background workers waste writes maintaining inboxes for dormant accounts that never log in; and a single celebrity post with 2,000,000 followers generates 2,000,000 cache writes. At 10,000 writes/s per worker pool, fanning out one celebrity post takes 200 seconds, saturating Kafka consumer lag and delaying ordinary users’ posts behind a head-of-line queue.

Pure Pull (Fan-Out on Read)

Under pure fan-out on read, publishing writes a single record to the author’s own outbox. When a member opens their feed, the aggregator queries the recent posts of every followed account and merges them in memory (Interactive Trace 15.B).

Pure pull eliminates write amplification and wasted work for inactive readers, and follow or unfollow changes reflect instantaneously. Its penalty is paid on the frequent read path: a member following 200 accounts triggers 200 parallel outbox fetches on every feed load, subjecting tail latency to the straggler distribution (max of 200 network RPCs).

Hybrid Fan-Out and Threshold Calibration

Real social graphs exhibit extreme degree skew: in code/feedsim, modeling 1,000 ordinary accounts (200 followers each, 2 posts/day, 20 reads/day) alongside one celebrity account (2,000,000 followers, 10 posts/day) reveals that the single celebrity generates 20,000,000 of the 20,400,000 daily push copies (98.0% of total write load). Conversely, pure pull executes 4,000,500 daily outbox fetches, 99.5% of which come from ordinary accounts.

Hybrid fan-out partitions authors by a follower threshold $T_{\text{celeb}}$ (10,000 in the simulation, typically 50,000 to 100,000 in production systems such as Twitter/X) (Figure 15-3).

StrategyPublish WorkRead WorkDelivery LagDormant-Member Overhead
Pure Push (Fan-Out on Write)O(followers) per post1 inbox lookupProportional to fan-out queue depth (minutes for celebrities)High unless inactive TTL eviction is enforced
Pure Pull (Fan-Out on Read)O(1) (1 outbox append)O(followed_accounts) parallel fetches0 ms (immediate)Zero
Hybrid (T_celeb, Chosen)O(followers) capped at T_celeb; O(1) above cutoff1 inbox lookup + K cached celebrity outboxes (K <= 15)< 5 s normal; 0 ms celebrityBounded by 30-day active-user push filter

Calibrating $T_{\text{celeb}}$ mathematically: An author with $F$ followers publishing $P$ posts/day and read by fraction $\alpha$ of active followers reading $R$ feeds/day costs $F \cdot P$ write operations under push versus $\alpha \cdot F \cdot R$ outbox reads under pull. Because celebrity outboxes sit in L1/Redis RAM (serving reads 10x cheaper than cross-shard inbox writes), setting $T_{\text{celeb}}$ around 50,000 to 100,000 followers keeps worst-case single-post push latency under 2 seconds while ensuring that 99.9% of users follow fewer than 15 accounts above the cutoff.

Hot-celebrity outbox protection: When a mega-celebrity with 50 million followers posts during a breaking news event, hundreds of thousands of feed aggregators simultaneously read outbox:{celeb_id}. To prevent a single Redis shard from melting under hot-key read traffic, each Feed Aggregator maintains a short-TTL (2 to 5 s) in-process L1 cache of hot celebrity outboxes refreshed via singleflight coalescing, capping backend Redis QPS per celebrity strictly at aggregator_count / TTL regardless of reader concurrency.

15.5 Cursor Pagination, Candidate Ranking, and Consistency Mechanics

Keyset Cursor Pagination vs. Offset Pagination

Offset pagination (OFFSET 20 LIMIT 20) breaks structurally on live feeds where new posts are continuously prepended at the head of the timeline (Interactive Trace 15.C).

Every new insertion shifts indices downward (causing duplicate posts on the next page), and every deletion shifts indices upward (omitting unseen posts without notice). Moreover, deep offsets force O(offset) scans in sorted indices. We replace positional offsets with an opaque keyset cursor encoding the (created_at_ms, post_id) pair of the last item returned on the preceding page. The next page queries ZREVRANGEBYSCORE inbox:{user_id} (cursor_score -inf LIMIT 0 20 and fetches celebrity outbox entries strictly older than cursor_score, achieving O(log N + limit) seek performance with zero boundary drift.

Authoritative Read-Time Filtering and Multi-Stage Ranking

Attempting to purge references from millions of follower inboxes whenever a post is deleted, moderated, or an author is unfollowed is slow and error-prone. We enforce a strict invariant: precomputed inboxes are candidate hints, never authoritative visibility decisions. During read-time hydration, the Feed Aggregator applies three deterministic filters in memory:

  1. Drop any post whose author_id is no longer in the reader’s current follow set or appears in the reader’s block/mute set.
  2. Drop any post whose hydrated record carries a non-null deleted_at tombstone or active trust-and-safety suppression flag.
  3. Attach parent posts alongside replies when the parent has not yet arrived in the reader’s inbox, preventing orphaned reply anomalies.

For engagement-ranked feeds (Meta Multifeed, LinkedIn FollowFeed, X Home), the hybrid inbox + celebrity merge supplies the L0 candidate pool (~500 recent post IDs). A lightweight L1 filter prunes stale or seen candidates down to ~150 items using a per-user Bloom filter of recently impressed post IDs, and an L2 ML scoring tier predicts engagement probabilities (P(click), P(reply), P(dwell)) within a 40 ms timeout budget. Because ranked order can change between requests, the aggregator freezes the top 100 scored post_ids in a short-lived session cache (TTL = 10 min) keyed by session_id and serves subsequent pages deterministically from that frozen snapshot.

Consistency Properties Visible to Members

Even though feed delivery is eventually consistent, three user-facing invariants prevent jarring product defects:

  • Author read-own-writes: Because background Kafka fan-out can lag by 1 to 5 s, the Feed Aggregator unconditionally merges the member’s own outbox:{user_id} at read time, guaranteeing an author never reloads their timeline and thinks a newly published post disappeared.
  • Monotonic reads within a session: Consistent hashing of user_id onto a primary Redis cache replica prevents a reader from observing a post on replica A and seeing it vanish on a lagging replica B seconds later.
  • Lazy inbox reconstruction on cache miss: If a member’s inbox is evicted after 30 days of inactivity or lost during a Redis shard outage, the aggregator executes a one-time collect-on-read rebuild over the member’s followed accounts, populates inbox:{user_id} asynchronously, and serves the first page immediately.

Operational SLIs, SLOs, and Alert Thresholds

  • Feed Read Availability SLI: Percentage of GET /v1/feeds/{id} calls returning 200 OK (including graceful chronological fallback), targeting 99.95% monthly; page when 5-minute error rate exceeds 0.5%.
  • Feed Read Latency SLI: p99 <= 200 ms, p50 <= 50 ms; alert when p99 exceeds 200 ms for 5 consecutive minutes.
  • Fan-Out Freshness SLI: Elapsed time between post commit timestamp and Redis ZADD completion across 99% of active followers, targeting p99 <= 5 s; alert above 10 s.
  • Empty-Feed / Hydration-Drop SLI: Fraction of requests returning zero items for members with >= 5 followed accounts; sudden spikes detect broken social-graph lookups or cache corruption.

15.7 Simulation Verification

Reproduce the push, pull, and hybrid fan-out cost benchmark. Run cargo run --release -p feedsim inside distributed-systems-from-the-ground-up/code/ to simulate 1,000 ordinary accounts (200 followers each, 2 posts/day, 20 reads/day) alongside 1 celebrity account (2,000,000 followers, 10 posts/day) under pure push, pure pull, and hybrid fan-out (cutoff = 10,000).

$ cargo run --release -p feedsim
copy on write for every account:   20400000 copies per day
collect on read for every account:  4000500 lists fetched per day
mixture, copy unless the author has over 10000 followers:
      400000 copies per day,    20005 lists fetched per day

From these measurements, we observe the exact quantitative impact of the hybrid boundary:

  1. Pure push blow-up: 1,000 ordinary accounts generate 400,000 daily copies (1,000 * 2 * 200), while the single celebrity account generates 20,000,000 copies (10 * 2,000,000), accounting for 98.04% of total system write work (20,400,000 copies/day).
  2. Pure pull read amplification: Skipping precomputed inboxes forces 20,000 daily feed reads across 200 followed ordinary accounts plus 1 celebrity, totaling 4,000,500 outbox fetches per day.
  3. Hybrid efficiency gain: Applying the 10,000-follower cutoff collapses total daily operations to 400,000 push copies plus 20,005 celebrity outbox fetches (420,005 total operations), cutting total work by 48.6x compared to pure push and 9.5x compared to pure pull while eliminating celebrity head-of-line fan-out storms completely.

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Fan-Out on Write (Push)Precomputing follower timelines asynchronously on post publication by inserting compact post references into each follower’s cached inbox.
Fan-Out on Read (Pull)Assembling a reader’s timeline dynamically at request time by fetching and merging recent posts from every followed author’s outbox.
Hybrid Fan-OutPartitioning authors at a follower-count threshold so ordinary accounts push to follower inboxes while high-follower celebrity accounts merge on read via K-way merge.
Keyset Cursor PaginationRequesting the next page of a live stream relative to an immutable (timestamp, post_id) marker rather than a positional offset, preventing duplicates and skips under concurrent writes.

16. Object Store: System Design

A distributed object store persists immutable binary blobs ranging from kilobyte thumbnails to multi-terabyte archival datasets and serves them by flat key within a bucket over HTTP. At exabyte scale spanning tens of thousands of spinning disks and NVMe drives, hardware failure ceases to be an anomaly and becomes a continuous background process: with a 2% annual drive failure rate across 20,000 disks, roughly one drive fails every single day, while firmware defects and magnetic decay introduce unannounced silent bit corruption.

In this chapter, we design an S3-compatible distributed object store that converts fragile commodity hardware into eleven-nines durability (99.999999999% annual object survival). By restricting the data model to immutable whole-object replacement rather than POSIX random-access file mutation, we separate strongly consistent object metadata from erasure-coded chunk storage, eliminate in-place update divergence, and execute continuous background checksum scrubbing and prioritized repair before correlated failures can exhaust redundancy.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, functional requirements, durability and read-after-write consistency SLOs, explicit non-goals, and petabyte-scale disk and metadata capacity bounds
  • S3-style HTTP/2 object contracts (PUT, GET, Range partial reads, multipart upload lifecycle, presigned capability URLs) and metadata manifest schemas
  • separation of the control plane (metadata cluster, failure-domain placement controller, background scrubber and garbage collector) from the stateless chunking and erasure-coding data plane
  • Reed-Solomon RS(6, 3) coding over GF(2^8), failure-domain placement across three availability zones, Copyset correlation control, continuous bit-rot scrubbing, and MTTR-driven durability
  • write-chunks-first atomic metadata commits, resumable multipart sealing, small-object Haystack packing, versioning, and grace-period garbage collection
  • failure-mode mitigation matrices, operational SLIs, production architectures (Amazon S3, Ceph RADOS, Facebook Haystack and f4, Azure Storage LRC), and verification via code/objectsim

16.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Actors and Use Cases

We organize the object storage boundary around three actor groups (Figure 16-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Application ClientUpload/download object (PUT / GET /v1/buckets/{b}/{key}), multipart upload (Init -> UploadPart -> Complete), list prefix (GET /v1/buckets/{b}?prefix=p)Media pipeline uploads a 50 GB master video in parallel 64 MB parts and video players stream arbitrary byte ranges via presigned URLs
Bucket OwnerConfigure versioning, lifecycle tiering, and bucket IAM policy; delete objects (DELETE /v1/buckets/{b}/{key})Compliance team enables immutable versioning to prevent accidental overwrites and transitions objects older than 30 days to erasure-coded cold storage
Storage OperatorManage hardware decommissioning, monitor bit-rot scrubbers, tune repair bandwidth, and verify garbage collectionAutomated fleet orchestration drains a failing rack and verifies Reed-Solomon reconstruction completes within target MTTR

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0An application can upload an immutable object from 0 bytes up to 5 TB under a flat string key inside a named bucket (using single-request PUT up to 5 GB and resumable multipart upload up to 5 TB).
1An application can download an entire object or an arbitrary byte interval via HTTP Range requests (206 Partial Content).
2An application can list keys within a bucket in lexicographical order by prefix with cursor pagination.
3Every returned byte is verified end-to-end against cryptographic or CRC32C checksums; corrupted data is repaired transparently from surviving redundancy or rejected with an explicit error rather than returned without warning.
4Applications can issue time-bounded HMAC-signed presigned URLs authorizing direct browser or device transfers against the object gateway.
5Buckets support optional object versioning and safe deletion with asynchronous reclamation of unreferenced storage chunks.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0Durability99.999999999% (11 nines) annual object survival across single-disk, node, rack, and single-AZ outagesRS(6, 3) erasure coding spread evenly across 3 AZs (3 shards per AZ) plus continuous bit-rot scrubbing and prioritized < 1 hour MTTR repair
1ConsistencyStrong read-after-write consistency for all PUT, DELETE, and LIST metadata operations (PC/EC quorum commit)Metadata resides in a Raft-replicated sharded key-value cluster; chunk bytes are immutable and content-addressed, eliminating version skew
2Availability99.95% regional API availability (<= 21.6 minutes/month)Stateless API gateways across three AZs; RS(6, 3) serves reads even if an entire AZ (3 shards) is offline simultaneously
3LatencyTime-to-first-byte p50 <= 25 ms, p99 <= 100 ms (metadata lookup + parallel shard read)Decouples metadata index from sequential disk I/O; replicates small hot objects (< 1 MB) 3 ways to avoid erasure-coding fan-out overhead
4Scale1,000,000,000 (1 billion) objects totaling 100 PB logical dataDemands 1.5x erasure-coded overhead (150 PB raw) instead of 3.0x replication (300 PB raw), saving 150 PB of physical drives

Non-Goals and Scope Boundaries

Object stores achieve petabyte scale specifically by omitting expensive POSIX file-system guarantees:

  • No in-place partial overwrites or appends: Modifying a single byte requires uploading a new immutable object version; POSIX byte-range locking and random writes belong to block stores or distributed file systems.
  • No atomic directory renames: Slashes inside keys (such as 2026/11/video.mp4) are visual prefix conventions only; renaming a prefix requires copying each underlying object metadata entry.
  • No cross-tenant deduplication: Although content-addressed chunks support deduplication within a single tenant or backup domain (as demonstrated in code/objectsim), public multi-tenant stores prohibit cross-customer deduplication because timing side channels would allow one tenant to probe whether another tenant holds a specific file.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

We contrast raw hardware requirements for 100 PB of logical customer data (1 billion objects) under 3-way replication versus RS(6, 3) erasure coding:

Resource DimensionArithmetic DerivationProvisioned Bound
Raw Storage (3-Way Replication)100 PB * 3.0 copies300 PB raw (20,834 drives of 16 TB at 90% fill)
Raw Storage (RS(6, 3) Chosen)100 PB * (9 / 6) = 100 PB * 1.5 overhead150 PB raw (10,417 drives of 16 TB at 90% fill, saving 10,417 drives)
Logical Chunks (64 MB / 4 MB)100 PB / 64 MB = 1.56 billion chunks (25 billion at 4 MB)1.56 billion 64 MB chunks (~14.0 billion RS shards)
Metadata Store Capacity1,000,000,000 objects * 1 KB avg manifest + index1.0 TB logical (3.0 TB raw across 20 Raft shards x 3 replicas)
Storage Node Fleet (RS(6, 3))10,417 disks / 36 disks per dense storage chassis~290 dense storage nodes (~97 nodes per AZ across 3 AZs)
Daily Expected Disk Failures10,417 disks * 2% AFR / 365 days~0.57 failed disks per day (roughly 4 drive replacements per week)
Scrubbing Read BandwidthFull 150 PB scrub every 14 days: 150 PB / (14 * 86,400 s)124 GB/s cluster-wide (~12 MB/s sequential background read per disk)

Sizing the background scrubber at ~12 MB/s per drive consumes under 8% of a modern 16 TB HDD’s 180 MB/s sequential throughput while guaranteeing every byte on disk is checksum-verified every two weeks.

16.2 External API and Data Contracts

The gateway exposes an HTTP/2 REST interface patterned after Amazon S3, carrying content integrity digests in headers and isolating binary payload streaming from metadata coordination.

External HTTP Contracts

Multipart upload lifecycle (objects > 100 MB up to 5 TB):

  1. POST /v1/buckets/{b}/{key}?uploads allocates an upload_id in the Multipart Coordinator (200 OK).
  2. PUT /v1/buckets/{b}/{key}?partNumber=1&uploadId={id} streams each 64 MB part independently in parallel and returns a verified per-part ETag (200 OK). Failed parts retry independently without restarting the entire transfer.
  3. POST /v1/buckets/{b}/{key}?uploadId={id} submits the ordered list of (part_number, etag) pairs; the coordinator atomically commits the final object manifest into the Metadata Cluster (200 OK). Until step 3 commits, no reader observes the object.

Metadata and Chunk Placement Schemas

-- Strongly consistent sharded metadata store (range-partitioned on (bucket_id, object_key)
-- to support lexicographical prefix listing, with prefix-hash salting on hot buckets)
CREATE TABLE object_manifests (
    bucket_id        BIGINT        NOT NULL,
    object_key       VARCHAR(1024) NOT NULL,
    version_id       UUID          NOT NULL,
    is_latest        BOOLEAN       NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
    is_delete_marker BOOLEAN       NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
    size_bytes       BIGINT        NOT NULL,
    etag             VARCHAR(128)  NOT NULL,
    storage_class    SMALLINT      NOT NULL, -- 1=REPLICATED_3X, 2=RS_6_3, 3=RS_10_4
    chunks_json      JSONB         NOT NULL, -- Ordered [{chunk_id, offset, length, pg_id, crc32c}]
    created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ   NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (bucket_id, object_key, version_id)
);

-- Placement group directory maintained by the Placement Controller
CREATE TABLE placement_groups (
    pg_id            BIGINT        PRIMARY KEY,
    coding_scheme    VARCHAR(16)   NOT NULL, -- 'RS_6_3' or 'REP_3'
    shard_nodes      JSONB         NOT NULL, -- 9 ordered (az_id, rack_id, node_id, disk_id) tuples
    epoch            BIGINT        NOT NULL, -- Monotonic fencing epoch on membership change
    state            VARCHAR(16)   NOT NULL  -- 'HEALTHY', 'DEGRADED', 'RECOVERING'
);

16.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We isolate namespace metadata, failure-domain topology management, and background durability maintenance inside the control plane while keeping the high-throughput byte-streaming path stateless and horizontally scalable (Figure 16-2).

Component Responsibilities

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Metadata Cluster (20 Raft shards x 3 replicas)ControlAuthoritative (bucket, key, version) -> chunk_manifest table and multipart upload stateLeader failure triggers Raft election in 1 to 3 s; synchronous 3-AZ quorum ensures strict read-after-write visibility
Placement ControllerControlCluster hardware topology (AZ -> Rack -> Host -> Disk), active placement groups (pg_id), epoch fencingGateways cache placement maps locally with epoch verification; brief controller outage pauses rebalancing without halting reads or writes
Scrubber, Repair, and GC TierControlDisk scan watermarks, degraded placement-group priority queue, unreferenced-chunk grace tableRuns continuously off the request path; rate-limited to protect foreground client IOPS
Object API Gateway (200 stateless hosts)DataRequest authentication, presigned-URL verifier, 64 MB streaming chunker, SIMD RS(6, 3) codec, CRC32C verifierAuto-scaled across three AZs; losing a host mid-upload leaves unreferenced staging chunks reclaimed by GC without corrupting metadata
Multipart CoordinatorDataIn-flight staging manifests for large multi-part uploadsPersists part commits to Metadata Cluster; background reaper expires incomplete uploads after 7 days
Storage Nodes (290 dense hosts)DataImmutable content-addressed shard blobs and per-shard CRC32C metadata on raw disksLoss of any disk, host, rack, or entire AZ (<= 3 shards per stripe) is masked transparently by RS(6, 3) reconstruction

Write and Read Lifecycles

Write path (PUT /v1/buckets/{b}/{key}):

  1. The Object API Gateway verifies caller credentials (or presigned HMAC token + expiration), validates bucket policy, and streams incoming bytes in 64 MB chunks (4 MB in code/objectsim).
  2. For each chunk, the gateway computes its cryptographic content hash (SHA-256) and hardware-accelerated CRC32C. For small hot objects (< 1 MB), it selects a 3-way replicated placement group; for large objects (>= 1 MB), it splits the 64 MB chunk into 6 equal 10.67 MB data shards and computes 3 Reed-Solomon parity shards via SIMD GF(2^8) arithmetic.
  3. The gateway writes all 9 shards concurrently to the 9 distinct disks assigned to the chosen Placement Group (3 shards in AZ-1, 3 in AZ-2, 3 in AZ-3). A chunk write succeeds once at least 8 of 9 shards acknowledge durable fsync (strict quorum with immediate asynchronous repair of the 9th shard if one disk is transiently slow), or all 9 under strict full-stripe durability mode.
  4. Atomic metadata commit (last step): Only after every chunk of the object is durably persisted on storage nodes does the gateway write the single object_manifests row to the Metadata Cluster and return 201 Created. An interrupted upload never exposes a half-written or dangling object name.

Read path (GET /v1/buckets/{b}/{key} with optional Range):

  1. The gateway queries the Metadata Cluster for the object’s latest manifest (or explicit version_id) and determines the exact subset of chunks intersecting the requested byte range [start, end].
  2. For each required chunk, the gateway reads the 6 primary data shards in parallel from the Placement Group’s storage nodes (preferring AZ-local replicas when reading replicated hot chunks) and verifies every shard’s CRC32C on arrival.
  3. If any data shard fails its checksum or times out (hedged tail request after 20 ms), the gateway fetches parity shards from surviving nodes, reconstructs the missing data shard in memory via RS(6, 3) matrix inversion, streams the verified byte slice to the client, and enqueues an asynchronous repair event for the corrupt shard.

16.4 Durability Engineering: Reed-Solomon Erasure Coding, Placement, and Scrubbing

From Parity Addition to Reed-Solomon RS(6, 3) over GF(2^8)

3-way replication provides simple, fast reads and 1-to-1 repair, yet wastes 200 PB of raw capacity for every 100 PB of stored data. Erasure coding eliminates most of that overhead by storing computed parity shards instead of full duplicates. Interactive Trace 16.A builds intuition using ordinary arithmetic addition over 3 data values and 1 sum.

To tolerate $m > 1$ simultaneous failures without integer overflow, production object stores execute Reed-Solomon RS(k, m) coding over the finite Galois Field $\text{GF}(2^8)$, where every byte is a polynomial element of degree at most 7, addition is bitwise XOR, and multiplication executes modulo an irreducible degree-8 polynomial (0x11d). Given $k = 6$ data shards arranged as a vector $\mathbf{d}$, multiplying by a $9 \times 6$ systematic Cauchy generator matrix $\mathbf{G}$ (whose top $6 \times 6$ submatrix is the identity matrix $\mathbf{I}6$) produces the $6$ unaltered data shards plus $3$ parity shards (P1, P2, P3). Because every $6 \times 6$ submatrix of a Cauchy matrix is guaranteed invertible over $\text{GF}(2^8)$, any 6 surviving shards out of 9 uniquely recover all 6 original data shards via $\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{G}{\text{surv}}^{-1} \mathbf{y}_{\text{surv}}$.

Modern CPUs execute GF(2^8) multiply-accumulate via 4-bit nibble lookup tables using AVX2/AVX-512 VPSHUFB (or ARM NEON VTBL) instructions at > 10 GB/s per core, making CPU encoding overhead negligible compared to disk and network bandwidth.

Durability SchemeStorage OverheadFault Tolerance (f)Normal Read Fan-OutSingle-Shard Repair Read CostPrimary Use Case
3-Way Replication3.00x (300 PB / 100 PB)Any 2 losses1 shard (lowest latency)1 shard readSmall objects (< 1 MB), metadata, ultra-hot blobs
Reed-Solomon RS(6, 3) (Chosen)1.50x (150 PB / 100 PB)Any 3 losses (full AZ outage)6 parallel shards6 shards readWarm and standard multi-AZ objects (>= 1 MB)
Reed-Solomon RS(10, 4)1.40x (140 PB / 100 PB)Any 4 losses10 parallel shards10 shards readCold archival blobs (Facebook f4)
Azure LRC (12, 2, 2)1.33x (133 PB / 100 PB)Any 3 losses (most 4-loss patterns)12 parallel shards6 shards read (half local group)Cloud cold storage minimizing cross-rack repair traffic

Failure-Domain Placement, Copysets, and Background Scrubbing

Redundancy count alone guarantees nothing if shards share a correlated failure domain: placing all 9 shards in the same rack loses the entire object when one top-of-rack switch fails. Our Placement Controller maps every RS(6, 3) stripe strictly across 9 distinct disks, 9 distinct hosts, and 3 distinct Availability Zones (3 shards per AZ: {D1, D2, P1} in AZ-1, {D3, D4, P2} in AZ-2, {D5, D6, P3} in AZ-3) (Figure 16-3).

This topology ensures that even if an entire Availability Zone goes offline (3 shards unreachable simultaneously), the 6 surviving shards across the remaining two AZs satisfy k = 6, preserving both zero data loss and full read availability without interruption. Furthermore, following the Copysets analysis (Cidon et al. 2013), rather than picking 9 random nodes from 290 hosts per chunk (which spreads combinations across nearly every possible 4-node subset so any correlated 4-node power failure destroys some chunk), we constrain shards onto fixed Placement Groups (PGs) of 9 nodes. Copysets dramatically lower the probability of data loss during correlated cluster-wide power outages while bounding repair coordination state.

To defeat silent bit corruption on cold archive drives that applications may not read for years, every storage node runs a rate-limited local bit-rot scrubber that sweeps every disk sector every 14 days, verifying stored bytes against each shard’s recorded CRC32C and content hash (Interactive Trace 16.B).

Why MTTR governs eleven-nines durability: Durability is governed by the race between Mean Time To Repair (MTTR) and subsequent independent failures inside the exposure window. Under RS(6, 3), losing 1 shard triggers prioritized reconstruction onto a healthy replacement disk in the same AZ. Shrinking MTTR from 1 week (168 hours) down to 1 hour shrinks the exposure window for compound failures by orders of magnitude. To balance stability against speed, the Placement Controller applies a 10-minute grace delay before starting repair on an unreachable host (avoiding terabyte storms during rolling OS reboots) and schedules repairs in strict deficit priority (stripes missing 2 shards jump ahead of stripes missing 1 shard), throttled below 20% of inter-rack bandwidth.

16.5 Small-Object Packing, Multipart Sealing, and Safe Garbage Collection

Small-Object Packing (Haystack Pattern)

Erasure coding a 20 KB thumbnail across 9 disks in 3 AZs wastes 9 network RPCs, 9 disk seeks, and metadata space exceeding the object payload itself. Following Facebook’s Haystack design, storage nodes pack millions of small objects (< 1 MB) sequentially into large append-only 64 GB volume files (3-way replicated across 3 AZs) accompanied by a compact in-memory (chunk_id -> volume_id, offset, length) index. Serving a small object therefore requires one single disk seek with zero filesystem directory or inode traversal overhead. As objects age into cold tiers, an offline compaction worker aggregates thousands of immutable small objects into 64 MB packed containers and erasure-codes the resulting container with RS(6, 3).

Versioning and Grace-Period Garbage Collection

Replication and erasure coding protect against hardware failure, never against software defects or accidental operator DELETE commands, because a mistaken deletion is faithfully committed to the metadata quorum. Enabling bucket versioning converts every DELETE into an append-only is_delete_marker = TRUE metadata record and retains prior version_id manifests until lifecycle rules explicitly expire them.

When an object version is permanently expired, its metadata entry disappears immediately, while physical shard deletion runs asynchronously in the background Garbage Collector (GC). Deleting chunks immediately creates a notorious data-loss race under content addressing or concurrent multipart commits:

  1. The GC scans metadata at time $t_0$ and marks chunk c9 as unreferenced.
  2. At time $t_1$, a concurrent upload produces identical chunk c9, sees c9 already exists on storage nodes, and commits a new manifest referencing c9.
  3. At time $t_2$, the GC deletes c9 from its stale $t_0$ candidate list, permanently corrupting the newly uploaded object.

We eliminate this race with a two-phase mark-and-grace protocol: the GC only reclaims chunks that have remained unreferenced continuously for a 24-hour grace window (t_now - last_referenced_at > 24 h) and acquires an epoch-fenced tombstone lock before reclaiming storage blocks, while any upload reusing an existing chunk refreshes last_referenced_at atomically prior to manifest commit.

16.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure Mode and Mitigation Matrix

Failure ModeBlast RadiusDetection SignalAutomated Mitigation
Single HDD / NVMe Drive Failure1 shard degraded per hosted Placement Group; zero client errorsSMART I/O error or storage-node health reportImmediate degraded read via surviving shards (RS(6, 3) reconstructs transparently); Placement Controller schedules prioritized rebuild onto spare drive within 1 hour
Entire Availability Zone Outage3 of 9 shards unreachable per stripe; zero data lossCross-AZ heartbeat quorum lossGateways read remaining 6 shards across the 2 healthy AZs; new writes spill onto temporary 2-AZ/3-rack placement groups and rebalance automatically after AZ recovery
Silent Disk Bit Rot1 corrupt shard returns altered bytes without OS errorRead-path CRC32C mismatch or 14-day background scrubber failureGateway rejects bad shard, reconstructs clean data from parity, serves verified bytes to client, and overwrites bad shard on disk
Abandoned Multipart Upload LeakOrphaned staging chunks accumulate without visibility on storage nodesUncommitted staging byte quota alert (> 2% cluster raw capacity)Lifecycle reaper automatically aborts and deletes staging parts older than 7 days
Metadata Prefix HotspotSequential keys (logs/2026-11-20/00001...) concentrate writes on one metadata Raft shardPer-shard write latency p99 > 50 msDynamic range splitting splits hot key ranges automatically across metadata shards within minutes

Operational SLIs, SLOs, and Alert Thresholds

  • Data Integrity SLI: Zero unrecoverable CRC32C or SHA-256 checksum failures served to clients (target = 0); any unrecoverable stripe (>= 4 simultaneous shard losses) triggers an immediate Sev-1 durability incident.
  • Under-Replicated Stripe Age SLI: Maximum age of any Placement Group with >= 2 missing shards must stay below 30 minutes; alert if repair backlog exceeds 1% of total stripes.
  • Read-After-Write Availability and TTFB SLI: 99.95% success rate on PUT/GET; p99 time-to-first-byte <= 100 ms for regional reads.
  • Scrubbing Coverage SLI: 100% of active disks must complete a full checksum scrub within every 14-day rolling window; alert on any node whose last scrub timestamp exceeds 16 days.

Production Benchmarks

Production SystemDurability SchemeMetadata & Placement EngineArchitectural Distinction

Ceph RADOSConfigurable 3x replication or RS(k, m) per poolCRUSH deterministic pseudo-random placement algorithm across Placement GroupsEliminates central lookup table on data path; clients compute exact OSD targets from compact cluster map + CRUSH(pg_id)
