16.7 Simulation Verification

Reproduce content-addressed chunking, deduplication, and silent bit-rot repair. Run cargo run --release -p objectsim inside distributed-systems-from-the-ground-up/code/ to split a 10 MB blob into 4 MB content-addressed chunks replicated across 6 storage nodes, verify zero-write deduplication on an identical upload, inject a 1-byte bit flip on node 4, and verify transparent checksum detection and automated self-healing on read.

$ cargo run --release -p objectsim
video.mp4, 10 MB: 3 chunks written, 0 already there
copy-of-video.mp4, the same bytes: 0 chunks written, 3 already there
chunks on each of the 6 nodes: 2 1 0 1 2 3
1 byte is damaged in the copy of chunk 1 on node 4
video.mp4 read back: 10485760 bytes, equal to the original: true, copies repaired: 1

From this execution transcript, we verify three core invariants of the storage engine:

  1. Chunking and deduplication: Splitting video.mp4 (10,485,760 bytes) at a 4 MB boundary produced 3 chunks replicated 3 times across 6 nodes (9 total copies distributed as 2 1 0 1 2 3). Re-uploading identical bytes under copy-of-video.mp4 wrote 0 new chunks, reusing all 3 existing content-addressed chunks while adding only a second metadata entry.
  2. End-to-end corruption detection: Injecting a single-byte silent corruption into chunk 1 on node 4 did not leak altered bytes to the reader; checksum verification caught the mismatch immediately during GET.
  3. Read-repair self-healing: The reader fell back to a healthy replica, returned all 10,485,760 bytes bit-for-bit identical (equal to the original: true), and restored full redundancy (copies repaired: 1).

16.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Content AddressingNaming immutable data chunks by a cryptographic hash of their byte payload, enabling intrinsic integrity checks and deduplication.
Reed-Solomon RS(k, m)Maximum-distance separable erasure coding over GF(2^8) splitting data into k data shards and m parity shards so any k of k + m shards reconstruct the original data.
Failure DomainA physical or logical boundary (disk, server, rack power supply, availability zone) whose components can fail simultaneously due to a shared fault.
Placement Group (Copyset)A fixed group of storage disks spanning distinct failure domains that hosts stripes together, bounding correlated multi-node data-loss probability.
Bit-Rot ScrubbingContinuous background verification reading every chunk on every disk in rotation against stored checksums to detect silent media corruption before redundancy expires.
Multipart UploadA three-phase protocol (Init, parallel UploadPart, atomic Complete) allowing multi-terabyte objects to transfer resumable parts while exposing the final object atomically.
Presigned URLA time-limited HMAC-authenticated HTTP URL delegating one specific object operation directly to a client without proxying bytes through application servers.

17. Video Streaming Platform: System Design

A two-hour high-definition film occupies roughly 4.5 GB. A viewer pressing play on a fluctuating mobile network or a fiber-connected television expects the first frame within a second and continuous playback without freezes, even while millions of viewers stream simultaneously across continents. Video accounts for the majority of global internet downstream traffic, turning a streaming platform into a large-scale content-processing pipeline paired with a bandwidth-constrained global delivery fabric.

In this chapter, we design a global adaptive video streaming platform grounded in one foundational architectural simplification: a video is transformed into a sequence of short, immutable HTTP files. Slicing every video into time-aligned 4-second segments across multiple quality renditions converts stateful media streaming into stateless HTTP object delivery. Origin storage reuses the erasure-coded object store (Chapter 16), global CDN edge caches serve immutable segments from ISP-adjacent disks without per-viewer state, and the client player independently adapts playback quality to live network conditions on every segment boundary.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, functional requirements, startup-latency and rebuffer SLOs, explicit non-goals, and petabyte-ingest and terabit-egress capacity bounds
  • external HTTP/2 contracts for resumable master ingest, HLS/DASH CMAF playback manifests, immutable segment delivery, and catalogue metadata schemas
  • separation of the control plane (ingest coordination, DAG scheduler, manifest and DRM service), offline transcoding plane, and multi-tier CDN playback plane
  • chunked parallel DAG transcoding across closed-GOP keyframes, unified CMAF packaging, per-title VMAF bitrate optimization, and permanent source archival
  • client-side Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) control algorithms (throughput margin, BBA, BOLA, MPC), CDN origin shielding against stampedes, egress economics, and low-latency live streaming
  • failure-mode mitigation matrices, QoE SLIs, production architectures (Netflix Open Connect, YouTube, Twitch LL-HLS), and simulation verification via code/streamsim

17.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Actors and Use Cases

We organize the streaming platform boundary around three external actor groups (Figure 17-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Content Creator / StudioInitiate resumable upload (POST /v1/videos), monitor encoding status (GET /v1/videos/{id})Studio or creator uploads a 10 GB 4K mezzanine file in parallel parts and tracks parallel ABR transcoding progress until publication
Video ViewerFetch playback manifest (GET /v1/videos/{id}/manifest.m3u8), stream segments (GET /{id}/{bitrate}/seg-{n}.m4s)Mobile or television player fetches the manifest, starts playback within 1 second, seeks arbitrarily, and switches resolution automatically across network fluctuations
Platform OperationsManage DRM license keys, pre-warm blockbuster releases onto edge caches, and tune CDN origin shieldsRelease engineering pre-positions a major premiere across global ISP edge caches overnight before launch hour

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0A creator can upload a source video up to 10 GB (or multi-hundred-gigabyte studio mezzanine files) using resumable multipart HTTP transfers.
1The platform transcodes every uploaded video into a multi-bitrate ABR ladder (240p to 1080p / 4K) sliced into time-aligned 4-second closed-GOP segments packaged as unified CMAF files for both HLS and DASH players.
2A viewer’s player fetches a manifest listing available renditions and segment URLs, starting initial playback within 2 seconds (1 second to first segment).
3The player dynamically adapts bitrate on any 4-second segment boundary in response to changing link throughput and buffer occupancy without playback discontinuity.
4A viewer can seek to any timestamp in the video by requesting the corresponding segment index directly without downloading preceding video data.
5The platform enforces playback entitlement checks and optional DRM key delivery before issuing signed manifest and segment URLs.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0Playback Availability99.95% global playback availability (<= 21.6 minutes/month)Multi-CDN DNS steering and ISP-embedded edge PoPs isolate playback from origin or single-CDN outages
1Startup & Rebuffer QoETime-to-first-frame p95 <= 1.0 s; rebuffer ratio < 0.2% of total watch hoursPlayers initiate playback on a low-bitrate rung (400 kbps) and maintain a 10 to 30 s ABR safety buffer
2ConsistencyStrong consistency for catalogue metadata and video publication state; immutable segments require zero cache coherenceSegments carry Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable; eventual visibility delay equals transcode completion time
3Ingest & Egress Scale10,000,000 concurrent viewers (~25 Tbps aggregate egress) and 500 hours of video uploaded per minuteEgress exceeds single-region datacenter capacity by two orders of magnitude, mandating multi-tier CDN caching and Origin Shields
4Transcode Throughput60-minute 4K upload playable within 5 to 10 minutesProhibits single-node sequential encoding; mandates chunked GOP-aligned DAG transcoding across spot compute pools

Non-Goals and Scope Boundaries

We exclude the following workloads from this chapter’s architecture:

  • Sub-second interactive video conferencing: Two-way video calls require sub-200 ms UDP/RTP media transport (WebRTC with ICE/STUN/TURN and SFU routers) that sacrifices retransmission reliability for conversational immediacy; HTTP segmented streaming serves Video-on-Demand (VoD) and one-to-many broadcasts (2 to 30 s latency).
  • Recommendation engines and social comments: Content discovery feeds follow the fan-out and ranking design of Chapter 15.
  • Low-level codec mathematics: We treat H.264, HEVC, and AV1 compression kernels as black-box encoders parameterized by closed-GOP keyframe cadence, bitrate caps, and perceptual VMAF quality targets.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

We size aggregate egress bandwidth, daily transcode storage growth, and object counts for 10,000,000 concurrent viewers averaging 2,500 kbps (720p) and 500 hours of new video uploaded per minute across a 4-rung ladder (400, 1,200, 2,500, 5,000 kbps; total 9,100 kbps):

Resource DimensionArithmetic DerivationProvisioned Bound
Aggregate Playback Egress10,000,000 viewers * 2,500 kbit/s25,000 Gbit/s (25 Tbps / 3.125 TB/s sustained)
Segment Request Rate10,000,000 viewers / 4 s per segment2,500,000 HTTP GET requests/s across global CDN edges
Encoded Storage per Video Hour(400 + 1,200 + 2,500 + 5,000) kbit/s * 3,600 s / 84.095 GB (~4.1 GB per hour across 4 renditions)
Daily New Encoded Storage500 hrs/min * 60 * 24 = 720,000 hrs/day * 4.1 GB2.95 PB/day (~1.08 EB/year logical before RS(6, 3) coding)
Daily New Segments Created720,000 hrs/day * (3,600 / 4) * 4 renditions2.59 billion immutable segment objects per day
Transcode Compute Fleet720,000 video hrs/day * 4 rungs = 2.88M encode-hours/day (~2x real-time CPU)~240,000 vCPUs (~3,750 64-core spot/ASIC transcode hosts)

Two numbers dominate the economics: 25 Tbps of egress (impossible to serve from centralized cloud origins without ISP-embedded CDNs) and 2.95 PB/day of newly encoded segments (motivating unified CMAF packaging and popularity-gated multi-codec encoding).

17.2 External API and Data Contracts

Playback splits into a lightweight, authenticated API call to retrieve the manifest and DRM token, followed by hundreds of unauthenticated (or signed-cookie) immutable HTTP GET segment fetches directly against CDN edge nodes.

Fetch an immutable 4-second CMAF media segment from the CDN Edge:

GET /8842/1200/seg-17.m4s HTTP/2

Setting Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable guarantees that every intermediate proxy, ISP cache, and edge PoP retains segments indefinitely until LRU/LFU eviction without ever issuing conditional If-None-Match origin revalidation traffic.

Catalogue and Transcode Job Schemas

-- Strongly consistent video catalogue and publication state machine
CREATE TABLE videos (
    video_id          BIGINT       PRIMARY KEY,
    creator_id        BIGINT       NOT NULL,
    title             VARCHAR(256) NOT NULL,
    duration_ms       INTEGER      NOT NULL,
    raw_object_key    VARCHAR(512) NOT NULL,  -- Permanent archival source in Object Store
    state             VARCHAR(24)  NOT NULL,  -- 'UPLOADING', 'TRANSCODING', 'READY', 'FAILED'
    drm_key_id        UUID         NULL,
    created_at        TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL
);

-- Individual chunked transcode DAG tasks scheduled by the Job Scheduler (Chapter 12)
CREATE TABLE transcode_tasks (
    task_id           UUID         PRIMARY KEY,
    video_id          BIGINT       NOT NULL REFERENCES videos(video_id),
    chunk_index       INTEGER      NOT NULL,  -- e.g., 60-second GOP-aligned source slice
    rendition_kbps    INTEGER      NOT NULL,  -- 400, 1200, 2500, 5000, 15000
    codec             VARCHAR(16)  NOT NULL,  -- 'h264', 'hevc', 'av1'
    status            VARCHAR(16)  NOT NULL,  -- 'PENDING', 'LEASED', 'DONE', 'FAILED'
    output_prefix     VARCHAR(512) NOT NULL,
    UNIQUE (video_id, chunk_index, rendition_kbps, codec)
);

17.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We partition the video platform into three distinct operational planes separated by both latency sensitivity and geography: a Control Plane for upload coordination, DAG scheduling, and manifest/DRM authorization; an Offline Media Plane for CPU-heavy parallel transcoding and durable origin storage; and a globally distributed CDN Playback Plane (Figure 17-2).

Component Responsibilities

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Upload and Ingest APIControlMultipart session credentials, source container inspection metadataStateless fleet; broken creator uploads resume from last acknowledged 64 MB part via Object Store multipart protocol
DAG Job SchedulerControlTranscode task dependency graph (Split -> Encode -> Package -> Publish)Lease-based distributed scheduler (Chapter 12); crashed worker lease expires and another spot worker re-runs one 60 s chunk idempotently
Manifest and DRM License ServiceControlVideo catalogue cache, viewer entitlement rules, Widevine/FairPlay/PlayReady license keysActive-active multi-region tier; edge-cached manifests continue serving active streams during brief control-plane hiccups
Raw & Packaged Object Store (Origin)Offline MediaMaster mezzanine files + all immutable 4 s .m4s segments (Chapter 16)Erasure-coded RS(6, 3) across 3 AZs; zero single-disk or single-AZ durability loss
Transcode Worker FleetOffline MediaEphemeral chunk buffers, hardware/CPU encoders (FFmpeg, SVT-AV1, ASICs)Runs on preemptible spot capacity; 100% idempotent outputs allow instant preemption without losing completed chunks
Origin Shield + CDN Edge PoPsPlayback DataMulti-tier NVMe/HDD segment caches (> 98% edge offload) in ISP PoPs worldwideOrigin Shield collapses regional misses into 1 origin fetch; Anycast DNS routes around failed PoPs automatically

Ingest-to-Playback Lifecycles

Upload and transcode lifecycle:

  1. The creator invokes POST /v1/videos, receiving presigned multipart upload URLs targeting the Raw Object Store. Once all parts complete, the Upload API validates the container header and persists state = 'TRANSCODING'.
  2. The DAG Job Scheduler launches a lightweight GOP Splitter job that demuxes the master video at closed-GOP keyframe boundaries into independent 60-second source chunks (zero pixel decoding required).
  3. For a 60-minute film across 4 bitrate rungs, the scheduler fans out 60 * 4 = 240 independent transcode jobs onto preemptible Transcode Workers. Each worker encodes its 60-second slice, aligns IDR keyframes strictly every 4.000 seconds, encrypts segments with Common Encryption (CENC), and writes 15 immutable .m4s segments directly to the Packaged Origin Store.
  4. Once all DAG leaf jobs report DONE, a CMAF Packager writes the HLS (.m3u8) and DASH (.mpd) manifests and atomically transitions the catalogue row to state = 'READY'.

Playback lifecycle:

  1. A viewer presses play; the player requests GET /v1/videos/8842/manifest.m3u8 from the Manifest Service, which checks entitlement, issues a DRM license (if required), and returns CDN segment templates plus a short-lived signed cookie.
  2. Because the player has not yet measured network throughput, it requests seg-0.m4s from the lowest bitrate rung (400 kbps, 200 KB) from the nearest CDN Edge PoP so the first frame renders in < 500 ms.
  3. Every 4 seconds (or sooner while filling the initial buffer), the player’s ABR controller inspects measured download throughput and current buffer occupancy to pick the optimal bitrate rung for seg-(n+1).m4s.
  4. If the CDN Edge PoP misses a cold segment, it forwards the request to the regional Origin Shield, which coalesces concurrent misses across dozens of PoPs into a single GET against the Packaged Object Store, caches the response, and returns it down the hierarchy.

17.4 Chunked Parallel DAG Transcoding and Unified CMAF Packaging

Parallel GOP-Level Transcoding and Per-Title Optimization

Encoding a 2-hour 4K master sequentially on a single multi-core server requires hours of wall-clock time, making timely publication impossible and turning mid-job hardware faults into costly restarts. Splitting the source at closed Group of Pictures (GOP) keyframe boundaries eliminates inter-chunk dependencies completely (Figure 17-3, top panel). Every 60-second slice across every bitrate rung executes in parallel on a separate machine, shrinking a 4-hour sequential encode into roughly 5 minutes of wall-clock latency while bounding any single worker crash to 1 minute of re-work.

Mandatory IDR alignment across rungs: Video compression stores most frames (P-frames and B-frames) as motion deltas referencing neighboring frames. For a player to switch cleanly from seg-17.m4s at 2,500 kbps to seg-18.m4s at 1,200 kbps without visual artifacts or decoder stalls, every rendition must place an Instantaneous Decoder Refresh (IDR) keyframe at the exact same presentation timestamp (t = 0.0 s, 4.0 s, 8.0 s, ...). Choosing a 4-second segment duration balances rapid ABR switching and fast seeking against compression efficiency (shorter 1 s segments force frequent keyframes that inflate bitrate by 15% to 25% and quadruple HTTP request rates).

Popularity-tiered and per-title encoding: Because video views obey a steep power law where most user-generated uploads receive fewer than 50 views, encoding every upload with slow multi-pass AV1 presets wastes millions of dollars in CPU time. Production platforms run a two-tier encoding policy:

  1. Immediate baseline publish: Encode all uploads rapidly in H.264 (240p, 480p, 720p) so creators can publish within minutes.
  2. Per-title / per-shot convex-hull optimization: For videos crossing a popularity threshold (or all premium studio titles), analyze scene complexity using perceptual metrics (VMAF) to generate a custom bitrate ladder: low-motion animation achieves transparent 1080p quality at 1.5 Mbps, whereas high-motion sports requires 6.0 Mbps. Retaining the original mezzanine master permanently in cold object storage allows re-encoding the entire popular catalog years later as superior codecs (AV1, VVC) mature without compounding generation loss.

Unified CMAF Packaging (HLS + DASH Deduplication)

Historically, Apple ecosystems demanded MPEG-2 Transport Stream (.ts) segments under HLS (RFC 8216), while web browsers, Android devices, and smart TVs demanded fragmented MP4 (.m4s) segments under MPEG-DASH (ISO/IEC 23009-1). Storing and caching both container formats doubled origin storage (+2.95 PB/day) and halved CDN edge cache hit ratios. Adopting CMAF (Common Media Application Format) stores one single canonical set of fragmented MP4 (.m4s) media segments referenced simultaneously by both .m3u8 HLS playlists and .mpd DASH manifests, halving storage footprint and concentrating 100% of edge cache capacity onto shared byte objects.

17.5 Client-Side ABR Control, CDN Origin Shielding, and Live Streaming

Client-Side Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) Control Theory

Moving adaptation logic out of servers into the client player is the single largest scalability enabler in video streaming: the server never tracks per-viewer congestion state, while the player directly observes exact segment download times, viewport resolution, decoder thermal limits, and remaining playback buffer.

Interactive Trace 17.A steps through a throughput-based ABR rule (80% safety margin on the preceding download speed) as a viewer’s connection plunges from 6,000 kbps to 1,500 kbps and 700 kbps before recovering.

In Interactive Trace 17.A, we observe an intrinsic physical constraint: throughput estimators always lag reality by at least one segment. When bandwidth drops abruptly from 6,000 kbps to 1,500 kbps during piece 4, the player has already requested a 2,500 kbps segment that takes 6.7 seconds to arrive. Only the 8.7 seconds of previously buffered video prevents a visible freeze. Production players therefore combine throughput estimation with explicit buffer-state feedback:

ABR AlgorithmControl SignalCore MechanismProduction Trade-Off
Throughput-Based (EWMA + Margin)Recent segment download rateSelects highest rung <= 0.8 * throughput_ewmaSimple and fast at startup; oscillates on spiky cellular networks when TCP congestion windows fluctuate
BBA (Buffer-Based Approach, Netflix)Current playback buffer occupancy $B(t)$Maps $B(t)$ linearly across reservoir $[B_{\min}, B_{\max}]$ to bitrate ladderCuts rebuffer events by 10% to 20% during steady state; requires throughput bootstrap during initial empty-buffer startup
BOLA (Lyapunov Optimization)Buffer level + logarithmic utility $v_m$Chooses rung maximizing $(V \cdot v_m + \gamma p - B(t)) / S_m$Mathematically near-optimal balance of average bitrate vs. rebuffer probability; default in dash.js
MPC / Pensieve (Hybrid)Throughput forecast + buffer + switching penaltyOptimizes multi-step QoE reward (bitrate minus rebuffer and flicker penalties)Highest QoE across diverse networks; higher implementation complexity

All production ABR policies enforce two asymmetric QoE laws: never rebuffer to chase sharper pixels (viewers abandon streams far more rapidly after a single stall than after 15 seconds of 480p video), and apply hysteresis (step down immediately on buffer drain, step up only after multiple consecutive healthy segments) to avoid jarring resolution flicker. Players also cap maximum forward buffer to 15 to 30 seconds: downloading 10 minutes ahead wastes enormous egress bandwidth whenever viewers abandon a video after 90 seconds.

Multi-Tier CDN Architecture and Origin Shielding

Delivering 25 Tbps globally requires placing thousands of edge cache servers directly inside last-mile ISP networks (the model pioneered by Netflix Open Connect appliances, where ISPs host free NVMe/HDD caching boxes inside regional peering facilities so > 95% of bytes never traverse paid transit networks).

To protect the Packaged Origin Store from thundering-herd cache stampedes during viral launches or live events, the CDN inserts a mid-tier Origin Shield (one designated regional cache cluster sitting between hundreds of edge PoPs and the origin):

  1. When 200 edge PoPs miss seg-0.m4s of a newly released blockbuster within the same millisecond, all 200 requests converge on the Origin Shield.
  2. The Origin Shield applies request coalescing (collapsed forwarding): it issues exactly one GET to the Packaged Origin Store and streams the arriving bytes simultaneously to all 200 waiting edge PoPs.
  3. For scheduled major premieres, the control plane executes proactive overnight off-peak pre-positioning, pushing top-title segments to ISP edge disks when network links are idle (02:00 to 06:00 local time). For cold long-tail catalog items, edge caches pin only the prefix (seg-0 through seg-2, first 12 s) so playback starts instantaneously from the edge while the Origin Shield fetches seg-3+ asynchronously only if the viewer continues watching.

Live Streaming and Low-Latency CMAF Extensions

Live broadcasts reuse the identical segmented HTTP + CDN architecture, replacing static playlists with a sliding-window manifest updated every 4 seconds as live encoders emit new segments (Cache-Control: public, max-age=1). Because a player waits for a full 4-second segment to finish encoding plus 3 buffered segments before display, standard HLS/DASH incurs 15 to 30 seconds of glass-to-glass live latency. Low-Latency HLS (LL-HLS) and LL-DASH cut live latency to 2 to 4 seconds by publishing 200 to 500 ms CMAF partial chunks over HTTP/2 chunked transfer encoding while the parent 4-second segment is still being encoded, paired with blocking playlist reloads that eliminate polling jitter.

17.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure Mode and Mitigation Matrix

Failure ModeBlast RadiusDetection SignalAutomated Mitigation
Regional CDN PoP OutageElevated startup latency for viewers in one metro areaSynthetic edge probe failure or BGP withdrawalAnycast / GeoDNS steers viewers to next-nearest healthy PoP within 30 s; active players fail over automatically on the next 4-second segment URL
Origin Stampede on Premiere LaunchRisk of saturating Origin Object Store egress linksOrigin GET RPS spikes > 5x baselineOrigin Shield request coalescing collapses duplicate PoP misses into 1 origin fetch; overnight pre-warming eliminates cold misses for major titles
Transcode Worker Preemption / CrashSingle 60-second chunk delayed by 1 to 3 minutesTask lease heartbeat timeout in DAG Job SchedulerScheduler reassigns the failed (video_id, chunk_index, rung) task to another spot worker; all other chunks continue undisturbed
Corrupt Source Container / Codec FailureSingle creator upload fails to reach READY stateEncoder exit code or VMAF/ffprobe validation failureDead-letter queue isolates malformed file after 3 retries and surfaces structured diagnostic error to the creator dashboard
Manifest / DRM Service DegradationNew playback starts fail; active viewers already streaming continue uninterruptedManifest API 5xx > 0.5% or p99 > 500 msMulti-region active-active failover; clients cache DRM keys across entire session duration so live playback survives control-plane blips

Operational SLIs, SLOs, and Alert Thresholds

  • Video Startup Failure Rate (VSF) SLI: Fraction of viewer play clicks failing to render frame 1 within 10 s, targeting < 0.5%; page on-call above 1.0% over 5 minutes.
  • Time-to-First-Frame (TTFF) SLI: p95 <= 1.0 s on broadband and <= 2.0 s on cellular networks; alert on > 20% regional regression.
  • Rebuffer Ratio SLI: (Total stall duration / Total watch duration), targeting < 0.2% globally; segmented by ISP ASN and CDN provider to trigger automated multi-CDN steering away from congested networks.
  • CDN Cache Hit Ratio (CHR) and Origin Offload SLI: Byte hit ratio >= 96% at edge PoPs and >= 99.5% combined with Origin Shield; drop below 94% indicates cache key fragmentation or broken Cache-Control headers.

17.7 Simulation Verification

Reproduce the adaptive bitrate (ABR) throughput and buffer simulation. Run cargo run --release -p streamsim inside distributed-systems-from-the-ground-up/code/ to step through 10 consecutive 4-second video segments across a 400 / 1200 / 2500 / 5000 kbps ladder as link bandwidth drops from 6,000 kbps to 1,500 kbps and 700 kbps before recovering to 6,000 kbps.

$ cargo run --release -p streamsim
piece  speed  chosen  download  buffered
    1   6000     400     0.3 s     4.0 s
    2   6000    2500     1.7 s     6.3 s
    3   6000    2500     1.7 s     8.7 s
    4   1500    2500     6.7 s     6.0 s
    5   1500    1200     3.2 s     6.8 s
    6    700    1200     6.9 s     4.0 s
    7    700     400     2.3 s     5.7 s
    8   3200     400     0.5 s     9.2 s
    9   6000    2500     1.7 s    11.5 s
   10   6000    2500     1.7 s    13.9 s
time without video after the start: 0.1 s

From this simulation transcript, we quantify three critical dynamics of adaptive streaming:

  1. Fast cold start: Starting piece 1 on the 400 kbps rung downloads in 0.3 s and populates 4.0 s of immediate buffer, immediately revealing the 6,000 kbps link capacity so piece 2 upgrades directly to 2,500 kbps.
  2. Buffer absorption of 1-segment estimator lag: When throughput collapses by 75% at piece 4 (6,000 -> 1,500 kbps), the in-flight 2,500 kbps segment requires 6.7 s to finish (2.7 s longer than its 4.0 s playback duration), draining the buffer from 8.7 s to 6.0 s without stalling. A second drop to 700 kbps at piece 6 takes 6.9 s and drains the buffer from 6.8 s to 4.0 s before the player steps down to 400 kbps at piece 7.
  3. Near-zero stall time across severe link degradation: Across an 8.6x bandwidth drop (6,000 -> 700 kbps), maintaining a 20% throughput safety margin plus a modest 4 to 14 s buffer kept total post-start rebuffering to 0.1 s (< 0.25% of the 40-second clip).

17.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
ABR (Adaptive Bitrate Streaming)Client-side control loop selecting the optimal encoded rendition for each upcoming video segment based on measured link throughput and playback buffer occupancy.
Closed GOP / IDR KeyframeA self-contained sequence of compressed video frames beginning with an Instantaneous Decoder Refresh frame, allowing clean bitrate switching and seeking on segment boundaries.
CMAF (Common Media Application Format)Unified fragmented MP4 (.m4s) segment container readable by both HLS and MPEG-DASH players, halving origin storage and CDN cache duplication.
DAG Transcoding PipelineSplitting a source video at keyframe boundaries into independent time chunks encoded concurrently across distributed workers and joined into unified manifests.
Origin ShieldA mid-tier regional CDN cache cluster using request coalescing to collapse concurrent edge-PoP misses into a single origin fetch.
BBA / BOLABuffer-based and Lyapunov-optimal ABR algorithms that govern bitrate selection directly from buffer occupancy to minimize rebuffer stalls.
LL-HLS / LL-DASHLow-latency streaming extensions delivering 200 to 500 ms partial CMAF chunks before a full segment finishes encoding, reducing live delay to 2 to 4 seconds.

References

  • R. Pantos and W. May, IETF RFC 8216, HTTP Live Streaming, 2017.
  • ISO/IEC 23009-1, Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (DASH), 2022.
  • T.-Y. Huang, R. Johari, N. McKeown, M. Trunnell, and M. Watson, “A Buffer-Based Approach to Rate Adaptation: Evidence from a Large Video Streaming Service”, ACM SIGCOMM, 2014.
  • X. Yin, A. Jindal, V. Sekar, and B. Sinopoli, “A Control-Theoretic Approach for Dynamic Adaptive Video Streaming over HTTP”, ACM SIGCOMM, 2015.
  • K. Spiteri, R. Urgaonkar, and R. K. Sitaraman, “BOLA: Near-Optimal Bitrate Adaptation for Online Videos”, IEEE INFOCOM, 2016.
  • H. Mao, R. Netravali, and M. Alizadeh, “Neural Adaptive Video Streaming with Pensieve”, ACM SIGCOMM, 2017.
  • Netflix Technology Blog, “Per-Title Encode Optimization”, 2015, and “High Quality Video Encoding at Scale”, 2015.

18. Real-Time Chat: System Design

A real-time messaging platform delivers conversational text and media across unreliable mobile networks while upholding strict perceptual invariants: messages must appear on online recipients’ screens in under half a second, survive hours or days of offline disconnection without loss, never duplicate under retries, and render in the exact same causal order on every participant’s device. Users detect violations immediately because an out-of-order reply or a repeated message renders a conversation visibly broken.

In this chapter, we design a globally scalable real-time chat system supporting 50,000,000 concurrent online connections and 20,000,000,000 messages per day. By separating minimal stateful WebSocket Gateways from stateless Chat Routers and anchoring every conversation to a strongly consistent per-conversation monotonic sequence number, we collapse reliable delivery, gap detection, duplicate suppression, multi-device synchronization, and offline recovery into a single cursor arithmetic protocol.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, functional requirements, sub-500 ms delivery and ordering SLOs, explicit non-goals, and 50-million-connection gateway and storage capacity bounds
  • WebSocket wire frames, idempotent HTTP/2 message submission, cursor catch-up APIs, and time-bucketed Cassandra/ScyllaDB message schemas
  • separation of the control plane (presence heartbeat service, Redis session directory, APNs/FCM offline push relay) from stateful WebSocket gateways and partitioned message logs
  • transport selection (polling, long polling, WebSocket), gateway connection isolation, monotonic per-conversation sequencing, client_id deduplication, and offline cursor recovery via interactive traces
  • 1:1 versus large-group fan-out, multi-device cursors and cumulative watermarks, viewport-scoped presence control, hot-channel storage partitioning, and Signal Double Ratchet E2EE implications
  • failure-mode mitigation matrices, operational SLIs, production architectures (WhatsApp Erlang/FreeBSD, Discord ScyllaDB, Slack, Facebook Messenger MQTT), and verification via code/chatsim

18.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Actors and Use Cases

We organize the real-time messaging boundary around three external actor groups (Figure 18-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Chat MemberMaintain WebSocket (WSS /v1/ws), send message (POST /v1/conv/{id}/messages), sync cursor (GET /v1/conv/{id}/messages?after=seq), send read/delivery watermarksMobile or desktop client sends messages reliably across elevator disconnects and synchronizes state consistently across phone, tablet, and laptop
External Push Relay (APNs / FCM)Dispatch wake-up notification for offline devicesOperating system wakes a suspended background application or renders an alert when a message commits while the recipient has no open WebSocket
Platform OperationsOrchestrate rolling gateway drains, scale hot-channel partitions, and monitor delivery latencySRE drains stateful gateway hosts in small batches so reconnecting phones spread TLS handshakes cleanly across healthy gateways

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0A member can send text and media-reference messages to 1:1 conversations and group channels (from 2 members up to 100,000 community members).
1Every online recipient device receives a newly committed message over its persistent WebSocket connection within 500 ms (p99).
2Every message within a conversation is assigned a strict gapless monotonic sequence number (1, 2, 3, ...), ensuring all participants observe an identical total message order.
3Retried message submissions carrying the same caller-generated client_id are stored and sequenced exactly once (end-to-end send idempotency).
4A device reconnecting after any offline interval recovers all missed messages deterministically by presenting its local last_received_seq cursor, suppressing out-of-order gaps and duplicate deliveries.
5The system supports multi-device synchronization per user, cumulative sent / delivered / read watermarks, scoped online presence, and optional End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) over opaque ciphertext payloads.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0Delivery Latencyp50 <= 80 ms, p99 <= 500 ms end-to-end (sender submit to online receiver render, intra-region)Mandates persistent full-duplex WebSockets (RFC 6455) and in-memory Redis session directory lookups (< 2 ms)
1Durability & OrderingZero loss of any message confirmed as sent; strict linearizable per-conversation sequence order (PC/EC)Durable quorum commit in the conversation shard leader precedes both the sender sent ACK and recipient gateway push
2Availability99.95% sending and receiving availability (<= 21.6 minutes/month)Multi-AZ stateful gateway pools with client exponential-backoff reconnects; session directory treated strictly as a hint
3Secondary ConsistencyEventual consistency (1 to 10 s) for presence status, typing indicators, and read watermarksKeeps secondary signals off the durable message commit path so presence storms never block chat messages
4Scale50,000,000 concurrent online connections and 20,000,000,000 messages per day (~231,500 msg/s avg, ~1,000,000 msg/s peak)Demands 500+ tuned WebSocket gateways (100,000 sockets/host) and horizontally sharded LSM-tree message storage

Non-Goals and Scope Boundaries

We exclude the following capabilities so the architecture remains centered on reliable real-time messaging:

  • Real-time audio and video calling: Interactive voice/video calls operate over UDP/SRTP (WebRTC) with jitter buffers and media SFUs rather than reliable TCP/WebSocket message logs.
  • Full-text search inside E2EE conversations: Because end-to-end encrypted payloads are opaque ciphertext on servers, E2EE search executes locally over each device’s decrypted SQLite index.
  • Rich media storage and transcoding: Attached images, voice notes, and video clips are uploaded out-of-band to the Object Store (Chapter 16) and referenced by immutable signed object IDs inside chat frames.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

We size gateway concurrency, socket memory, write throughput, and message storage for 50,000,000 concurrently online devices and 20,000,000,000 daily messages averaging 200 bytes per record:

Resource DimensionArithmetic DerivationProvisioned Bound
WebSocket Gateway Fleet50,000,000 open sockets / 100,000 sockets per host500 gateway hosts (~167 hosts per AZ across 3 AZs; +20% headroom = 600 hosts)
Per-Gateway Socket Memory100,000 sockets * ~40 KB (kernel TCP + TLS state + user-space ring buffers)~4.0 GB RAM per gateway (fits comfortably inside standard 32 GB instances)
Session Directory RAM (Redis)50,000,000 active device sessions * 128 B (user_id, device_id, gw_id, ttl)6.4 GB raw (~19.2 GB across 12 sharded Redis nodes with replication)
Message Write Rate (Avg / Peak)20,000,000,000 / 86,400 s = 231,481 msg/s; 4x peak event burst231,500 msg/s avg, 926,000 msg/s peak
Daily Message Storage Growth20,000,000,000 msg/day * 200 B4.0 TB/day logical (12.0 TB/day raw at 3x replication; ~1.46 PB/year logical)
Presence Heartbeat Traffic50,000,000 devices / 30 s lease renewal interval1.67 million lightweight lease renewals/s (handled via batched per-gateway heartbeats)

Notice a key systems optimization in the final row: if 50,000,000 devices each issued individual Redis EXPIRE RPCs every 30 seconds, the Session Directory would endure 1.67M ops/s of presence overhead alone. Instead, gateways keep per-socket liveness locally over WebSocket PING/PONG frames and renew their host-level session lease in bulk batches, cutting Session Directory RPC volume by two orders of magnitude.

18.2 External API and Data Contracts

Clients maintain one persistent TLS-encrypted WebSocket (WSS /v1/ws) for low-latency bidirectional push frames and use idempotent HTTP/2 (or multiplexed WebSocket RPCs) for message submission and cursor catch-up.

External Wire and HTTP Contracts

Send a message (idempotent via Idempotency-Key / client_id):

POST /v1/conv/301/messages HTTP/2
Host: api.chat.example
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Idempotency-Key: u9a1-phone-a-000512
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "client_id": "u9a1-phone-a-000512",
  "ciphertext_b64": "YW55IGNpcGhlcnRleHQ...",
  "content_type": "text/plain"
}

HTTP/2 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "conversation_id": "301",
  "seq": 42,
  "client_id": "u9a1-phone-a-000512",
  "committed_at": "2026-11-20T13:08:05.112Z"
}

Catch up after disconnection (GET /v1/conv/{id}/messages?after=seq):

GET /v1/conv/301/messages?after=1&limit=100 HTTP/2
Host: api.chat.example
Authorization: Bearer <token>

HTTP/2 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "conversation_id": "301",
  "messages": [
    { "seq": 2, "sender_id": "u_bob", "body": "hello?", "committed_at": "2026-11-20T13:07:10Z" },
    { "seq": 3, "sender_id": "u_bob", "body": "we are starting", "committed_at": "2026-11-20T13:07:15Z" },
    { "seq": 4, "sender_id": "u_bob", "body": "table 4", "committed_at": "2026-11-20T13:07:22Z" }
  ],
  "has_more": false
}

Server-to-client WebSocket push frame (WSS /v1/ws):

{
  "type": "message.push",
  "conversation_id": "301",
  "seq": 42,
  "sender_id": "u_alice",
  "client_id": "u9a1-phone-a-000512",
  "payload": "YW55IGNpcGhlcnRleHQ...",
  "committed_at": "2026-11-20T13:08:05.112Z"
}

Partitioned Message Store Schema (ScyllaDB / Cassandra Layout)

Messages are append-only and read overwhelmingly as contiguous recent ranges (seq > cursor). Partitioning solely by conversation_id causes unbounded partition growth for multi-year channels; adding a 10-day time bucket keeps every partition bounded below 100 MB while keeping recent range scans inside a single partition:

-- Wide-column LSM-tree table (ScyllaDB / Cassandra) optimized for sequential range catch-up
CREATE TABLE conversation_messages (
    conversation_id BIGINT,
    time_bucket     INT,           -- floor(unix_seconds / 864000) -> 10-day bucket
    seq             BIGINT,        -- Strict monotonic per-conversation sequence number
    client_id       TEXT,          -- Sender-generated UUID for write deduplication
    sender_id       BIGINT,
    payload_bytes   BLOB,          -- Plaintext or Signal Double Ratchet ciphertext
    committed_at    TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY ((conversation_id, time_bucket), seq)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (seq ASC);

-- Per-user shared read watermark (synchronized across phone, tablet, and desktop)
CREATE TABLE read_watermarks (
    user_id         BIGINT,
    conversation_id BIGINT,
    last_read_seq   BIGINT,
    updated_at      TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, conversation_id)
);

18.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We isolate session discovery, presence liveness, and offline push notification dispatch inside the control plane while dedicating 500 lightweight stateful WebSocket Gateways and partitioned message sequencers to the low-latency delivery data plane (Figure 18-2).

Component Responsibilities

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Session Directory (Redis Cluster)ControlEphemeral (user_id, device_id) -> gateway_id mapping with 30 s lease TTLTreated strictly as a routing hint; losing a shard delays live push until devices renew or reconnect, while zero messages are lost
Presence Heartbeat ServiceControlOnline/idle status with 15 to 30 s offline grace debounce and viewport subscription mapsEventual consistency; isolates high-fan-out presence churn from message delivery
Offline Push Relay (Chapter 13)ControlAPNs / FCM device push tokens and badge countersAsynchronous queue-backed dispatch; wakes suspended mobile apps so they reconnect and pull via cursor
WebSocket Gateways (500 stateful hosts)Data100,000 live TLS/WebSocket file descriptors per host (epoll/kqueue), auth contextMinimal proxy logic so feature deploys never drop sockets; host crash triggers jittered client reconnect + cursor catch-up
Chat Router and Sequencer (200 hosts)DataStateless routing tier + conversation-sharded sequencer leases (dedup LRU + monotonic next_seq)Auto-scaled across three AZs; consistent hashing routes each conversation_id to its owning sequencer shard
Partitioned Message Store (100 shards x 3 replicas)DataDurable ordered conversation logs and client_id deduplication tableQuorum 3-AZ commit ensures confirmed messages survive any disk, host, or AZ failure

End-to-End Message Lifecycle

  1. Client Submit: Sender’s device generates a random UUID client_id (u9a1), renders the message optimistically as pending in the local UI, and sends it over its open WebSocket to Gateway A (or via POST /v1/conv/{id}/messages).
  2. Deduplication and Sequencing: Gateway A forwards the frame to the owning Chat Router and Sequencer for conversation_id = 301. The sequencer checks (conversation_id, sender_id, client_id) against its deduplication store. If seen previously, it returns the original seq without writing; otherwise it assigns the next monotonic seq = 42 and commits durably to the Partitioned Message Store quorum.
  3. Sender sent ACK: Immediately upon durable quorum commit, the sequencer replies {seq: 42} to Gateway A -> Sender’s device, which transitions the UI message from pending to sent and slots it at position 42.
  4. Live Push or Offline Wakeup: The Chat Router queries the Session Directory for every recipient’s active (device_id -> gateway_id) mappings (plus the sender’s other logged-in devices). For every online device (for example, Receiver on Gateway B), the router pushes {conv: 301, seq: 42, payload} over an internal gRPC stream to Gateway B, which writes the WebSocket frame down the recipient’s socket. For recipients with no active session, the router enqueues a wake-up alert to the Offline Push Relay (APNs/FCM).
  5. Delivery & Read Watermarks: Once Receiver’s device persists seq = 42 locally, it sends a lightweight cumulative delivery_ack(conv=301, seq=42) watermark back up its WebSocket, which routes to the sender’s online devices.

18.4 Stateful Gateways, Sequencing, Idempotency, and Offline Catch-Up

Transport Comparison: Why Persistent WebSockets Win

Ordinary HTTP request-response forces clients to initiate every exchange. Three patterns overcome server-to-client push, with sharply different network and CPU costs:

Transport PatternDelivery LatencyIdle Request OverheadServer Per-Client StateSuitability at 50M Devices
Short Polling (1 s)0 to 1,000 ms (500 ms avg)50,000,000 empty HTTP requests/s (4.3 trillion/day)NoneUnviable; wastes massive radio battery and server CPU
HTTP Long PollingNear-zero (< 100 ms)Re-establishes request every 30 s + after every message1 held HTTP socketFallback only for restrictive corporate proxies blocking WebSocket upgrades
WebSocket (RFC 6455) / MQTT (Chosen)Near-zero (< 50 ms)Zero HTTP headers; lightweight 2-byte ping frames every 30 s1 persistent TCP/TLS socket (~40 KB RAM)Standard production choice for real-time mobile and web messaging

Isolating Stateful Gateways and Preventing Reconnect Storms

Holding 100,000 long-lived TLS connections per server introduces a critical operational hazard: restarting a gateway binary drops 100,000 active sessions instantaneously. Two architectural rules contain this blast radius:

  1. Strip all business logic from gateways: Gateways terminate TLS, validate auth tokens on handshake, maintain the in-memory socket_id -> fd table, and forward frames over multiplexed internal gRPC pools to stateless Chat Routers. Because gateways rarely change code, feature deployments occur dozens of times daily with zero socket churn.
  2. Jittered client reconnection backoff: When a gateway host crashes unexpectedly, 100,000 mobile devices detect TCP teardown within seconds. If all 100,000 phones reconnect immediately, the resulting TLS handshake storm can cascade across healthy gateways. Client SDKs therefore apply truncated exponential backoff with full jitter (sleep = random(0, min(30s, 1s * 2^attempt))), spreading reconnection load smoothly over 15 to 30 seconds.

Idempotent Send and Per-Conversation Cursor Recovery

Mobile links drop acknowledgements routinely. Without deduplication, retrying an unacknowledged send appends the same text under two consecutive sequence numbers. Interactive Trace 18.A walks through client_id deduplication across a lost confirmation.

On the receiving side, wall-clock timestamps fail because phone clocks skew by seconds or minutes, placing replies ahead of questions. Assigning strict gapless integers (1, 2, 3, ...) per conversation at the shard leader enables every recipient device to maintain one integer cursor (last_displayed_seq) and enforce a deterministic three-branch state machine on every incoming frame m:

  • m.seq == cursor + 1: Display m immediately and advance cursor = m.seq.
  • m.seq > cursor + 1 (Gap detected): Do not display m out of order (optionally buffer in memory); immediately issue GET /v1/conv/{id}/messages?after={cursor} to fetch the missing interval cleanly.
  • m.seq <= cursor (Duplicate): Discard m without modifying UI state.

Interactive Trace 18.B steps through all three faults (disconnect gap, out-of-order frame arrival, and duplicate redelivery) on a single mobile phone.

In Figure 18-3, we combine the online push path and offline cursor catch-up path, showing why the server never tracks per-device delivery queues: whether a phone entered a subway tunnel for 10 seconds or remained powered off for 7 days, recovery executes the identical GET ?after={cursor} range query.

18.5 Group Fan-Out, Presence Control, Hot Channels, and E2EE

1:1 vs. Large-Group Fan-Out and Multi-Device Sync

For 1:1 chats and ordinary group conversations (<= 500 members), the Chat Router resolves active sessions for all members in one batched Redis MGET, groups recipients by target gateway_id, and dispatches one coalesced RPC per gateway.

For massive broadcast channels (10,000 to 500,000 members in Slack workspaces or Discord communities), pushing every message body immediately to 100,000 sockets creates the same write/egress fan-out storm analyzed in Chapter 15. Large channels therefore switch automatically at a membership threshold (N > 500) to subscription-scoped pub/sub: only gateways hosting members who currently have that specific channel open in the foreground subscribe to the channel’s live fan-out topic; all other members receive an eventual unread badge (latest_seq) and pull messages lazily from their cursor when opening the channel.

Multi-device users (phone + laptop + tablet) require zero extra storage duplication: every device tracks its own local delivered_seq cursor independently so a powered-off laptop catches up fully on boot, while a single per-user read_watermarks table (max(last_read_seq)) synchronizes unread counters immediately across all devices.

Controlling Presence Fan-Out and Hot Channels

Unfiltered presence broadcasting (pushing "online" / "offline" to all 500 contacts every time a mobile radio toggles between Wi-Fi and LTE) routinely generates 5x to 10x more network traffic than actual chat messages. Three controls bound presence cost:

  1. Viewport-scoped subscriptions: Clients subscribe only to presence updates for contacts currently visible on screen (typically 15 to 30 rows), unsubscribing immediately upon scrolling away.
  2. Offline hysteresis debounce (15 to 30 s): When a WebSocket disconnects, the Presence Service delays broadcasting offline for 20 seconds; brief cellular handoffs reconnect within the grace window with zero status flicker.
  3. Ephemeral typing frames: Typing indicators ("Alice is typing") bypass persistent storage completely and expire client-side after 5 seconds.

On the storage tier, a single viral Discord channel receiving 500 messages/s and 50,000 concurrent readers creates an extreme hot partition on (conversation_id, time_bucket). Production deployments place a Read-Through Request-Coalescing Service in front of ScyllaDB (Discord’s Rust Data Services tier) that holds the hottest 50 recent messages of active channels in memory and coalesces 10,000 identical catch-up range queries into a single storage read.

End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) Architectural Consequences

Enabling E2EE via the Signal Double Ratchet protocol preserves the entire messaging pipeline unchanged: servers still assign seq numbers, commit opaque payload_bytes, route frames through WebSocket gateways, and replay missed ranges by cursor. Every property depending on server visibility, however, shifts to client devices:

  • Key distribution and group rekeying: For 1:1 chats, the server hosts a signed public PreKey Bundle (X3DH) so a sender can initiate an encrypted session even while the recipient is offline. For encrypted groups, each sender distributes a symmetric Sender Key encrypted pairwise to every group member; removing any member forces every remaining participant to rotate Sender Keys (O(N) pairwise key exchanges), capping encrypted group sizes practically around 1,000 members (addressed at larger scale by IETF MLS / TreeKEM, O(log N)).
  • Offline notifications and history sync: APNs/FCM notifications carry either an opaque wake-up signal or encrypted payload decrypted by a mobile notification service extension, and newly linked devices must transfer historical decryption keys directly from an existing authenticated device over an encrypted local channel.

18.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure Mode and Mitigation Matrix

Failure ModeBlast RadiusDetection SignalAutomated Mitigation
WebSocket Gateway Crash100,000 connected devices drop sockets (0.2% of fleet); zero messages lostGateway health check failure and sudden drop in active socket countClients reconnect to healthy gateways using full-jitter exponential backoff (1 to 30 s) and issue GET ?after=cursor to recover any messages sent during the gap
Session Directory (Redis) Shard LossLive push temporarily misses 1/12 of users until sessions refreshRedis cluster slot error or push-miss fallback ratio spikeDurable store still commits every message; gateways re-register live session leases automatically within 30 s, and offline push / cursor sync heals missed live frames
Message Store Shard Leader Failure1 to 3 s write pause for 1% of conversations (1 of 100 shards)Raft leader heartbeat loss / sequencer commit timeoutFollower wins election within 1 to 3 s; clients retry with identical client_id, guaranteeing zero duplicates and monotonic seq continuity
Hot Community Channel OverloadSingle ScyllaDB partition saturates disk/CPU under 50,000 concurrent readersPer-partition read latency p99 > 100 msRead-through request-coalescing cache layer collapses identical GET ?after=seq bursts into 1 storage read; 10-day time buckets prevent unbounded partition growth
APNs / FCM Push Provider OutageDelayed background wake-up banners for offline phones; online chats unaffectedPush relay error rate > 5% or queue depth surgeCircuit breaker queues alerts with TTL expiry (5 min); users opening the app recover all messages cleanly via cursor sync

Operational SLIs, SLOs, and Alert Thresholds

  • End-to-End Online Delivery Latency SLI: Elapsed time from server commit to recipient device delivery_ack on online 1:1 sessions, targeting p99 <= 500 ms (intra-region); alert if p99 > 800 ms for 5 minutes.
  • Message Commit Availability & Durability SLI: 99.95% write success rate on POST /v1/conv/{id}/messages with zero sequence gaps (max_seq - count == 0 per conversation audit).
  • Gateway Connection Churn SLI: Rolling 1-minute disconnect rate across the gateway fleet; spikes above 3% per minute indicate network brownouts or accidental simultaneous gateway restarts.
  • Cursor Catch-Up Latency SLI: p99 <= 150 ms for GET /v1/conv/{id}/messages?after=seq (100-message page), ensuring snappy conversation recovery immediately after subway or tunnel reconnects.

Production Benchmarks

Production SystemGateway / Transport LayerStorage & Sequencing EngineArchitectural Distinction
WhatsAppErlang/OTP (ejabberd-derived) on tuned FreeBSD holding 2 to 3 million sockets per serverMnesia / ephemeral relay queues (store-and-forward deleted after delivery) + client SQLite historyFamous extreme socket density per host and strict Signal E2EE where servers retain zero permanent plaintext history
DiscordElixir gateway cluster (Guild actors) over WebSockets + Rust Data Services coalescerMigrated from MongoDB -> Cassandra -> ScyllaDB ((channel_id, bucket) + Snowflake ID)Documented scaling past trillions of messages; Rust request-coalescing middleware eliminated Cassandra/ScyllaDB hot-channel partition storms
SlackStateful Channel Servers (Flannel edge cache) over WebSocketsVitess-sharded MySQL per workspaceUses workspace-scoped edge caches (Flannel) to offload bootstrap metadata and presence fan-out during enterprise morning login spikes

18.7 Simulation Verification

Reproduce sequence-gap detection, cursor catch-up, and duplicate suppression. Run cargo run --release -p chatsim inside distributed-systems-from-the-ground-up/code/ to simulate a phone receiving message 1 online, disconnecting while messages 2, 3, and 4 commit on the server, receiving message 4 alone out of order, reconnecting with cursor 1, and receiving a duplicate redelivery of message 3.

$ cargo run --release -p chatsim
the phone is online
  phone shows 1: are you coming?
the phone loses its connection, and 3 messages are sent
  server stores 2: hello?
  server stores 3: we are starting
  server stores 4: table 4
message 4 reaches the phone alone, over a connection that drops again
  phone ignores 4: message 2 is missing
the phone reconnects and reports that it has message 1
  phone shows 2: hello?
  phone shows 3: we are starting
  phone shows 4: table 4
the server repeats message 3, because an acknowledgement was lost
  phone ignores 3: already shown
messages on the server: 4, shown on the phone: 4

From this execution transcript, we validate all three invariants of the per-conversation cursor protocol:

  1. Out-of-order protection: When message 4 arrived while the phone’s cursor stood at 1, the rule 4 > 1 + 1 prevented rendering message 4 ahead of missing messages 2 and 3.
  2. Exact gap recovery: Reporting cursor 1 upon reconnect allowed the server to replay the exact suffix [2, 3, 4] without tracking any per-device delivery queue on the server.
  3. Idempotent duplicate suppression: When a lost acknowledgement triggered a duplicate delivery of message 3 while the cursor stood at 4, the rule 3 <= 4 discarded the duplicate cleanly, terminating with 4 messages on the server and the exact same 4 messages displayed once in strict order on the phone.

18.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
WebSocket (RFC 6455)A full-duplex persistent framing protocol upgraded from HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 allowing low-latency bidirectional push over a single TCP/TLS connection.
Stateful GatewayA minimal edge server dedicated exclusively to terminating and maintaining hundreds of thousands of long-lived client sockets, isolated from stateless application logic.
Session DirectoryAn in-memory lease-based mapping ((user_id, device_id) -> gateway_id) used as a fast routing hint for live message push.
Per-Conversation Sequence NumberA strict gapless monotonic integer (1, 2, 3, ...) assigned by a conversation’s shard leader that defines the single canonical message order for all participants.
Client Sync CursorThe highest contiguous sequence number persisted and displayed by a specific device, used to detect gaps, suppress duplicates, and fetch missed history deterministically.
Cumulative Watermark ReceiptA single integer (delivered_seq or read_seq) acknowledging all messages up to and including that sequence number in one idempotent update.
Double Ratchet / Sender KeysCryptographic primitives of the Signal E2EE protocol deriving fresh per-message keys for forward secrecy and post-compromise security.

References
