19. Payment System: System Design

A distributed payment platform orchestrates monetary transfers across payers, merchants, and external banking rails while maintaining an immutable, zero-sum accounting ledger. In contrast to caches, news feeds, or rate limiters where bounded staleness or occasional duplicate execution is an acceptable engineering trade-off, financial infrastructure operates under strict legal and monetary invariants: double-charging a card withdraws real funds from a customer’s account, and recording an uncollected payment causes unrecoverable inventory loss. In this chapter, we design an architecture that places transactional correctness, auditability, and idempotent state recovery strictly ahead of raw availability.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, verifiable functional requirements, strong-consistency SLOs, and storage, TPS, and 7-year audit capacity bounds
  • idempotent HTTP/2 payment APIs, strict payment state machines, and relational ledger DDL using signed integer minor units
  • PCI-DSS Cardholder Data Environment (CDE) isolation, EMV network tokenization, and non-CDE payment core architecture
  • Stripe-style atomic-phase execution and recovery points that eliminate database locks during slow external PSP RPCs while modeling network timeouts as a first-class UNKNOWN state
  • immutable double-entry ledger invariants, deterministic rounding/remainder allocation, and K-way hot-account sub-account sharding to eliminate row-lock serialization
  • transactional outbox with WAL CDC, saga compensation semantics, and T+0 to T+2 three-way financial reconciliation across internal ledger, PSP clearing files, and bank statements
  • failure matrices, financial SLIs, production architectures (Stripe, Adyen, Uber LedgerStore, TigerBeetle), and verification via code/paysim

19.1 Requirements and Capacity Envelope

What appears to a shopper as an instantaneous checkout click is a multi-day distributed workflow spanning four autonomous parties: the issuing bank (holding the cardholder’s account), the card network (Visa or Mastercard, routing messages and enforcing dispute rules), the acquiring bank / Payment Service Provider (PSP) (settling funds on behalf of the merchant), and the payment platform we design here. Every card payment traverses four distinct lifecycle stages: Authorization (seconds; verifies funds and places a hold without moving cash), Capture (at shipment; confirms the final amount <= authorized amount), Settlement (T+1 to T+3 batch transfer of actual cash between banks), and Refund or Chargeback Dispute (possible for up to 120 to 180 days). Because external banking networks cannot participate in a distributed two-phase commit (2PC) with our internal databases, we achieve financial correctness through idempotent state machines, immutable accounting journals, and automated reconciliation.

Actors and Use Cases

Three classes of external actors interact across the boundary of the payment platform (Figure 19-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Merchant / Checkout ServiceAuthorize, capture, or charge (POST /v1/payments)Collect payment for an order using an opaque card token and caller-supplied Idempotency-Key
Merchant / Support SystemFull or partial refund (POST /v1/payments/{id}/refunds)Reverse all or part of a captured charge via append-only compensating ledger transactions
External PSP / Card NetworkAsynchronous status webhook and T+1 clearing fileReport delayed capture outcomes, interchange fees, FX settlement rates, or cardholder disputes
Finance / AuditorAccount journal query and daily three-way reconciliationProve that every account balance equals the exact sum of its immutable ledger rows and matches bank statements

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0The platform supports both single-step (authorize + capture) and two-step (authorize, followed by full or partial capture) charges in any ISO-4217 currency.
1Every mutating endpoint mandates a caller-supplied Idempotency-Key. Retries bearing the same key and identical request payload return the original cached result (including declines) with zero duplicate side effects; reusing a key with a different payload returns 422 Unprocessable Content.
2Every monetary state transition records balanced debit and credit entries in an append-only ledger whose signed integer amounts sum strictly to zero per transaction and currency (SUM(delta_minor) == 0). Existing rows are never updated or deleted.
3The platform supports full and multi-partial refunds whose cumulative amount never exceeds the captured amount, recorded exclusively as new reversing ledger entries.
4Raw Primary Account Numbers (PANs) and CVVs are strictly confined to an isolated PCI-DSS Cardholder Data Environment (CDE) and never enter the payment core, ledger database, message broker, or application logs.
5An automated pipeline reconciles internal ledger records daily against PSP clearing files and bank settlement statements, surfacing unexplained cash breaks within 24 hours.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0ConsistencyStrict ACID Serializability / Linearizability across idempotency keys, payment state, and ledger entriesSynchronous 3-AZ quorum commit (PC/EC): refuse new charges during a quorum partition rather than risking unverified or duplicate mutations
1DurabilityZero loss of any committed payment or ledger entry under any single host, disk, or AZ failure; 7-10 year immutable audit retention3-AZ synchronous replication (Raft or PostgreSQL synchronous standby in a remote AZ) plus continuous encrypted WAL archival to WORM object storage
2Availability99.99% core API availability (<= 4.3 minutes/month) excluding external PSP outagesActive-active stateless orchestrators across three AZs; automated multi-PSP failover routing when a single acquirer degrades
3LatencyCore internal orchestration overhead p99 <= 40 ms (excluding 200-3,000 ms external PSP RTT)Prohibits holding database transactions open during external network I/O; relies on short local ACID phases
4Scale1,000 sustained payments/s (5,000 peak flash-sale TPS)86.4 million payments/day; requires hot-account sharding so high-fan-in merchant or fee rows do not serialize database writes

Capacity and Resource Envelope

Financial infrastructure is constrained by transactional lock contention, cross-AZ synchronous fsync latency, and multi-year regulatory retention, rather than raw network bandwidth:

Resource DimensionDerivationProvisioned Bound
Daily Payment Volume1,000 payments/s * 86,400 s86.4M payments/day
Daily Ledger Journal Rows86.4M payments * 3 entries (payer debit, merchant credit, platform-fee credit)~259M rows/day
Daily Storage Growth259M rows * ~180 B (tuple + indexes) + 86.4M payment and idempotency rows (~300 B)~72 GB/day (~26 TB/year)
7-Year Audit RetentionHot NVMe tier (90 days: ~6.5 TB) + immutable compressed Parquet/WORM archive (7 years)~6.5 TB active NVMe; ~35 TB cold WORM archive
Peak ACID Write Rate5,000 peak TPS * 2 short local DB transactions/payment (Phase 1 intent + Phase 3 finalize)10,000 ACID tx/s -> partitioned PostgreSQL (by merchant_id / account shard) or distributed SQL plus hot-account sharding

19.2 External API, State Machine, and Data Contracts

Idempotent HTTP/2 Payment API

Because HTTP POST is not inherently idempotent, every mutating request requires a caller-supplied Idempotency-Key header (scoped uniquely per (merchant_id, idempotency_key)). Monetary values are represented strictly as signed 64-bit integers in the currency’s smallest minor unit paired with an ISO-4217 currency code (4000 with "EUR" denotes 40.00 EUR; 500 with "JPY" denotes 500 JPY, which has zero fractional subunits).

Create a payment (initial attempt):

POST /v1/payments HTTP/2
Host: pay.example
Authorization: Bearer sk_live_merchant_42
Idempotency-Key: order-7
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "payer_account": "acct_ada",
  "merchant_account": "acct_shop_42",
  "payment_method_token": "tok_9f2a8c11",
  "amount_minor": 4000,
  "currency": "EUR",
  "capture_mode": "automatic"
}

HTTP/2 201 Created
Location: /v1/payments/pay_9001
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "payment_id": "pay_9001",
  "state": "CAPTURED",
  "amount_minor": 4000,
  "currency": "EUR",
  "psp_reference_id": "psp_ref_01J9X7"
}

Four behavioral contracts ensure idempotency protection holds under real network failures:

  1. Atomic Persistence: The idempotency key record, payment state transition, and ledger entries commit inside the same ACID database transaction. A crash can never commit a charge without also persisting its deduplication key.
  2. Caching Terminal Failures: Declines (such as 422 Unprocessable Content for insufficient funds) are cached under the key identically to successes. If a merchant already informed a customer that order-8 failed, a delayed retry must replay 422 rather than charging the card later once funds arrive.
  3. Concurrent In-Flight Exclusion: When a second request bearing an active Idempotency-Key arrives while the first is still running, the unique key lock returns 409 Conflict with Retry-After: 1 instead of launching a concurrent duplicate PSP call.
  4. Payload Fingerprinting: Storing the SHA-256 hash of the canonical request payload detects accidental key reuse (such as submitting 40000 cents under a key originally bound to 4000 cents) and rejects the call with 422 Unprocessable Content.

Strict Payment State Machine and Relational Schema

Every payment transitions along a directed acyclic state machine guarded at the database layer by optimistic version checks (WHERE payment_id = $1 AND state = 'PENDING_PSP' AND version = $2), making illegal transitions (such as DECLINED -> CAPTURED or double-capturing a settled charge) structurally impossible:

CREATED -> PENDING_PSP -> AUTHORIZED -> CAPTURED -> SETTLED
                |             |            |
                v             v            v
            DECLINED        VOIDED   PARTIALLY_REFUNDED -> REFUNDED / DISPUTED

Before examining the DDL below, note the role of each table: idempotency_keys tracks the request SHA-256 digest, current recovery_point, and serialized HTTP reply; payments holds the canonical state machine and the deterministic psp_reference_id shared with the external acquirer; and ledger_entries records immutable signed minor-unit deltas verified by a deferrable transaction-commit trigger asserting SUM(delta_minor) == 0 per (tx_id, currency).

CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
    merchant_id      TEXT        NOT NULL,
    idem_key         TEXT        NOT NULL,
    request_sha256   BYTEA       NOT NULL,
    recovery_point   TEXT        NOT NULL, -- 'STARTED' | 'PENDING_PSP' | 'FINISHED'
    response_status  INT,
    response_body    JSONB,
    locked_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    expires_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (merchant_id, idem_key)
);

CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id       TEXT        PRIMARY KEY,
    merchant_id      TEXT        NOT NULL,
    psp_reference_id TEXT        NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    amount_minor     BIGINT      NOT NULL CHECK (amount_minor > 0),
    currency         CHAR(3)     NOT NULL,
    state            TEXT        NOT NULL,
    version          BIGINT      NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
    entry_id         BIGINT      GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    tx_id            UUID        NOT NULL,
    account_id       TEXT        NOT NULL,
    currency         CHAR(3)     NOT NULL,
    delta_minor      BIGINT      NOT NULL CHECK (delta_minor <> 0),
    created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- Deferrable constraint trigger verifies SUM(delta_minor) = 0 per (tx_id, currency) at COMMIT.

19.3 System Architecture: PCI-DSS Isolation and Async Clearing

We enforce two explicit structural boundaries across the payment platform: a security boundary isolating raw card numbers inside a minimal PCI-DSS Cardholder Data Environment (CDE), and a transactional boundary separating short local ACID commits from slow external PSP network calls and multi-day settlement pipelines (Figure 19-2).

Component Responsibilities and Failure Domains

ComponentCompliance ScopeState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Tokenization Vault and HSMPCI-DSS CDEEncrypted PAN <-> opaque token (tok_*), HSM key materialIsolated VPC with direct egress allow-list to card networks; active-active across three AZs; keeps the entire payment core out of PCI audit scope
Payment API GatewayNon-CDENone (stateless mTLS, auth, fail-closed rate limit)Multi-AZ active-active deployment; rejects malformed or unauthorized calls at ingress
Payment Orchestrator (x12)Non-CDENone (stateless atomic-phase runner)Pod crash mid-flight leaves durable PENDING_PSP recovery point in DB; caller retries or pollers resume safely
Core Ledger and Idempotency DBNon-CDEidempotency_keys, payments, ledger_entries, outbox_events3-AZ synchronous quorum (Raft or Postgres sync standby); rejects writes during quorum loss rather than risking split-brain double charges
CDC Outbox Relay (Debezium)Async TierWAL replication slot offsetStreams committed outbox_events into Kafka with at-least-once delivery; downstream consumers deduplicate by event_id
Pending Poller and WebhooksAsync TierPolling queue and webhook deduplication keysResolves UNKNOWN payments via PSP status queries and verifies HMAC-signed PSP webhooks
T+1 / T+2 Reconciliation EngineAsync TierClearing and bank statement snapshotsExecutes deterministic three-way join across internal ledger, PSP clearing files, and bank cash statements

19.4 Atomic-Phase Idempotency and Unknown Outcomes

Opening a database transaction, holding row locks while issuing a remote HTTP call to an external PSP (200 ms to 5,000 ms), and committing when the PSP replies fails catastrophically under production concurrency. By Little’s Law (L = lambda * W), sustaining 1,000 TPS across a 2-second PSP slowdown holds 2,000 database connections and row locks open simultaneously, exhausting connection pools and cascading a single acquirer’s latency spike into a total platform outage.

Following the pattern documented by Stripe and Airbnb, we decompose every payment into Atomic Phases separated by durable recovery points, enforcing one strict invariant: no external network RPC may ever execute inside an open database transaction (Figure 19-3).

Treating UNKNOWN as a First-Class Durable State

When Phase 2 times out after 5 seconds, receives an HTTP 502, or suffers an orchestrator crash before reading the socket, the outcome at the issuing bank is genuinely unknown. Marking the payment DECLINED on timeout invites the customer to retry with a new order, double-charging their card when the first charge actually settled. Conversely, blindly re-submitting a new charge without the deterministic psp_reference_id persisted in Phase 1 causes the PSP to process two separate charges.

Instead, the payment remains durably in PENDING_PSP until one of three convergent paths resolves it:

  1. Idempotent Caller Retry: A retry carrying the same Idempotency-Key reads recovery_point = 'PENDING_PSP', skips Phase 1, and queries or re-submits to the PSP using the persisted psp_reference_id.
  2. Signed PSP Webhook: When the PSP completes settlement asynchronously, its HMAC-verified webhook triggers Phase 3 via a conditional transition (WHERE state = 'PENDING_PSP').
  3. Background Status Poller: A sweeper inspects payments remaining in PENDING_PSP past 30 seconds, queries the PSP status endpoint with exponential backoff, and drives them to CAPTURED, DECLINED, or manual operations escalation after 24 hours.

Advance through the interactive step-by-step trace below to observe how durable PENDING intent and a stable PSP reference resolve a dropped network reply without double-charging:

19.5 Immutable Double-Entry Ledger and Hot-Account Sharding

Mutating a single accounts.balance column in place destroys audit provenance and permits partial-update corruption if a crash occurs between debiting one account and crediting another. Financial systems instead implement double-entry bookkeeping: every monetary movement appends an immutable set of journal rows whose signed minor-unit deltas sum strictly to zero (SUM(delta_minor) == 0). Any bug that fails to balance a transfer violates the database constraint and aborts the transaction before committing corrupt state.

Exact Monetary Arithmetic and Deterministic Rounding

Binary IEEE-754 floating-point values (f32/f64) cannot represent decimal tenths exactly (0.10 + 0.20 != 0.30 in binary), accumulating unexplained cent discrepancies across millions of percentage fees and currency conversions. Storing all amounts as signed 64-bit integer minor units paired with an ISO-4217 currency code guarantees exact integer arithmetic. Whenever a percentage fee or multi-way payout split produces a fractional cent (such as dividing 100 cents across 3 recipients), the ledger applies a deterministic rounding policy (round-half-even or largest-remainder allocation) and routes the exact integer remainder to a designated remainder account so the transaction remains strictly zero-sum.

Executing code/paysim validates idempotent replay (order-7, order-9), cached refusal replay (order-8), and zero-sum conservation (10,000 cents total before and after all operations):

$ cargo run --release -p paysim
start: {"ada": 10000, "shop": 0}, total 10000
order-7: 4000 cents from ada to shop: Done, ada has 6000
order-7: 4000 cents from ada to shop: Done, ada has 6000
order-8: 9000 cents from ada to shop: Refused, ada has 6000
order-9: 6000 cents from ada to shop: Done, ada has 0
order-9: 6000 cents from ada to shop: Done, ada has 0
end: {"ada": 0, "shop": 10000}, total 10000

Inspect the append-only journal mechanics across two charges and an immutable reversing refund below:

Eliminating Hot-Account Row-Lock Serialization

At 1,000-5,000 TPS, maintaining a single materialized balance row per account introduces severe row-level lock contention on high-fan-in accounts such as acct:platform_fees, a global PSP clearing account, or a flagship merchant during a flash sale. Executing SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 'platform_fees' FOR UPDATE on every payment serializes all concurrent transactions behind a single database row lock, collapsing write throughput regardless of cluster size.

We eliminate hot-account serialization through two complementary designs (Figure 19-4):

  1. K-Way Sub-Account Sharding (Credit-Heavy Clearing and Fee Accounts): Partition high-TPS credit accounts logically into K sub-accounts (merchant_42#0 through merchant_42#15) selected deterministically by hash(payment_id) % K. Concurrent credits lock independent rows across K buckets, scaling throughput linearly by factor K. A periodic asynchronous rollup worker writes balance checkpoints (SUM(sub_accounts #0..#15)), bounding read query cost to entries created since the latest checkpoint.
  2. Single-Threaded Partitioned Ledger Engines (High-TPS Debit Accounts): Debit accounts enforcing strict synchronous non-negative overdraft checks cannot split debits arbitrarily across independent rows without risking concurrent overdrafts. Workloads demanding 100,000+ debit TPS on hot accounts route account partitions to dedicated single-threaded, memory-first, Raft-replicated ledger engines (such as TigerBeetle) that execute batched double-entry transfers sequentially in microseconds with zero SQL lock overhead.

Cross-Service Consistency: Transactional Outbox and Sagas

Publishing a PaymentCaptured event to Kafka directly from application code after committing the database transaction creates a dual-write hazard: a process crash between the two commits money without notifying order fulfillment, whereas publishing before commit emits phantom events on rollback. Phase 3 resolves this by inserting an outbox_events row inside the exact same ACID transaction as the ledger entries. A Change Data Capture (CDC) relay (such as Debezium tailing the PostgreSQL WAL) streams committed outbox rows into Kafka with at-least-once delivery, while downstream consumers deduplicate by event_id.

For business workflows spanning independent services (inventory reservation, loyalty points, and card capture), an orchestrator executes a Saga: a sequence of local transactions paired with idempotent compensating transactions on failure. Reversible local steps (inventory holds) execute before irreversible external steps (card capture) so partial failures unwind cleanly.

19.6 Three-Way Reconciliation and Multi-Currency FX

Because external PSPs, card networks, and settlement banks operate outside our ACID boundary, internal records can diverge from actual bank cash due to delayed chargebacks, silent PSP duplicate processing, FX rate movement between authorization (T+0) and settlement (T+2), or variable interchange fees. We run an automated Three-Way Financial Reconciliation Pipeline daily to detect and classify these breaks (Figure 19-5).

Clearing Suspense Accounts and Multi-Currency Conservation

Double-entry accounting prevents premature merchant payouts by routing captured funds through explicit clearing suspense accounts:

  1. On Capture (T+0): Debit clearing:psp_receivable, Credit merchant:pending_payout and platform:fee_revenue.
  2. On Bank Settlement (T+2): Debit bank:operating_cash, Credit clearing:psp_receivable. When cross-currency settlement occurs (for example, payer billed EUR and merchant settled USD), each currency maintains an independently balanced zero-sum pair bridged through explicit fx:trading_eur and fx:trading_usd clearing accounts so single-currency conservation holds everywhere.
  3. Deterministic Break Classification: Unmatched records route into Timing Differences (in-flight UTC cutoff items aged out after 72 hours), Fee or FX Variances (auto-booked to a tracked variance account within configured tolerances), and Critical Breaks (duplicate charges or missing bank cash), which page on-call engineers and automatically freeze affected merchant payout releases until resolved.

19.7 Security, Failure Modes, Production Systems, and Verification

PCI-DSS Scope Minimization and Network Tokenization

Storing, transmitting, or logging raw 16-digit PANs pulls every server, database, message broker, and log aggregator touching that data into full PCI-DSS Level 1 audit scope. The checkout client submits raw card fields directly to the isolated Tokenization Vault (via hosted iframe or direct TLS session into the CDE), receiving an opaque token (tok_9f2a8c11) safe for storage in the Non-CDE core. Modern platforms additionally replace static PANs with EMV Network Tokens (Visa Token Service and Mastercard MDES), which automatically update expired credentials and cryptographically bind tokens to a single merchant domain, raising authorization approval rates while removing raw PAN exposure.

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ScenarioBlast RadiusAutomated Recovery and Preserved Invariant
Client Connection Drops Before ReplySingle paymentClient retries with same Idempotency-Key; returns cached response or resumes from PENDING_PSP with zero double charge
PSP Timeout / 5xx in Phase 2Single payment or one acquirer railZero DB locks held; payment remains PENDING_PSP (UNKNOWN) and resolves via webhook or status poller using psp_reference_id; circuit breaker routes new traffic to secondary PSP
Core Ledger Primary Crash / AZ LossAll writes for 1-3 sSynchronous 3-AZ quorum promotes up-to-date standby with zero RPO (0 lost transactions); incoming charges receive 503 during failover
Duplicate PSP Webhook DeliverySingle paymentConditional transition WHERE state = 'PENDING_PSP' plus unique webhook event_id table guarantees single application
High-TPS Merchant Row-Lock SpikeHot merchant / fee accountK=16 logical sub-account sharding eliminates serial row locks while async rollup preserves exact master balances
Bank Settlement ShortfallFinancial integrityT+2 three-way reconciliation raises a Critical Break alert within 24 hours and holds affected payout disbursements

Financial Observability: SLIs and Alerts

Four specialized signals monitor financial integrity beyond standard HTTP metrics: authorization approval rate segmented by issuer BIN, country, and PSP (a sudden > 3% drop exposes acquirer regressions even while HTTP status remains 200); a continuous ledger conservation verifier asserting SUM(delta_minor) == 0 per tx_id and currency (SEV-1 on any non-zero sum); pending payment aging alerting when payments linger in PENDING_PSP past 15 minutes; and unreconciled suspense aging escalating funds remaining in clearing:psp_receivable past T+3.

How Production Systems Implement Payments

Production SystemCore ArchitectureArchitectural Distinction
StripeAtomic-phase idempotency keys, sharded relational ledger, isolated PCI vaultFormalized recovery-point idempotency strictly separating ACID transactions from external network RPCs, paired with multi-acquirer smart retries
AdyenUnified platform connected directly to Visa/Mastercard card schemesRemoves intermediate gateway hops to cut latency and boost authorization rates; native three-way settlement reconciliation
Uber (LedgerStore)Immutable, cryptographically tamper-evident append-only double-entry storeEnforces immutability and Merkle-tree audit verification at the storage engine layer across billions of daily entries
TigerBeetlePurpose-built distributed financial accounting database (Viewstamped Replication + io_uring)Executes strict double-entry transfers in single-threaded deterministic batches (1M+ TPS), eliminating SQL hot-account lock contention natively

Verification in the Repository

Run the payment ledger and idempotency simulation. Execute cargo run --release -p paysim in code/ to verify idempotent deduplication (order-7, order-9), cached insufficient-funds refusal replay (order-8), and strict zero-sum double-entry conservation across all operations.

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Atomic Phase / Recovery PointStructuring a payment workflow into short local ACID transactions separated from slow external RPCs so retries resume cleanly without holding DB locks across network I/O.
Double-Entry LedgerAppend-only accounting model in which every monetary transfer records balanced debit and credit rows summing strictly to zero per currency.
Hot-Account ShardingPartitioning high-TPS credit accounts (such as platform fees or clearing suspense accounts) into K logical sub-accounts to remove serial database row-lock contention.

Chapter 20: Ticket Booking: System Design

A high-contention ticket booking platform sells finite, non-fungible inventory, such as stadium seats, cinema seats, or airline cabins, where each seat can belong to at most one confirmed buyer. While this invariant is trivial under sequential single-node execution, real ticket drops combine extreme ingress bursts (millions of concurrent buyers arriving within seconds of an on-sale opening) with long, unreliable checkout phases spanning external payment authorization. In this chapter, I design a distributed booking architecture that enforces zero double-selling through event-sharded relational state machines and atomic compare-and-swap holds, while absorbing flash-sale demand behind a cryptographically gated virtual waiting room.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, verifiable functional requirements, strong-consistency SLOs, explicit non-goals, and flash-sale capacity bounds
  • idempotent HTTP/2 seat-map, hold, and booking APIs, HMAC admission tokens, and relational DDL for seat inventory and booking uniqueness
  • control-plane vs. data-plane separation across the virtual waiting room, event-sharded inventory tier, seat-map cache, and payment saga engine
  • flash-sale admission control with randomized pre-sale lottery pools, HMAC-signed pass tokens, and layered anti-bot rate limits
  • per-seat state machine (AVAILABLE -> HELD -> BOOKED), conditional CAS SQL predicates, multi-seat deadlock-free locking, and compensating payment sagas
  • failure matrices, booking SLIs/SLOs, production architectures (Ticketmaster, Stripe, Cloudflare Waiting Room), and verification via code/bookingsim

20.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Every ticket purchase crosses two distinct operational regimes. Before checkout, millions of prospective buyers browse venue layouts and wait for a sale to open; this traffic is overwhelmingly read-heavy and tolerates bounded staleness of one to two seconds. Once a buyer selects seats and enters payment details, the platform enters a strict transactional regime where every state transition on a seat must serialize across concurrent callers and survive orchestrator crashes or delayed payment network replies.

Actors and Use Cases

Three external actor classes interact across the boundary of the ticket booking platform, as illustrated in Figure 20-1.

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Ticket BuyerJoin queue, inspect seat map (GET /v1/shows/{id}/seats), place timed hold (POST /v1/shows/{id}/holds), and confirm booking (POST /v1/bookings)Wait in a virtual queue during a stadium concert drop, reserve two adjacent seats for 10 minutes, and complete checkout idempotently
Event OrganizerConfigure venue layout, seat pricing tiers, and admission pacing (PUT /v1/shows/{id}/layout)Publish a 50,000-seat stadium manifest and throttle checkout ingress to 500 admitted buyers per second
Payment ProcessorAuthorize, capture, refund, and deliver signed settlement webhooks (POST /v1/webhooks/payment-settled)Confirm card capture asynchronously or execute an automated compensating refund if a seat lease expired

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0A buyer can view a showing’s seat map reflecting each seat’s current status (AVAILABLE, HELD, or BOOKED) with bounded staleness.
1A buyer holding a valid admission token can place a timed hold on one or more seats for a configurable TTL (5 to 10 minutes).
2A multi-seat hold request executes atomically: the buyer receives all requested seats or none.
3At any instant, each seat of a showing is held by or booked to at most one buyer; expired holds become immediately claimable without waiting for background cleanup.
4A buyer can confirm a held booking by supplying a payment token and an Idempotency-Key; duplicate submissions return the original confirmation without double-charging.
5If payment succeeds after the seat lease has expired and another buyer has claimed the seat, the system rejects the booking and triggers an automatic compensating refund.
6During flash sales, the system queues excess arrivals in a virtual waiting room and admits buyers into the booking tier at a controlled rate.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0ConsistencyStrict ACID Serializability / Linearizability for seat holds and booking confirmations; eventual consistency (<= 2 s lag) for seat-map readsEvent-sharded 3-AZ synchronous quorum relational database (PC/EC) for seat inventory; CDN and read-through cache for seat maps
1Availability99.95% booking API availability (<= 21.6 minutes/month); fail closed on inventory quorum lossRefuse new holds if a shard loses majority quorum rather than risking split-brain double sales
2LatencySeat-map read p99 <= 50 ms; seat-hold CAS p99 <= 150 ms; booking confirmation orchestration overhead p99 <= 200 ms (excluding external PSP RTT)Single-shard local ACID transactions with zero database locks held during external payment network calls
3Flash-Sale Scale100,000 active showings; 2,000,000 buyer arrivals within 60 seconds (~33,333 arrivals/s) for a single flagship eventEdge-hosted virtual waiting room absorbs arrival spikes and caps core booking ingress to 500 admitted buyers/s per event shard
4Abuse ResistanceBounded holds per buyer account/session (<= 6 seats) and cryptographic enforcement of queue orderHMAC-signed short-lived admission tokens validated at the Booking API gateway; layered IP, device, and account rate limits

Non-Goals and Explicit Scope Boundaries

To focus on inventory correctness and flash-sale stability, we explicitly exclude the following concerns from this design:

  • Secondary ticket resale and peer-to-peer transfers: Transferring issued barcodes between accounts introduces escrow and ticket-reissuance workflows outside primary inventory allocation.
  • Airline revenue management and dynamic overbooking optimization: Deliberately overselling physical capacity relies on historical no-show statistical models; our inventory invariant enforces exact configured capacity limits.
  • Full card-network PCI-DSS tokenization internals: We rely on opaque payment tokens (tok_*) and the idempotent payment platform architecture designed in Chapter 19 rather than handling raw PANs inside the booking core.
  • Venue physical turnstile validation: Offline barcode scanning at stadium gates consumes issued ticket manifests asynchronously and operates independently of online seat locking.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

Ticket booking storage requirements are modest compared to media or telemetry platforms; the binding engineering constraints are flash-sale ingress burst absorption and per-row write contention on desirable seats.

Resource DimensionDerivationProvisioned Bound
Active Seat Inventory100,000 active showings * 300 average seats/showing30,000,000 seat rows
Seat Table Storage (Hot NVMe)30M rows * 180 B (tuple, version, lease fields, primary + secondary indexes)~5.4 GB active working set (fits entirely in database buffer pool RAM)
Annual Confirmed Bookings50M bookings/year * 350 B (booking + saga journal rows)~17.5 GB/year
Peak Flash-Sale Arrival Rate2,000,000 arrivals / 60 s at on-sale opening~33,333 queue-join req/s handled at CDN edge
Waiting-Room Polling Bandwidth2,000,000 queued clients polling every 10 s * 512 B JSON payload200,000 req/s; ~820 Mbit/s edge egress
Core Inventory Admitted Write RatePacing controller admits 500 buyers/s per flagship show shard * 2 CAS writes (hold + confirm)1,000 ACID tx/s per shard; 50,000 stadium seats clear in ~100 to 180 s
Cached Seat-Map Read Traffic5,000 concurrent admitted browsers refreshing every 2 s2,500 req/s absorbed by 2 s TTL edge/Redis cache (0.5 origin queries/s per showing)

20.2 External API and Data Contracts

All mutating endpoints accept HTTP/2 JSON payloads, require a valid bearer identity, and enforce a caller-supplied Idempotency-Key header. During gated flash sales, callers must also present the signed X-Admission-Token header issued by the virtual waiting room; requests lacking a valid, unexpired signature fail fast at the API gateway with 403 Forbidden.

Seat-Map Read Endpoint

GET /v1/shows/881/seats HTTP/2
Host: tickets.example
Authorization: Bearer usr_eyJhbGci...
X-Admission-Token: v1.show881.usr42.1760436600.9f8e7d6c...

HTTP/2 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: public, max-age=2
ETag: "show881-v40912"

{
  "show_id": 881,
  "snapshot_at": "2026-10-14T10:00:00Z",
  "seats": [
    { "seat_id": "A1", "tier": "orchestra", "price_minor": 12500, "state": "AVAILABLE", "version": 4 },
    { "seat_id": "A2", "tier": "orchestra", "price_minor": 12500, "state": "HELD", "version": 7 },
    { "seat_id": "A3", "tier": "orchestra", "price_minor": 12500, "state": "BOOKED", "version": 9 }
  ]
}

The Cache-Control: public, max-age=2 header declares that the seat map is advisory and may lag the authoritative seat store by up to two seconds. Clients pass the returned version (or allow the server to evaluate current state directly) when attempting a hold.

Atomic Multi-Seat Hold Endpoint

POST /v1/shows/881/holds HTTP/2
Host: tickets.example
Authorization: Bearer usr_eyJhbGci...
X-Admission-Token: v1.show881.usr42.1760436600.9f8e7d6c...
Idempotency-Key: 5d1c-hold-1
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "seat_ids": ["A1", "A4"]
}

HTTP/2 201 Created
Location: /v1/shows/881/holds/hld_7730
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "hold_id": "hld_7730",
  "show_id": 881,
  "seat_ids": ["A1", "A4"],
  "expires_at": "2026-10-14T10:10:00Z",
  "total_minor": 25000,
  "currency": "USD"
}

If any requested seat is already held (with an unexpired lease) or booked, the transaction rolls back all seats in the batch and returns 409 Conflict with an RFC 9457 application/problem+json body identifying the contested seat IDs:

HTTP/2 409 Conflict
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "/problems/seat-unavailable",
  "title": "One or more requested seats are no longer available",
  "status": 409,
  "unavailable_seats": ["A1"]
}

Idempotent Booking Confirmation Endpoint

POST /v1/bookings HTTP/2
Host: tickets.example
Authorization: Bearer usr_eyJhbGci...
Idempotency-Key: 5d1c-book-1
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "hold_id": "hld_7730",
  "show_id": 881,
  "payment_token": "tok_83hf91a"
}

HTTP/2 201 Created
Location: /v1/bookings/bkg_55102
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "booking_id": "bkg_55102",
  "show_id": 881,
  "seat_ids": ["A1", "A4"],
  "state": "CONFIRMED",
  "payment_id": "pay_9001"
}

If the buyer’s hold expired prior to payment submission, the endpoint returns 410 Gone before invoking the payment processor. If a network retry repeats Idempotency-Key: 5d1c-book-1 after a lost response, the service returns the persisted 201 Created confirmation without issuing a second charge.

Relational Inventory and Booking Schema

All seats belonging to a single show_id reside on the same relational shard so multi-seat holds execute inside a local ACID transaction without distributed two-phase commit (2PC). Two structural defenses protect the invariant: every seat row carries a monotonic version and hold_expires_at timestamp, and the booking_seats table enforces a UNIQUE (show_id, seat_id) constraint as an application-independent database backstop.

CREATE TABLE seats (
    show_id         BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    seat_id         TEXT        NOT NULL,
    tier            TEXT        NOT NULL,
    price_minor     BIGINT      NOT NULL CHECK (price_minor > 0),
    state           TEXT        NOT NULL CHECK (state IN ('AVAILABLE', 'HELD', 'BOOKED')),
    hold_id         TEXT,
    holder_user_id  TEXT,
    hold_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    booking_id      TEXT,
    version         BIGINT      NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    PRIMARY KEY (show_id, seat_id)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_seats_active_holds
    ON seats (show_id, hold_expires_at)
    WHERE state = 'HELD';

CREATE TABLE bookings (
    booking_id      TEXT        PRIMARY KEY,
    show_id         BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    user_id         TEXT        NOT NULL,
    hold_id         TEXT        NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    idem_key        TEXT        NOT NULL,
    payment_id      TEXT        UNIQUE,
    state           TEXT        NOT NULL CHECK (state IN ('PENDING_PAYMENT', 'CONFIRMED', 'COMPENSATED', 'FAILED')),
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    UNIQUE (user_id, idem_key)
);

CREATE TABLE booking_seats (
    show_id         BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    seat_id         TEXT        NOT NULL,
    booking_id      TEXT        NOT NULL REFERENCES bookings(booking_id),
    PRIMARY KEY (show_id, seat_id) -- Second line of defense against double booking
);

20.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We isolate flash-sale crowd management and operational configuration from the synchronous transactional seat path by splitting the platform into a Control Plane and a Data Plane, as depicted in Figure 20-2.

Control Plane Responsibilities

The control plane governs traffic shaping, shard routing, and asynchronous housekeeping without sitting on the critical per-seat checkout path:

  • Queue Pacing Controller: Computes the admission release rate per showing (tokens/s) by monitoring inventory database CPU, lock-wait latency, and remaining seat counts. When a showing sells out, the controller flips the waiting-room state to SOLD_OUT, immediately terminating polling for millions of queued browsers.
  • Event Shard Directory: Maintains the mapping from show_id to its assigned 3-AZ synchronous relational shard. High-demand stadium shows receive dedicated shards prior to on-sale openings so a flagship concert drop cannot degrade latency for concurrent theater or cinema shows.
  • Lease Sweeper Worker: Periodically scans idx_seats_active_holds to reset expired HELD rows back to AVAILABLE and invalidate cached seat maps. Correctness never depends on sweeper punctuality because the hot-path SQL predicates treat any row with hold_expires_at < now() as available immediately.

Data Plane Responsibilities

The data plane executes the synchronous buyer journey across four decoupled tiers:

ComponentState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Virtual Waiting Room (Edge)Queue positions, randomized lottery ranks, HMAC signing keysRuns across CDN edge PoPs; node failure reconstructs queue rank from signed client queue cookies; already admitted buyers retain valid pass tokens
Seat Map CDN and CacheEventual read-only seat availability snapshots (2 s TTL)Cache miss or Redis outage falls back to a single coalesced read replica query per showing per 2 seconds (singleflight)
Booking API and Inventory ServiceStateless (X-Admission-Token verification, CAS SQL, idempotency)Multi-AZ stateless pods; pod crash mid-request allows safe client retry via Idempotency-Key
Event-Sharded Seat DBseats, bookings, booking_seats, outbox_events (3-AZ sync quorum)Primary crash promotes synchronous standby within 1 to 3 s with zero RPO (0 lost bookings); writes pause until quorum recovers
Payment Saga EngineDurable saga journal and transactional outboxResumes interrupted payment confirmations or issues compensating refunds via Chapter 19 idempotent payment calls

20.4 Deep Dive: Flash-Sale Virtual Waiting Room and Admission Control

When 2,000,000 buyers arrive within 60 seconds for 50,000 stadium seats, 97.5% of arrivals cannot end in a purchase. Exposing the inventory database directly to 33,333 concurrent hold requests per second saturates database connection pools, triggers massive row-lock thrashing on front-row seats, and collapses throughput for everyone.

Pre-Sale Lottery Pool and FIFO Pacing

If queue order were determined strictly by arrival timestamp at 10:00:00.000 UTC, automated ticket bots colocated near edge PoPs with sub-millisecond jitter would capture the entire front of the queue. Instead, we divide admission into two phases:

  1. Pre-Sale Lobby (T - 30 min to T = 0): Every authenticated buyer arriving before the opening enters an unordered lobby pool. At T = 0, the waiting room applies a cryptographically seeded permutation (Fisher-Yates shuffle or HMAC-derived sort key over (show_id, user_id, epoch_secret)) to assign each lobby participant a uniform random queue rank. Buyers arriving after T = 0 append strictly in FIFO order behind the randomized lobby cohort.
  2. Controlled Token Release: Each second, the Queue Pacing Controller advances a monotonic admitted_rank_watermark in edge KV storage by R slots (for example, R = 500 buyers/s). Queued clients poll a lightweight edge endpoint every 10 seconds displaying their remaining offset (rank - watermark).

Cryptographically Signed HMAC Admission Tokens

Once a client’s rank <= admitted_rank_watermark, the edge waiting room mints a stateless, short-lived admission token signed with HMAC-SHA256 using a key rotated every hour via KMS:

payload   = base64url("v1|" + show_id + "|" + user_id + "|" + issued_at + "|" + expires_at + "|" + nonce)
signature = HMAC_SHA256(edge_signing_key, payload)
token     = payload + "." + base64url(signature)

Every call to POST /v1/shows/{id}/holds must include X-Admission-Token. The Booking API verifies three conditions in constant time without calling the waiting room: (1) valid HMAC signature, (2) show_id and user_id match the authenticated caller and path, and (3) now() < expires_at (typically a 15-minute shopping window). Direct API scraping attempts that bypass the waiting room fail at ingress in under 1 ms without touching the inventory database.

Layered Anti-Bot and Hold-Hoarding Defenses

Malicious resellers often attempt inventory hoarding: holding hundreds of seats across automated sessions without paying to starve legitimate buyers and force resale demand. We counter this at three layers:

  1. Waiting-Room Gate: Requires account verification (phone or payment-instrument history) and adaptive proof-of-interaction challenges before issuing a lottery rank.
  2. Per-Account Hold Quotas: Enforces a strict cap (such as at most 6 held or booked seats per (show_id, user_id)) inside the Inventory Service transaction and tracks abandoned-hold velocity per account and IP subnet using sliding-window rate limiters (Chapter 7).
  3. General Admission Counter Sharding: For unnumbered standing-room events (such as 5,000 floor tickets), updating a single remaining_count row serializes all concurrent buyers on one database lock. We pre-split capacity into K = 50 sub-counters of 100 places each, routing buyers to hash(user_id) % K and probing adjacent non-empty shards only as buckets approach zero.

20.5 Deep Dive: Seat State Machine, Conditional CAS, and Payment Sagas

At the core of the Inventory Service lies the race condition that breaks unsynchronized read-modify-write implementations. If two servers read seat 12, observe state = 'AVAILABLE', and independently write their respective buyers’ IDs, both buyers receive confirmation for the same seat. Advance through the interactive trace below to inspect how separating the read from the write permits double booking, and how a conditional write eliminates the race.

Per-Seat State Machine and Conditional CAS SQL

We model every numbered seat as a three-state machine (AVAILABLE -> HELD -> BOOKED) guarded by monotonic version fencing and explicit hold_expires_at timestamps, as shown in Figure 20-3.

To acquire a single seat without holding long pessimistic locks, the Inventory Service executes a single atomic conditional UPDATE that treats expired holds as immediately available:

UPDATE seats
SET state           = 'HELD',
    hold_id         = $1,
    holder_user_id  = $2,
    hold_expires_at = now() + INTERVAL '10 minutes',
    version         = version + 1
WHERE show_id = $3
  AND seat_id = $4
  AND (
      state = 'AVAILABLE'
      OR (state = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < now())
  )
RETURNING seat_id, version, hold_expires_at;

If the database returns 1 row, the caller holds an exclusive lease on the seat. If 0 rows match, another transaction already won the race (or the seat is BOOKED), and the API immediately returns 409 Conflict with zero lock queuing.

Multi-Seat Atomicity and Deadlock Prevention

When a group requests multiple seats (["A1", "A4", "A2"]), the Inventory Service sorts the requested seat_ids lexicographically (["A1", "A2", "A4"]) before executing the batch UPDATE inside one shard-local ACID transaction:

UPDATE seats
SET state           = 'HELD',
    hold_id         = $1,
    holder_user_id  = $2,
    hold_expires_at = now() + INTERVAL '10 minutes',
    version         = version + 1
WHERE show_id = $3
  AND seat_id = ANY($4::text[]) -- pre-sorted lexicographically
  AND (
      state = 'AVAILABLE'
      OR (state = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < now())
  )
RETURNING seat_id;

Sorting seat_ids establishes a strict global lock-acquisition order across concurrent transactions, making circular wait (deadlock) structurally impossible. If the count of returned rows is strictly less than array_length($4, 1), the service issues ROLLBACK, releasing every partial hold atomically and returning 409 Conflict listing the contested seats.

Comparing Concurrency Control Strategies

MechanismContention BehaviorDB Connections Held While WaitingApplication-Bug Safety
Pessimistic Lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE)Losing callers block in a row-lock queue until the holder commitsYes; slow holders stall pool capacityNone if a code path omits FOR UPDATE
Optimistic Conditional CAS (UPDATE ... WHERE)One caller wins immediately; losers fail fast with 409 ConflictNo; zero waiting across transactionsRelies on predicate discipline on every mutation
Database Uniqueness Constraint (PRIMARY KEY (show_id, seat_id))Second insert into booking_seats fails with unique-violation errorNoEnforced by storage engine regardless of application bugs

Our architecture combines Conditional CAS on seats for fast contention resolution with the booking_seats primary key constraint as an unbypassable final invariant check.

Lease Expiry, Late-Payment Races, and Saga Compensation

Because checkout requires a buyer to enter payment credentials and await external card-network authorization (200 ms to 15 s), a hold can expire while payment is in flight. Step through the interactive trace below to observe how an expired hold allows a second buyer to acquire the seat cleanly and how the system rejects the first buyer’s late confirmation.

Following the atomic-phase pattern from Chapter 19, we never hold a database transaction open while invoking the external payment service. Instead, the Payment Saga Engine executes three short local phases around the payment RPC:

  1. Phase 1: Conditional Grace-Window Extension (Local ACID, < 5 ms): Before charging the card, the saga atomically verifies the hold is still owned by the caller and extends hold_expires_at by a 60-second payment grace buffer while inserting a PENDING_PAYMENT row in bookings and a durable saga journal step: 
    UPDATE seats
SET hold_expires_at = now() + INTERVAL '60 seconds',
    version         = version + 1
WHERE show_id = $1 AND hold_id = $2 AND holder_user_id = $3
  AND state = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at >= now();
    If 0 rows update, the hold already lapsed; the saga aborts with 410 Gone and zero card charge occurs.
  2. Phase 2: External Payment Capture (No DB Locks Held): The saga invokes the Payment Platform (POST /v1/payments) using Idempotency-Key = hold_id, guaranteeing at most one card charge across orchestrator retries.
  3. Phase 3: Fenced Booking Confirmation or Automatic Compensation (Local ACID, < 5 ms): Upon payment approval, the saga conditionally transitions the seats to BOOKED and inserts rows into booking_seats: 
    UPDATE seats
SET state = 'BOOKED', booking_id = $1, version = version + 1
WHERE show_id = $2 AND hold_id = $3 AND holder_user_id = $4 AND state = 'HELD';
    In the extreme case where an external payment took longer than the 60-second grace buffer and another buyer claimed the seat in the meantime, the fenced UPDATE returns 0 rows (or booking_seats raises a uniqueness violation). The saga never overrides the inventory invariant: it marks the booking COMPENSATED, writes an outbox event triggering an idempotent full refund (POST /v1/payments/{id}/refunds), and informs the buyer.

20.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ScenarioBlast RadiusAutomated Recovery and Preserved Invariant
Buyer Abandons Checkout Mid-HoldHeld seats unavailable for up to 10 minhold_expires_at < now() predicate immediately releases seats to subsequent CAS callers at exact expiry
Payment Gateway Latency Spike (> 60 s)Single checkout sessionPhase 1 grace extension absorbs typical slowness; if lease still expires and another buyer claims the seat, Phase 3 fencing fails and triggers automatic compensating refund
Client Retries POST /v1/bookings After Dropped ReplySingle bookingUNIQUE (user_id, idem_key) replays original 201 Created confirmation without double-charging or failing on the consumed hold
Event Shard Primary Crash or AZ OutageSingle event shard for 1 to 3 s3-AZ synchronous Raft/PostgreSQL standby promotes with zero RPO; callers receive 503 Service Unavailable during election and retry safely
Seat Map Cache OutageRead latency rises brieflySingleflight coalescing reconstructs showing snapshots from read replicas at <= 1 query per showing per 2 seconds
Flash-Sale Bot Storm (33k+ req/s)Waiting-room ingress tierEdge PoPs absorb queue joins; Booking API rejects forged or missing HMAC admission tokens in < 1 ms without hitting the database

Operational SLIs and SLOs

We monitor four domain-specific Service Level Indicators alongside standard HTTP saturation metrics:

  1. Inventory Conservation Invariant (Zero-Tolerance Audit): Continuous background verification asserting zero duplicate (show_id, seat_id) rows in booking_seats and zero seats marked BOOKED without a matching CONFIRMED booking (SEV-1 page on any non-zero violation).
  2. Hold Contention Ratio (409 / total hold attempts): Normal values sit below 15%; spikes above 60% signal stale seat-map caching or excessive admission pacing (R set too high relative to remaining seats).
  3. Late-Payment Compensation Rate: Fraction of authorized payments requiring automatic refund due to lease expiration (SLO < 0.01%). Elevated rates indicate payment gateway latency approaching the Phase 1 grace window.
  4. Waiting-Room Pacing Stability: Difference between configured target admission rate R and observed Booking API hold-attempt rate, ensuring admission tokens are neither hoarded nor bypassed.

How Production Systems Implement Ticket Booking

Production SystemCore ArchitectureArchitectural Distinction
Ticketmaster (Smart Queue and Inventory Core)Edge virtual waiting room with randomized pre-sale lobby, event-partitioned inventory services, verified-fan account gatingIsolates stadium on-sale bursts behind multi-layered bot scoring and randomized lobby ranking before admitting buyers to strongly consistent seat locks
Cloudflare Waiting RoomEdge-native FIFO and random-lottery queue running on globally distributed PoPs with signed admission cookiesKeeps millions of polling browsers completely off origin infrastructure while dynamically adjusting admission rates based on active checkout sessions
Stripe Checkout and Payment IntentsAtomic-phase idempotency keys paired with PaymentIntent state machines and webhook settlementProvides the external compensating-refund and idempotent capture substrate required by booking sagas to guarantee zero double charges
Alibaba / JD Flash-Sale Inventory EnginesPre-sharded in-memory Lua atomic counter decrements (Redis/Tair) backed by asynchronous durable order queuesTrades per-seat numbering for extreme throughput (100,000+ stock decrements/s) on fungible SKU counts, followed by asynchronous database reconciliation

20.7 Simulation Verification

To verify conditional seat holds, contention rejection, lease expiry without a background reaper, and late-payment fencing, run the bookingsim crate in the repository’s code/ workspace:

$ cargo run --release -p bookingsim
minute 0: ada holds seat 1: true
minute 1: bob holds seat 1: false
minute 1: bob holds seat 2: true
minute 3: bob pays for seat 2: true
minute 6: ada's hold has run out. bob holds seat 1: true
minute 7: ada pays for seat 1: false
minute 8: bob pays for seat 1: true
seat 0: Free
seat 1: Sold { buyer: "bob" }
seat 2: Sold { buyer: "bob" }

The observed transcript confirms four invariants on a three-seat hall with a 5-minute hold TTL:

  • At minute 1, Bob’s attempt to hold seat 1 fails (false) because Ada holds an active lease; Bob successfully acquires seat 2 and confirms it at minute 3.
  • At minute 6, after Ada’s 5-minute lease expires, Bob’s conditional hold on seat 1 succeeds immediately (true) without requiring a background sweeper.
  • At minute 7, Ada’s delayed payment attempt for seat 1 is fenced out (false), preserving single-owner exclusivity so Bob completes the purchase at minute 8.

Run the ticket booking simulation. Execute cargo run --release -p bookingsim in code/bookingsim to reproduce conditional CAS holds, automatic lease expiration, and fenced late-payment rejection.

20.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Compare-and-Swap (CAS) HoldAn atomic conditional database update that transitions a seat to HELD only if it is currently AVAILABLE or its existing hold_expires_at timestamp has passed.
Fencing PredicateA conditional check (WHERE hold_id = $2 AND state = 'HELD') on booking confirmation that rejects delayed payment completions after lease expiry.
HMAC Admission TokenA cryptographically signed, short-lived pass minted by the virtual waiting room and verified statelessly at the Booking API to enforce queue pacing.
Inventory HoardingAutomated abuse in which bots reserve large blocks of seats with no intention of paying, countered by per-account hold caps and waiting-room vetting.
Payment Saga CompensationAn automated idempotent refund triggered when an external payment succeeds after the corresponding seat lease has already been reclaimed by another buyer.
Virtual Waiting RoomAn edge-hosted queueing and randomized lottery tier that absorbs flash-sale bursts and meters buyer ingress to match core database throughput.

Chapter 21: Ride Hailing: System Design

A ride-hailing platform matches moving passengers with nearby idle drivers under two opposing data-management constraints. Driver coordinates arrive continuously at hundreds of thousands to millions of updates per second, yet every coordinate becomes obsolete within three to four seconds and requires zero disk durability for live matching. Trip lifecycles, by contrast, carry binding financial and physical invariants: a ride must be assigned to at most one driver, a driver must hold at most one active ride, and every state transition must survive process crashes. In this chapter, I design a geographically partitioned architecture that splits ephemeral in-memory spatial indexing from strongly consistent trip state management, combining H3/S2 spatial indexing, road-network ETA ranking, exclusive dispatch offer locks, and cell-level surge aggregation.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, verifiable functional requirements, split-consistency SLOs, explicit non-goals, and GPS ingestion capacity bounds
  • HTTP/2 and WebSocket APIs for GPS heartbeats, idempotent ride requests, exclusive driver acceptance, and live trip tracking, alongside relational trip DDL
  • control-plane vs. data-plane separation across region partitioning, cell-sharded RAM indexes, road-graph ETA engines, and Raft-backed trip stores
  • H3 hexagonal and S2 Hilbert-curve spatial indexing compared with geohash boundary distortion, plus TTL-leased driver heartbeat ingestion
  • adaptive k-ring cell expansion, Contraction Hierarchies ETA ranking, serialized 15-second exclusive offer locks, and H3 cell-level surge pricing aggregation
  • failure matrices, dispatch SLIs/SLOs, production architectures (Uber H3/DISCO, Lyft, Google S2), and verification via code/nearbysim

21.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

One-dimensional B-tree indexes order records along a single key and cannot efficiently answer two-dimensional proximity queries: intersecting a latitude range scan with a longitude range scan examines thousands of irrelevant drivers across an entire city. To reduce candidate lookup time from O(N) across the entire fleet to O(K) local candidates, we project spherical coordinates onto discrete hierarchical spatial cells and pair that volatile read/write tier with a durable state machine for trip assignments.

Actors and Use Cases

Three external actor classes interact across the boundary of the ride-hailing platform, as illustrated in Figure 21-1.

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Driver ClientStream GPS heartbeats (POST /v1/drivers/{id}/positions or persistent binary stream) and accept/decline offers (PUT /v1/rides/{id}/assignments/{drv})Broadcast (lat, lon, heading, speed) every 3 to 4 seconds while online and accept a 15-second dispatch offer
Rider ClientRequest ride (POST /v1/rides) and follow approaching vehicle (WS /v1/rides/{id}/stream)Submit pickup and dropoff coordinates with an Idempotency-Key, view ETA, and watch live vehicle telemetry
City OperationsConfigure regional dispatch policy and surge caps (PUT /v1/regions/{city}/policy)Adjust ring search radius, offer TTL, and dynamic pricing thresholds during concerts, storms, or airport surges

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0Online drivers transmit GPS coordinates every 3 to 4 seconds; drivers who cease reporting automatically vanish from active matching within 15 seconds.
1A rider can request a ride specifying pickup and dropoff coordinates with a caller-supplied Idempotency-Key so retries never summon two vehicles.
2The platform discovers nearby available drivers via spatial cell indexing, ranks candidates by road-network Estimated Time of Arrival (ETA), and offers the ride sequentially.
3Each ride is assigned to at most one driver, and each driver is concurrently offered or assigned to at most one ride.
4Once assigned, the rider receives real-time location updates of the approaching driver and durable state transitions across the trip lifecycle (REQUESTED -> OFFERED -> ACCEPTED -> ARRIVING -> IN_PROGRESS -> COMPLETED).
5The system continuously aggregates real-time rider demand and idle driver supply per spatial cell to compute dynamic surge pricing multipliers.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0Spatial Lookup LatencyNearby candidate discovery + ETA ranking p99 <= 100 ms; full end-to-end match initiation <= 250 msLock-free or fine-grained sharded in-memory spatial index co-located with precomputed Contraction Hierarchies road graphs
1Split ConsistencyEventual consistency (<= 4 s staleness) for live driver coordinates; strict ACID Linearizability for trip state and driver assignmentDual storage architecture: volatile RAM spatial index for heartbeats (AP), 3-AZ Raft-replicated relational/KV store for trips (CP)
2Availability99.95% ride request availability per metro region (<= 21.6 minutes/month)Independent regional deployments (a failure in London never impacts Tokyo); volatile location index rebuilds automatically in 4 seconds

Non-Goals and Explicit Scope Boundaries

To keep our architectural focus on real-time spatial matching and dispatch exclusivity, we exclude the following concerns:

  • Turn-by-turn navigation and map-tile rendering: Client map SDKs render vector tiles and compute voice navigation instructions independently of backend dispatch.
  • Multi-passenger pooled carpooling optimization (Ride-Share Routing): Dynamic vehicle-routing with time windows (VRPTW) for shared trips extends the single-rider matching problem with combinatorial detour constraints.
  • Driver background verification, payout disbursements, and tax reporting: Offline compliance workflows and settlement payouts build on the payment ledger architecture in Chapter 19.
  • Offline map-data ingestion from OpenStreetMap or satellite imagery: Road-graph compilation runs in batch map-engineering pipelines outside the real-time dispatch plane.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

In ride hailing, write throughput on driver heartbeats exceeds rider matching reads by more than two orders of magnitude, while the total memory footprint of all live driver positions fits comfortably in RAM.

Resource DimensionDerivationProvisioned Bound
Sustained GPS Write Rate500,000 active drivers / 4 s interval (or / 3 s in dense metros)125,000 to 167,000 updates/s (~1M updates/s at global mega-scale)
In-Memory Driver State500,000 drivers * 128 B (driver_id, lat, lon, h3_cell, status, expires_at, heading)~64 MB raw state (~256 MB with hash-table and cell-set overhead)
GPS Ingress Bandwidth167,000 updates/s * 64 B compact protobuf/binary frame~10.7 MB/s (~86 Mbit/s) per mega-region
Spatial Search Candidate Fan-OutCenter cell + 1-ring (7 H3 hexagons or 9 S2 squares) * ~20 idle drivers/cell~140 to 180 candidate drivers filtered to top 10 to 20 for road-graph ETA
Daily Completed Trips1,000 peak req/s * 0.35 average utilization * 86,400 s~30,000,000 rides/day

21.2 External API and Data Contracts

Driver telemetry runs over persistent bidirectional HTTP/2 (gRPC) or WebSocket connections using compact binary payloads, while trip creation and offer acceptance expose explicit idempotent REST semantics.

Driver Location Heartbeat Contract

POST /v1/drivers/7056/positions HTTP/2
Host: rides.example
Authorization: Bearer drv_eyJhbGci...

In production mobile clients, the same logical payload serializes into a 48 to 64 byte Protocol Buffers message pushed over a long-lived TLS stream so cellular radios avoid repeated TCP/TLS handshakes.

  "ride_id": "ride_501",
  "state": "REQUESTED",

  "estimated_pickup_sec": 240
}

Exclusive Driver Offer Acceptance Endpoint

PUT /v1/rides/ride_501/assignments/7056 HTTP/2
Host: rides.example
Authorization: Bearer drv_eyJhbGci...
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "offer_id": "off_9912",
  "offer_version": 3
}

HTTP/2 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "ride_id": "ride_501",
  "driver_id": "7056",
  "state": "ACCEPTED",
  "version": 4
}

Using PUT on a driver-scoped assignment URI makes retries by the accepted driver naturally idempotent. If the 15-second offer lease has expired or another driver has already accepted, the endpoint returns 409 Conflict.

Active Trip Telemetry Stream

Once state = 'ACCEPTED', the rider client opens GET /v1/rides/ride_501/stream (Upgrade: websocket). The Location Gateway fans out the assigned driver’s GPS heartbeats directly onto the rider’s socket (using the session routing model from Chapter 18) until the trip reaches COMPLETED or CANCELLED.

Durable Trip Store Schema

The volatile spatial index holds only RAM structs, whereas the strongly consistent Trip Store persists every trip state transition and active offer lease:

CREATE TABLE rides (
    ride_id          TEXT             PRIMARY KEY,
    city_id          TEXT             NOT NULL,
    rider_id         TEXT             NOT NULL,
    idem_key         TEXT             NOT NULL,
    driver_id        TEXT,
    pickup_lat       DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL,
    pickup_lon       DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL,
    pickup_h3_cell   BIGINT           NOT NULL,
    dropoff_lat      DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL,
    dropoff_lon      DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL,
    surge_multiplier NUMERIC(4,2)     NOT NULL DEFAULT 1.00,
    state            TEXT             NOT NULL CHECK (state IN (
                         'REQUESTED', 'OFFERED', 'ACCEPTED', 'ARRIVING',
                         'IN_PROGRESS', 'COMPLETED', 'CANCELLED', 'NO_DRIVER'
                     )),
    active_offer_id  TEXT,
    offer_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    version          BIGINT           NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ      NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    UNIQUE (rider_id, idem_key)
);

CREATE TABLE driver_active_locks (
    driver_id        TEXT        PRIMARY KEY,
    ride_id          TEXT        NOT NULL UNIQUE REFERENCES rides(ride_id),
    lock_type        TEXT        NOT NULL CHECK (lock_type IN ('OFFER', 'TRIP')),
    expires_at       TIMESTAMPTZ -- NULL once transitioned to active TRIP
);

21.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

Because rides never cross geographic continents, we deploy independent regional cells per metropolitan area (or metro cluster) and separate operational policy management from real-time telemetry ingestion and dispatch, as shown in Figure 21-2.

Control Plane Responsibilities

  • Cell Partition Map: Assigns coarse parent H3/S2 spatial regions to specific shards of the Cell-Sharded Spatial Index using consistent hashing (Chapter 1) with dynamic splitting in high-density urban cores.
  • Dispatch Policy Store: Publishes per-city parameters (default H3 search resolution, maximum k-ring escalation depth, 15-second offer TTL, and batch-matching window duration) to stateless Dispatch Engine nodes.
  • Surge and Supply Monitor: Consumes cell-level counts of AVAILABLE drivers and incoming REQUESTED rides over sliding 60-second windows, publishing smoothed surge multipliers per H3 resolution-7/8 hexagon.

Data Plane Responsibilities

The data plane deliberately combines two storage tiers at opposite ends of the consistency-durability spectrum:

ComponentStorage Engine & ConsistencyFailure Impact and Mitigation
Location GatewayStateless persistent TLS/WebSocket terminatorsDriver mobile SDKs reconnect automatically to healthy gateways within 1 to 3 s
Cell-Sharded Spatial IndexEphemeral in-memory hash maps partitioned by parent cell ID (Eventual, zero disk fsync)Node crash loses one city partition’s live positions; incoming 3 to 4 second driver heartbeats rebuild the index completely within 4 seconds
Road-Graph Routing and ETA EngineIn-memory Contraction Hierarchies road graph with live edge-weight updates from GPS streamStateless replicas per region; fallback to straight-line Haversine distance multiplied by historical city speed if traffic feed lags
Dispatch Engine and Offer LockStateless matching coordinator + atomic single-driver lease storeCrash mid-offer leaves durable OFFERED state and offer_expires_at in Trip Store; another coordinator resumes immediately upon TTL expiry
Trip Store3-AZ Raft-replicated relational/KV database (Strict Linearizability, full durability)Leader crash promotes synchronous follower in 1 to 3 s with zero lost trips

21.4 Deep Dive: Spatial Indexing (H3, S2, Geohash) and Heartbeat Ingestion

Choosing the spatial cell geometry directly determines boundary edge cases, neighbor-lookup arithmetic, and surge-pricing uniformity.

Comparing Geohash, Google S2, and Uber H3

  1. Geohash (Latitude/Longitude Rectangles): Interleaves quantized latitude and longitude bits into a base-32 string where longer shared prefixes denote finer nested rectangles. Although simple to compute, geohash suffers from severe latitude distortion (cells narrow dramatically toward the poles) and edge discontinuity (two points separated by 10 meters across the equator or prime meridian share zero prefix characters). Furthermore, every rectangular cell has two distinct neighbor distances: 4 edge-adjacent neighbors at distance d and 4 corner-adjacent neighbors at distance sqrt(2) * d.
  2. Google S2 (Cube-Projected Hilbert Curve): Projects the Earth’s sphere onto six cube faces and enumerates hierarchical quadtree cells along a Hilbert space-filling curve into 64-bit unsigned integers (S2CellId). The Hilbert curve preserves locality far better than Z-order curves (used by geohash), enabling arbitrary geographic regions to be covered by a small union of contiguous 64-bit integer intervals. S2 cells remain square-like and still have 8 neighbors at two distinct center-to-center distances.
  3. Uber H3 (Hierarchical Hexagonal Grid): Projects the Earth onto an icosahedron and tiles each face with regular hexagons across 16 resolutions (each parent hexagon contains approximately 7 child hexagons, plus exactly 12 pentagons globally placed over ocean areas). Hexagons provide a decisive mathematical advantage for mobility platforms: every hexagon has exactly 6 neighbors whose centers lie at the exact same Euclidean distance from the center cell. This symmetry eliminates diagonal corner bias during k-ring radius searches, smooths gradient calculations for surge pricing, and guarantees uniform area across latitudes.
PropertyGeohashGoogle S2Uber H3
Cell ShapeRectangle (lat/lon aligned)Spherical quadrilateralRegular hexagon (+ 12 pentagons)
Neighbor Center Distances2 distinct distances (d and 1.414 d)2 distinct distances (d and 1.414 d)1 uniform distance across all 6 neighbors
Area Distortion Across GlobeSevere near polesLow (quadratic projection)Minimal (gnomonic icosahedron projection)
Exact Parent-Child ContainmentExact (1 -> 32 or 1 -> 4)Exact (1 -> 4 quadtree)Approximate (1 -> 7 aperture-7 tiling)
Primary StrengthZero-dependency string prefixingExact polygon containment and range scansUniform k-ring search and smooth surge spatial aggregation

High-Throughput Driver Heartbeat Write Path

When a driver’s client transmits (driver_id, lat, lon, ts) every 3 to 4 seconds, the Location Gateway computes the driver’s target H3 index at the city’s matching resolution (typically H3 Resolution 8, edge length ~461 m, area ~0.74 km^2, or Resolution 9, edge length ~174 m) and routes the update to the owning Spatial Index shard via the Cell Partition Map:

  1. In-Place Same-Cell Update (Common Path, > 90% of Heartbeats): The shard looks up driver_id in its local DriverMap. If new_cell == old_cell, it overwrites (lat, lon, heading, expires_at = now + 15 s) in place with zero structural allocations.
  2. Cell-Boundary Crossing: If new_cell != old_cell, the shard removes driver_id from CellMap[old_cell] and inserts it into CellMap[new_cell]. If new_cell belongs to a neighboring index shard, the gateway sends an asynchronous remove to the old shard and an upsert to the new shard; even if the remove drops, the 15 s TTL lease evicts the stale ghost entry automatically.
  3. Silent Offline Eviction via TTL Leases: When a driver enters a tunnel, kills the app, or loses battery, no disconnect packet arrives. Because every entry carries expires_at = last_seen + 15 s, both read-time filtering (entry.expires_at > now) and a lightweight periodic bucket sweep remove silent drivers without distributed failure detectors.
  4. Dual-Path Billing Persistence: For drivers currently in state IN_PROGRESS, the Location Gateway asynchronously forks the GPS coordinate onto a partitioned Kafka topic (trip-breadcrumbs) so fare reconciliation and dispute resolution have durable history without adding disk latency to the matching RAM index.

21.5 Deep Dive: k-Ring Expansion, ETA Ranking, Exclusive Dispatch, and Surge Aggregation

Finding candidate drivers and assigning exactly one car to one rider requires uniting spatial retrieval, road-network graph routing, and strongly consistent distributed locking, as depicted in Figure 21-3.

Adaptive k-Ring Expansion and Road-Graph ETA Ranking

Querying only the rider’s single cell misses an idle driver parked 30 meters away on the opposite side of a cell boundary. The Dispatch Engine therefore executes an adaptive k-ring search:

  1. Ring 1 Lookup (k = 1): Computes the rider’s H3 cell and fetches gridDisk(center_cell, 1) (the center cell plus its 6 surrounding hexagons, or 9 squares in an S2/Cartesian grid), issuing parallel in-memory scatter reads to the owning shards (typically 1 shard, or 2 shards near a partition border).
  2. Ring Escalation (k = 2 or Coarser Parent): In dense downtown cores, Ring 1 yields 50 to 200 idle drivers immediately. In sparse suburbs at 03:00 local time, if Ring 1 returns fewer than K_min = 10 free drivers, the engine expands to Ring 2 (19 H3 cells or 25 squares) and up to a configurable city radius cap (for example, 5 km) before returning NO_DRIVER.
  3. Road-Network ETA Ranking via Contraction Hierarchies: Euclidean straight-line distance misleads whenever rivers, highways, medians, or one-way streets separate driver and rider. The Dispatch Engine passes the top 20 to 30 spatially closest candidates to the Routing and ETA Engine. Running textbook Dijkstra on a continental road graph per request is far too slow; instead, the engine precomputes Contraction Hierarchies (CH) (or Customizable Contraction Hierarchies, CCH) over arterial shortcuts, answering exact shortest-path drive times in under 1 ms per candidate while continuously updating road-segment travel speeds from the fleet’s own GPS telemetry stream.

Exclusive Single-Driver Offer Protocol and CAS Assignment

Broadcasting a ride offer simultaneously to five drivers minimizes dispatch latency but forces four drivers who tapped “Accept” to see a withdrawn offer, degrading driver retention and triggering race storms. Instead, we execute an exclusive serialized offer protocol with bounded 15-second leases. Advance through the interactive trace below to observe how sequential offers, offer expiry, and conditional writes prevent double assignment even when an earlier driver’s acceptance arrives late.

Two atomic database invariants enforce strict one-to-one exclusivity inside the Trip Store:

  1. Acquiring an Exclusive Offer Lease: Before pushing an offer notification to driver D1, the Dispatch Engine atomically claims D1 in driver_active_locks (succeeding only if D1 has no unexpired OFFER or TRIP lock) and transitions the ride to OFFERED with active_offer_id = off_1 and offer_expires_at = now() + INTERVAL '15 seconds'. This guarantees D1 never receives overlapping offers from two simultaneous riders.
  2. Conditional CAS Acceptance: When driver D2 responds PUT /v1/rides/ride_501/assignments/7056, the Trip Store executes a single ACID transaction: 
    UPDATE rides
SET state           = 'ACCEPTED',
    driver_id       = $1,
    active_offer_id = NULL,
    version         = version + 1
WHERE ride_id         = $2
  AND state           = 'OFFERED'
  AND active_offer_id = $3
  AND offer_expires_at >= now()
RETURNING ride_id, version;
    Alongside upgrading driver_active_locks.lock_type from 'OFFER' to 'TRIP' (expires_at = NULL). If D1’s delayed acceptance arrives after off_1 expired and off_2 was accepted by D2, the predicate active_offer_id = $3 matches 0 rows and returns 409 Conflict.

Batch Matching and Cell-Level Surge Pricing Aggregation

Greedy first-come-first-served matching can produce globally suboptimal pairings when two nearby riders request trips within 1 second of each other. In dense urban zones, the Dispatch Engine buffers incoming requests within an H3 resolution-6 region for a short batch window (2 to 5 seconds) and solves a minimum-weight bipartite matching (Hungarian algorithm or min-cost max-flow) over the (riders x candidate_drivers) ETA matrix, reducing aggregate pickup wait times across the city by 15% to 25%.

Simultaneously, the Surge and Supply Monitor aggregates real-time demand_count (unmatched ride requests and fare-estimate views) and supply_count (idle drivers with valid leases) inside each H3 resolution-7/8 hexagon every 30 seconds. Because hexagons share identical edge-to-edge neighbor geometry, applying a spatial smoothing kernel across each cell and its 6 neighbors eliminates sharp price cliffs across street boundaries where walking 20 meters would otherwise drop a fare by half.

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ScenarioBlast RadiusAutomated Recovery and Preserved Invariant
Driver Phone Enters Tunnel or CrashesSingle driver15-second TTL lease expires automatically; driver leaves spatial index without sending a disconnect message
Spatial Index Shard CrashOne geographic sub-region for <= 4 sReplacement shard starts empty; incoming 3 to 4 second GPS heartbeats reconstruct full fleet visibility automatically

Operational SLIs and SLOs

Four domain-specific Service Level Indicators track dispatch health beyond raw HTTP error rates:

  1. Spatial Index Freshness (p99 Heartbeat Ingestion Lag): Measures time from client GPS timestamp to Spatial Index visibility (SLO <= 500 ms); rising lag indicates gateway saturation or GC pauses.
  2. Time to First Offer and Match Completion Rate: Tracks p95 elapsed seconds from POST /v1/rides to driver ACCEPTED (SLO <= 30 s) and percentage of requests reaching NO_DRIVER.
  3. ETA Prediction Error (MAE): Compares predicted pickup ETA at dispatch against actual driver arrival timestamp; persistent positive drift alerts to stale road-graph traffic edge weights.
  4. Exclusivity Audit Invariant: Continuous background verifier confirming zero active rides share a driver_id and zero ACCEPTED rides lack a matching driver_active_locks entry (SEV-1 on any non-zero violation).

How Production Systems Implement Ride Hailing
