TermDefinition
Contraction Hierarchies (CH)A road-graph preprocessing technique that inserts shortcut edges along major arterial corridors, accelerating shortest-path ETA queries to under one millisecond.
Exclusive Offer LockA time-bounded lease (15 s) binding one candidate driver to at most one pending ride offer so concurrent matchers cannot double-offer the same vehicle.

Chapter 22: Search Autocomplete: System Design

A real-time search autocomplete (typeahead) service proposes complete queries as a user types each character into a search input. Compared with full-text search, autocomplete amplifies request volume by an order of magnitude (emitting up to one request per keystroke rather than one per submitted query) while enforcing an end-to-end latency budget under 100 milliseconds, of which network round-trip time consumes the majority. Because server-side execution must finish within 10 to 20 milliseconds at p99, any design that scans or ranks matching queries online collapses on short prefixes such as a or k. In this chapter, I design a read-only, edge-cached serving architecture backed by precomputed top-K prefix trie snapshots, offline MapReduce and Flink exponential-decay aggregation, lock-free blue-green snapshot swaps, frequency-balanced prefix sharding, and layered safety and privacy filtering.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, verifiable functional requirements, sub-20 ms server SLOs, explicit non-goals, and keystroke QPS and RAM capacity bounds
  • cacheable HTTP/2 GET suggestion APIs, client out-of-order sequence guards, blocklist moderation contracts, and compact immutable trie snapshot schemas
  • control-plane and offline build pipeline separation from the lock-free, read-only online serving data plane
  • precomputed top-K prefix trie nodes achieving O(L) lookup, exponential frequency decay, fast-lane Flink trending overlays, and double-buffered atomic snapshot swaps
  • load-balanced prefix range sharding across serving nodes, client debouncing, CDN caching trade-offs, k-anonymity privacy gates, and PII/profanity filtering
  • failure matrices, typeahead SLIs/SLOs, production architectures (Google Suggest, Elasticsearch FST, Meta Typeahead, Microsoft Top-k Completion), and verification via code/typeahead

22.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Autocomplete is an advisory acceleration layer whose failure must never block core search submission. This asymmetry permits aggressive offline precomputation, multi-tier HTTP caching, and eventual consistency (minutes to hours for the global corpus, under one minute for breaking trends) in exchange for predictable sub-20 ms server tail latency at 1,000,000+ global requests per second.

Actors and Use Cases

Three external actor classes interact across the boundary of the search autocomplete service, as illustrated in Figure 22-1.

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Searcher (Browser / Mobile Client)Fetch top-K completions (GET /v1/suggestions?q={prefix})Type ka with client debouncing and receive ["kafka", "karaoke near me", "kayak"] within 100 ms end-to-end
Search BackendEmit completed query events asynchronously to the Query Log StreamLog normalized submitted searches (never raw partial prefixes) for offline MapReduce decay and real-time Flink trend detection
Trust and Safety OperationsPublish moderation exclusions (PUT /v1/blocklist)Remove defamatory, violent, or leaked PII completions across all edge serving replicas within minutes

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0Given a normalized UTF-8 prefix string q (1 to 20 characters), the service returns up to K = 5 (configurable up to 10) highest-ranked matching query completions.
1Suggestions are ranked by time-decayed historical search frequency so recent sustained interest outranks stale multi-year totals.
2Breaking queries that surge dramatically within the last 60 minutes appear in suggestions within 1 to 2 minutes without waiting for a full batch rebuild.
3Every candidate query must satisfy a minimum distinct-user privacy threshold (k-anonymity) before entering any suggestion snapshot.
4Automated policy filters scrub PII patterns and prohibited terms during offline trie builds, and an emergency edge blocklist suppresses reported suggestions within minutes.
5The service degrades gracefully: if the autocomplete tier is unreachable or slow, the client allows uninterrupted typing and search submission.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0LatencyEnd-to-end keystroke-to-display <= 100 ms; origin server p99 <= 20 ms (p50 <= 3 ms)Zero online subtree traversal or sorting; all top-K lists precomputed at every trie node and held entirely in RAM

Non-Goals and Explicit Scope Boundaries

To focus on low-latency prefix indexing and snapshot distribution, we exclude the following extensions from the base architecture:

  • Per-user personalized search history ranking: Personal history completions are typically stored locally in browser IndexedDB or fetched from a small per-user cache and merged client-side ahead of global typeahead results.
  • Full-text fuzzy edit-distance spelling correction: Supporting Levenshtein edit distance >= 2 across arbitrary mid-word typos requires phonetic/BK-tree or trigram indexes rather than strict prefix tries.
  • Multi-language morphology and CJK input-method composition (IME): Character composition states prior to word commit require locale-specific tokenizers outside standard prefix lookup.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

Autocomplete is constrained by tail latency on hot short prefixes and in-memory working set size across prefix shards.

Origin Egress Bandwidth200,000 req/s * 256 B average JSON response~51 MB/s (~410 Mbit/s)

22.2 External API and Data Contracts

Because global suggestions for a given normalized prefix are identical across users within a locale, the read endpoint uses a cacheable HTTP/2 GET with explicit Cache-Control headers so both browsers and CDN edge PoPs absorb the majority of short-prefix load.

Prefix Suggestion Lookup Endpoint

GET /v1/suggestions?q=ka&locale=en-US&limit=5&seq=14 HTTP/2
Host: search.example
Accept: application/json

HTTP/2 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate=60
X-Snapshot-Version: v108

{
  "prefix": "ka",
  "seq": 14,
  "suggestions": [
    { "text": "kafka", "score": 900, "source": "main" },
    { "text": "karaoke near me", "score": 800, "source": "main" },
    { "text": "kayak", "score": 450, "source": "main" }
  ]
}

Three contract details govern client correctness and caching efficiency:

  1. Prefix Echo and Sequence Guard (seq): Network replies can arrive out of order: a slow reply for ka (seq=14) may arrive after a fast reply for kaf (seq=15). The browser discards any response whose seq < latest_sent_seq or whose echoed prefix no longer matches the active input box, and aborts superseded in-flight HTTP requests via AbortController.
  2. Caching Empty Results: A prefix with zero completions (such as q=kafx) still returns 200 OK with "suggestions": [] and Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, protecting origin shards against repeated cache-penetration misses on typos.
  3. Cache TTL vs. Takedown Latency Trade-Off: Setting max-age=300 (5 minutes) rather than 5 hours bounds the maximum time a newly blocklisted offensive term can linger in downstream browser or edge caches.

Emergency Blocklist Control Endpoint

PUT /v1/blocklist/terms HTTP/2
Host: admin.search.example
Authorization: Bearer ops_eyJhbGci...
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "locale": "en-US",
  "action": "DENY_EXACT_OR_SUBSTRING",
  "pattern": "redacted-harmful-phrase",
  "reason": "policy-ticket-4921"
}

HTTP/2 202 Accepted
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "blocklist_version": 841,
  "propagation_slo_sec": 60
}

Compact Immutable Trie Snapshot Schema

Rather than storing pointer-heavy heap objects or repeating full query strings across millions of ancestor nodes, the offline builder serializes each shard snapshot into two contiguous memory-mapped (mmap) binary arrays:

1. String Pool (arena.bin):
   Contiguous UTF-8 bytes of all distinct eligible completions, addressed by u32 offset + u16 len.

2. Trie Node Array (trie_shard_k.bin):
   struct TrieNode {
       char_code:       u16,       // UTF-16 / compressed byte edge label
       first_child_idx: u32,       // Contiguous child slice start (binary-searched)
       child_count:     u16,       // Number of outgoing edges
       top_k_ids:       [u32; 5],  // Indexes into String Pool, pre-sorted by score
       top_k_scores:    [u32; 5],  // Fixed-point decayed scores for merge with trending overlay
   }

Storing integer string_pool offsets instead of duplicated text cuts RAM consumption by 4x to 6x, eliminates garbage-collection pause spikes, and enables instant zero-parse loading via mmap.

22.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We strictly decouple asynchronous query aggregation and snapshot compilation from the read-only serving path, as illustrated in Figure 22-2.

Control and Offline Build Plane

No online request ever writes to a serving trie. Instead, an offline pipeline compiles immutable versioned artifacts:

  • Query Log Stream (Kafka): Receives completed search submissions (sampled uniformly at 10% to 100%) asynchronously from the Search Backend, adding zero latency to search execution.
  • Batch Aggregator (Spark / MapReduce) and Fast-Lane Streamer (Flink): Normalizes query strings (Unicode NFKC, lowercase, whitespace collapsing), tracks distinct-user counts via HyperLogLog sketches, applies exponential frequency decay, and emits two outputs: hourly/daily global scores and 1-minute breaking-trend deltas.
  • Safety Filter and Trie Builder: Scrubs PII (email addresses, phone numbers, national IDs via regex and NER classifiers) and policy-prohibited phrases, then constructs per-shard precomputed top-K trie binary blobs (v108) stored in immutable object storage.
  • Snapshot Rollout Controller: Validates candidate snapshots against canary prefix regression suites (verifying non-empty top queries, bounded size delta, and zero blocklist leaks) before orchestrating a staggered push to serving replicas.

Online Data Plane

ComponentState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Browser ClientIn-memory prefix cache, debounce timer (50 to 100 ms), monotonic seq counterCaches recent prefix replies locally so backspace is instantaneous; aborts slow requests after 80 ms so search stays unaffected
CDN Edge CachePublic HTTP cache keyed by (locale, normalized_prefix) (300 s TTL)Absorbs ~80% of global volume, especially single-character and two-character prefixes; serves stale-while-revalidate during brief origin blips
Prefix Router (L7 LB)Prefix range partition map (aa..ap -> shard 0, …)Stateless routing across 3 AZs; retries read-only GET idempotently on another shard replica on timeout
In-Memory Trie ReplicasRead-only mmap trie snapshot (v108), tiny trending hash map (< 50 MB), and hot blocklist set (< 10 MB)Zero write locks; every replica within a shard holds an identical immutable snapshot and serves reads concurrently

22.4 Deep Dive: Precomputed Top-K Trie, Exponential Decay, and Atomic Snapshot Swap

A sorted array or uncached prefix trie finds the starting node for prefix ka in O(log N) or O(L) time, yet still must enumerate and sort every completion in the subtree beneath ka. On short prefixes such as k or s, that subtree holds millions of queries, making online sorting incompatible with a 10 to 20 ms server budget.

Precomputed Top-K Nodes Achieving O(L) Lookup

Because the top 5 completions of any prefix p depend only on the query corpus and remain invariant across callers between rebuilds, we compute them bottom-up once during the offline build and store the sorted top-K list directly inside every trie node, as depicted in Figure 22-3.

During offline assembly, a single post-order traversal computes each node’s top-K list by merging the top-K lists of its immediate children plus any query terminating at the node itself. For an alphabet of 26 lowercase characters and K = 5, each node evaluates at most 26 * 5 + 1 = 131 entries, yielding total build complexity linear in the number of trie nodes (O(N_nodes * K)). At query time, traversing a prefix of length L <= 20 requires at most L pointer or array hops and zero subtree scanning. Advance through the interactive trace below to follow how each keystroke resolves in a single precomputed lookup.

Exponential Frequency Decay and Fast-Lane Trending Overlay

Raw cumulative counts freeze past events at the top of suggestions indefinitely. To balance historical stability with recency, the batch aggregator computes an exponentially weighted moving score at every time bucket t (hourly or daily):

S(t) = alpha * C(t) + (1 - alpha) * S(t - 1)

With an hourly decay factor alpha = 0.35, the weight of a query’s volume from h hours ago decays geometrically by (1 - alpha)^h = 0.65^h, ensuring that sustained current demand smoothly overtakes stale peaks without abrupt cliff effects at midnight boundaries.

Because a full global trie rebuild takes 15 to 45 minutes in MapReduce/Spark, breaking news queries (such as an unexpected sports result or major outage) would otherwise lag by an hour. We close this freshness gap with a two-tier hybrid serving lookup:

  1. Main Immutable Trie (~32 GB per cluster, rebuilt hourly): Covers the entire 100M-query corpus with decayed scores.
  2. Trending Overlay Table (< 50 MB, updated every 60 s by Apache Flink): Consumes the live Kafka query stream over a 15-minute sliding window, computing z-score velocity (recent_rate - baseline_rate) / stddev. Only queries exceeding a surge threshold (and passing distinct-user k-anonymity and safety filters) enter the tiny trending prefix map.
  3. Online Merge (< 0.2 ms): Each serving replica looks up prefix p in both the main trie and the small trending map, merges the two sorted top-5 lists by boosted score, strips any terms present in the hot emergency blocklist, and returns the final 5 suggestions.

Lock-Free Double-Buffered Blue-Green Snapshot Swap

Updating a live trie in place under 200,000 concurrent reads/s introduces reader-writer lock contention, memory fragmentation, and partial-update inconsistency. Instead, every serving node performs a double-buffered atomic pointer swap:

  1. While serving traffic from Arc<TrieSnapshot> (v107), a background loader downloads v108 from object storage, verifies its SHA-256 checksum, maps it into memory (mmap), and warms critical top-level pages (L <= 3) via synthetic prefix probes.
  2. Once warmed and verified, the loader executes a single atomic pointer swap (atomic_ptr.store(v108, Ordering::Release)).
  3. In-flight requests holding references to v107 complete without interruption; once the reference count of v107 drops to zero, the process unmaps v107. If canary metrics detect an anomaly in v108, the Rollout Controller reverts the pointer back to v107 in under one second.

22.5 Deep Dive: Prefix Sharding, Caching, and Safety/Privacy Controls

Frequency-Balanced Prefix Range Sharding

Partitioning the 27.5 GB trie directly by the first ASCII letter (a through z across 26 shards) creates extreme load skew: English queries starting with s, c, or p carry more than 20 times the volume of x, q, or z. We compare two production sharding schemes:

  • Measured-Load Prefix Range Sharding (Preferred for Locality): The offline Trie Builder inspects observed query-frequency histograms and computes variable-length lexicographic boundaries so every shard carries roughly equal RAM and QPS (for example, aa..an on Shard 0, ao..az on Shard 1, while w..z share Shard 15). Prefix routing requires a tiny in-memory boundary table at the L7 router and keeps consecutive prefixes co-located on the same shard for warm CPU L2/L3 cache locality during multi-keystroke typing sessions.
  • Consistent Hashing by Prefix String: Hashes every full prefix string uniformly across shards. This eliminates range-rebalancing logic automatically when storing flat prefix-to-top-K tables, at the cost of splitting a single user’s typing sequence (k, ka, kaf) across different machines and losing shared trie-node prefix compression.

PII Scrubbing, k-Anonymity, and Moderation Hygiene

Because autocomplete surfaces crowd-sourced text directly beneath the search bar, two classes of failures carry severe legal and reputational risk:

  1. Private Data Leakage (k-Anonymity Gate): A user accidentally pasting a Social Security number, street address, or medical record into a search box must never expose that string to strangers typing the same opening characters. The aggregator enforces strict distinct-user k-anonymity (requiring at least k = 100 distinct authenticated users or unique IP/cookie HyperLogLog estimates across multiple days, never raw query count, since one user can repeat a private query 500 times) combined with deterministic regex scrubbing for digits resembling credit cards, phones, and emails.
  2. Defamatory, Hateful, and Unsafe Completions: High search volume around an unverified rumor or harmful query can elevate it into top-K predictions. Defense operates in depth: (a) deterministic blocklists and ML safety classifiers filter candidates during offline snapshot assembly at zero online latency cost, and (b) an in-memory Emergency Exclusion Set pushed to all serving nodes within 60 seconds strips newly reported terms on the read path immediately without waiting for the next hourly snapshot build.

22.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ScenarioBlast RadiusAutomated Recovery and Preserved Invariant
Origin Serving Tier OutageUncached long prefixes (L >= 3) return empty suggestionsCDN edge continues serving cached hot prefixes (stale-while-revalidate); browser timeout (80 ms) ensures core search submission works uninterrupted
Corrupted or Empty Trie Snapshot (v108)Canary shard onlyRollout Controller canary gate aborts promotion; if already promoted, instant atomic pointer rollback reinstates v107 in < 1 s
Offline Batch Aggregator FailsGlobal corpus freshness lags past 1 hourServing replicas continue serving v107 indefinitely without downtime; Flink trending overlay keeps breaking news current
Out-of-Order Network Replies at ClientSingle user’s dropdown flickerClient checks response.seq >= latest_seq and response.prefix == input_box, discarding stale late responses cleanly

Hot Single-Letter Prefix Burst (q=a)Edge PoP onlyCache-Control: public, max-age=300 absorbs 99.9%+ of hot short-prefix bursts at CDN edge; origin sees near-zero traffic

Operational SLIs and SLOs

Four domain-specific Service Level Indicators track autocomplete quality and responsiveness:

  1. Origin Lookup Latency (p99 <= 20 ms, p50 <= 3 ms): Monitored per prefix shard to detect memory-page faults after snapshot swaps or GC jitter.
  2. Client-Observed End-to-End Latency and Timeout Drop Rate: Telemetry from browsers measuring actual keystroke-to-render duration (p95 <= 100 ms) and percentage of requests cancelled or timed out.
  3. Suggestion Click-Through Rate (CTR) and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR): Measures ranking quality; a sudden CTR drop after a v108 rollout signals normalization mismatch or broken decay weights.
  4. Snapshot Staleness and Blocklist Propagation Lag: Alerts if the active serving snapshot age exceeds 2 hours or if any replica lags the latest blocklist_version by more than 60 seconds.

How Production Systems Implement Search Autocomplete

Production SystemCore ArchitectureArchitectural Distinction
Google SuggestGlobally distributed prefix-sharded in-memory trees, real-time trending pipelines, strict policy/safety classifiers, and locale-aware rankingCombines global decayed volume with geographic locality, fresh breaking-event overlays, and automated enforcement of published prediction safety policies
Elasticsearch Completion SuggesterFinite State Transducer (FST) stored in Lucene segment files and loaded directly into off-heap memoryCompresses both shared prefixes and shared suffixes into a deterministic weighted automaton, answering top-K prefix queries in microseconds with minimal RAM
Meta (Facebook) TypeaheadBrowser-side bootstrapped personal graph + parallel backend type-specific indexes merged by a stateless aggregatorPreloads a user’s immediate social connections into browser RAM before the first keystroke so personal queries resolve in < 1 ms with zero network RTT
Microsoft Top-k Completion (RMQ / Path-Compressed Trie)Space-efficient path-compressed trie annotating internal nodes with max-subtree scores and priority-queue traversalAvoids storing redundant top-K lists at every node when memory budgets are tight, achieving near-optimal space with bounded top-K extraction time

22.7 Simulation Verification

To verify prefix lookup, frequency-ordered top-K ranking, and empty-prefix handling, execute the typeahead crate in the repository’s code/ workspace:

$ cargo run --release -p typeahead
k    -> kubernetes (950), kafka (900), karaoke near me (800)
ka   -> kafka (900), karaoke near me (800), kayak (450)
kaf  -> kafka (900), kafka vs rabbitmq (300)
ke   -> key value store (700), keyboard (650)
ra   -> raft (600), rate limiter (500)
x    -> no suggestion

The observed output validates the precomputed prefix-table behavior across six representative prefixes:

  • Short prefix k immediately returns the top 3 completions across the entire k* subtree (kubernetes (950), kafka (900), karaoke near me (800)) ordered strictly by descending score.
  • Narrowing from k to ka and kaf progressively refines the candidate set down to kafka (900) and kafka vs rabbitmq (300).
  • Prefix x returns an explicit empty result (no suggestion), matching our API contract for cacheable empty 200 OK responses.

22.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
DebouncingDelaying outgoing autocomplete requests by a short quiet window (50 to 100 ms) after each keystroke to avoid wasting bandwidth on intermediate letters while typing rapidly.
Double-Buffered Snapshot SwapLoading a new immutable trie version alongside the active snapshot and flipping a single atomic read pointer lock-free so zero online queries stall during updates.
Exponential Frequency DecayWeighting historical query counts via S(t) = alpha * C(t) + (1 - alpha) * S(t - 1) so recent popularity outranks outdated cumulative volume.
Finite State Transducer (FST)A compact directed acyclic automaton that shares both common prefixes and common suffixes across keys while associating numeric weights with paths.
k-Anonymity ThresholdAdmitting a query into autocomplete only after at least k distinct users have issued it, preventing private single-user searches from leaking to strangers.
Precomputed Top-K TrieA prefix tree in which every internal node stores the pre-sorted top-K completions of its entire subtree, reducing lookup complexity to O(L) pointer hops.
Sequence-ID Out-of-Order GuardTagging each client request with a monotonic integer seq and discarding late responses whose seq trails a newer keystroke.

Chapter 23: Web Crawler: System Design

A distributed web crawler traverses the public web graph continuously, discovering billions of URLs, fetching HTML and structured resources, and feeding deduplicated documents into downstream search indexers or archival corpora. Although breadth-first graph traversal requires ten lines of code in memory, operating against the live internet introduces five severe distributed systems constraints: the graph contains tens of billions of vertices that mutate while being traversed, infinite dynamically generated spider traps lure workers into unbounded loops, more than a quarter of pages duplicate existing content across distinct URLs, DNS resolution saturates standard resolvers, and every origin server belongs to an external operator who will block any crawler that violates politeness limits. In this chapter, I design a host-partitioned crawler built around the Mercator two-stage politeness frontier, RFC 9309 robots.txt compliance, Bloom-filter and RocksDB URL deduplication, 64-bit SimHash near-duplicate detection, and multi-layered spider-trap defenses.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, verifiable functional requirements, strict politeness SLOs, explicit non-goals, and petabyte-scale crawl capacity bounds
  • operator control APIs for seed injection and host policy overrides, monotonic cursor page-feed contracts, and frontier/host metadata schemas
  • control-plane vs. data-plane separation across the Seed Coordinator, DNS and robots.txt caches, host-partitioned frontier shards, async fetcher pools, and object storage
  • Mercator two-stage politeness frontier (priority front queues, per-host back queues, and next-fetch min-heap), consistent-hash host ownership, and adaptive 429 backoff
  • URL canonicalization, sharded Bloom filter + RocksDB seen-set deduplication, 64-bit SimHash / MinHash near-duplicate detection, spider-trap budgets, and conditional 304 revisit scheduling
  • failure matrices, crawl SLIs/SLOs, production architectures (Googlebot, Mercator, IRLbot, Common Crawl), and verification via code/crawlsim

23.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Web crawling exhibits an unusual error-tolerance asymmetry. Missing 0.5% of long-tail URLs due to a Bloom filter false positive, or re-fetching a small fraction of pages after a worker crash, causes negligible harm to a search index. Violating per-host politeness, however, harms external website operators, triggers IP-block blacklists, and degrades the crawler’s global reach. Every architectural boundary in this design therefore treats per-host politeness as a strict invariant while allowing approximate deduplication and eventual consistency across the broader crawl loop.

Actors and Use Cases

Three external actor classes interact across the boundary of the distributed web crawler, as illustrated in Figure 23-1.

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Crawl OperatorInject seed URLs (POST /v1/seeds) and override host rules (PUT /v1/hosts/{host}/rules)Bootstrap a fresh crawl from high-authority seed domains or cap page budgets and crawl delays for a sensitive partner host
Target Web HostPublish robots.txt directives and respond to polite HTTP/TLS GET requestsSpecify disallowed URL prefixes, optional Crawl-delay, ETag validators, and 429 Too Many Requests rate signals
Search IndexerConsume deduplicated crawl stream (GET /v1/pages?after={cursor})Read unique newly fetched or modified documents in monotonic sequence order without re-parsing mirrors or infinite traps

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0Starting from operator-supplied seed URLs, the system discovers, normalizes, and fetches reachable web pages by following extracted hyperlinks.
1Before fetching any page on an origin host, the crawler retrieves, parses, caches, and strictly obeys that host’s robots.txt exclusion rules (RFC 9309).
2The crawler enforces strict per-host politeness: at most one in-flight request per host (or configured concurrency cap) separated by a minimum crawl delay (>= 1 s default, scaled dynamically on slow or 429 responses).
3The crawler deduplicates normalized URLs against a durable seen set so the same URL is not re-crawled unnecessarily within a single crawl epoch.
4The crawler identifies exact duplicate pages (via SHA-256 content hash) and near-duplicate mirrors (via 64-bit SimHash) before persisting to the page store and downstream feed.
5The crawler defends against infinite spider traps through per-host depth caps, page budgets, URL length caps, and path-repetition filters.
6The crawler revisits previously fetched pages at adaptive intervals driven by observed change frequency, using HTTP If-None-Match / If-Modified-Since conditional headers.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0Scale and Throughput10,000,000,000 (10B) pages crawled per 30-day cycle (~3,860 pages/s sustained; 10,000 pages/s burst)Horizontal partitioning across 40+ disk-backed frontier shards and 300+ asynchronous non-blocking fetcher workers (epoll/io_uring)
1Politeness<= 1 active request per origin host at any instant; >= 1 s inter-request pause (100% enforcement across cluster)Consistent-hash partitioning by hostname ensures exactly one frontier machine owns all scheduling state for a given host
2DurabilityFrontier queues, host politeness state, and URL-seen database survive machine restarts without losing days of graph discoveryDisk-backed frontier queues (RocksDB/segmented logs) with replica checkpoints; pages written to replicated object storage (Chapter 16)
3ConsistencyEventual consistency across URL deduplication (<= 1% Bloom filter false-positive skip rate acceptable, or 0% with RocksDB backing)Loose asynchronous batch forwarding of cross-host links over Kafka eliminates synchronous cross-shard locks
4RobustnessZero worker crashes or memory exhaustion from malformed HTML, decompression bombs, slow-loris streams, or infinite redirectsHard per-fetch socket timeout (10 s), max body byte cap (10 MB), max redirect hops (5), and sandboxed streaming HTML parsers

Non-Goals and Explicit Scope Boundaries

To keep our focus on distributed crawling, politeness, and deduplication, we exclude the following concerns:

  • Full headless-browser JavaScript rendering at 100% coverage: Executing Chromium/V8 for single-page applications multiplies CPU cost by 20x to 50x; production crawlers route only a selective subset of JS-heavy domains to a separate rendering pool after static HTML fetch.
  • Inverted-index construction, PageRank computation, and query serving: Downstream search engines consume our immutable object store and change feed asynchronously.
  • Authenticated crawling behind login walls or anti-bot gates: This architecture crawls strictly public, robots.txt-permitted web resources and never circumvents access controls.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

Web crawling is bounded simultaneously by distinct active hosts in the frontier (politeness concurrency), URL-seen memory/disk footprint, and petabyte-scale object storage.

Resource DimensionDerivationProvisioned Bound
Sustained Fetch Rate10,000,000,000 pages / (30 days * 86,400 s)~3,858 pages/s (provisioned for 5,000 pages/s)
Minimum Active Hosts for Politeness5,000 pages/s * 1 s minimum delay (or 2 s average delay)>= 10,000 distinct ready hosts active simultaneously
Ingress Network Bandwidth5,000 pages/s * 100 KB average HTML payload * 8 bits~4.0 Gbit/s sustained HTTP ingress

URL-Seen In-Memory Bloom Filter10B URLs * 10 bits (~0.8% false-positive rate)~12.5 GB total RAM (~1.6 GB/shard) fronting RocksDB

23.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We partition the crawler into a Control Plane that governs host ownership, compliance policies, and DNS caching, and a streaming Data Plane that executes the continuous Frontier -> Fetch -> Parse -> Deduplicate -> Store pipeline, as illustrated in Figure 23-2.

Control Plane Responsibilities

  • Seed Coordinator: Maintains the consistent-hash ring mapping normalized hostnames (hash(host)) onto Frontier shards. Adding or removing a frontier node rebalances only 1/N of hosts while preserving single-owner politeness guarantees.
  • Host Policy and Trap Guard: Distributes operator overrides, domain authority page budgets, and regex trap rules to all parsers and frontier shards.
  • Robots and DNS Cache: Caches parsed robots.txt directives (24-hour TTL, honoring Cache-Control and negative caching on 404 for 24 hours; fail-closed backoff on 5xx) and resolved IP addresses (honoring DNS record TTLs) so fetchers never block on external UDP resolvers.

Data Plane Responsibilities

ComponentState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Politeness Frontier (x40 Shards)Disk-backed priority front queues, per-host back queues, and min-heap of next_ready_at timesHost-partitioned with WAL replication to standby; shard crash fails over its host partitions to standby without losing discovered URLs
Fetcher Worker Pool (x300 Nodes)Ephemeral in-flight HTTP/TLS sockets (thousands of async connections per node)Worker crash drops in-flight URLs; frontier tracks leased URLs with a 60-second lease timeout and re-enqueues unacknowledged URLs
HTML Parser and Normalizer (x60 Nodes)Stateless streaming HTML/UTF-8 parserCrash replays page from durable fetch buffer; strict byte/nesting limits isolate malformed markup
URL Seen Filter (x8 Shards)In-memory Bloom filter backed by on-disk RocksDB 128-bit URL hash tableCrash reloads from replicated NVMe RocksDB shard; cross-host new URLs route in batches via Kafka to owning frontier shard
Content DeduplicatorExact SHA-256 hash store + 64-bit SimHash permutation tablesPrevents duplicate mirrors from entering object storage or triggering redundant downstream link expansion
Page Object Store and Change FeedCompressed unique HTML artifacts (s3://crawl-pages/...) + append-only sequence logErasure-coded multi-AZ object storage (Chapter 16) serves downstream indexers via cursor pagination

23.4 Deep Dive: Mercator Two-Stage Politeness Frontier and robots.txt Compliance

A single FIFO frontier queue fails immediately on the live web. Because pages link heavily to other pages on the same domain, a FIFO queue produces long runs of consecutive URLs targeting one host (news.example/1, news.example/2, …). Either the crawler launches parallel requests and floods news.example (triggering an IP ban), or workers sit idle waiting on news.example’s crawl delay while thousands of other hosts sit ready behind it in the queue.

Mercator Two-Stage Frontier Architecture

Following the classic Mercator architecture, we decouple what is important to crawl (priority) from when a host may be contacted (politeness) using two distinct queue stages, as depicted in Figure 23-3.

  1. Stage 1: Priority Front Queues (F Queues): Incoming unseen URLs are scored by a URL Prioritizer using domain authority (in-link count / PageRank), expected freshness (news homepages vs. static archives), and shallow path depth, then appended to one of F disk-backed priority queues (P1 High through PF Low). A Biased Selector draws from P1 far more frequently than from PF (for example, weighted probabilities 0.6 / 0.3 / 0.1), preventing starvation of low-priority URLs while favoring high-value pages.
  2. Stage 2: Per-Host Back Queues (B Queues) and Min-Heap: The frontier maintains B active back queues (typically B = 3x to 5x the number of fetcher threads per shard), enforcing one strict invariant: every non-empty back queue contains URLs belonging to exactly one origin host. A Host-to-Queue Table maps host -> back_queue_id, and a Min-Heap orders all active back queues by their earliest legal fetch timestamp next_ready_at.
  3. Polite Dispatch Loop: When a fetcher worker asks for work, the frontier pops the root of the min-heap (B1, ready at t = 10.0 s). If now < B1.next_ready_at, the worker sleeps until 10.0 s (in practice, with 10,000+ hosts, the root is always immediately ready). The frontier pops one URL from B1, hands it to the fetcher, and computes the next allowed timestamp dynamically from the server’s own response time: 
    next_ready_at = fetch_complete_time + max(min_crawl_delay_ms, 10 * last_rtt_ms)
    Multiplying observed response latency by 10 automatically slows down against struggling small servers while moving briskly across well-provisioned origins. If a host returns HTTP 429 Too Many Requests or 503 Service Unavailable, the frontier respects any Retry-After header and applies exponential backoff (2x per failure up to 24 hours). When B1 empties, the frontier pulls from the Biased Selector until a fresh host populates B1.

Advance through the interactive step-by-step trace below to observe how per-host queues and a 2-second host interval keep fetchers busy across three hosts without ever violating politeness.

Host-Ownership Sharding and robots.txt Compliance

Enforcing politeness locally on each machine breaks if two frontier nodes hold queues for news.example simultaneously, doubling its incoming request rate. Partitioning frontier shards strictly by consistent_hash(origin_host) guarantees a single authoritative scheduler and robots.txt cache entry per host. Because 80% to 85% of hyperlinks on a web page point to other pages on the same host, host partitioning also minimizes cross-node network forwarding: only the remaining 15% to 20% of cross-host links travel through Kafka batches to remote shards.

Before fetching any path on a newly encountered host, the fetcher requests https://{host}/robots.txt with an identifiable User-Agent string and contact URL, obeying RFC 9309 longest-match Allow/Disallow prefix precedence:

  • 2xx: Parse directives and cache for 24 hours (or Cache-Control max-age).
  • 4xx (including 404 Not Found): Assume full crawl permission and negative-cache for 24 hours.
  • 5xx or timeout: Assume temporary disallow (fail closed) and retry with exponential backoff so the crawler never hammers an unhealthy origin.

23.5 Deep Dive: URL Deduplication, SimHash Near-Duplicates, and Spider-Trap Defenses

URL Canonicalization and Hybrid Bloom Filter + RocksDB Seen Set

Before checking whether a discovered link has already been queued, the parser applies deterministic URL canonicalization: lowercasing scheme and host, stripping default ports (:80, :443), removing URL fragments (#section), resolving relative dot-segments (/a/../b -> /b), sorting query parameters lexicographically, and stripping known tracking parameters (utm_*, fbclid, sessionid).

Checking 50,000+ extracted links per second against 10 billion seen URLs (~800 GB as raw 80-byte strings) exceeds single-node RAM. We resolve this with a two-tier sharded lookup (partitioned by hash(host) so every shard validates its own host’s links locally):

  1. Tier 1: In-Memory Sharded Bloom Filter (12.5 GB total across 8 shards at 10 bits/URL): Answers “definitely unseen” in under 100 ns with zero disk I/O. If the crawl tolerates missing ~0.8% of new URLs due to Bloom false positives, the filter alone suffices.
  2. Tier 2: On-Disk RocksDB 128-Bit Hash Table (160 GB NVMe SSD): For exact deduplication (0% false-positive drops), any positive Bloom hit probes the local RocksDB LSM-tree keyed by xxHash128(canonical_url). Because most newly discovered links on the web are duplicates, batching RocksDB point lookups and keeping an LRU cache of hot URLs (such as site navigation links appearing on every page) eliminates > 90% of SSD reads.

Exact Checksums and 64-Bit SimHash Near-Duplicate Detection

Roughly 25% to 30% of fetched web pages duplicate content already stored under another URL (http vs. https, www vs. apex domain, printer-friendly views, syndicated articles). Exact duplicates are caught immediately by hashing normalized body text with SHA-256.

Near-duplicates, however, differ slightly in timestamps, ad banners, or view counters, causing cryptographic hashes like SHA-256 to diverge completely. Following Google’s Manku et al. algorithm, we compute a locality-sensitive 64-bit SimHash fingerprint for every fetched document:

  1. Extract overlapping word shingles (for example, 3-word n-grams) from the visible text and assign TF-IDF weights.
  2. Hash each shingle to a 64-bit integer; maintain a 64-element float vector V, adding +weight to V[i] if bit i of the hash is 1, or -weight if 0.
  3. Collapse V into a 64-bit fingerprint F where bit i = 1 if V[i] > 0, else 0.
  4. Near-Duplicate Index Lookup (Hamming Distance <= 3): Two pages whose 64-bit fingerprints differ in at most k = 3 bit positions are classified as near-duplicates. Comparing against 10 billion fingerprints linearly is infeasible; instead, by the pigeonhole principle, partitioning each 64-bit fingerprint into 4 blocks of 16 bits (or 6 blocks across permuted sorted tables) guarantees that any two fingerprints with Hamming distance <= 3 share at least one exact 16-bit prefix block. Probing 4 sorted permutation tables reduces candidate comparisons from billions to a handful of entries in microseconds.

Spider-Trap Containment and Adaptive Revisit Scheduling

Dynamically generated websites create infinite URL spaces: online calendars linking day-1 -> day-2 -> ... forever, e-commerce faceted filter permutations (?color=red&size=m&sort=asc), or symlinks causing recursive path loops (/a/b/a/b/a/b/...). Because no algorithm can decide in general whether an arbitrary web server generates an infinite graph, we enforce four orthogonal hard bounds:

  1. Per-Host Authority-Weighted Page Budget (IRLbot Model): Every host receives a finite page budget per crawl epoch proportional to its external in-degree (number of distinct referring domains), preventing low-authority traps from consuming crawler capacity.
  2. Depth and URL-Length Limits: Cap link-hop depth from the host root (default max_depth = 8), maximum URL length (2,048 bytes), and repeated path segments (reject any URL where a path component repeats >= 3 times).
  3. Hard Fetch Resource Limits: Enforce strict TCP connect (3 s), total download (10 s), max payload (10 MB), and redirect hop (<= 5) limits to block slow-loris and gzip-bomb traps.
  4. Adaptive Revisit Scheduling: Rather than revisiting every page uniformly or strictly proportional to change frequency (Cho and Garcia-Molina proved that proportional revisiting wastes budget on ultra-volatile pages that grow stale immediately), we schedule conditional revisits (If-None-Match: "<etag>") prioritizing moderate-change, high-importance pages, confirming unchanged documents via lightweight 304 Not Modified responses.

23.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ScenarioBlast RadiusAutomated Recovery and Preserved Invariant
Fetcher Worker Crashes Mid-DownloadIn-flight URLs on 1 workerFrontier lease (60 s) expires without completion ACK; URL returns to host back queue for retry
Frontier Shard Machine Crash1/40 of origin hosts pause brieflyReplicated WAL promotes standby shard owning those host partitions; zero loss of discovered queue state
Target Origin Returns 429 or 503Single external origin hostFrontier honors Retry-After and exponentially increases crawl_delay_ms; after 5 consecutive failures, quarantines host for 24 hours
Infinite Calendar or Faceted Filter TrapSingle origin hostPer-host page_budget, max_depth, and path-repetition guards halt expansion before frontier disk fills
Malformed HTML or Gzip Decompression BombSingle fetch taskStreaming byte-counter aborts download at 10 MB decompressed limit; sandboxed parser drops corrupt document without crashing worker
External Recursive DNS SlowdownFetcher connection setupDedicated in-cluster DNS Resolver Cache absorbs 95%+ of lookups; circuit breaker pauses uncached host resolution rather than exhausting worker threads

Operational SLIs and SLOs

Four domain-specific Service Level Indicators govern crawl efficiency and external safety:

  1. Per-Host Politeness Violation Rate: Audit metric verifying zero inter-request intervals below min_crawl_delay_ms or robots.txt Disallow violations (SLO = 0.000%, SEV-1 on any violation).
  2. Useful-Byte Yield (Unique / Total Fetched Ratio): Percentage of fetched bytes passing exact SHA-256 and SimHash deduplication (target >= 65%); sudden drops signal an uncontained spider trap or URL normalization regression.
  3. Frontier Queue Starvation and Active Host Count: Tracks number of distinct ready hosts in the min-heap (target >= 10,000 active hosts) and fetcher thread utilization.
  4. HTTP Status Distribution (2xx / 304 / 4xx / 429 / 5xx): Rising 429 or 403 share signals overly aggressive default crawl delays or IP reputation issues requiring immediate pacing adjustment.

How Production Systems Implement Web Crawling

Production SystemCore ArchitectureArchitectural Distinction
GooglebotMassively distributed host-partitioned crawler with adaptive crawl-budget optimization, SimHash near-dedup, and decoupled Chromium Evergreen JS rendering pipelineDynamically computes per-host crawl capacity from live error/latency telemetry and splits fast static HTML fetching from GPU/CPU-intensive JavaScript rendering
Mercator (Compaq SRC)Two-stage frontier (priority front queues + per-host back queues + politeness min-heap) with disk-backed URL-seen batchingDefined the canonical politeness frontier data structure still used across modern large-scale crawlers
IRLbot (Texas A&M)Single-server extreme-efficiency crawler using disk-based DRUM (Disk Repository with Update Management) batch seen-set checks and STAR domain-budgetingCrawled 6.38 billion pages in 41 days from a single machine, demonstrating that authority-weighted per-domain budgets are essential to defeat spider traps
Common Crawl (Apache Nutch / StormCrawler)Open-source distributed politeness-partitioned crawler publishing petabyte-scale monthly WARC archives on S3Exposes public, standardized WARC/WET crawl snapshots with strict RFC 9309 compliance for open web research and ML corpora

23.7 Simulation Verification

To verify per-host politeness scheduling, URL-seen deduplication, and per-host spider-trap page budgets, execute the crawlsim crate in the repository’s code/ workspace:

$ cargo run --release -p crawlsim
t= 0  fetch news/
t= 1  fetch calendar/day-1, shop/
t= 2  fetch news/a
t= 3  fetch calendar/day-2, shop/item-1
t= 4  fetch news/b
t= 5  fetch calendar/day-3, shop/item-2
t= 7  fetch calendar/day-4
pages fetched: 10
links to addresses already seen: 7
links not followed because a host had given 4 pages: 1

The observed transcript confirms all three core crawler invariants across three hosts (news, calendar, shop) configured with a 2-second per-host politeness interval and a 4-page per-host trap budget:

  • Zero politeness violations: news is fetched strictly at t = 0, 2, 4; calendar at t = 1, 3, 5, 7; and shop at t = 1, 3, 5. No host is ever contacted twice within 2 seconds, while fetchers remain busy across interleaved hosts.
  • URL deduplication: 7 links pointing to already-discovered URLs are filtered out cleanly before re-entering the frontier.
  • Spider-trap containment: The infinite calendar/day-1 -> day-2 -> day-3 -> day-4 -> day-5 chain terminates cleanly at calendar/day-4, dropping day-5 (1 link blocked by the 4-page host cap).

23.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Bloom FilterA compact probabilistic bit-array set membership structure (~10 bits/element) with zero false negatives and a tunable low false-positive rate.
Mercator FrontierA two-stage URL scheduler combining priority front queues (deciding crawl importance) with per-host back queues and a next-fetch min-heap (enforcing politeness).
Politeness ConstraintRestricting crawler concurrency to at most one active request per origin host separated by a minimum crawl delay so external servers are never overloaded.
Robots Exclusion Protocol (robots.txt)Standardized site-root directives (RFC 9309) specifying disallowed URL paths and crawler policies that compliant crawlers fetch and cache prior to crawling.
SimHashA locality-sensitive 64-bit document fingerprint in which near-duplicate pages differ in at most a few bits (small Hamming distance), enabling fast mirror detection.
Spider Trap (Crawler Trap)A dynamically generated or cyclical URL structure (such as an infinite calendar or faceted filter graph) capable of producing unbounded distinct URLs.
URL CanonicalizationNormalizing case, default ports, relative paths, fragments, and query parameter order so equivalent URLs map to a single canonical key.

Chapter 24: Metrics and Monitoring: System Design

A distributed metrics and monitoring platform continuously collects numeric telemetry across tens of thousands of services, compresses billions of daily data points into specialized time-series storage, serves interactive range queries during live incidents, and pages on-call engineers when user-facing service levels degrade. Monitoring exhibits an asymmetric workload profile: continuous, relentless append-only writes of tiny (timestamp, float64) samples paired with sparse ad-hoc reads that suddenly spike during outages across multi-month ranges. Above all, a monitoring system carries a strict failure-isolation mandate: because engineers depend on metrics precisely when production infrastructure breaks, the telemetry plane must run on independent compute, networking, and storage so a production outage cannot silence its own alarms. In this chapter, I design a horizontally sharded time-series database (TSDB) and alerting platform incorporating pull and push ingestion, Gorilla delta-of-delta and XOR compression, inverted label-index cardinality defenses, two-hour WAL-backed head blocks compacted to immutable object storage, spike-preserving rollups, and hysteresis-guarded multi-window alert evaluation.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, verifiable functional requirements, high-availability write SLOs, explicit non-goals, and compression-adjusted capacity bounds
  • Prometheus OpenMetrics scrape exposition, Remote Write ingestion, PromQL range-query APIs, alert rule definitions, and TSDB chunk/index schemas
  • control-plane vs. data-plane separation across isolated target discovery, sharded TSDB ingesters, object-store compaction, query engines, and Dead-Man’s Switch watchdogs
  • pull vs. push ingestion trade-offs, mergeable histograms vs. non-aggregatable percentiles, Gorilla delta-of-delta timestamp and XOR float64 compression, and inverted label-index cardinality defense
  • two-hour WAL head blocks flushed to immutable object-store TSDB blocks, multi-stat downsampling rollups (min, max, sum, count), and Pending -> Firing alert evaluation with hysteresis
  • failure matrices, telemetry SLIs/SLOs, production architectures (Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, Google Monarch, Grafana Mimir), and verification via code/metricsim

24.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Every telemetry data point belongs to a time series uniquely identified by a metric name and a sorted set of key=value labels (for example, http_requests_total{service="payments",az="us-east-1a",status="500"}). Three metric primitives cover nearly all operational signals: counters (monotonically increasing totals from which queries derive rates across intervals, surviving missed scrapes cleanly), gauges (instantaneous point-in-time readings such as queue depth or resident memory), and histograms (cumulative counts across duration buckets that can be summed across hosts and time windows to compute exact or relative-error-bounded tail percentiles like p99).

Actors and Use Cases

Three external actor classes interact across the boundary of the metrics and alerting platform, as illustrated in Figure 24-1.

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Instrumented ServiceExpose /metrics for pull scraping or transmit Remote Write batches (POST /api/v1/write)Report request counters, latency histogram buckets, and memory gauges every 10 seconds across 100,000 service instances
SRE / On-Call EngineerExecute range queries (GET /v1/series?query=...) and register alert expressions (PUT /v1/alerts/{name})Inspect 6-hour p99 checkout latency across availability zones and configure a 5-minute burn-rate error alert
Incident PagerReceive grouped firing alerts and periodic dead-man’s switch heartbeatsDeduplicate cascading dependency alarms into one actionable page and trigger escalation if the monitoring pipeline stalls

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0The platform collects numeric time-series samples (counters, gauges, and cumulative histograms) from long-lived services via pull scraping and accepts pushed batches from ephemeral short-lived jobs.
1Engineers can select and aggregate arbitrary subsets of time series by label matchers (service="payments", status=~"5..") over any historical time window.
2The query engine computes fleet-wide latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) by aggregating histogram bucket counts across instances and intervals.
3Raw samples are retained at full 10-second resolution for 15 days and automatically downsampled into 5-minute and 1-hour multi-stat rollups (min, max, sum, count) retained for 2 years.
4Engineers define PromQL-style alert rules specifying an expression, threshold, and sustained for duration; the evaluator suppresses transient flapping and fires absence alerts when critical series cease arriving.
5Firing alerts route through grouping, inhibition, and deduplication pipelines before paging responders, guarded by an external Dead-Man’s Switch watchdog.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0Ingestion Scale10,000,000 active time series sampled every 10 s (1,000,000 samples/s sustained; 3,000,000 samples/s burst)Horizontally sharded TSDB ingesters partitioned by hash(series_labels) with lock-free append-only in-memory head chunks
1Query Latencyp99 <= 1.0 s for 6-hour incident dashboards; p99 <= 3.0 s for 1-year downsampled trend queriesSeparate read/query tier from write ingesters; route long-range queries automatically to 5-minute or 1-hour rolled-up blocks
2FreshnessNewly scraped samples become queryable and alert-evaluable within <= 30 sQuery Engine fans out to both active RAM head blocks on ingesters and immutable historical blocks in object storage
3Availability and Isolation99.9% write and alert availability (<= 43.2 minutes/month) with zero shared fate against monitored production systemsDedicated monitoring VPC, separate AWS/GCP account or failure zone, and independent pager egress path
4Tiered DurabilityTolerates losing a few seconds of un-replicated live points on crash; zero loss of flushed historical blocks (11 nines durability)Write-ahead log (WAL) + 2x or 3x ingester replication without synchronous cross-AZ consensus (AP writes); 2-hour blocks flushed to replicated object storage
5Cardinality DefenseHard per-tenant active-series caps (<= 500,000 series/service) to prevent unbounded label OOM cascadesIngress distributor rejects or relabels violating series while emitting a cardinality-breach meta-metric

Non-Goals and Explicit Scope Boundaries

To maintain sharp boundaries across the three pillars of observability, we exclude the following systems from the TSDB core:

  • Unstructured application log indexing: Per-request JSON logs containing unbounded user_id or order_id fields belong in dedicated inverted-text or columnar log stores (such as Loki, Elasticsearch, or ClickHouse), never as TSDB labels.
  • Distributed request tracing: Following an individual RPC tree across microservices (OpenTelemetry spans / Jaeger / Tempo) stores high-cardinality trace IDs outside numeric metric aggregation.
  • Continuous CPU/heap flame-graph profiling: Stack-trace sampling uses specialized symbol-table profiles rather than scalar time series.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

Time-series storage capacity changes by an order of magnitude once Gorilla bit-level compression is applied:

Resource DimensionDerivationProvisioned Bound
Sustained Sample Ingestion10,000,000 active series / 10 s scrape interval1,000,000 samples/s (86.4B samples/day)
Uncompressed Daily Storage86.4B samples * 16 B (8 B int64 timestamp + 8 B float64 value)1.38 TB/day (~504 TB/year)
Gorilla-Compressed Daily Storage86.4B samples * 1.5 to 2.0 B/sample (1.37 B typical in Gorilla; 2.0 B byte-aligned)~130 to 173 GB/day (~8x to 11x reduction)
15-Day Raw Retention (Object Store)173 GB/day * 15 days~2.6 TB immutable 2-hour TSDB blocks
2-Year Hourly Rollup Storage10M series * 17,520 hours * 4 stats (min, max, sum, count) * 2 B~1.4 TB compressed historical rollups
Ingester Head-Block RAM (2-Hour Window)10M series * 720 samples/2h * 2 B + ~1 KB/series inverted label index overhead~14.4 GB raw chunks + ~10 GB label index (~25 to 30 GB per full replica; ~75 to 90 GB at 3x replication across 40 ingesters)

24.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

To protect alert delivery and telemetry durability during production incidents, we isolate the monitoring cluster on independent infrastructure and separate control-plane discovery and watchdog logic from the high-throughput ingestion and query data plane, as illustrated in Figure 24-2.

Control Plane Responsibilities

  • Target Discovery: Reads service registries (Kubernetes API, Consul, cloud instance tags) to push live lists of /metrics scrape targets to regional Collection Agents without manual host files.
  • Alert Rule Registry: Stores versioned PromQL alert definitions, multi-window SLO burn-rate rules, and temporary maintenance silences.
  • Dead-Man’s Switch Watchdog: A minimal external probe running in an independent region or cloud provider. The internal Alert Evaluator continuously fires an always-true synthetic alert (vector(1)) to the watchdog every 60 seconds; if the watchdog stops receiving that heartbeat for 3 consecutive minutes, it pages SRE through an independent escalation channel.

Data Plane Responsibilities

ComponentState HeldFailure Impact and Mitigation
Collection Agents (Scrapers)Target list + short local retry bufferConsistent-hash sharded across target services; HA pairs scrape critical targets in parallel and deduplicate on ingestion
Write DistributorStateless consistent-hash router + per-tenant cardinality limiterRoutes every sample by hash(metric_name + sorted_labels) to RF = 3 (or RF = 2) TSDB Ingesters; rejects runaway label cardinality at ingress
Sharded TSDB IngestersActive 2-hour Gorilla head chunks in RAM + local NVMe Write-Ahead Log (WAL)Single ingester crash leaves zero query gaps because RF = 3 peer ingesters hold identical samples; restart replays local WAL in < 30 s
Object-Store Blocks and CompactorImmutable 2-hour, 24-hour, and downsampled (5m, 1h) blocks in S3/GCSCompactor merges overlapping 2-hour blocks from replicas into deduplicated, erasure-coded long-term Parquet/TSDB blocks
PromQL Query EngineStateless query planner + short-TTL sub-query result cacheStrictly isolated from write path with per-query memory (2 GB), max-series (100k), and timeout (30 s) guardrails so incident dashboard floods never stall ingestion
Alert Evaluator and AlertmanagerActive Pending/Firing alert state + silence/grouping tableRuns in redundant HA pair; Alertmanager groups related alerts (for example, 50 services failing behind 1 database) into a single incident notification

24.4 Deep Dive: Pull vs. Push Ingestion, Gorilla Compression, and Cardinality Defense

Pull vs. Push Ingestion Trade-Offs

DimensionPull Model (HTTP Scrape)Push Model (Remote Write / OTLP)
Failure DetectionFailed scrape immediately sets synthetic up == 0 metric, distinguishing dead instances from idle onesSilent service crash looks identical to zero traffic unless paired with external absence alerts
Backpressure ControlCollectors govern scrape cadence and can shed non-critical targets during overloadServices can DDoS the monitoring tier simultaneously during traffic storms or restarts
Short-Lived Batch JobsCron or Lambda jobs finishing in 3 seconds exit before the 10-second scrape arrivesJobs push final counters cleanly before process termination
Network TopologyRequires collector-to-service reachability across VPC/NAT boundariesServices behind restrictive firewalls push outbound over TLS

Production platforms combine both models cleanly: regional Collection Agents pull from long-lived services every 10 seconds to obtain free health checks (up == 1) and centrally paced load, while ephemeral batch jobs and edge clients push via protobuf Remote Write (POST /api/v1/write) into the Write Distributor.

Gorilla Delta-of-Delta Timestamp and XOR Value Compression

Storing raw (int64 timestamp, float64 value) pairs consumes 16 bytes/sample, requiring 1.38 TB/day at 1M samples/s. Because consecutive samples in a time series arrive at regular scrape intervals (10 s) and vary gradually, we apply the Gorilla bit-level streaming encoder inside every 2-hour chunk, as depicted in Figure 24-3.

  1. Timestamp Delta-of-Delta (DoD) Packing: For sample n, compute the first delta dt_n = t_n - t_(n-1) and the second-order difference D = dt_n - dt_(n-1). On a regular 10-second scrape cadence (t = 100, 110, 120), dt_1 = 10, dt_2 = 10, and D = 0. Gorilla encodes D using variable-length bit prefixes:
    • D == 0: write single bit '0' (1 bit total, a 64x reduction over 64-bit timestamps).
    • D in [-63, 64]: write '10' followed by a 7-bit signed integer (9 bits).
    • D in [-255, 256]: write '110' followed by a 9-bit signed integer (12 bits).
    • D in [-2047, 2048]: write '1110' followed by a 12-bit signed integer (16 bits).
    • Otherwise: write '1111' followed by a 32-bit signed value (36 bits).
  2. Float64 Bitwise XOR Encoding: IEEE-754 double-precision numbers for slowly varying gauges or rates share identical sign, exponent, and leading mantissa bits. Computing xor = bits(v_n) ^ bits(v_(n-1)) produces long runs of leading and trailing zero bits:
    • If xor == 0 (value unchanged): write single bit '0' (1 bit total).
    • If xor != 0 and its non-zero meaningful bits fall within the previous sample’s leading/trailing zero window: write '10' followed only by the meaningful bits.
    • Otherwise: write '11', 5 bits encoding leading-zero count, 6 bits encoding meaningful-bit length, and the meaningful bits themselves.

Advance through the interactive step-by-step trace below to observe how encoding differences shrinks timestamps and values dramatically compared with raw 16-byte storage.

Because decoding sample k requires scanning from the beginning of its compressed bit stream, samples are segmented into fixed 120-sample chunks (20 minutes at 10-second intervals) inside 2-hour blocks, bounding random-access decode cost to microseconds.

Inverted Label Index and Cardinality Explosion Defense

To answer label-filtered queries like http_requests_total{service="payments", status="500"} in milliseconds, every TSDB block maintains an inverted index mapping each (label_key, label_value) pair to a sorted posting list of integer series_ids. Query resolution intersects the posting lists for service="payments" and status="500", yielding the exact matching series IDs before decoding their Gorilla chunks.

This inverted index creates the single most destructive operational failure mode in monitoring systems: cardinality explosion. Every unique combination of label values allocates a distinct series_id, inverted index entries, and an active RAM Gorilla head chunk (~1 to 2 KB per series). Adding a single unbounded label such as user_id (1,000,000 values) or raw url_path to a metric with 100 hosts and 5 HTTP statuses multiplies 500 series into 500,000,000 series, exhausting ingester RAM within minutes. We enforce three defenses:

  1. Ingestion-Time Relabeling Rules: Drop or normalize high-cardinality labels (replacing /users/98123/profile with route template /users/:id/profile) at the Collection Agent before samples enter the Write Distributor.
  2. Per-Tenant Active-Series Quotas: The Write Distributor tracks active series_id counts per service/tenant and rejects new series creations above the configured quota (429 + cardinality-limit alert) rather than letting one misconfigured deployment OOM the shared TSDB cluster.
  3. Observability Pillar Routing: Enforce organizational lint rules keeping TSDB labels strictly bounded (< 100 distinct values per label) while routing user_id and request_id diagnostics to structured logs and distributed traces.

24.5 Deep Dive: Block Compaction, Spike-Preserving Rollups, and Alert Hysteresis

Two-Hour WAL Head Blocks and Immutable Object-Store Compaction

TSDB ingesters separate live mutable writes from immutable cold storage using an LSM-inspired lifecycle:

  1. In-Memory Head Block (0 to 2 hours): Newly arriving samples append to both a sequential local NVMe Write-Ahead Log (for crash recovery) and per-series RAM Gorilla chunks. No disk random writes occur during steady-state ingestion.
  2. Immutable 2-Hour Flush: At the end of every 2-hour window, the ingester seals the head block, builds its compact sorted inverted index, writes an immutable block to object storage (S3/GCS), and truncates the corresponding WAL segment.
  3. Background Compaction and Parquet/TSDB Tiering: Stateless Compactor workers merge 2-hour blocks from multiple HA replicas (deduplicating identical samples) into larger 12-hour and 24-hour immutable blocks (or columnar Parquet files for analytical long-term retention), reducing object-store metadata lookups during multi-week queries.

Why Averages Mislead and Spike-Preserving Rollups

Averaging response times hides tail latency that degrades user experience: if 99% of requests finish in 40 ms and 1% stall at 2,000 ms, the mean is a deceptively calm 60 ms, yet a user page triggering 50 backend fan-out RPCs has a 1 - 0.99^50 = 39.5% chance of hitting a 2-second stall. Moreover, precomputed per-host percentiles (p99) are mathematically non-aggregatable: the fleet p99 across two servers cannot be derived from their individual p99 values. Services must therefore emit mergeable cumulative histogram buckets (or relative-error exponential / DDSketch histograms) so the Query Engine sums counts across hosts before computing quantiles.

The exact same hazard affects long-term downsampling rollups. Rendering a 1-year graph on a 2,000-pixel monitor cannot scan 3.15 million raw 10-second points per series, so the Compactor downsamples blocks older than 15 days into 5-minute and 1-hour rollups. Reducing a 1-minute window containing 57 seconds at 40 ms and 3 seconds at 900 ms to a single arithmetic average (83 ms) erases the outage completely. Each rollup point therefore stores a 4-tuple of aggregates: min, max, sum, and count, preserving exact averages (sum / count) alongside peak spikes (max) and floors (min).

Multi-Window Alert Evaluation with Hysteresis

Noisy alerting causes pager fatigue, eroding on-call responsiveness during genuine incidents. We enforce four architectural rules in the Alert Evaluator:

  1. Symptom-Based SLO Alerts: Page on user-facing symptoms (error budget burn rate, p99 checkout latency, failed payment ratio) rather than low-level machine causes (CPU > 85%) that may reflect healthy batch utilization.
  2. State Machine with Pending -> Firing Hysteresis: When an alert expression evaluates true at t = 0, it transitions from INACTIVE to PENDING without paging. Only if the condition holds continuously across every 30-second evaluation for the configured for_seconds window (for example, 300 s) does it transition to FIRING and dispatch to Alertmanager. Adding a keep_firing_for_seconds cooldown (hysteresis) prevents rapid flapping across a noisy threshold boundary.
  3. Absence / Missing-Data Guards: A threshold rule error_rate > 0.01 evaluates to an empty vector when a service crashes completely and stops emitting metrics, leaving the alert silent during total outage. Every critical service therefore pairs symptom alerts with an explicit absence rule (absent(up{service="payments"}) == 1 for 2 minutes).
  4. Grouping and Inhibition in Alertmanager: Groups simultaneous alerts sharing cluster or service labels into one consolidated incident page, and inhibits downstream dependency alerts when an upstream root-cause alert (such as DatabasePrimaryDown) is already firing.

24.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ScenarioBlast RadiusAutomated Recovery and Preserved Invariant
Monitored Production Cluster OutageZero impact on monitoring planeMonitoring runs in isolated VPC/account with independent network egress; up == 0 and absence alerts fire reliably
Single TSDB Ingester CrashZero data loss or query gapWrite Distributor writes to RF = 3 ingesters; peers serve active 2-hour head blocks while crashed node replays local WAL on restart
Runaway High-Cardinality Label DeployViolating service’s new series onlyWrite Distributor enforces per-tenant active-series cap, rejecting offending series while keeping shared cluster RAM stable
Incident Dashboard Query StormQuery latency rises slightlySeparate query tier enforces per-query timeouts (30 s) and max-series caps; TSDB ingestion and alert evaluation remain completely unaffected
Alert Evaluator or Alertmanager FreezeAlert evaluation stallsRedundant HA evaluator continues running; if both stall, external Dead-Man’s Switch watchdog detects missing heartbeat within 3 minutes and pages SRE
Object-Store Transient Read ErrorHistorical range queries (> 2 h)Real-time alerting and recent 2-hour incident graphs serve directly from ingester RAM head blocks without object-store dependency

Operational SLIs and SLOs

Four meta-monitoring Service Level Indicators (“watching the watcher”) track the telemetry platform’s own health:

  1. Sample Ingestion Drop Rate: Fraction of incoming scraped or pushed samples dropped due to overload or timeout (SLO < 0.01%).
  2. End-to-End Ingestion-to-Query Freshness (p99): Elapsed seconds from sample timestamp to visibility in PromQL queries (SLO <= 30 s).
  3. Alert Evaluation Loop Duration and Missed Cycles: Verifies every 30-second rule group finishes within its interval (SLO: 0 skipped evaluation ticks per hour).
  4. Dead-Man’s Switch Heartbeat Continuity: End-to-end synthetic alert fired every 60 seconds through the full Evaluator -> Alertmanager -> Pager pipeline (SLO: 99.99% delivery continuity).

How Production Systems Implement Metrics and Monitoring

Production SystemCore ArchitectureArchitectural Distinction
PrometheusPull-based collector + local embedded TSDB using Gorilla compression, 2-hour WAL head blocks, and PromQLEstablished the OpenMetrics exposition standard, pull-based up health probing, and inverted label-index TSDB architecture
VictoriaMetricsHigh-efficiency Go TSDB with merged LSM-style storage parts, zstd-layered delta/XOR encoding, and native high-cardinality index cachingAchieves sub-byte-per-sample compression (~0.4 to 0.8 B/point) and significantly lower RAM per active series than standard TSDB layouts
Google MonarchPlanet-scale globally distributed push-based in-memory TSDB structured in regional leaves, zone aggregators, and global root query mixersPrioritizes strict regional failure isolation (zero global dependency for local alerting) and high-fan-in streaming aggregation
Grafana Mimir / ThanosHorizontally sharded, multi-tenant Prometheus-compatible TSDB separating stateless distributors, replicated ingesters, object-store compactors, and query frontendsExtends Prometheus semantics to billions of active series with per-tenant cardinality limits, split-by-interval query caching, and unlimited S3/GCS block retention

24.7 Simulation Verification

To verify delta-based time-series compression and the difference between average and maximum downsampling rollups on transient latency spikes, execute the metricsim crate in the repository’s code/ workspace:

$ cargo run --release -p metricsim
3600 points, 1 for every second of an hour
plain, 16 bytes for each point: 57600 bytes
each point as its change from the one before: 7223 bytes, 2.0 bytes for each point
minute 20, kept as its average: 83 ms
minute 20, kept as its largest value: 900 ms

The observed output validates two core TSDB mechanics over 3,600 one-second response-time samples:

  • Compression efficiency: Storing raw 16-byte (timestamp, value) points consumes 57,600 bytes, whereas byte-aligned delta encoding shrinks the hour to 7,223 bytes (2.0 bytes/point, an 8x reduction; bit-packed Gorilla XOR pushes this further to ~1.37 bytes/point).
  • Spike preservation in rollups: During minute 20 (57 seconds at ~40 ms plus a 3-second spike at 900 ms), an average-only rollup records 83 ms and conceals the incident, whereas recording max preserves the 900 ms spike alongside min, sum, and count.

Run the metrics compression and rollup simulation. Execute cargo run --release -p metricsim in code/metricsim to reproduce the 8x delta compression reduction (57,600 to 7,223 bytes) and verify how max rollups preserve the 900 ms spike that an 83 ms average hides.

24.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Cardinality ExplosionUnbounded growth in active time series caused by placing high-cardinality identifiers (such as user_id or request_id) into metric labels, exhausting inverted-index RAM.
Dead-Man’s SwitchAn always-firing synthetic heartbeat alert verified by an independent external watchdog to detect silent stalls in the monitoring or paging pipeline.
Delta-of-Delta (DoD) CompressionEncoding regular time-series timestamps as the second-order difference D = (t_n - t_(n-1)) - (t_(n-1) - t_(n-2)), compressing jitter-free intervals to 1 bit.
Downsampling (Rollup)Aggregating high-resolution historical points into coarser intervals (5m, 1h) storing min, max, sum, and count to accelerate long-range queries without hiding spikes.
Gorilla XOR EncodingCompressing adjacent IEEE-754 floating-point metric values by bitwise XORing consecutive readings and packing only the non-zero significant window.
Hysteresis (for: / Cooldown)Requiring an alert condition to persist across consecutive evaluations before firing (and keeping it firing briefly after recovery) to eliminate noisy flapping.
Mergeable HistogramRecording request durations into cumulative or exponential buckets whose counts can be summed across instances before computing accurate fleet percentiles.
