Chapter 25: File Synchronization

A cloud file synchronization service maintains a coherent directory tree across laptops, desktops, and mobile devices even when endpoints disconnect for hours or weeks. In contrast to the single-leader replicated stores examined in Chapter 3, every client device acts as an autonomous write origin that modifies local files without consulting a central coordinator. Two offline devices can mutate the same document concurrently and reconnect days later; no leader election protocol can prevent those divergent writes while the devices remain partitioned. In this chapter, I design a synchronization architecture that transfers only mutated byte ranges across wide-area links, arbitrates concurrent revisions without data loss, and converges disconnected replicas through strongly consistent metadata paired with an immutable content-addressed block store.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, functional and non-functional requirements, non-goals, and exabyte-scale capacity bounds
  • content-addressed chunk APIs, conditional manifest commits (If-Match), monotonic change-cursor feeds, and relational metadata schemas
  • control-plane and data-plane separation across the Metadata Service, Content-Addressed Block Store, Garbage Collector, and Delta Notification Bus
  • FastCDC content-defined chunking, cross-version deduplication security boundaries, and Merkle directory tree diffing
  • optimistic concurrency control, conflict-copy branching, tombstone lifecycle management, long-poll notification hints, and epoch-safe garbage collection
  • failure recovery matrices, synchronization SLIs, real-world production architectures (Dropbox Magic Pocket, Google Drive, iCloud Drive), and simulation verification via code/syncsim

25.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Cloud file synchronization combines two contrasting storage workloads inside one product boundary. File payloads are large, opaque, and immutable once hashed, which suits horizontally scalable erasure-coded object storage. Directory hierarchies, access control lists, version numbers, and change cursors are compact, frequently mutated, and require strict transactional ordering to detect concurrent edits. We isolate these two concerns from the outset so high-throughput bulk transfers never saturate the transactional metadata tier.

Actors and Use Cases

Three classes of actors interact across the synchronization service boundary (Figure 25-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Desktop / Mobile ClientUpload changed chunks (PUT /v1/blocks/{sha256}) and commit manifests (PUT /v1/files/{id})Local filesystem watcher detects a saved presentation, computes FastCDC chunks, uploads one changed block, and advances version 3 to version 4
Collaborator DeviceSubscribe to delta notifications and catch up (GET /v1/changes?cursor=<seq>)A teammate’s laptop wakes on a delta hint, fetches new manifest entries, downloads missing blocks, and atomically swaps the local file
Offline DeviceBranch conflicting offline editsA phone edits version 3 in airplane mode, reconnects after version 4 commits, receives 412 Precondition Failed, and saves a conflict copy
Storage OperatorGarbage-collect orphan blocks and enforce quotasBackground sweeper reclaims unreferenced chunks whose 30-day version retention and tombstone grace periods have expired

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0Any file creation, modification, rename, or deletion on one authorized device propagates to all other devices subscribed to the same namespace.
1A device that disconnects for days or weeks catches up on every missed namespace mutation upon reconnecting using a durable change cursor.
2Only mutated chunks of a modified file cross the wide-area network; unchanged byte ranges are deduplicated against existing server blocks.
3When two devices independently modify the same base file version, the service detects the conflict atomically and preserves both revisions without discarding data.
4Users can inspect revision history and restore any prior version of a modified file within a 30-day retention window.
5Users can recover deleted files from explicit tombstones within a 30-day retention window before underlying blocks become eligible for garbage collection.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0DurabilityEleven nines (99.999999999%) annual chunk durability; zero loss of committed metadata versionsErasure-coded multi-AZ chunk storage (6+3 Reed-Solomon) paired with 3-AZ synchronous Raft/Paxos metadata replication
1ConsistencyStrict serializability for metadata commits (If-Match CAS); eventual convergence across offline devicesMetadata store rejects concurrent commits on stale versions via single-shard ACID transactions; edge devices reconcile asynchronously
2Propagation Latencyp99 <= 5 s from manifest commit on origin device to delta notification delivery on connected peer devicesPersistent WebSocket or HTTP/2 long-poll notification tier decoupled from bulk block transfers
3Bandwidth EconomyWAN bytes transferred scale with O(changed bytes) rather than O(total file size) even under prepended insertionsFastCDC content-defined chunking replaces fixed-offset slicing to localize boundary shifts
4Scale100M active users, 10B files, 1 EB logical content, 40M concurrent online devicesAccount-sharded metadata cluster, stateless notification edge fleet, and direct client-to-object-store pre-signed chunk I/O

We explicitly combine two consistency models in Requirement 1. Client replicas are eventually consistent by physical necessity because an offline laptop cannot participate in synchronous quorum writes. The central metadata service is strongly consistent so every conditional version commit observes a single authoritative parent revision.

Non-Goals and Out-of-Scope Boundaries

To keep the architectural boundary crisp, we exclude four capabilities from this design:

  • Real-time character-level collaborative editing: Simultaneous sub-second co-editing of structured text requires Operational Transformation or Sequence CRDTs rather than opaque byte-chunk synchronization; we design that architecture in Chapter 26.
  • Distributed POSIX byte-range locks (fcntl / flock): Acquiring advisory or mandatory file locks across wide-area networks stalls offline editors and degrades availability during transient partitions.
  • Cross-tenant zero-knowledge encryption with global deduplication: End-to-end client encryption with per-user random keys produces distinct ciphertexts for identical plaintext blocks, preventing cross-user deduplication; we scope deduplication within a single tenant or shared namespace unless convergent encryption trade-offs are explicitly accepted.
  • Full-text content indexing and semantic search: Extracting text from PDFs or office documents runs in an asynchronous downstream indexing pipeline consuming the same change log rather than on the critical sync path.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

File synchronization is constrained by exabyte-scale block storage durability, 40 million concurrent notification sockets, and strongly consistent metadata write QPS.

Resource DimensionDerivationProvisioned Bound
Concurrent Online Devices100M users * 2 devices/user * 20% online40M open notification connections (~400 edge pods at 100k sockets/pod)
Metadata Mutation Rate100M users * 20 file ops/day / 86,400 s (3x peak factor)~23,150 avg commits/s; ~70,000 peak commits/s
Logical vs. Physical Block Storage1 EB logical content; ~30% cross-version dedup savings -> 700 PB unique; 6+3 Reed-Solomon (1.5x)~1.05 EB raw disk capacity across multi-AZ block clusters
Total Unique Chunks700 PB / 4 MB average chunk size~175B unique chunks (~250B logical chunk references)
Hot Metadata Footprint10B files * 500 B (path, ACL, version, ~12 to 25 SHA-256 pointers)~5 TB active metadata (~15 TB with 3x replication across 32 shards)
Aggregate Block Bandwidth23,150 commits/s * 1.5 avg mutated chunks * 1 MB avg delta size~35 GB/s sustained ingress; ~70 GB/s sustained egress (2x fanout)

25.2 External API and Data Contracts

We design the wire protocol around two invariants: upload blocks before committing metadata, and guard every metadata commit with an optimistic version precondition. Because blocks are addressed by their SHA-256 cryptographic digest, block uploads are inherently idempotent and retry-safe without extra server coordination.

Chunk Existence and Direct Block Upload

Before transferring bytes, the sync client submits the ordered list of SHA-256 chunk hashes produced by its local FastCDC scanner and asks the control plane which blocks are absent in the target namespace.

POST /v1/namespaces/ns_881/chunks:exists HTTP/2
Host: sync.example
Authorization: Bearer tok_client_laptop
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "digests": [
    "9f2c8b14e0a3...",
    "41aa77d0c91e...",
    "c07e5519f8b2..."
  ]
}

HTTP/2 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "missing": [
    {
      "digest": "c07e5519f8b2...",
      "upload_url": "https://blocks.sync.example/v1/blocks/c07e5519f8b2...?sig=hmac_v1_...",
      "expires_at": "2026-10-14T10:15:00Z"
    }
  ]
}

The client streams each missing payload directly to the Data Plane Block Gateway via the pre-signed URL. The gateway recomputes SHA-256 over the incoming byte stream, rejects corrupted payloads with 400 Bad Request if the computed digest does not match the path parameter, persists the erasure-coded block, and returns 201 Created (or 200 OK if an identical concurrent upload already completed).

PUT /v1/blocks/c07e5519f8b2...?sig=hmac_v1_... HTTP/2
Host: blocks.sync.example
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
Content-Length: 4194304

<4194304 raw bytes>

Conditional Manifest Commit and Idempotent Retries

Once every missing chunk is durable, the client commits the updated file manifest to the Metadata Service using an HTTP If-Match precondition naming the parent version and a caller-generated Idempotency-Key protecting against dropped commit acknowledgements.

PUT /v1/namespaces/ns_881/files/7 HTTP/2
Host: sync.example
Authorization: Bearer tok_client_laptop
If-Match: "3"
Idempotency-Key: laptop-op-99214
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "path": "/docs/architecture.pdf",
  "chunks": ["9f2c8b14e0a3...", "41aa77d0c91e...", "c07e5519f8b2..."],
  "size_bytes": 11842010,
  "mtime_ms": 1760436012000
}

HTTP/2 200 OK
ETag: "4"
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "file_id": 7,
  "version": 4,
  "cursor_seq": 5121,
  "manifest_sha256": "e3b0c44298fc..."
}

If a second device submits a commit carrying If-Match: "3" after version 4 has committed, the Metadata Service checks idempotency_key first. If the key matches the committed revision 4, the server replays 200 OK so a retried laptop commit after a dropped socket never triggers a false conflict. If the key differs, the server rejects the stale commit with 412 Precondition Failed:

HTTP/2 412 Precondition Failed
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "/problems/version-conflict",
  "title": "File modified concurrently by another device",
  "status": 412,
  "current_version": 4,
  "current_etag": "\"4\"",
  "last_modified_by": "device_laptop_01"
}

Cursor-Based Delta Change Feed

All peer devices, whether waking from a real-time notification hint or reconnecting after 30 days offline, fetch missed namespace transitions through one unified paginated endpoint:

GET /v1/namespaces/ns_881/changes?cursor=5120&limit=500 HTTP/2
Host: sync.example
Authorization: Bearer tok_client_phone

HTTP/2 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "changes": [
    {
      "seq": 5121,
      "file_id": 7,
      "op": "UPSERT",
      "path": "/docs/architecture.pdf",
      "version": 4,
      "chunks": ["9f2c8b14e0a3...", "41aa77d0c91e...", "c07e5519f8b2..."]
    },
    {
      "seq": 5122,
      "file_id": 12,
      "op": "TOMBSTONE",
      "path": "/docs/draft.md",
      "version": 2
    }
  ],
  "next_cursor": 5122,
  "has_more": false
}

Relational Metadata Schema

We shard the strongly consistent metadata store by namespace_id so every single-file commit, rename, and change_log sequence increment commits inside one local ACID transaction without distributed two-phase commit overhead.

CREATE TABLE files (
    namespace_id     BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    file_id          BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    parent_dir_id    BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    name             TEXT        NOT NULL,
    version          BIGINT      NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    state            TEXT        NOT NULL, -- 'ACTIVE' | 'TOMBSTONE'
    manifest_sha256  BYTEA       NOT NULL,
    last_idem_key    TEXT        NOT NULL,
    updated_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    deleted_at       TIMESTAMPTZ,
    PRIMARY KEY (namespace_id, file_id),
    UNIQUE (namespace_id, parent_dir_id, name) WHERE state = 'ACTIVE'
);

CREATE TABLE file_versions (
    namespace_id     BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    file_id          BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    version          BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    chunk_digests    BYTEA[]     NOT NULL,
    size_bytes       BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    author_device_id TEXT        NOT NULL,
    created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (namespace_id, file_id, version)
);

CREATE TABLE change_log (
    namespace_id     BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    seq              BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    file_id          BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    op               TEXT        NOT NULL, -- 'UPSERT' | 'RENAME' | 'TOMBSTONE'
    version          BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    payload_json     JSONB       NOT NULL,
    created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (namespace_id, seq)
);

CREATE TABLE namespace_blocks (
    namespace_id     BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    chunk_sha256     BYTEA       NOT NULL,
    byte_length      INT         NOT NULL,
    last_referenced  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (namespace_id, chunk_sha256)
);

Notice the partial unique index UNIQUE (namespace_id, parent_dir_id, name) WHERE state = 'ACTIVE': multiple tombstoned files that previously occupied the same path can coexist safely in history while active filenames remain strictly unique within a directory.

25.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We partition the synchronization service into a lightweight Control Plane handling metadata consistency, ACL enforcement, delta notifications, and garbage collection, and a high-bandwidth Data Plane transferring immutable blocks directly between client agents and erasure-coded storage (Figure 25-2).

Component Responsibilities and Failure Domains

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Recovery
Client Sync AgentEdgeLocal directory tree, SQLite local index, last applied cursorCrashes or prolonged offline periods recover cleanly by scanning local disk against SQLite state and resuming from cursor
Metadata and CAS APIControlStateless (auth, ACL check, manifest validation, pre-signed URL minting)Load balancer routes around failed pods immediately; Idempotency-Key prevents duplicate commits on retry
Metadata Store (3-AZ)Controlfiles, file_versions, change_log, namespace_blocks (sharded by namespace_id)Synchronous 3-AZ Raft/PostgreSQL quorum elects a new primary in 1 to 3 s with zero committed metadata loss
Delta Notification BusControlIn-memory map of namespace_id -> subscribed WebSocket/long-poll socketsPod crash drops connections; clients reconnect with exponential jitter and issue a catch-up GET /changes?cursor= call
GC and Quota SweeperControlSweep watermarks and unreferenced candidate queuesIdempotent batch jobs restart from last scanned shard; 30-day delayed sweep archive protects active uploads
Block GatewayDataStateless streaming SHA-256 verifier and erasure-coding clientFailed chunk upload leaves no metadata pointer; client retries the exact same content-addressed PUT
Content-Addressed Block StoreDataImmutable 4 MB chunks keyed by SHA-256 across multi-AZ storage nodesErasure coding (6+3 Reed-Solomon) survives simultaneous loss of up to 3 storage nodes or 1 full AZ
Edge Download CacheDataHot shared blocks in NVMe/RAM LRU caches near POPsCache miss falls through to origin block store; content addressing eliminates cache invalidation complexity because chunks are immutable

End-to-End Change Propagation Walkthrough

  1. Local Debounce and Chunking: The desktop agent receives filesystem notifications (FSEvents on macOS, inotify on Linux, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows). It waits for a 1 to 2 s quiet window so partially written application saves are not uploaded prematurely, then slices the file with FastCDC and hashes each chunk with SHA-256.
  2. Missing-Chunk Discovery: The agent sends POST /v1/namespaces/{ns}/chunks:exists to the Metadata API and receives pre-signed upload URLs for only the chunks absent from the namespace.
  3. Parallel Direct Data-Plane Upload: The agent streams missing chunks concurrently over HTTP/2 to the Block Gateway, which verifies each SHA-256 digest and commits the erasure-coded stripes to the Content-Addressed Block Store.
  4. Atomic Control-Plane Commit: The agent issues PUT /v1/namespaces/{ns}/files/{id} with If-Match: "3". Inside one ACID transaction on the namespace shard, the Metadata Store verifies that every listed chunk exists in namespace_blocks, checks version = 3, increments to version = 4, inserts the file_versions row, and appends seq = 5121 to change_log.
  5. Hint Fanout: After the transaction commits (via transactional outbox or CDC tailing change_log), the Metadata tier publishes a lightweight invalidation hint (ns_881, seq=5121) to the Delta Notification Bus, which pushes a wake-up frame to every online peer device in ns_881.
  6. Peer Convergence: Each waking device calls GET /v1/namespaces/ns_881/changes?cursor=5120, diffs the incoming chunk list against its local block cache, downloads only missing chunks from the Edge Cache or Block Gateway, reassembles the new file into a hidden staging path, calls fsync, and atomically rename()s it into place before advancing its persisted cursor.

25.4 Content-Defined Chunking, Deduplication, and Merkle Tree Diffing

The bandwidth efficiency of a file synchronization service rests on how a byte stream is partitioned into addressable chunks and how two directory trees locate their differences (Figure 25-3).

Defeating Fixed-Block Boundary Shifts with FastCDC

Dividing a file at fixed offsets (every 4 MB, for example) handles in-place overwrites well but collapses whenever bytes are inserted or removed near the start of a file. Prepending a single byte shifts every subsequent offset by +1, altering the byte contents of every downstream fixed block and invalidating 100% of the file’s SHA-256 checksums. The client is forced to re-upload the entire file despite a one-byte edit.

Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) anchors cut points to local byte patterns instead of global file offsets. A sliding window advances byte by byte across the file while maintaining a rolling hash H. Whenever the low-order k bits of H equal zero ((H & ((1 << k) - 1)) == 0), the scanner terminates the current chunk. Because each boundary depends exclusively on the bytes immediately preceding it, inserting bytes at offset 0 alters only the first chunk; once the scanner reaches the original boundary bytes, the rolling hash hits the same cut condition and realigns every remaining chunk identically.

Classic CDC implementations used Rabin fingerprinting (polynomial division over GF(2)), which requires multiple arithmetic operations per byte and limits single-core throughput to roughly 100 to 200 MB/s. Modern synchronization engines adopt FastCDC (Xia et al., USENIX ATC 2016), which introduces three production optimizations:

  1. Gear Rolling Hash: Replaces Rabin polynomial modulo arithmetic with a 256-entry 64-bit random lookup table G[byte]: fp = (fp << 1) + G[input[i]]. Computing the rolling hash takes one shift, one table lookup, and one addition per byte, saturating 1 to 2 GB/s per CPU core.
  2. Minimum and Maximum Size Clamping with Cut-Point Skipping: To avoid pathological tiny chunks (inflating metadata) or giant chunks (hurting deduplication), we enforce [MinSize, MaxSize] bounds (for example, 1 MB minimum, 4 MB target average, 8 MB maximum for large files; or 2 KB / 8 KB / 64 KB for fine-grained backup tiers). FastCDC skips hash evaluation completely for the first MinSize bytes of every chunk, eliminating redundant CPU work.
  3. Normalized Chunking: Pure geometric cut distributions produce high variance in chunk lengths. FastCDC uses a stricter bitmask (MaskS, one extra zero bit) between MinSize and AvgSize and a looser bitmask (MaskL, one fewer zero bit) between AvgSize and MaxSize, tightening chunk sizes closely around the target mean without losing boundary realignment.

Deduplication Scope and Side-Channel Security

Content-addressed deduplication yields three storage and network wins: identical blocks inside a single file, unchanged blocks across 30 days of file versions, and identical files shared across a team namespace are stored once. However, cross-tenant deduplication introduces a well-known cryptographic oracle vulnerability. If an attacker guesses the SHA-256 hash of a sensitive corporate contract and probes POST /v1/chunks:exists, receiving "missing": [] confirms that another tenant uploaded that exact document, and skipping the upload lets the attacker bind their own manifest to a block they never possessed.

We close this side channel by combining two controls:

  • Namespace-Scoped Existence Visibility: The namespace_blocks table records chunk ownership per namespace_id. A client only skips uploading a chunk if namespace_blocks confirms that the chunk is already authorized within that namespace.
  • Proof-of-Ownership (PoW) for Cross-Namespace Physical Dedup: Inside the Data Plane Block Store, physical deduplication across namespaces may still occur transparently after the client uploads the ciphertext or completes a random byte-range challenge proving possession of the full chunk payload.

Merkle Directory Tree Diffing for Reconnection and Audits

While incremental edits rely on monotonic change_log cursors, two scenarios require full-tree comparison: initial cold-start sync onto a device that already holds a partial local copy (for example, after reinstalling the OS or migrating an archive), and periodic consistency audits verifying that a client did not drop a local filesystem event without notice.

Streaming metadata for 500,000 files on every reconnect wastes bandwidth and database IOPS. Instead, both the client SQLite index and the server namespace maintain a Merkle Directory Tree:

  • Every file leaf node computes H(file) = SHA256(name || version || manifest_sha256).
  • Every directory internal node computes H(dir) = SHA256(sorted_child_hashes).

During reconciliation, the client sends its root hash H(root) to the server. If the root hashes match, synchronization finishes in O(1) with a single round trip. If they differ, the client descends only the subdirectories whose hashes diverge, pruning intact subtrees in O(K log N) messages for K mutated files out of N total files.

25.5 Optimistic Concurrency, Conflict Branching, Tombstones, and Garbage Collection

Detecting concurrent edits accurately and managing the lifecycle of deleted files and unreferenced chunks account for the majority of subtle production defects in file synchronization engines.

Optimistic Concurrency and Conflict-Copy Branching

Because disconnected clients edit independently, every manifest commit carries If-Match: "<base_version>". The Metadata Store executes a single-row atomic conditional update:

UPDATE files
   SET version = version + 1,
       manifest_sha256 = $3,
       last_idem_key = $4,
       updated_at = now()
 WHERE namespace_id = $1
   AND file_id = $2
   AND version = $5
   AND state = 'ACTIVE';

If two devices commit simultaneously against version 3, serializable isolation guarantees that exactly one update affects 1 row and advances the file to version 4, while the second affects 0 rows and returns 412 Precondition Failed. Advance through Interactive Trace 25.A to examine how an offline laptop and phone diverge from version 3 and how the server prevents silent overwrite.

Once the phone receives 412 Precondition Failed, the system must apply a deterministic resolution policy:

  • Last-Write-Wins (LWW): Overwriting version 4 with the phone’s bytes hides the conflict from the user but destroys the laptop’s edits without warning. LWW is unacceptable for general-purpose user files.
  • Conflict-Copy Branching (Default Policy): The phone downloads version 4 into the original path (notes.txt), renames its own diverged local copy to a deterministic conflict path (notes (Phone conflicted copy 2026-10-14).txt), and commits that branch as a brand-new file (version = 1). Both devices converge to holding both files, zero bytes are lost, and the human author decides how to reconcile binary or document edits.
  • Content-Aware Auto-Merge: Possible only for structured formats (plain text, source code, or collaborative rich text documents) where the service understands internal syntax, which is the exact domain of Chapter 26.

Local Client Reconciliation: Tombstones, Renames, and OS Quirks

Dropbox’s engineering postmortem on rewriting its desktop sync engine (Nucleus) highlighted that the hardest correctness invariants live inside the three-tree local reconciliation loop comparing: (1) the Remote Server Tree, (2) the Last-Synced Baseline Tree, and (3) the Current Local Filesystem Tree.

  1. Explicit Tombstones vs. Absence: If a file is missing from the server’s active directory listing, a client comparing only current state cannot distinguish “deleted on another device” from “newly created locally and not yet uploaded.” Recording deletions as explicit TOMBSTONE entries in change_log (and comparing against the Last-Synced Baseline Tree) resolves the ambiguity deterministically.
  2. Metadata-Only Renames and Moves: Moving a 10 GB video between folders updates (parent_dir_id, name) inside files and emits a RENAME entry in change_log without touching the Block Store. Even if a client OS watcher reports a move as separate UNLINK and CREATE events, local FastCDC hashing and namespace_blocks lookup ensure zero payload bytes cross the network.
  3. Cross-Platform Path Collisions: Linux filesystems are case-sensitive (Report.pdf and report.pdf coexist), whereas default macOS APFS and Windows NTFS volumes are case-insensitive. The control plane enforces case-insensitive uniqueness per directory (or automatically renames colliding sync targets with a (Case Conflict) suffix on case-insensitive clients) and strips reserved characters (:, ?, *, trailing spaces on Windows).

Notification Hints Paired with Durable Cursors

We never rely on WebSocket or long-poll notifications to carry authoritative file deltas. A transient edge proxy restart or mobile radio handoff can drop a push frame at any instant. Instead, the Delta Notification Bus delivers ephemeral, loss-tolerant wake-up hints (namespace_id = ns_881 changed). Upon receiving a hint (or upon reconnecting or hitting a low-frequency fallback heartbeat every 5 minutes), the client polls GET /v1/namespaces/{ns}/changes?cursor=<last_seq>. Separating the unreliable signal from the durable cursor keeps the notification tier entirely stateless in memory while guaranteeing zero missed mutations.

Epoch-Safe Garbage Collection for Unreferenced Chunks

Deleting a chunk immediately when a file is modified or removed would corrupt other files sharing that chunk via deduplication and violate the 30-day version-restore contract. Worse, unguarded online reference counting suffers from a classic distributed race: Client A uploads chunk C (refcount 0), the GC sweeper scans C and deletes it before Client A submits its manifest commit PUT /v1/files/7, leaving a dangling manifest pointing to missing bytes.

We eliminate GC races with Two-Phase Epoch Mark-and-Sweep plus Delayed Deletion:

  1. Upload Lease Window: Newly uploaded blocks receive an immutable creation timestamp created_at and are exempt from garbage collection for a mandatory upload grace period (for example, 24 hours), bounding the maximum duration of an in-flight chunked upload.
  2. Offline Mark Phase: A periodic MapReduce/Spark job scans a consistent snapshot of file_versions (including active files and versions/tombstones within the 30-day retention window) and emits the set of live chunk_sha256 digests.
  3. Quarantine and Sweep Phase: Chunks present in the Block Store with created_at < snapshot_time - 24h and absent from the live set are moved to a Delayed Sweep Archive (soft-deleted metadata flag) for 7 additional days before physical erasure-coded stripe reclamation. Any emergency recovery or audit anomaly can halt the physical sweep before irreversible disk deletion occurs.

25.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ScenarioBlast RadiusAutomated Recovery and Preserved Invariant
Client Disconnects Mid-UploadSingle file uploadAlready-uploaded chunks remain durable in the content-addressed Block Store; client resumes by querying chunks:exists and uploading only remaining blocks
Dropped Response to Manifest CommitSingle file commitClient retries PUT /v1/files/{id} with identical If-Match and Idempotency-Key; server detects matching last_idem_key and returns 200 OK without spawning a spurious conflict copy
Two Offline Devices Edit Same FileSingle fileSecond commit receives 412 Precondition Failed; client downloads authoritative version and branches its local edit into a named conflict copy
Notification Edge Pod Crash~100k online socketsClients reconnect with jittered backoff and immediately execute GET /changes?cursor= to recover any missed hints
Metadata Shard Primary FailureWrites to 1/32 of namespaces for 1 to 3 sSynchronous 3-AZ Raft/PostgreSQL standby promotes with zero RPO; clients retry idempotently
Local OS Watcher Overflow (IN_Q_OVERFLOW)Single client deviceSync agent triggers an automatic Merkle tree diff against local SQLite state and server root hash to detect missed filesystem edits
GC Sweeper Races with Slow UploadUncommitted chunk24 h upload grace period plus 7 d Delayed Sweep Archive quarantine prevents premature deletion of live or in-flight blocks

Synchronization SLIs and SLOs

Four domain-specific Service Level Indicators track synchronization health beyond standard HTTP status codes:

  1. End-to-End Sync Propagation Latency (p95, p99): Measured via synthetic canary pairs modifying a 100 KB file in Region A and recording when the peer agent in Region B finishes the atomic local rename(). SLO: p99 <= 5 s.
  2. Delta Deduplication Efficiency Ratio: 1 - (bytes_uploaded / total_modified_file_bytes) tracked per client version. A sudden drop exposes rolling-hash regressions or misaligned chunk parameters.
  3. Spurious Conflict Rate: Percentage of manifest commits returning 412 where the client and server manifest_sha256 values are identical (indicating broken retry idempotency or local clock/watcher bugs). Target: < 0.001%.
  4. Quiescent Tree Convergence Invariant: Periodic Merkle-root comparison between simulated multi-device test fleets and server state; any persistent root mismatch after 30 s of network quiescence triggers a release-blocking SEV-1 failure.

How Production Systems Implement File Synchronization

Production SystemCore Storage & Metadata ArchitectureArchitectural Distinction
DropboxMagic Pocket (exabyte erasure-coded block store), Edgestore (sharded MySQL metadata), Nucleus (Rust client sync engine)Uses 4 MB fixed blocks paired with rsync-style binary delta transfers for modified blocks; migrated its client engine to Rust to verify three-tree state machine invariants formally
Google DriveColossus distributed filesystem, Spanner globally consistent metadata, Drive Push Notification channelsStrongly consistent global metadata via TrueTime; unifies opaque binary sync with native Google Docs OT co-editing under one namespace ACL graph
Apple iCloud DriveCloudKit metadata zones + multi-cloud chunked asset storage (ChunkEngine)Uses content-defined chunking and client-side per-file encryption keys wrapped in user-specific keybags, trading cross-tenant deduplication for strong privacy
SyncthingDecentralized peer-to-peer Block Exchange Protocol (BEP) over TLS/QUICEliminates the central metadata server completely by exchanging vector clocks and per-folder block indexes directly between devices, branching conflicts identically via timestamped copies

25.7 Simulation Verification

Running code/syncsim verifies both core invariants of this chapter: (1) FastCDC boundary stability under a single-byte prepend to a 65,536-byte file compared against fixed 1,024-byte slicing, and (2) atomic optimistic concurrency conflict detection when two offline devices commit against base version 3.

$ cargo run --release -p syncsim
a file of 65536 bytes, and the same file with 1 byte added at the start
cuts every 1024 bytes: 65 chunks, 65 to upload again
cuts that depend on the content: 62 chunks, 1 to upload again
the server holds version 3. the laptop and the phone both change it while offline
laptop uploads, based on version 3: accepted as version 4
phone uploads, based on version 3: conflict: the server is at version 4, written by the laptop

Inspect the observed ratio directly: prepending 1 byte invalidates 65 / 65 (100%) of fixed-offset chunks, whereas content-defined chunking isolates the mutation to 1 / 62 (1.6%) of chunks, reducing WAN upload bandwidth by 98.4%. On the control plane, the laptop’s conditional upload based on version 3 commits cleanly as version 4, and the phone’s subsequent upload carrying base version 3 is deterministically flagged as a conflict against version 4.

Run the file synchronization simulation. Execute cargo run --release -p syncsim in code/ to reproduce the fixed-block vs. content-defined chunking comparison (65/65 vs. 1/62 dirty chunks) and the offline version-3 optimistic concurrency conflict trace.

25.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Content-Addressed Storage (CAS)Storage model in which every immutable block is addressed by the cryptographic hash (SHA-256) of its contents, enabling automatic deduplication and idempotent retries.
Content-Defined Chunking (CDC)Slicing a byte stream at positions where a rolling hash over a sliding window matches a fixed bitmask, preventing insertions from shifting downstream chunk boundaries.
FastCDCHigh-throughput CDC algorithm combining a table-driven Gear rolling hash, minimum-length cut skipping, and normalized dual-mask chunking.
Merkle Directory TreeHierarchical hash tree where file leaves hash their version and manifest digest and directories hash their sorted children, enabling O(K log N) full-tree diffing.
Optimistic Concurrency (If-Match)Conditional metadata update that succeeds only when the server’s current version matches the client’s declared base version, turning concurrent writes into explicit conflicts.
Conflict-Copy BranchingConflict resolution policy that preserves the winning revision under the original path and saves the rejected concurrent revision under a disambiguated sibling filename.
Monotonic Change CursorPer-namespace strictly increasing sequence number allowing online and long-offline clients to fetch every missed metadata transition via one paginated feed.
TombstoneExplicit metadata record representing a file deletion so offline clients distinguish remote deletions from newly created local files and can restore deleted items during a retention window.

  • A. Tridgell and P. Mackerras, “The rsync algorithm”, Australian National University Technical Report TR-CS-96-05, 1996.

Chapter 26: Collaborative Editing

A real-time collaborative document editor allows dozens of authors to modify the same text simultaneously, rendering each author’s own keystrokes instantaneously while streaming remote edits and live cursor positions across all participants within a fraction of a second. In Chapter 25, we handled concurrent offline edits to opaque files by branching a conflict copy and deferring resolution to a human user. In a live co-editing session, concurrent edits occur dozens of times per minute whenever two authors type within one network round-trip time of each other. Presenting manual conflict copies on every keystroke is unworkable; the editor must merge concurrent operations automatically while preserving every participant’s intent and guaranteeing that every replica converges to the exact same byte sequence. In this chapter, I design a collaborative editing architecture built around local-first execution, Operational Transformation and Sequence CRDTs, sticky document gateways, and snapshot-compacted operation logs.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, functional and non-functional requirements, non-goals, and multi-million-session capacity bounds
  • document hydration APIs, WebSocket operation and state-vector sync protocols, ACL enforcement, and append-only operation log schemas
  • control-plane session coordination and fencing epochs separated from sticky collaboration gateways, presence buses, and snapshot compaction
  • positional divergence, Jupiter server-serialized Operational Transformation, and causal Sequence CRDTs (RGA, YATA, and Fugue) versus fractional indexing
  • tombstone retention, epoch-based garbage collection, server-compacted snapshots with operation log tails, ephemeral carets, and selective local undo
  • failure recovery matrices, convergence SLIs, production architectures (Google Docs, Figma, Yjs, Automerge), and simulation verification via code/editsim

26.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Building a responsive collaborative editor creates an unavoidable distributed systems tension. Human perception detects typing lag above 16 to 50 ms, which forbids waiting for a 50 to 200 ms wide-area round trip to a central coordinator before painting a character on screen. Every client must therefore apply local edits immediately to its own in-memory replica and propagate deltas asynchronously. Once every client accepts uncoordinated writes, replicas apply the same set of operations in different arrival orders. The central engineering invariant is Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC): any two replicas that have received the same set of operations must hold identical document state, regardless of delivery order or duplicate transmission.

Actors and Use Cases

Three actor roles interact across the collaborative editing boundary (Figure 26-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Co-Author BrowserApply concurrent edits (WS /v1/docs/{id}/ops) and stream ephemeral presenceTwo engineers edit separate paragraphs of a design doc while seeing each other’s colored carets and selections move live
Offline Mobile EditorBuffer local edits offline and reconcile on reconnectA reviewer edits a document on a commuter train for 40 minutes, then exchanges a compact state vector on reconnect to merge missed remote ops
Document AdminEnforce sharing ACLs (PATCH /v1/docs/{id}/permissions) and restore historical snapshotsAn owner revokes write access from a former contractor mid-session and rolls a corrupted section back to revision 4400

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0Up to 100 concurrent authors can edit the same document simultaneously without locking paragraphs or manually merging conflicts.
1Each author’s own keystrokes render locally in under 16 ms without waiting for server acknowledgement.
2Edits committed by one online author propagate and render on all other connected authors’ screens within 200 ms.
3Once all operations are delivered, every participant’s replica converges to an identical document state regardless of arrival order.
4Connected authors observe live remote cursor positions, text selections, and active collaborator presence.
5An author working offline can continue editing uninterrupted and automatically merge buffered local operations upon reconnection.
6Authorized users can inspect immutable document revision history and restore any prior snapshot cleanly.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0ConvergenceStrong Eventual Consistency (SEC) across all replicas with zero permanent state divergenceMathematical commutativity and idempotency via Sequence CRDTs (or server-serialized Jupiter OT)
1DurabilityZero loss of any server-acknowledged operation under single-node or AZ failureAppend-only operation log replicated synchronously across 3 AZs before acknowledging to the sender
2ConsistencyEventual between client replicas; linearizable for server log ordering, ACL revocations, and gateway ownership leasesSticky document ownership fenced by monotonic lease epochs from a consensus-backed Session Coordinator
3LatencyLocal apply < 16 ms (60 Hz frame budget); remote fanout p99 <= 200 ms; cold document open p99 <= 400 msSticky in-memory gateway pods eliminate cross-pod hops; periodic binary snapshots cap cold-open replay length
4Scale10M concurrently open documents, 20M open WebSocket sessions, up to 100 co-authors per documentPartitioned WebSocket gateways + sticky doc_id routing + client-side 50 to 100 ms micro-batching of keystrokes

Non-Goals and Out-of-Scope Boundaries

We exclude four concerns from the scope of this architecture:

  • Arbitrary opaque binary synchronization: Large media files, archives, and disk images lack fine-grained merge semantics and belong to the content-addressed chunk sync pipeline in Chapter 25.
  • Serverless peer-to-peer WebRTC mesh topology: Pure client-to-client synchronization without a server authority complicates corporate RBAC enforcement, instant permission revocation, and durable cloud backup.
  • Multi-document ACID transactions: Atomic edits spanning multiple distinct documents simultaneously are excluded; each document is an independent concurrency and consistency domain.
  • Real-time audio and video calling: Media streams use separate RTP/WebRTC SFU infrastructure outside the document operation pipeline.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

Collaborative editing is bounded by in-memory working sets across sticky session servers, WebSocket fanout bandwidth, and sustained append throughput to the operation log.

Resource DimensionDerivationProvisioned Bound
Concurrent WebSocket Sessions10M open docs * 2 average connected authors20M open sockets (~200 edge/gateway pods at 100k sockets/pod)
Raw Keystroke Generation Rate20M authors * 10% actively typing * 5 keystrokes/s10M raw character edits/s at global peak
Batched Wire Operation RateClient batches keystrokes over 100 ms windows (~5 chars/batch)~2M WebSocket operation frames/s across the fleet
Operation Log Write Bandwidth10M raw ops/s * 30 B (compressed run-length batches reduce to ~60 B per 5-op frame)~120 to 300 MB/s sustained append across 32 log shards (~4 to 10 MB/s per shard)
In-Memory Working Set10M open docs * 50 KB average in-RAM CRDT/text + metadata500 GB aggregate RAM (~300 sticky gateway pods with 4 GB doc heap each, keeping < 50% headroom)
Daily Operation Storage120 MB/s avg * 86,400 s (assuming 40% daily utilization factor)~4.1 TB/day raw op log; compacted snapshots prune stale op tails after retention policy

26.2 External API and Data Contracts

A client opens a document through an HTTP/2 hydration endpoint to fetch the latest compacted snapshot plus the operation tail, then upgrades to a persistent bidirectional WebSocket connection routed to the sticky gateway shard owning that doc_id.

Document Hydration and History Endpoints

GET /v1/docs/doc_8812 HTTP/2
Host: docs.example
Authorization: Bearer tok_author_ada

HTTP/2 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "doc_id": "doc_8812",
  "doc_epoch": 12,
  "snapshot_seq": 4400,
  "head_seq": 4410,
  "state_vector": { "site_1": 1902, "site_2": 2508 },
  "snapshot_b64": "AQIDBAUG...",
  "tail_ops_b64": ["CgsMDQ4P...", "ERITFBUW..."],
  "gateway_ws_url": "wss://gw-shard-07.docs.example/v1/docs/doc_8812/ops?epoch=12"
}

To inspect historical versions or audit authorship, clients query paginated revisions:

GET /v1/docs/doc_8812/operations?after_seq=4400&limit=100 HTTP/2
Host: docs.example
Authorization: Bearer tok_author_ada

PATCH /v1/docs/doc_8812/permissions HTTP/2
Host: docs.example
Authorization: Bearer tok_admin_ada
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "principal_id": "user_bob",
  "role": "VIEWER"
}

Bidirectional WebSocket Sync Protocol

Once connected to wss://gw-shard-07.docs.example/v1/docs/doc_8812/ops, clients and the sticky gateway exchange framed binary (Protobuf or compact varint) messages represented below in JSON for clarity.

1. Offline Reconnection Handshake (State-Vector Exchange):

{
  "type": "SYNC_STEP_1",
  "doc_id": "doc_8812",
  "doc_epoch": 12,
  "state_vector": { "site_1": 1902, "site_2": 2490 }
}

The gateway computes the exact set difference between its current state vector and the client’s vector, streaming only missing operations in SYNC_STEP_2. If the client’s doc_epoch predates a mandatory tombstone garbage-collection epoch (client_epoch < server_min_epoch), the gateway responds with EPOCH_EXPIRED, directing the client to download the latest compacted snapshot and rebase its unacked local edits cleanly.

2. Operation Delta Submission and Idempotent Acknowledgement:

{
  "type": "OP_BATCH",
  "doc_id": "doc_8812",
  "client_op_id": "site_1:1903",
  "doc_epoch": 12,
  "ops": [
    { "kind": "INS", "id": [1903, 1], "origin_left": [1, 1], "origin_right": [2, 1], "text": "h" }
  ]
}

{
  "type": "OP_ACK",
  "doc_id": "doc_8812",
  "client_op_id": "site_1:1903",
  "server_seq": 4412
}

Because every CRDT operation carries a globally unique (lamport_clock, site_id) identifier (client_op_id), retrying an OP_BATCH after a transient socket drop is strictly idempotent: both the gateway’s in-memory CRDT state and the durable operation log ignore already-applied identifiers and replay the matching OP_ACK.

3. Ephemeral Presence and Cursor Update:

{
  "type": "PRESENCE",
  "author_id": "user_ada",
  "anchor_id": [1903, 1],
  "head_id": [1903, 1],
  "color": "#2563eb"
}

Presence frames bypass the durable operation log entirely and are fanned out in memory to peer sockets with throttling (<= 10 Hz per client).

Durable Storage Schema

We separate high-frequency sequential appends (doc_operations) from periodic compressed checkpoints (doc_snapshots) and access control rules (doc_acls).

CREATE TABLE documents (
    doc_id             TEXT        PRIMARY KEY,
    doc_epoch          BIGINT      NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    min_valid_epoch    BIGINT      NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    latest_snapshot_seq BIGINT     NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    head_seq           BIGINT      NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    updated_at         TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE doc_operations (
    doc_id             TEXT        NOT NULL,
    server_seq         BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    client_op_id       TEXT        NOT NULL,
    author_id          TEXT        NOT NULL,
    payload_bytes      BYTEA       NOT NULL,
    created_at         TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (doc_id, server_seq),
    UNIQUE (doc_id, client_op_id)
);

CREATE TABLE doc_snapshots (
    doc_id             TEXT        NOT NULL,
    snapshot_seq       BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    doc_epoch          BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    state_vector_json  JSONB       NOT NULL,
    object_store_uri   TEXT        NOT NULL,
    byte_size          INT         NOT NULL,
    created_at         TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (doc_id, snapshot_seq)
);

CREATE TABLE doc_acls (
    doc_id             TEXT        NOT NULL,
    principal_id       TEXT        NOT NULL,
    role               TEXT        NOT NULL, -- 'OWNER' | 'EDITOR' | 'VIEWER'
    acl_version        BIGINT      NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    PRIMARY KEY (doc_id, principal_id)
);

26.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

To keep remote edit fanout under 200 ms while enforcing live access control and durable persistence, we divide the platform into a consensus-backed Control Plane managing ownership leases and permissions, and a sticky, memory-first Data Plane executing delta merges and fanout (Figure 26-2).

Component Responsibilities and Failure Domains

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Recovery
Local CRDT Client EngineEdgeFull document CRDT state, local undo stack, IndexedDB offline op queueBrowser crash or network drop preserves unsent edits in IndexedDB; reconnect triggers state-vector sync
Session CoordinatorControlConsistent hash ring + consensus-backed doc_id -> (gateway_pod, lease_epoch) mapReplicated across 3 AZs (etcd/Consul/ZooKeeper); revokes expired gateway heartbeats within 5 s and assigns a new fenced owner
ACL and Auth ServiceControldoc_acls table and permission invalidation topicLive role downgrade (EDITOR -> VIEWER) pushes an immediate revocation event to the owning gateway pod to reject further write frames
Sticky Collaboration GatewaysDataIn-memory merged CRDT state and open WebSockets for assigned doc_idsPod crash drops sockets for its assigned documents; clients reconnect (1 to 3 s) to the newly elected owner pod hydrated from snapshot + op-log tail
Presence and Pub/Sub BusDataEphemeral caret, selection, and cross-AZ relay subscriptions (no disk persistence)Pod loss drops transient cursor frames; clients re-emit presence automatically on the next heartbeat or pointer move
Append-Only Operation LogDataDurable doc_operations partitioned by doc_id across 3-AZ synchronous replicasPrimary log shard failover takes 1 to 3 s with zero loss of acknowledged edits; lease fencing tokens block stale gateway writes
Snapshot Compactor & Object StoreDataPeriodic compressed CRDT snapshots (doc_snapshots + S3/GCS blobs)Stateless background workers resume compaction from latest_snapshot_seq; failure only increases tail replay length temporarily

End-to-End Operation Path

  1. Zero-Latency Local Apply: Author A types h. The client CRDT engine inserts the character locally in < 1 ms, renders the frame within the 16 ms budget, buffers the delta in IndexedDB, and flushes an OP_BATCH over its open WebSocket to the sticky gateway owning doc_8812.
  2. ACL Check and Lease-Fenced Durability: Gateway Pod A verifies Author A’s live EDITOR role, merges the delta into its in-memory CRDT state, and appends the payload to the 3-AZ doc_operations log tagged with its active lease_epoch fencing token.
  3. Acknowledgement and Low-Latency Fanout: Once the 3-AZ log confirms durability, Gateway Pod A returns OP_ACK to Author A and immediately broadcasts the delta over in-memory WebSockets to Author B and all other connected editors on the same shard.
  4. Asynchronous Compaction: After 500 new operations (or 60 s of active editing), the Snapshot Compactor folds the latest snapshot plus the op-log tail into a new binary checkpoint in object storage and advances latest_snapshot_seq.

26.4 Why Positional Edits Diverge: Operational Transformation vs. Sequence CRDTs

Representing a document edit by an integer array index (insert('h', 1) or delete(3)) works only inside a single-writer editor where no concurrent operation can shift indices while an edit is in flight. When two co-authors edit concurrently without coordination, integer indices go stale immediately. Advance through Interactive Trace 26.A to observe how concurrent positional edits by Ada and Bob against "cat" diverge permanently into "chast" and "chats".

Two distinct algorithmic families resolve positional divergence: Operational Transformation (OT), which keeps integer indices and rewrites incoming operations to compensate for concurrent shifts, and Sequence CRDTs, which replace mutable integer indices with immutable globally ordered identifiers.

Operational Transformation and the Jupiter Architecture

In OT, a transformation function T(op_a, op_b) -> op_a' adjusts op_a so that applying op_a' after op_b produces the same document state as applying op_b' after op_a. In the "cat" trace, transforming Bob’s Ins('s', 3) against Ada’s concurrent Ins('h', 1) shifts Bob’s target index right by 1 to Ins('s', 4), yielding "chats" on both replicas.

Ensuring convergence across arbitrary peer-to-peer networks requires every transformation pair to satisfy two mathematical laws:

  • TP1 (Convergence Property 1): Applying op_a followed by T(op_b, op_a) produces the exact same state as applying op_b followed by T(op_a, op_b).
  • TP2 (Convergence Property 2): Transforming a third operation op_c against (op_a, T(op_b, op_a)) yields the exact same transformed operation as transforming op_c against (op_b, T(op_a, op_b)).

Designing rich-text OT functions that satisfy TP2 across arbitrary deletion ranges, formatting spans, and table mutations proved notoriously error-prone; formal model checkers later uncovered subtle divergence bugs in multiple published decentralized OT algorithms.

Production OT systems (beginning with Xerox PARC’s Jupiter in 1995 and adopted by Google Docs) bypass TP2 entirely through an architectural constraint: every operation routes through a single central server that fixes a linear total order. Each client synchronizes exclusively with the server rather than directly with peers, maintaining at most one unacknowledged operation batch in flight while buffering subsequent keystrokes locally. Because transformations occur strictly along a 2-dimensional client-versus-server grid, only TP1 is required. The trade-off is structural: OT depends on the central server to serialize revisions and requires re-transforming every queued edit against the entire missed server log when an offline client reconnects.

Sequence CRDTs: Immutable Identifiers and Causal Broadcast

Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) eliminate transformation functions altogether by replacing volatile array offsets with immutable, globally unique character identifiers. Because an insertion references immutable identifiers rather than mutable integer positions, concurrent insertions commute natively: applying op_1 then op_2 yields the exact same sequence as applying op_2 then op_1. Step through Interactive Trace 26.B to see how immutable character names remove position drift.

While the intuition of assigning dense numeric keys between neighbors is clear, production Sequence CRDTs diverge sharply in how they construct identifiers. Comparing fractional indexing against causal position identifiers exposes two critical production pathologies:

  1. Fractional Indexing (Logoot / LSEQ / Treedoc): Assigns each character a variable-length path drawn from a dense totally ordered space (for example, inserting between 10 and 20 picks 15; inserting between 15 and 16 appends another digit level 15.5). Two weaknesses limit fractional indexing in long-lived text documents:
    • Unbounded Identifier Growth: Repeated insertions at the same cursor (such as prepending lines at the top of a log) deepen path arrays linearly with edit count, inflating per-character metadata.
    • Character Interleaving Anomaly: As demonstrated by Kleppmann et al. (PaPoC 2019), if Ada types "hello" and Bob concurrently types "world" at the exact same position in a fractional-indexing CRDT, their independently chosen fractional keys can fall between each other, garbling the converged text into "hweolrllod".
  2. Causal Position Identifiers (RGA, YATA, and Fugue): Instead of dense numerical coordinates, modern Sequence CRDTs identify every character by a fixed-size Lamport pair (lamport_clock, site_id) and specify its position by referencing immutable causal anchors: the existing character immediately to its left (origin_left), and in YATA and Fugue, the character immediately to its right (origin_right) at the moment of insertion (Figure 26-3).

In RGA (Replicated Growable Array), concurrent siblings sharing the same origin_left are ordered in descending (lamport_clock, site_id) order. Because each author’s sequential keystrokes chain off their own preceding character ('e' anchors after 'h', 'l' after 'e'), typing "hello" and "world" concurrently keeps each author’s contiguous run intact ("worldhello" or "helloworld"). YATA (used in Yjs) adds origin_right to eliminate additional edge cases, and Fugue (Weidner and Kleppmann, 2023) extends the tree-based left/right origin rule to eliminate backward interleaving (when authors type right-to-left or insert at the start of a paragraph) as well as forward interleaving.

Causal Sequence CRDTs require causal delivery: an insertion referencing origin_left = (1, 1) cannot be integrated until (1, 1) exists locally. The client engine enforces this via per-site state vectors ({ site_1: max_clock_1, site_2: max_clock_2 }), buffering any out-of-order delta in a small pending queue until its causal predecessor arrives. Furthermore, to avoid storing 24 to 32 bytes of metadata per 1-byte ASCII character, production engines (Yjs and Automerge) apply run-length encoding: a contiguous burst of 80 characters typed sequentially by one author is stored as a single struct with one starting (clock, site_id), one origin_left, and a string length of 80, splitting the block only if a later edit inserts or deletes inside the middle of the run.

Comparing Central-Server OT and Causal Sequence CRDTs

Architectural DimensionCentral-Server OT (Jupiter)Causal Sequence CRDT (YATA / Fugue)
Position AddressingVolatile integer offsets adjusted on arrivalImmutable causal anchors (lamport_clock, site_id)
Convergence MechanismServer total order + TP1 transformation pairsCommutative, associative, idempotent merge rules
Offline & Local-First ErgonomicsHard: long offline queues require expensive server-side re-transformation on reconnectNative: offline edits merge cleanly in any order via compact state-vector sync
Memory & Metadata FootprintVery low (~1x raw text size; no tombstones required in live state)Moderate (~1.5x to 3x raw text with run-length encoding; grows with tombstones)
Core Engineering ComplexityProving TP1 correctness across rich-text formatting, tables, and undoTombstone garbage collection, columnar binary compaction, and causal buffering
Typical Production FitAlways-online web suites with complex rich-text schemas (Google Docs)Offline-capable local-first apps, developer tools, and distributed workspaces (Yjs, Linear, Zed, Automerge)

26.5 Tombstones, Garbage Collection Epochs, Presence, Undo, and Log Compaction

Operating a Sequence CRDT across millions of long-lived documents requires solving four lifecycle problems beyond initial convergence.

Tombstones and Server-Coordinated GC Epochs

When Author A deletes character (1, 1) concurrently while offline Author B inserts (5, 2) with origin_left = (1, 1), physically removing (1, 1) from Author A’s memory would leave Author B’s incoming operation referencing a nonexistent anchor and break convergence. A CRDT therefore marks deleted characters as tombstones: hidden from the visible text buffer, yet retained in the structural index (often stripped of their character payload so only (id, length, deleted=true) metadata remains).

Over months of heavy editing in a living engineering specification, tombstones can outnumber visible characters by 10x to 50x, inflating memory consumption and document load times. In a purely peer-to-peer system where an unknown offline device might reappear two years later, safe tombstone deletion is undecidable without global causal stability tracking. Because our architecture uses a central sticky gateway and durable log, we bound tombstone growth cleanly using GC Epochs:

  1. During periodic snapshot compaction, the Snapshot Compactor identifies tombstones older than a configured retention horizon (for example, 30 days) whose causal dependencies are fully closed across all non-deleted siblings.
  2. The Compactor writes a new compacted snapshot stripping those expired tombstones, bumps doc_epoch (12 -> 13), and advances min_valid_epoch once all active gateways roll over.
  3. Any mobile client reconnecting after 45 days offline sends doc_epoch = 11 < min_valid_epoch. The gateway rejects direct delta merge with EPOCH_EXPIRED, transmits the fresh epoch = 13 snapshot, and the client computes a deterministic diff of its unacknowledged offline edits against the fresh snapshot before submitting them as fresh epoch = 13 operations.

Snapshot Compaction and Operation Log Tail

Replaying 500,000 individual keystrokes every time a user opens a mature document violates the 400 ms cold-open SLO. We combine an immutable append-only operation log (for zero-loss durability and complete revision history) with periodic binary snapshots stored in object storage:

  • Every 500 appended operations (or after 60 s of active mutations), the Snapshot Compactor hydrates the prior snapshot, applies the incremental tail, serializes the resulting CRDT state using columnar run-length delta encoding (where clocks, site IDs, lengths, and UTF-8 text sit in separate compressed byte streams), and writes the checkpoint to S3/GCS.
  • Opening a document requires exactly one object-store fetch plus replaying at most 500 recent operations (< 20 ms CPU time), keeping cold-open latency constant regardless of total document age.

Ephemeral Presence, Selective Local Undo, and Semantic Limits

Three user-facing mechanics require specialized treatment in multi-author sessions:

  1. Anchored Ephemeral Carets: Caret and selection updates are transient and never written to disk; losing a cursor update matters for 50 ms until the next pointer event arrives. Each remote caret binds to an immutable CRDT character identifier (clock, site_id) rather than a raw integer offset so concurrent insertions upstream never misplace another author’s visible cursor.
  2. Selective Local Undo: Reversing the globally most recent operation in a shared document would undo a teammate’s typing unexpectedly. Each client therefore maintains a per-author undo stack recording only its own operations. Invoking Undo on a CRDT does not delete history; it emits a new compensating operation (marking the author’s previously inserted range as tombstoned, or re-inserting previously deleted content at its original causal anchors) while preserving intervening edits made by peers.
  3. Convergence Is Syntactic, Not Semantic: Mathematical convergence guarantees that every replica ends with identical bytes, not that the combined prose matches human intent. If Ada and Bob simultaneously fix the typo "teh" by deleting it and retyping "the", both replicas converge cleanly to "thethe". Collaborative editors rely on low-latency colored presence carets as a social coordination layer so co-authors naturally avoid editing the exact same word at the exact same instant.

Collaborative Editing SLIs and SLOs

  1. Local Input-to-Paint Latency: p99 <= 16 ms measured via browser PerformanceObserver around local CRDT apply and DOM layout.
  2. Remote Edit Fanout Latency (E2E): Measured from Author A’s WebSocket send timestamp to Author B’s remote render timestamp across regions; SLO: p99 <= 200 ms.
  3. Document Hydration Latency: Time from GET /v1/docs/{id} to interactive editable state; SLO: p99 <= 400 ms (alerts if average uncompacted op-log tail exceeds 1,000 ops).
  4. Replica Convergence Integrity Check: Gateways periodically broadcast a lightweight rolling state hash (Merkle/XOR checksum of visible text) alongside heartbeat frames; any client whose quiescent text hash disagrees with the gateway triggers an immediate telemetry alert and automated state-vector resync.

26.7 Simulation Verification

Running code/editsim directly compares unadjusted positional edits against Operational Transformation and CRDT identifier ordering on the canonical "cat" concurrent-edit workload (ada inserts h at 1; bob inserts s at 3), followed by a concurrent same-position insertion tie-break test.

$ cargo run --release -p editsim
both start from "cat". ada puts h at 1, bob puts s at 3
changes applied as they are:     ada sees "chast", bob sees "chats"
positions adjusted:              ada sees "chats", bob sees "chats"
a name for every character:      ada sees "chats", bob sees "chats"
both type between a and t:       ada sees "carnt", bob sees "carnt"

The simulation transcript confirms three exact properties: applying raw positional offsets without coordination causes permanent replica divergence ("chast" vs. "chats"); transforming concurrent indices (OT) and assigning immutable character identifiers (CRDT) both achieve exact convergence to "chats" regardless of delivery order; and deterministic (clock, site_id) tie-breaking resolves concurrent insertions at the exact same boundary identically ("carnt") on every replica.

Run the collaborative editing simulation. Execute cargo run --release -p editsim in code/ to verify raw positional divergence (chast vs. chats), Operational Transformation convergence, Sequence CRDT commutativity, and deterministic tie-breaking (carnt).

26.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC)Convergence guarantee stating that any two replicas having received the same set of operations hold identical state, regardless of arrival order or duplicates.
Operational Transformation (OT)Concurrency control technique that rewrites incoming positional operations against concurrent intervening edits before applying them.
Jupiter ProtocolClient-server OT architecture in which a central server fixes a single total revision order, eliminating the need for decentralized TP2 transformations.
Sequence CRDTConflict-free replicated list data structure whose insert and delete operations commute natively using immutable identifiers rather than mutable array indices.
RGA / YATA / FugueCausal Sequence CRDT algorithms anchoring each inserted element to immutable neighbor identifiers (lamport_clock, site_id) to prevent character interleaving.
State VectorCompact map { site_id -> max_clock } summarizing all causal operations observed by a replica, used to compute minimal delta diffs on reconnection.
TombstoneHidden deletion marker preserved in a CRDT structure so concurrent operations referencing the deleted element’s identifier can still locate their anchor.
GC EpochMonotonic server-managed compaction generation allowing expired tombstones to be stripped safely while forcing ancient offline clients to rebase cleanly.

Chapter 27: Stock Exchange

An electronic stock exchange matches buyers and sellers of financial instruments under strict legal rules governing fairness, auditability, and microsecond latency. Whenever an incoming buy limit price meets or exceeds the lowest resting sell price, the central matching engine executes a trade immediately and disseminates the resulting book update to every market participant simultaneously. Unlike web services that scale horizontally by distributing requests across stateless thread pools backed by relational databases, an electronic exchange achieves sub-100-microsecond tail latency through the opposite pattern: every symbol’s limit order book runs inside a single deterministic thread pinned to an isolated CPU core, holding all state in pre-allocated memory with zero locks and zero database calls on the critical path. In this chapter, I design a low-latency stock exchange covering binary order entry, pre-trade risk enforcement, intrusive O(1) order book data structures, LMAX Disruptor ring buffers, and active-passive deterministic standby replication.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, verifiable functional and non-functional requirements, non-goals, and trading-day capacity bounds
  • binary SBE/OUCH order entry wire layouts, UDP multicast L3 market data frames, control-plane risk APIs, and order idempotency contracts
  • control-plane surveillance and risk limits separated from the zero-allocation deterministic matching data plane and microsecond latency budgets
  • price-time priority limit order book mechanics and intrusive doubly-linked-list data structures delivering O(1) cancellations with zero heap allocation
  • single-threaded mechanical sympathy, cache-line-padded LMAX Disruptor ring buffers, pre-trade risk enforcement, and deterministic active-passive standby failover via replicated sequencer journals
  • failure recovery matrices, exchange SLIs, production architectures (LMAX, Nasdaq, IEX, CME Globex), and simulation verification via code/matchsim

27.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Financial exchanges operate under three regulatory and physical constraints that dictate every downstream architectural choice. First, price-time priority is legally enforceable: among two resting orders at the same price, the order accepted earlier by the exchange must execute first without ambiguity. Second, wire-to-wire determinism is mandatory: regulators and surveillance teams must be able to replay the exchange’s input log bit-for-bit after market close and reconstruct the exact book state and trade sequence at any microsecond. Third, algorithmic trading firms compete on single-digit microseconds, meaning tail-latency jitter from garbage collection, OS scheduling, mutex contention, or disk fsync directly degrades market quality.

Actors and Use Cases

Three external actors interact across the electronic stock exchange boundary (Figure 27-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Trading Firm / BrokerSubmit, modify, and cancel orders over persistent binary FIX/SBE sessionsA co-located market maker submits NewOrderSingle (BUY 50 ACME @ 1005), cancels stale quotes in < 50 us, and receives ExecutionReport fills
Market Data SubscriberConsume real-time L2/L3 order book deltas via UDP multicastInstitutional algorithms reconstruct the live order book locally from sequenced multicast packets and recover dropped frames via TCP replay
Clearing and SurveillanceAudit trades, enforce risk limits/kill switches, and settle cash/shares (T+1)Exchange operators configure firm credit caps, halt a volatile symbol via circuit breaker, and forward drop-copy fills to clearing houses (DTCC)

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0Authorized firms can submit limit orders (BUY or SELL integer quantity at an integer tick price), market orders, and Immediate-or-Cancel (IOC) orders for any listed symbol.
1Authorized firms can cancel or reduce any open resting order that has not yet been completely filled.
2Incoming aggressive orders match against resting opposite-side orders strictly by price-time priority (best price first; earliest sequence number first at equal price).
3Every trade executes at the price of the passive resting order in the book, with any unfilled remainder of a limit order resting in the book at its limit price.
4Every incoming order passes pre-trade risk validation (credit cap, fat-finger price collar, rate limit, and firm kill-switch check) before mutating any order book.
5Every order book addition, modification, cancellation, and trade execution publishes a sequenced L3 market data delta simultaneously to all subscribers.
6Every executed trade streams asynchronously to drop-copy clearing pipelines and an immutable regulatory audit journal.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0FairnessUnambiguous global total order per matching partition independent of client or gateway wall clocksSingle authoritative sequencer assigns monotonic seq_id and exchange_ts_ns; equalized physical ingress fiber paths
1DeterminismBit-exact reproducible state machine across primary, standby, and post-close regulatory replayZero wall-clock reads inside matching loop, zero randomness, integer fixed-point ticks, single-threaded execution

3DurabilityZero loss of any sequenced input command or executed trade across single-host failureReplicated append-only sequencer journal across 3 nodes in 2 availability zones prior to external fill acknowledgement
4Availability99.99% uptime during trading hours (6.5 h/day); automatic failover < 50 msActive-passive deterministic hot standby continuously replaying the live journal in lockstep
5ConsistencyStrict linearizability: exactly one authoritative order book exists per symbol at any instantSymbol-sharded single-threaded matching cores with lease-fenced sequencer leadership

Non-Goals and Out-of-Scope Boundaries

Four surrounding financial systems sit outside this core matching architecture:

  • Post-trade T+1 netting, cash ledger, and bank settlement: Multilateral clearing (DTCC/NSCC) and double-entry monetary accounting operate asynchronously downstream using the exact transactional ledger architecture designed in Chapter 19.
  • Retail brokerage web/mobile portals: End-user authentication, order routing, and portfolio dashboards belong to broker-dealer front ends that aggregate retail orders before connecting to exchange gateways.
  • Multi-leg options and implied cross-symbol spreads: Complex derivatives matching requires combinatorial cross-book solvers outside single-symbol price-time matching.
  • Dark-pool hidden midpoint pegs: Non-displayed midpoint matching introduces distinct regulatory order-type rules omitted here to keep the displayed L3 limit book crystal clear.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

An electronic exchange is constrained by single-core instruction cache efficiency, microsecond network/journal tail latency, and market-open burst absorption, rather than raw disk capacity.

Resource DimensionDerivationProvisioned Bound
Daily Order & Cancel Volume500M messages across a 6.5 h (23,400 s) trading session (~92% cancels/updates)~21,370 avg msgs/s
Market-Open / Close Peak Burst10x to 25x average burst during opening auction and macro announcements~215,000 to 500,000 peak msgs/s exchange-wide

Total In-RAM Resting Order Pool5,000 symbols * 10,000 resting orders * 64 B per OrderNode~3.2 GB RAM total (~320 MB per matching shard; fits largely in L3 cache)
Market Data Multicast Bandwidth500,000 peak L3 deltas/s * 64 B wire frame (plus UDP/IP headers)~55 MB/s (~440 Mbps) easily carried on 10 GbE / 25 GbE multicast fabric

27.2 External API and Data Contracts

HTTP/1.1 and JSON introduce millisecond-scale overhead from TLS framing, text parsing, dynamic string allocation, and garbage collection. Production exchanges therefore run compact binary protocols over persistent kernel-bypass TCP sessions on the hot order-entry path, while reserving standard REST/JSON strictly for the low-frequency control plane.

Hot-Path Binary Wire Contracts (SBE / OUCH Style)

Every message uses Simple Binary Encoding (SBE) (standardized by the FIX Trading Community) or Nasdaq OUCH fixed-layout little-endian structs. Because every field occupies a fixed byte offset with zero optional heap allocations, the gateway decodes an incoming frame via a single bounds-checked pointer cast in under 100 nanoseconds. Monetary prices are strictly signed 64-bit integer ticks (price_ticks = 1005 represents $10.05 at $0.01 tick size), eliminating IEEE-754 floating-point comparison errors.

// Fixed 64-byte SBE NewOrderSingle frame (Order Entry -> Gateway -> Sequencer)
struct __attribute__((packed)) SbeNewOrder {
    uint16_t block_length;    // Fixed payload size (56 bytes)
    uint16_t template_id;     // 1 = NewOrderSingle
    uint32_t firm_id;         // Authenticated trading firm identifier
    uint64_t cl_ord_id;       // Caller-supplied idempotency key (unique per firm/session)
    uint32_t symbol_id;       // Dense integer symbol index (e.g., 42 = ACME)
    uint8_t  side;            // 1 = BUY, 2 = SELL
    uint8_t  ord_type;        // 1 = LIMIT, 2 = MARKET
    uint8_t  tif;             // 0 = DAY, 3 = IOC, 4 = FOK
    uint8_t  reserved;
    int64_t  price_ticks;     // Integer minor units (1005 = 10.05)
    uint64_t quantity;        // Whole share count (> 0)
    uint64_t seq_id;          // Populated strictly by Sequencer (0 on wire ingress)
    uint64_t exchange_ts_ns;  // Populated strictly by Sequencer (monotonic epoch ns)
};

// Fixed 48-byte SBE CancelOrder frame
struct __attribute__((packed)) SbeCancelOrder {
    uint16_t block_length;    // 40 bytes
    uint16_t template_id;     // 2 = CancelOrder
    uint32_t firm_id;
    uint64_t cl_ord_id;       // Idempotency key of cancel request
    uint64_t orig_order_id;   // Exchange-assigned order_id to cancel
    uint32_t symbol_id;
    uint32_t reserved;
    uint64_t seq_id;          // Populated by Sequencer
    uint64_t exchange_ts_ns;  // Populated by Sequencer
};

// Fixed 64-byte UDP Multicast L3 Market Data Delta (ITCH / MoldUDP64 payload)
struct __attribute__((packed)) MarketDataL3Delta {
    uint64_t seq_id;          // Global partition sequence (detects UDP packet gaps)
    uint64_t exchange_ts_ns;
    uint32_t symbol_id;
    uint8_t  event_type;      // 1=ADD, 2=CANCEL, 3=MODIFY, 4=TRADE
    uint8_t  side;
    uint16_t reserved;
    uint64_t order_id;        // Resting order affected
    int64_t  price_ticks;     // Execution or resting price
    uint64_t qty_delta;       // Filled or cancelled quantity
    int64_t  best_bid_ticks;  // Snapshot of top-of-book post-event
    int64_t  best_ask_ticks;
};

Order Idempotency and Session Recovery Contract

Every trading session maintains a monotonic client message sequence plus a per-session cl_ord_id idempotency key. If a firm’s TCP session drops before it reads an ExecutionReport, the firm reconnects using the same session_id and queries NextExpectedSeqNum (standard FIX/OUCH session recovery). Resubmitting a previously sequenced cl_ord_id returns the cached ExecutionReport without re-entering the matching engine, preventing catastrophic duplicate fills.

Control-Plane Risk and Surveillance API

Low-frequency administrative actions use authenticated REST/JSON over an isolated management network, translating into sequenced control commands injected into the matching pipeline so risk updates themselves remain deterministic on replay:

PUT /v1/risk/firms/firm_22/limits HTTP/2
Host: ctrl.exchange.example
Authorization: Bearer tok_risk_ops
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "max_order_qty": 100000,
  "max_notional_ticks": 5000000000,
  "price_collar_bps": 500,
  "max_orders_per_sec": 10000
}
