27.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

Electronic exchanges enforce a strict architectural boundary between the Control Plane (risk policy configuration, surveillance halts, symbol-to-shard mapping, and emergency kill switches) and the Deterministic Data Plane (kernel-bypass order ingress, pre-trade risk enforcement, total sequencing, in-memory matching, hot standby replication, and multicast dissemination), as illustrated in Figure 27-2.

Notice the deliberate omission of any dynamic L7 load balancer on the hot path. Every trading firm terminates onto a dedicated gateway port over a physically equalized fiber cable so no participant gains a structural hardware latency advantage before the sequencer. Every gateway forwards risk-cleared frames to the single authoritative Sequencer (or per-partition sequencer cluster), and each symbol belongs exclusively to one deterministic Matching Core.

Component Responsibilities and Failure Domains

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Recovery
Risk and Limit ManagerControlAuthoritative firm credit caps, price collars, symbol statusPersisted in 3-AZ relational store; pushes incremental updates asynchronously to Risk Engines and Sequencer
Surveillance and HaltsControlReal-time wash-trade detectors, volatility circuit breakers, kill-switch triggersInjects sequenced HaltSymbol or KillSwitch commands into the journal so primary and standby halt identically
Order Gateway (x16)DataKernel-bypass TCP sessions, FIX/SBE session seq maps, rate-limit token bucketsGateway failure drops its connected firms’ sessions; firms reconnect to backup gateways while resting orders remain intact (or auto-cancel if Cancel-on-Disconnect is enabled)
Pre-Trade Risk EngineDataIn-RAM per-firm open notional exposure, position counters, collar tablesCo-located in-process with gateway (or dedicated pre-sequencer stage); rejects fat-finger or over-limit orders in < 2 us before sequencing
Sequencer and Journal (3-node)DataMonotonic seq_id, replicated append-only binary journal (Aeron Cluster / Raft)Leader crash promotes hot standby sequencer from replicated journal quorum in < 50 ms with zero sequence regression
Matching Core + Hot Standby (x10 pairs)DataFull L3 limit order books for assigned symbol partition in pre-allocated RAMPrimary crash promotes deterministic Hot Standby holding the exact same book state in < 50 ms

27.4 Price-Time Priority Limit Order Book and Intrusive O(1) Data Structures

A limit order book for one symbol comprises two opposing priority queues: the Bid side (buy orders ranked highest price first) and the Ask side (sell orders ranked lowest price first). The gap between the Best Bid and the Best Ask is the spread. Whenever an incoming order’s limit price crosses the spread (buy price >= best ask, or sell price <= best bid), the engine matches against the front of the best opposite price level repeatedly until either the incoming order fills completely or no crossing price levels remain. Every fill trades at the passive resting order’s price, granting price improvement to aggressive orders. Advance through Interactive Trace 27.A to trace seven sequential orders arriving at an empty book and observe exact price-time priority matching.

Designing for 90% Cancellations with Zero Heap Allocation

On real equities exchanges, over 90% of submitted orders are cancelled or modified before ever executing as market makers continuously re-quote around changing prices. Using standard library containers such as std::map<Price, std::deque<Order>> or Rust BTreeMap<i64, VecDeque<Order>> suffers from two severe latency killers: cancelling an order in the middle of a VecDeque takes O(K) linear scan time at busy price levels, and allocating or freeing nodes dynamically triggers allocator lock contention or GC stop-the-world pauses.

Production matching engines combine four cache-resident structures to guarantee O(1) insert at tail, O(1) fill at head, O(1) arbitrary cancel, and zero dynamic allocations:

  1. Pre-Allocated Slab Arena (OrderNode Pool): At startup before market open, the engine allocates one contiguous array of N OrderNode structs (each padded to 64 bytes to occupy one CPU cache line) linked into an intrusive free list. Creating or releasing an order pops or pushes an index in 2 instructions with zero heap calls.
  2. Intrusive Doubly-Linked List per PriceLevel: Each OrderNode directly embeds prev_idx, next_idx, and level_ptr fields. Every PriceLevel maintains head_idx, tail_idx, order_count, and total_qty. Appending a new resting order updates tail_idx in O(1). Filling consumes from head_idx in O(1). Cancelling any order anywhere inside a 5,000-order queue splices prev_idx and next_idx directly in O(1) without scanning a single neighbor.
  3. Flat Open-Addressed OrderMap (order_id -> node_idx): A pre-sized power-of-2 hash table (using Fibonacci hashing and linear probing, kept below 50% load factor) maps order_id directly to its slab index in O(1) (1 cache miss).
  4. Indexed Price-Level Directory (best_bid / best_ask): For symbols trading within a bounded daily circuit-breaker band (+/- 20% around prior close), a dense tick array indexed by (price_ticks - base_tick) combined with a two-level hierarchical uint64_t bitset (__builtin_ctzll / tzcnt hardware instruction) locates the next non-empty price level after a level drains in O(1) (~3 CPU cycles). For wide-range instruments, a compact cache-aligned B-Tree (branching factor 16 to 32) keeps active top-of-book levels hot in L1/L2 cache while maintaining direct cached pointers to best_bid_level and best_ask_level.

Cancel/Replace Priority Rule: Reducing a resting order’s quantity modifies node.qty and level.total_qty in place in O(1) while preserving its time priority in the doubly-linked list. Increasing quantity or changing price must unlink the node and re-insert it at the tail of its target price level (losing time priority) so participants cannot abuse small early orders to reserve front-of-queue slots.

27.5 Single-Threaded Determinism, LMAX Disruptor, Pre-Trade Risk, and Active-Passive Standby

The single most counterintuitive lesson of exchange architecture is that one thread processing a single symbol partition beats a multi-threaded lock-protected book by an order of magnitude while simultaneously guaranteeing regulatory determinism.

Mechanical Sympathy and the LMAX Disruptor Ring Buffer

Executing one limit-order match against an L1/L2-cache-resident intrusive book takes roughly 200 to 800 nanoseconds. Acquiring an uncontended mutex, invalidating dirty cache lines via MESI coherence traffic across processor cores, or suffering a single Linux scheduler context switch costs 1 to 15 microseconds, exceeding the matching computation itself. Worse, OS thread scheduling introduces non-deterministic arrival ordering across locks, making exact replay impossible.

Popularized by LMAX Exchange (Thompson et al., 2011), modern matching engines pass sequenced messages from network/journal I/O threads into the pinned matching thread using a lock-free Disruptor Ring Buffer (Figure 27-3).

Four mechanical sympathy techniques eliminate microsecond jitter on modern x86-64 hardware:

  1. Power-of-2 Pre-Allocated Ring Buffer: Slots are allocated contiguously at startup (capacity = 2^20). Indexing slot seq uses bitwise masking (seq & (capacity - 1)), avoiding expensive integer modulo instructions and enabling hardware L1/L2 stride prefetching.
  2. Cache-Line Padding Against False Sharing: A CPU transfers memory between cores in 64-byte cache lines. If the producer cursor (prod_seq) and matching consumer cursor (match_seq) sit adjacent in memory, every write by the producer invalidates the consumer’s cache line even though they touch different variables (false sharing). Padding each atomic cursor to occupy its own 64-byte (or 128-byte on Intel spatial-prefetcher architectures) cache line eliminates coherence ping-pong.
  3. Single-Writer Principle and Acquire/Release Barriers: Each cursor has exactly one owning writer thread, allowing plain loads/stores paired with lightweight release/acquire memory fences (compiled to zero extra barrier instructions on x86-64 TSO) instead of costly LOCK CMPXCHG atomic read-modify-write loops.
  4. Core Pinning and Busy-Spin Polling: The matching thread is pinned to an isolated physical core (isolcpus, nohz_full, rcu_nocbs kernel boot flags, IRQ affinity moved away) and busy-spins on prod_seq.load(Acquire) with a PAUSE instruction, removing sleep/wake kernel futex latency entirely.

Pre-Trade Risk Controls and Determinism Discipline

Unchecked algorithmic bugs (such as Knight Capital’s $440M 45-minute trading loss in 2012) can destabilize markets within milliseconds. We enforce risk checks in two explicit layers:

  • Pre-Sequencer Risk (Gateway / Risk Stage): Checks session authentication, token-bucket message rate limits, static max order size, gross firm notional limits, and active firm kill-switch status. Rejecting invalid frames before the sequencer prevents flood traffic from polluting the journal or consuming matching CPU cycles.
  • In-Engine Deterministic Risk (Post-Sequencer): Checks invariants that depend on live order book state, specifically dynamic fat-finger price collars (rejecting an aggressive buy priced > 5% above the current reference mid-price), Self-Trade Prevention (STP) (cancelling resting or incoming orders belonging to the same firm_id rather than executing an illegal wash trade), and Limit-Up/Limit-Down (LULD) volatility halts. Because these run inside the single-threaded state machine, primary and standby make bit-identical accept/reject decisions.

Defending strict determinism requires disciplined engineering rules across the matching binary: never call clock_gettime() inside the matching loop (consume exchange_ts_ns exclusively from the sequenced input frame), forbid randomized hash-map seeds (std::collections::HashMap SipHash randomization breaks iteration determinism), ban floating-point arithmetic, and compile with deterministic single-threaded execution.

Deterministic Active-Passive Standby and Market Data Fanout

Holding the order book exclusively in RAM creates no durability risk because the sequenced input journal is the sole source of truth and the order book is a pure deterministic function of that log (State = fold(InitialEmptyBook, Journal)).

To avoid minutes of full-day replay during a mid-day hardware failure, every matching shard runs an isolated Hot Standby on a separate host in a second fault domain (Figure 27-3). Using a low-latency consensus log transport such as Aeron Cluster (Raft over UDP/IPC), the Sequencer replicates every incoming command to both the Primary and Standby journals simultaneously. The Hot Standby runs the exact same matching loop continuously, updating its own in-memory order book in lockstep (~20 to 50 us behind) while keeping its outbound network publisher muted. If the Primary misses heartbeats (or loses its Raft leadership lease), the Hot Standby unmutes its outbound publisher from last_published_seq + 1 and takes over active trading in < 50 ms with zero inconsistent state and zero lost resting orders.

To disseminate market data fairly without allowing a slow TCP subscriber to stall the matching core, the matching engine writes L3 deltas into an outbound ring buffer consumed by separate A/B Redundant UDP Multicast Publishers. Every multicast packet reaches all co-located subscribers within nanoseconds of each other over equal-length switch fanout. Subscribers detect any dropped UDP datagram via gaps in seq_id and fetch missed packets asynchronously over an out-of-band TCP retransmission channel.

27.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ScenarioBlast RadiusAutomated Recovery and Preserved Invariant

Runaway Trading Algorithm / Fat-Finger StormSingle firm or symbolPre-trade rate limiter, fat-finger price collar, and operator Kill Switch (POST /kill-switch) cancel all resting firm orders deterministically
Software Defect Discovered Mid-SessionSingle symbol partitionSurveillance halts symbol, replays immutable sequencer journal through patched engine binary, and verifies exact fill audit trail for regulators

Exchange Observability: SLIs and SLOs

  1. Wire-to-Wire Order Latency Histogram (p50, p99, p99.99): Measured via hardware PTP-synchronized NIC timestamps (optical tap at switch ingress and egress) without touching application CPU clocks. SLO: p99 <= 100 us, p99.99 <= 500 us.
  2. Primary-to-Standby Replay Lag: Difference between primary committed seq_id and hot-standby applied seq_id. Alert threshold: > 100 messages or > 500 us.
  3. Deterministic State Checksum Parity: Every 10,000 sequenced events, both primary and hot standby compute a rolling CRC32/XXHash over their top-of-book and fill counters and emit it to an out-of-band monitor; any single bit of divergence triggers an immediate SEV-1 halt investigation.
  4. Multicast Gap and Retransmission Rate: Fraction of L3 market data packets requiring TCP gap recovery; rising rates expose switch microburst buffer exhaustion before participants notice staleness.

How Production Systems Implement Electronic Exchanges

Production SystemCore ArchitectureArchitectural Distinction

NasdaqOUCH binary order entry, TotalView-ITCH / MoldUDP64 A/B UDP multicast, FPGA-accelerated ingressHardware FPGA pre-trade risk and binary framing push wire-to-wire matching latencies into the low tens of microseconds
IEX (Investors Exchange)Deterministic matching engine preceded by a 38-mile (350 us) coiled optical fiber Speed BumpUses physical signal propagation delay to neutralize cross-venue latency arbitrage while preserving deterministic internal order execution
CME GlobexiLink 3 (SBE binary) order entry + MDP 3.0 (SBE over UDP multicast) market dataStandardized FIX Simple Binary Encoding across global futures markets for zero-allocation decoding and deterministic hardware timestamping

27.7 Simulation Verification

Running code/matchsim executes a deterministic price-time priority limit order book across seven incoming orders, exercising resting spread formation, FIFO partial fills at identical prices (1005), multi-level book sweeps, and passive price improvement (order 7 selling with limit 995 fills at resting buy prices 1010 and 1000).

$ cargo run --release -p matchsim
order 1: sell 50 at 1010
order 2: sell 30 at 1005
order 3: sell 40 at 1005
order 4: buy 60 at 1000
order 5: buy 50 at 1005
    trade: 30 at 1005, order 5 with waiting order 2
    trade: 20 at 1005, order 5 with waiting order 3
order 6: buy 100 at 1010
    trade: 20 at 1005, order 6 with waiting order 3
    trade: 50 at 1010, order 6 with waiting order 1
order 7: sell 80 at 995
    trade: 30 at 1010, order 7 with waiting order 6
    trade: 50 at 1000, order 7 with waiting order 4
waiting to buy: 10 at 1000
waiting to sell: nothing
shares traded: 200

Verify every invariant directly from the transcript:

  • Price-Time FIFO Priority: When order 5 (buy 50 @ 1005) crosses the spread, it exhausts order 2 (30 shares) first before taking 20 shares from order 3, honoring arrival order at price 1005.
  • Remainder Resting: order 6 (buy 100 @ 1010) clears the remaining 20 shares of order 3 at 1005 and all 50 shares of order 1 at 1010, resting its unfilled 30 shares as the new best bid at 1010.
  • Passive Price Improvement & Conservation: order 7 (sell 80 @ 995) trades 30 shares at 1010 and 50 shares at 1000 (resting buyers’ prices), transferring 200 total shares and leaving exactly 10 shares of order 4 resting at 1000.

Run the deterministic matching engine simulation. Execute cargo run --release -p matchsim in code/ to verify price-time FIFO ordering, passive price execution, multi-level sweeps, and share conservation (200 shares traded, 10 remaining at 1000).

27.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Limit Order Book (LOB)Dual priority structure holding resting buy orders (highest price first) and sell orders (lowest price first) for a single tradable symbol.
Price-Time Priority (FIFO)Matching rule ranking orders strictly by best limit price first, and by earliest sequencer arrival number among orders at the same price.
SequencerAuthoritative single ordering component assigning monotonic seq_id and exchange_ts_ns timestamps to every input command before journaling.
LMAX DisruptorPre-allocated, cache-line-padded, lock-free power-of-2 ring buffer enabling sub-microsecond single-writer handoff between threads with zero allocations.
Mechanical SympathyDesigning data structures and concurrency boundaries to align with CPU cache lines, branch predictors, and memory fences rather than fighting hardware physics.
Simple Binary Encoding (SBE)FIX-standardized fixed-offset binary wire protocol allowing zero-copy, zero-allocation encoding and decoding of financial messages.
Pre-Trade Risk CheckIn-RAM validation of credit limits, order size caps, fat-finger price collars, and firm kill switches executed before an order mutates the book.
Active-Passive Deterministic StandbyIsolated replica consuming the exact same sequenced journal in lockstep to hold an identical order book ready for sub-50-ms failover.

Chapter 28: Click Aggregation

Online advertising platforms bill advertisers per valid click while simultaneously driving live campaign dashboards and real-time budget pacing. Counting clicks over a clean, ordered, finite file in an overnight batch job is elementary, yet running once per day leaves advertisers blind for 24 hours and allows exhausted budgets to overspend for hours. Real-time click streams invert every assumption of batch processing: mobile devices buffer clicks inside tunnels and flush them minutes or hours late, network packets arrive out of order, browsers retry unacknowledged beacons and create duplicates, and stream processors crash mid-window while holding partial aggregates in memory. Because advertisers pay real money per aggregated click, overcounting by 2% triggers billing disputes and undercounting by 2% forfeits revenue directly. In this chapter, I design a distributed real-time click aggregation pipeline combining stateless high-availability ingestion, event-time tumbling windows with heuristic watermarks, Chandy-Lamport asynchronous checkpointing, hot-ad two-stage pre-aggregation, and audit-grade batch reconciliation.

In this chapter, we cover

  • actors, use cases, verifiable functional and non-functional requirements, non-goals, and billion-click capacity bounds
  • high-availability click ingestion endpoints, live OLAP count/Top-K APIs, Avro event envelopes, and idempotent ReplacingMergeTree schemas
  • control-plane stream orchestration and schema management separated from the speed-layer streaming path and immutable archive reconciliation path
  • event-time versus processing-time semantics, client clock-skew clamping, heuristic watermarks with idle-partition handling, allowed lateness, and late-event side outputs
  • Chandy-Lamport asynchronous barrier snapshots for effectively-once state recovery, hot-ad salting with two-stage pre-aggregation, HyperLogLog distinct counts, and click-fraud deduplication
  • failure recovery matrices, streaming SLIs, production architectures (Apache Flink, Google MillWheel and Photon, Meta Scuba), and simulation verification via code/clicksim

28.1 Requirements, Actors, and Capacity Bounds

Click aggregation bridges two conflicting operational demands: sub-minute freshness for live advertiser dashboards and budget pacing, and exact financial completeness for end-of-month invoicing. No unbounded streaming system can guarantee both instantaneous emission and 100% completeness simultaneously because an arbitrary offline device can always deliver an older click later. We resolve this fundamental tension explicitly by publishing two clearly labeled grades of results: fast provisional counts emitted from the real-time stream within seconds, and immutable final counts produced after reconciling stragglers from an immutable raw-event archive.

Actors and Use Cases

Three external actors interact across the ad-click aggregation boundary (Figure 28-1).

ActorOperationConcrete Scenario
Visitor Browser / SDKReport raw ad-click telemetry (POST /v1/clicks)Mobile SDK emits a signed click beacon carrying a client-generated click_id and event_ts, retrying automatically on transient network timeouts
Advertiser DashboardQuery live 1-minute counts and Top-K campaigns (GET /v1/ads/{id}/clicks)A marketing analyst tracks campaign clicks minute-by-minute within 30 s of occurrence and watches real-time Top-K trending ads
Billing and Fraud EngineFilter invalid bot traffic and compute final invoicesFraud pipeline drops forged or high-velocity bot clicks; nightly reconciliation computes exact immutable daily totals for advertiser billing

Functional Requirements

No.Functional Requirement
0Every click beacon submitted by an authorized browser or mobile SDK is accepted with minimal latency and persisted durably with both its client event_ts and collector ingest_ts.
1The system aggregates valid clicks per advertisement into 1-minute event-time tumbling windows and exposes provisional counts within 30 s of each window’s close.
2Clicks delayed in transit are attributed to the exact minute in which they occurred (event_ts), rather than the minute in which they reached the server (ingest_ts).
3Duplicate click deliveries caused by client retries or at-least-once broker redelivery are deduplicated by click_id and counted at most once.
4The system exposes live Top-K advertisement rankings over recent sliding or tumbling windows and explicitly labels every returned count as PROVISIONAL or FINAL.
5Every raw click is retained immutably in long-term object storage so nightly reconciliation produces exact FINAL billing counts and historical bugs or fraud-rule updates can be reprocessed cleanly.

Non-Functional Requirements and SLOs

No.PropertyTarget SpecificationArchitectural Consequence
0AccuracyFINAL billing counts exact (0% drift from raw archive after fraud filter); PROVISIONAL counts within 1% of FINALEvent-time watermarking + allowed-lateness upserts paired with immutable raw Parquet archive reconciliation
1FreshnessProvisional 1-minute window counts visible in OLAP within 30 s (p99) of window endContinuous stateful stream processing (Flink) with tuned watermark lag (10 to 15 s) and streaming OLAP ingestion
2Ingestion Availability99.99% availability for POST /v1/clicks (strictly prioritized over dashboard query availability)Stateless edge collectors perform minimal validation and append directly to a 3-AZ Kafka log with zero synchronous dependency on downstream processors
3DurabilityZero loss of any 202 Accepted click across single broker or AZ failureKafka acks=all across 3 replicas (min.insync.replicas=2) plus continuous archival to erasure-coded object storage
4ConsistencyEventual and revisable for PROVISIONAL counts; immutable and strongly consistent once marked FINALIdempotent keyed upserts in OLAP (ReplacingMergeTree / upsert primary key) with explicit finality flag
5Scale1B clicks/day (~11.6k avg/s), 100,000 peak clicks/s, 1M active advertisementsPartitioned Kafka log, parallel stateful Flink subtasks with hot-ad salting, and distributed columnar OLAP

Observe the deliberate availability asymmetry in Requirement 2: a dashboard outage lasting 60 seconds is a temporary annoyance whose data remains intact, whereas a dropped POST /v1/clicks request destroys billable revenue permanently because the visitor will not click again. Decoupling stateless collectors behind a durable partitioned log isolates revenue-critical ingestion from downstream processing bugs or OLAP maintenance.

Non-Goals and Out-of-Scope Boundaries

Four surrounding ad-tech systems sit outside this aggregation pipeline:

  • Real-time bidding (RTB) ad selection: Serving auctions and ranking candidate ads within < 50 ms happens upstream before an impression or click token is minted.
  • Multi-day cross-device conversion attribution: Joining clicks against offline store purchases or 30-day app installs runs on offline data warehouses rather than sub-minute window operators.
  • Advertiser payment settlement and ledger accounting: Generating credit-card charges and double-entry merchant receivables belongs to the payment ledger architecture in Chapter 19.
  • Ad-hoc arbitrary BI SQL queries over raw logs: Interactive multi-terabyte scans execute over the Parquet/Iceberg lakehouse outside the latency-sensitive live OLAP serving tier.

Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds

Click aggregation is constrained by peak ingestion spikes, stateful per-window deduplication memory in RocksDB, hot-key partition skew, and multi-year raw archive retention.

Event Log Envelope and Idempotent OLAP Schema

Inside Kafka, enriched click records follow a compact Avro/Protobuf schema registered in the Schema Registry:

{
  "click_id": "0199f2a8-c110-7b2e-9a41-3f9c01e4b821",
  "ad_id": 7,
  "campaign_id": 402,
  "event_ts_ms": 1760436007412,
  "ingest_ts_ms": 1760436007890,
  "client_ip_hash": "a49f12c0e8b1...",
  "user_agent_hash": "7b22d10a91f4...",
  "is_valid_token": true
}

In the OLAP serving store (ClickHouse or Apache Pinot), window counts are stored as idempotent keyed replacements, never blind UPDATE counts SET c = c + delta increments. If a stream processor crashes after publishing a window count and replays the last checkpoint interval upon recovery, re-writing the exact computed total under the composite key (ad_id, window_start, window_sec) with a monotonic revision overwrites the row cleanly with zero double-counting:

CREATE TABLE ad_click_counts (
    ad_id            UInt64,
    campaign_id      UInt64,
    window_start     DateTime,
    window_sec       UInt16,
    click_count      UInt64,
    unique_users_est UInt64,
    status           Enum8('PROVISIONAL' = 1, 'FINAL' = 2),
    revision         UInt64,
    updated_at       DateTime64(3)
)
ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree(revision)
PARTITION BY toYYYYMMDD(window_start)
ORDER BY (ad_id, window_sec, window_start);

28.3 High-Level Architecture: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

We structure the aggregation platform around a clear split between Control Plane orchestration (schema enforcement, topic partitioning, Chandy-Lamport checkpoint coordination, and watermark management) and a dual-path Data Plane combining a low-latency streaming speed layer with an immutable raw-archive reconciliation tier (Figure 28-2).

Component Responsibilities and Failure Domains

ComponentPlaneState HeldFailure Impact and Recovery
Schema and Broker ControlControlAvro/Protobuf schema versions, Kafka partition assignments, topic ACLsStateless control APIs backed by consensus metadata; prevents schema-breaking collector deploys from poisoning stream jobs
Stream Job Manager (Flink)ControlTask graph topology, checkpoint barrier coordinator, latest completed checkpoint metadataActive-passive HA JobManager backed by ZooKeeper/Kubernetes leases; restarts failed tasks from last completed checkpoint in S3/GCS
Click Collectors (x40)Data (Speed)Stateless (HMAC token verification, clock-skew clamping, IP hashing, Kafka producer batching)Edge L7 LB routes around failed collectors immediately; zero lost requests
Kafka Event Log (x12)Data (Speed)7-day partitioned raw click log across 3 AZs (64 partitions)Broker failure promotes an in-sync replica in seconds with zero committed click loss (min.insync.replicas=2)
Stateful Stream Engine (x24)Data (Speed)Per-window counts, click_id dedup sets, HLL sketches, watermark trackers in local NVMe RocksDBTask crash restores incremental RocksDB snapshot + Kafka offsets atomically from object storage; effectively-once counts preserved
OLAP Serving Store (Pinot / ClickHouse)Data (Speed)Partitioned columnar window counts (ReplacingMergeTree / upsert tables)Replicated shards absorb single-node failure without query downtime; idempotent upserts survive stream replay cleanly
Raw Click Archive & Nightly BatchData (Batch)Immutable Zstd Parquet files on S3/GCS (73 TB/year) + Spark/Flink batch reconcilerStateless batch jobs re-read immutable Parquet partitions on failure to produce authoritative FINAL billing rows

End-to-End Click Path Walkthrough

  1. Stateless Edge Ingestion: A visitor clicks an advertisement. The browser or mobile SDK posts POST /v1/clicks to a stateless Collector. The Collector verifies the HMAC impression_token, stamps ingest_ts, clamps implausible client event_ts values, appends the Avro record to Kafka keyed by ad_id (or salted ad_id#salt for hot campaigns), and returns 202 Accepted.
  2. Parallel Archival: An independent Kafka Connect / Sink consumer streams every raw partition continuously into immutable hourly Zstd Parquet files in S3/GCS, establishing the permanent replayable source of truth.
  3. Stateful Event-Time Processing: Flink subtasks consume Kafka partitions, check click_id against local RocksDB dedup state, drop duplicates and high-velocity bot bursts, assign valid clicks to their 1-minute event-time tumbling window, and advance per-partition watermarks.
  4. Provisional Emission and Allowed Lateness: When the global watermark passes a window’s end boundary, the operator emits an idempotent PROVISIONAL count row to ClickHouse/Pinot. Late clicks arriving within the allowed-lateness grace period update RocksDB state and emit updated revisions; extreme stragglers route to a late-event side output.
  5. Final Billing Reconciliation: After a configured reconciliation cutoff (for example, T+2 hours or nightly at 02:00 UTC), the Batch Reconciler reads the complete raw Parquet partitions (or executes unified Kappa replay using identical Flink SQL/DataStream logic over historical storage), incorporates every late straggler and offline fraud classifier verdict, and upserts immutable status = 'FINAL' rows for invoicing.

28.4 Event-Time Semantics, Heuristic Watermarks, Windows, and Late-Event Handling

Every click event carries two distinct timestamps: event time (event_ts, when the visitor actually clicked on their device) and processing time (ingest_ts / processor wall clock, when the server received it). Aggregating by processing time answers the wrong business question (“how many beacons reached our servers during minute 10:01”) and corrupts reporting whenever a mobile carrier lags or a collector experiences a 5-minute pause, producing five empty minutes followed by an artificial 6x spike that bills an expired campaign.

Defending Against Malicious or Drifted Client Clocks

Relying blindly on raw device timestamps introduces its own hazard: a smartphone whose local clock is misconfigured to 1970 or 2031 would inject clicks into decades-old or far-future windows, inflating state or poisoning watermarks. Collectors enforce a clock-skew hygiene contract at ingestion:

  • Compute skew = client_send_ts - ingest_ts whenever the SDK reports its local transmission time alongside event_ts, correcting systematic device clock offsets via adjusted_event_ts = event_ts - skew.
  • Clamp future timestamps (adjusted_event_ts > ingest_ts + 5 s) down to ingest_ts, and flag or route clicks older than 7 days directly to an audit dead-letter archive so a corrupt device cannot stall watermark math.

Heuristic Watermarks and Idle-Partition Alignment

Dividing an infinite stream into finite tumbling windows ([12:00, 12:01), [12:01, 12:02)), sliding windows (5-minute span sliding every 1 minute for live Top-K trends), or session windows (grouping bursts per user separated by an inactivity gap) requires deciding when a window has received enough out-of-order events to close.

A heuristic watermark W(t) expresses the stream engine’s estimate of event-time completeness: "the processor assumes no further non-late events with event_ts < W(t) will arrive." Under a bounded-out-of-orderness generator with lag allowance L (for example, L = 10 s), each partition tracks:

partition_watermark = max_event_ts_observed_in_partition - L

When a downstream operator reads from P parallel upstream partitions, its combined watermark must equal min(partition_watermark_1, ..., partition_watermark_P) so a fast partition does not prematurely close windows for a slightly lagging partition. A subtle production pitfall arises when one partition receives zero clicks for several minutes (for example, a quiet geographic shard at 03:00 local time): its max_event_ts freezes, pinning min(...) and halting every window across the entire cluster. Production Flink deployments eliminate this stall by configuring an idle-source timeout (withIdleness(Duration.ofSeconds(15))), temporarily excluding quiet partitions from the minimum calculation until traffic resumes.

Advance through Interactive Trace 28.A to observe out-of-order arrivals, duplicate suppression, watermark window closure, and a one-minute late straggler on a 10-second tumbling window with 5-second watermark lag.

Allowed Lateness and Late-Event Side Outputs

Choosing the watermark lag L exposes an unavoidable latency-completeness trade-off: larger L captures more out-of-order mobile clicks before initial emission but delays dashboards by L seconds. Following the Google Dataflow / Apache Beam window lifecycle model, we decouple fast provisional emission from state retention using a three-stage policy (Figure 28-3).

  1. Watermark Trigger (W(t) >= 12:01:00): As soon as W(t) crosses the window end (12:01:00), the operator emits the initial PROVISIONAL count (revision = 1) to ClickHouse/Pinot, keeping dashboard latency under 15 to 30 s.
  2. Allowed Lateness Window (12:01:00 < W(t) <= 12:01:20): Rather than purging RocksDB state immediately at 12:01:00, the operator retains the window counter and click_id dedup set for a bounded grace period (for example, +20 s in Figure 28-3, or +5 min for mobile-heavy ad networks). Each late click arriving inside this grace window updates the state and emits a higher-revision idempotent upsert (revision = 2, 3, ...) that refines the live OLAP count cleanly.
  3. State Purge and Late-Event Side Output (W(t) > 12:01:20): Once the watermark exceeds window_end + allowed_lateness, the operator purges both the window counter and its click_id dedup set from RocksDB so state memory stays strictly bounded (~144 MB total). Any extreme straggler arriving hours later routes cleanly into a dedicated Late-Event Side Output stream, alerting operators if late-event volume spikes and ensuring the nightly FINAL reconciliation job captures every billable click.

28.5 Chandy-Lamport Asynchronous Barrier Snapshots, Hot-Ad Salting, and Click-Fraud Deduplication

Three internal stream-processing mechanisms separate an academic prototype from a production billion-click billing pipeline: fault-tolerant checkpointing, skew elimination, and multi-tier deduplication.

Exactly-Once Stateful Recovery via Asynchronous Barrier Snapshots

A stateful stream operator holds three tightly coupled pieces of state in memory and local NVMe RocksDB: its current Kafka partition offsets, open window partial counts, and seen click_id sets. If the processor persists Kafka offsets independently from its RocksDB state and crashes between the two writes, recovery either drops uncheckpointed clicks (underbilling) or replays already-counted clicks into stale counters (overbilling).

Apache Flink solves distributed stateful recovery without halting stream throughput using Asynchronous Barrier Snapshots (ABS) (Carbone et al., 2015), a streaming adaptation of the classical Chandy-Lamport distributed snapshot algorithm (1985):

  1. Barrier Injection: Every 30 to 60 seconds, the JobManager instructs every Kafka source subtask to record its current partition offset and inject an in-band checkpoint barrier (barrier_id = k) directly into the event stream alongside regular click records.
  2. Barrier Alignment: When a downstream stateful operator receives barrier_id = k on input channel A, it pauses processing further records from channel A (buffering them briefly) while continuing to drain channel B until barrier_id = k arrives on all input channels. This alignment defines an exact consistent cut across the entire distributed dataflow graph: every event before barrier_id = k is reflected in state, and every event after barrier_id = k belongs to checkpoint k + 1. (Under heavy backpressure, Flink can switch to unaligned checkpoints that snapshot in-flight channel buffers immediately to keep checkpoint duration bounded.)
  3. Asynchronous Incremental RocksDB Upload: Once aligned, the operator takes an instantaneous copy-on-write RocksDB checkpoint (hard-linking immutable local SSTable files in milliseconds), resumes processing clicks immediately, and uploads only newly generated SSTable deltas asynchronously to S3/GCS.
  4. End-to-End Effectively-Once Guarantee: When all operators acknowledge barrier_id = k, the JobManager commits checkpoint k atomically. On crash, every subtask restores its exact RocksDB state and rewinds its Kafka consumer to the exact paired offsets from checkpoint k. Any window already emitted between checkpoint k and the crash is recomputed identically and written to ClickHouse/Pinot via idempotent keyed upsert (ReplacingMergeTree), achieving end-to-end effectively-once aggregation.

Hot-Ad Salting, Two-Stage Pre-Aggregation, and HyperLogLog

Partitioning Kafka and Flink strictly by hash(ad_id) breaks down during major live events (a championship broadcast or flash sale), where one flagship advertisement can generate 25% of total platform clicks (25,000+ clicks/s). That single ad_id maps to one Flink subtask, saturating its CPU, blowing up backpressure, and freezing the global watermark while the other 23 subtasks sit largely idle.

Because addition is associative and commutative, we eliminate hot-ad skew with Two-Stage Salted Pre-Aggregation:

  • Stage 1 (Salted Local Pre-Aggregation): For normal ads, events hash by ad_id. For hot ads (detected dynamically via a lightweight Count-Min Sketch or campaign tier flag), the upstream partitioner appends a deterministic or random salt (ad_id, salt) where salt in 0..15 (K = 16). Sixteen parallel Stage-1 subtasks each process ~1,560 clicks/s and emit only one compact partial sum per window (16 messages/minute total).
  • Stage 2 (Global Window Rollup): A downstream operator strips the salt, re-keys strictly by (ad_id, window_start), and sums the 16 partial aggregates into the exact global count in microseconds.

Note a critical mathematical caveat when computing distinct clicking users (unique_users_est): unlike total click sums, exact unique counts cannot be added across salted partitions because the same user may land in both salt=3 and salt=11. Instead, each Stage-1 subtask populates a compact HyperLogLog (HLL) probabilistic sketch (12 KB per window for < 1% standard error), and Stage 2 merges the 16 HLL byte arrays associatively via element-wise max(reg_a[i], reg_b[i]) to produce an accurate global distinct-user estimate in constant memory.

Click-Fraud Filtering and Multi-Tier Deduplication

Ad-click pipelines are constant targets for automated click-fraud botnets attempting to drain competitors’ daily budgets. We defend accuracy across three layers:

  1. Cryptographic Impression Tokens: Every ad render mints a short-lived HMAC-signed impression_token encoding (impression_id, ad_id, expiry_ts, publisher_id). Stateless collectors reject forged beacons lacking a valid signature or expired beyond 30 minutes before they ever enter Kafka.
  2. Window-Bounded click_id Deduplication: Stateful operators store seen click_id keys inside RocksDB scoped to each window and automatically purge them when the watermark passes window_end + allowed_lateness, preventing unbounded dedup-table memory growth. For multi-datacenter active-active billing pipelines (such as Google Photon), cross-DC deduplication writes processed click_id records to a Paxos-replicated global key-value store to guarantee at-most-once billing even during full datacenter failovers.
  3. Streaming Velocity and Offline Fraud Classification: A lightweight Flink velocity filter flags abnormal click bursts (> 20 clicks/minute from one (client_ip_hash, user_agent_hash) fingerprint) into a suspected_fraud side output so live budgets pause safely, while heavier graph-based bot detectors run offline before finalizing FINAL nightly billing invoices.

28.6 Failure Modes, SLIs, and Production Systems

Failure and Recovery Matrix

Failure ScenarioBlast RadiusAutomated Recovery and Preserved Invariant
Flink TaskManager Host Crash1/24 of partitions pause 5 to 15 sJobManager restarts affected tasks from latest incremental RocksDB checkpoint + paired Kafka offsets; idempotent OLAP upserts yield zero double-counting
Idle Kafka Partition Stalls WatermarkGlobal provisional window emissions stallSource idleness timeout (15 s) temporarily excludes quiet partitions from min(partition_watermarks), resuming window closure immediately
Mobile Device Offline for 2 HoursSingle delayed click batchWatermark already purged the window; late clicks route cleanly to the Late-Event Side Output and are folded into FINAL billing counts by the nightly reconciler
Client Retry / Broker Redelivery StormDuplicate click beaconsWindow-scoped RocksDB click_id dedup set drops duplicates inside open/lateness windows; batch reconciler deduplicates globally by click_id
Viral Broadcast Ad Overwhelms One SubtaskSingle hot ad_id partitionTwo-stage salted pre-aggregation (K=16) spreads Stage-1 load evenly across subtasks while preserving exact Stage-2 totals
Buggy Aggregation Code Deployed for 48 HoursCorrupted provisional/final countsEngineers deploy patched logic and reprocess the immutable S3/GCS raw Parquet archive (or 7-day Kafka log), overwriting affected keys in OLAP via higher revision
OLAP Serving Store OutageLive dashboards degradedStateless Collectors continue returning 202 Accepted into Kafka uninterrupted; Flink checkpoints buffer safely and drain backlog once OLAP recovers

Streaming Observability: SLIs and SLOs

  1. Collector Ingestion Success Rate: Percentage of valid POST /v1/clicks requests durably committed to Kafka with 202 Accepted. SLO: >= 99.99% (SEV-1 page if < 99.95% over 2 minutes).
  2. End-to-End Provisional Freshness Lag: olap_emit_ts - window_end_ts measured per minute across all partitions. SLO: p99 <= 30 s.
  3. Watermark Lag and Partition Skew: current_wall_clock - global_watermark and max(partition_wm) - min(partition_wm). Rising skew immediately exposes a stuck partition, hot ad key, or broken idle-source configuration.
  4. Provisional-to-Final Billing Drift: Daily automated audit comparing SUM(PROVISIONAL) against SUM(FINAL) per campaign. SLO: < 1.0% drift; sudden drift spikes signal excessive mobile lateness, bot waves, or miscalibrated watermark lag L.
  5. Checkpoint Duration and Alignment Buffer Size: Alert if asynchronous RocksDB snapshot completion approaches 50% of the checkpoint interval (> 30 s), preventing cascading backpressure before recovery time degrades.

How Production Systems Implement Click Aggregation

Production SystemCore ArchitectureArchitectural Distinction
Apache FlinkDistributed stateful dataflow with Chandy-Lamport Asynchronous Barrier Snapshots + incremental RocksDB stateIndustry standard for unified event-time stream and batch processing (Kappa architecture) with native watermarks, allowed lateness, and side outputs
Google MillWheel & DataflowPer-key persistent state, low-watermark propagation, programmable Triggers + Accumulation modesFormalized the Dataflow Model separating what is computed (transformations), where in event time (windows), when in processing time (watermarks/triggers), and how refinements relate (retract/accumulate)

28.7 Simulation Verification

Running code/clicksim feeds an identical stream of out-of-order, duplicated, and late-arriving ad clicks through both a processing-time (arrival-time) counter and an event-time watermarked counter (10 s tumbling windows, 5 s watermark lag allowance) and compares both against ground truth.

$ cargo run --release -p clicksim
what happened:              0-10 s: 8, 10-20 s: 4, 20-30 s: 1
counted by arrival time:    0-10 s: 7, 10-20 s: 5, 20-30 s: 1, 60-70 s: 1
counted by event time:      0-10 s: 7, 10-20 s: 4
still open:                 20-30 s: 1
clicks received twice: 1, clicks too late for their window: 1

Inspect every metric confirmed by the simulation output:

  • Processing-Time Distortion: Counting by arrival time misattributes delayed clicks across buckets (10-20 s inflated to 5 instead of 4), fabricates a phantom 60-70 s: 1 bucket for a click that occurred in 0-10 s, and only lands on 7 for 0-10 s accidentally because a duplicate click partially cancels out two delayed arrivals.
  • Event-Time Watermark Accuracy: Counting by event time with deduplication drops the 1 duplicate click cleanly, attributes the 7 s delayed click correctly to 0-10 s, produces exact 10-20 s: 4, keeps 20-30 s: 1 open pending watermark advancement, and explicitly flags the 1 extreme straggler (clicks too late for their window: 1) so downstream late-event side outputs and nightly batch reconciliation restore the exact 0-10 s total of 8.

Run the streaming click aggregation simulation. Execute cargo run --release -p clicksim in code/ to observe processing-time distortion versus event-time watermarked windows, duplicate suppression (1 duplicate dropped), open-window buffering (20-30 s: 1), and late-straggler detection (1 late click).

28.8 Terminology and References

Engineering Glossary

TermDefinition
Event Time vs. Processing TimeEvent time is the instant an action occurred on the origin device; processing time is the wall-clock instant the server ingested or processed that event.
Tumbling / Sliding / Session WindowFinite event-time groupings: non-overlapping fixed intervals (tumbling), overlapping fixed-span intervals advancing by a shorter slide (sliding), and inactivity-delimited user bursts (session).
Heuristic WatermarkMonotonic progress timestamp W(t) estimating the event-time boundary before which the stream engine expects all non-late events to have arrived.
Allowed Lateness & Side OutputBounded post-watermark grace period retaining window state for incremental updates, after which extreme stragglers route to a separate side-output stream for batch reconciliation.
Asynchronous Barrier Snapshot (ABS)Flink’s Chandy-Lamport adaptation that aligns in-band stream barriers across input channels and snapshots RocksDB state plus Kafka offsets asynchronously without pausing ingestion.
Two-Stage Salted Pre-AggregationSpreading a hot key across K salted subtasks in Stage 1 to compute partial window sums, then folding only K compact summaries in Stage 2 to eliminate skew.
HyperLogLog (HLL)Probabilistic cardinality sketch estimating distinct counts within < 1% error using ~12 KB of associatively mergeable memory per window.
Lambda vs. Kappa ArchitectureLambda pairs a real-time speed layer with a separate nightly batch layer; Kappa uses one unified streaming codebase capable of replaying an immutable historical log to recompute results.
